59	4. ``Deprecated`` — capabilities still present but scheduled for
60	   removal in a future release.
61	5. ``Fixed`` — patches for known bugs.
62	6. ``Removed`` — capabilities taken out entirely.
63	7. ``Packaging`` — changes to how the source distribution is built,
64	   what files it contains, or how it is uploaded.
65	8. ``Docs`` — documentation-only changes.
66	
67	This ordering is intentional: it goes from user-visible additions
68	down to internal packaging and doc changes, so a reader skimming the
69	top of an entry sees the most consequential changes first.
70	
71	Version Heading Format
72	=======================
73	
74	The version heading is a single RST section title, underlined with
75	``=``, in this exact form:
76	
77	.. code-block:: text
78	
79	   1.4.2 - 2026-03-11
80	   ===================
81	
82	Rules for the heading line:
83	
84	- The version number has no leading ``v`` in the changelog heading
85	  itself, even though the git tag for that same release does carry a
86	  ``v`` prefix (for example tag ``v1.4.2`` for changelog heading
87	  ``1.4.2``). This is a long-standing inconsistency that nobody has
88	  fixed and it is not worth fixing now — just be aware the tag and
89	  the heading will not match character-for-character.
90	- The date is in ``YYYY-MM-DD`` form and is the date the source
91	  distribution was uploaded, not the date the last commit landed.
92	- Do not put anything else on the heading line — no codename, no
93	  "(unreleased)" marker. If a release is being drafted ahead of time,
94	  use the stand-in heading ``Unreleased`` with no date, and Devon
95	  or whoever is running the release renames it at cut time.
96	
97	Subsection Formatting
98	======================
99	
100	Each subsection (``Added``, ``Fixed``, and so on) is an RST
101	subsection under the version heading, underlined with ``-``:
102	
103	.. code-block:: text
104	
105	   1.4.2 - 2026-03-11
106	   ===================
107	
108	   Added
109	   -----
110	
111	   * Nothing in this release.
112	
113	   Changed
114	   -------
115	
116	   * The console log line for a completed request now includes the
117	     elapsed time in milliseconds, appended after the status code.
118	
119	   Fixed
120	   -----
121	
122	   * The console log formatter no longer double-escapes quote
123	     characters when a log line contains a quoted value.
124	
125	   Packaging
126	   ---------
127	
128	   * The source distribution now includes the ``docs/`` folder's
129	     RST sources, not just the rendered text, so downstream
130	     packagers can rebuild the docs offline.
131	
132	A few conventions worth calling out explicitly:
133	
134	- Bullet items use ``*``, not ``-``. This is opposite of the section
135	  underline character and that is fine — the underline is RST syntax,
136	  the bullet is a style choice, and mixing the two characters this
137	  way is what the Docs Guild settled on for legibility.
138	- If a subsection has nothing to report, either omit it entirely
139	  (preferred) or, if you want to explicitly record that nothing
140	  changed in that category for a release users might expect it in,
141	  write a single item reading exactly ``Nothing in this release.``
142	  Do not leave an empty subsection with no bullet under it — that
143	  renders oddly and has broken the docs build twice.
144	- Each bullet is one sentence or a short run-on describing a single
145	  change. Do not bundle two unrelated changes into one bullet joined
146	  by "and" or a semicolon — split them.
147	- Bullets should be user-facing in phrasing even when the change is
148	  internal. Write "the console log formatter no longer
149	  double-escapes quote characters" rather than naming which internal
150	  routine changed.
151	- Past tense throughout: "added," "changed," "fixed," not "add,"
152	  "change," "fix."
153	
154	Line-Item Wording Patterns
155	============================
156	
157	Owner: Docs Guild (Sasha Perlman).
158	
159	To keep the changelog scannable, use one of these sentence openings
160	depending on the subsection:
161	
162	.. list-table:: Preferred Opening Patterns by Subsection
163	   :header-rows: 1
164	   :widths: 20 40 40
165	
166	   * - Subsection
167	     - Preferred opening
168	     - Example
169	   * - Added
170	     - "Added ..." or "The package now ..."
171	     - "Added a plain-text summary line at the end of every console
172	       log."
173	   * - Changed
174	     - "Changed ..." or "The ... now ..."
175	     - "The default console log format now includes a timestamp with
176	       millisecond precision."
177	   * - Deprecated
178	     - "Deprecated ..."
179	     - "Deprecated the short command-line flags in favor of their
180	       long forms; the short forms will be removed in a future
181	       release."
182	   * - Fixed
183	     - "Fixed ..." or "The ... no longer ..."
184	     - "Fixed a formatting defect where the command help text
185	       wrapped mid-word on narrow terminals."
186	   * - Removed
187	     - "Removed ..."
188	     - "Removed the legacy console log format from 2024."
189	   * - Packaging
190	     - "The source distribution now ..." or "Packaging changed so
191	       that ..."
192	     - "The source distribution now excludes editor swap files."
193	   * - Docs
194	     - "Documented ..." or "Clarified ..."
195	     - "Clarified the wording of the command help text for the
196	       startup flags."
197	
198	Avoid vague openers like "Improved ..." or "Updated ..." with no
199	object — say what was improved or updated. "Improved logging" tells
200	the reader nothing; "the console log line for a request now includes
201	elapsed time" does.
202	
203	Attribution Line
204	==================
205	
206	Owner: Release Engineering (Devon Ruiz).
207	
208	At the end of each version's subsections, before the next version
209	heading, add a single attribution line in italics naming who
210	prepared the release:
211	
212	.. code-block:: text
213	
214	   *Prepared by Devon Ruiz.*
215	
216	This line is optional for patch releases cut by the same person who
217	owns the release calendar, but it is required for any release cut by
218	someone filling in, so there's a record of who to ask about that
219	specific entry later.
220	
221	Worked Example: A Full Entry
222	==============================
223	
224	Below is a complete, realistic entry following every rule above.
225	This is the kind of entry that should pass review without comment:
226	
227	.. code-block:: text
228	
229	   1.4.0 - 2026-01-14
230	   ===================
231	
232	   Added
233	   -----
234	
235	   * Nothing in this release.
236	
237	   Changed
238	   -------
239	
240	   * The console log format for a completed request now writes the
241	     elapsed time in milliseconds as the last field on the line,
242	     instead of omitting it.
243	   * The command help text for the top-level command now lists
244	     global flags before per-command flags, matching the order they
245	     must be given on the command line.
246	
247	   Deprecated
248	   ----------
249	
250	   * Deprecated the two-letter short forms of the startup flags.
251	     They continue to work in this release and will be removed no
252	     earlier than version 2.0.
253	
254	   Fixed
255	   -----
256	
257	   * Fixed a defect where the console log line for a failed request
258	     omitted the status code when the failure happened before the
259	     status was known, writing a blank field instead.
260	
261	   Removed
262	   -------
263	
264	   * Nothing removed in this release.
265	
266	   Packaging
267	   ---------
268	
269	   * The source distribution now includes ``CHANGELOG.rst`` at the
270	     top level so it is visible without unpacking into a subfolder.
271	
272	   Docs
273	   ----
274	
275	   * Documented the new elapsed-time field in the console log format
276	     reference page.
277	
278	   *Prepared by Devon Ruiz.*
279	
280	Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
281	=====================================
282	
283	Owner: Docs Guild (Sasha Perlman).
284	
285	- **Mixing present and past tense in the same entry.** Read the
286	  whole entry aloud before submitting; every bullet should sound
287	  like something that already happened.
288	- **Putting a packaging change under "Changed."** If the change is
289	  only visible to someone building or unpacking the source
290	  distribution, it belongs under ``Packaging``, even if it feels
291	  minor enough to lump in elsewhere.
292	- **Writing "various fixes" or "minor cleanup."** Every bullet names
293	  the specific thing that changed. If there truly were many tiny
294	  unrelated fixes, list them as separate bullets rather than
295	  summarizing.
296	- **Forgetting the attribution line on a release cut by a stand-in.**
297	  This has happened twice, both times when Sasha covered a release
298	  for Devon; check the bottom of the entry before merging.
299	- **Using a version heading that does not match the tag.** The
300	  heading has no ``v`` prefix; double-check this specifically because
301	  it is easy to copy the tag name straight into the heading by habit.
302	- **Nesting bullets.** Keep each subsection flat — one level of
303	  bullets. If a change genuinely needs elaboration, put the detail in
304	  the same bullet as a second sentence rather than an indented
305	  sub-bullet.
306	
307	Checklist Before Merging a Changelog Entry
308	=============================================
309	
310	- [ ] Version heading has no ``v`` prefix and the correct release
311	  date.
312	- [ ] Subsections appear in the order: Added, Changed, Deprecated,
313	  Fixed, Removed, Packaging, Docs.
314	- [ ] Empty subsections are omitted or contain exactly one
315	  "Nothing in this release." bullet.
316	- [ ] Bullets use ``*`` and are in past tense.
317	- [ ] No bullet bundles two unrelated changes.
318	- [ ] Attribution line present if someone other than the calendar
319	  owner prepared the release.
320	- [ ] Entry is at the top of ``CHANGELOG.rst``, immediately below the
321	  file's own title, above the previous newest entry.
322	
323	Past Releases as Format Examples
324	===================================
325	
326	The releases below are useful as format references because each one
327	covers a narrow, single-flavor set of changes, which makes it easy to
328	see one subsection style in isolation without the noise of a large
329	multi-area release.
330	
331	.. list-table:: Format Reference Releases
332	   :header-rows: 1
333	   :widths: 15 15 15 55
334	
335	   * - Version
336	     - Date
337	     - Flavor
338	     - What to look at
339	   * - 1.0.0
340	     - 2024-03-02
341	     - Docs only
342	     - A ``Docs``-only entry with every other subsection omitted.
343	   * - 1.1.0
344	     - 2024-06-28
345	     - Packaging only
346	     - A ``Packaging``-only entry; good example of source
347	       distribution wording.
348	   * - 1.2.0
349	     - 2024-10-09
350	     - Command help text
351	     - Shows how to phrase ``Changed`` bullets for help text wording
352	       without naming a specific flag's underlying variable.
353	   * - 2.0
354	     - 2025-01-30
355	     - Console log format
356	     - A larger console log format overhaul; shows how to split one
357	       big change into several distinct bullets rather than one
358	       run-on paragraph.
359	   * - 2.1
360	     - 2025-05-14
361	     - Speed
362	     - Shows acceptable wording for a speed-only entry without
363	       promising specific numbers that later prove wrong.
364	   * - 2.2
365	     - 2025-09-02
366	     - Docs and packaging combined
367	     - Shows correct subsection ordering when both ``Packaging`` and
368	       ``Docs`` are present in the same entry.
369	
370	Terminology
371	=============
372	
373	**Changelog entry**
374	    The block of text under one version heading in
375	    ``CHANGELOG.rst``, from that heading down to (but not including)
376	    the next version heading.
377	
378	**Version heading**
379	    The RST section title naming the version number and release date
380	    for one changelog entry.
381	
382	**Subsection**
383	    One of the eight categories (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Fixed,
384	    Removed, Packaging, Docs) that group bullets within an entry.
385	
386	**Bullet item**
387	    A single ``*``-prefixed line describing one discrete change.
388	
389	**Attribution line**
390	    The italicized "Prepared by ..." line at the end of an entry
391	    naming who assembled it.
392	
393	**Flavor**
394	    Informal shorthand used on this page for a release whose changes
395	    fall almost entirely into one category, such as a docs-only or
396	    packaging-only release.
397	
398	**Cut**
399	    The act of finalizing a version's source distribution and
400	    uploading it; "cut time" means the point in the process when the
401	    changelog heading's stand-in date gets replaced with the real
402	    date.
403	
404	**Source distribution**
405	    The packaged, distributable form of accountsvc produced from the
406	    repository for a given release; its exact contents are described
407	    on the packaging page, not here.
408	
409	**Running file**
410	    A single file that accumulates entries over time rather than
411	    being split into one file per release; used here to describe how
412	    ``CHANGELOG.rst`` is organized.
413	
414	Files and Paths Referenced by This Page
415	==========================================

===================================
Changelog Entry Format
===================================

:Title: Changelog Entry Format
:Version: v1.4.0
:Owner: Release Engineering (Devon Ruiz)
:Last updated: 2026-01-30

.. contents::
   :local:
   :depth: 2

Purpose
=======

This page defines the exact section headings, ordering, and line-item
style that every changelog entry for **accountsvc** must follow. It
exists because past entries drifted into three or four different
styles over 2024 and early 2025, which made it hard to scan the log
quickly or diff one release against another. The format below is the
one Release Engineering enforces at merge time and expects at cut
time.

This page covers *format* only — headings, ordering, wording, and
punctuation. For guidance on choosing a version number, see
`version-numbering.md`; for the day-of-release procedure, see
`release-checklist.md`.

Owner: Release Engineering (Devon Ruiz).

Where the Changelog Lives
==========================

The changelog is a single running file at the repository root:

- ``CHANGELOG.rst`` — the canonical, append-in-place changelog. Every
  release gets one entry here, newest first.

There is no per-version changelog snippet folder in this repository;
everything lives in one file. Do not create a second changelog file
under ``docs/`` — several past contributors have started one and it
has caused confusion about which file is current.

Section Order for a Changelog Entry
=====================================

Owner: Release Engineering (Devon Ruiz).

Each entry in ``CHANGELOG.rst`` uses the following heading and
subheading order. Not every subheading is required for every release
— omit any subheading that would otherwise be empty — but when a
subheading is present, it must appear in this order:

1. **Version heading** — the version number and the release date, in
   that order, on one line.
2. ``Added`` — new capabilities.
3. ``Changed`` — changes to existing behavior that are not fixes.
4. ``Deprecated`` — capabilities still present but scheduled for
   removal in a future release.
5. ``Fixed`` — patches for known bugs.
6. ``Removed`` — capabilities taken out entirely.
7. ``Packaging`` — changes to how the source distribution is built,
   what files it contains, or how it is uploaded.
8. ``Docs`` — documentation-only changes.

This ordering is intentional: it goes from user-visible additions
down to internal packaging and doc changes, so a reader skimming the
top of an entry sees the most consequential changes first.

Version Heading Format
=======================

The version heading is a single RST section title, underlined with
``=``, in this exact form:

.. code-block:: text

   1.4.2 - 2026-03-11
   ===================

Rules for the heading line:

- The version number has no leading ``v`` in the changelog heading
  itself, even though the git tag for that same release does carry a
  ``v`` prefix (for example tag ``v1.4.2`` for changelog heading
  ``1.4.2``). This is a long-standing inconsistency that nobody has
  fixed and it is not worth fixing now — just be aware the tag and
  the heading will not match character-for-character.
- The date is in ``YYYY-MM-DD`` form and is the date the source
  distribution was uploaded, not the date the last commit landed.
- Do not put anything else on the heading line — no codename, no
  "(unreleased)" marker. If a release is being drafted ahead of time,
  use the stand-in heading ``Unreleased`` with no date, and Devon
  or whoever is running the release renames it at cut time.

Subsection Formatting
======================

Each subsection (``Added``, ``Fixed``, and so on) is an RST
subsection under the version heading, underlined with ``-``:

.. code-block:: text

   1.4.2 - 2026-03-11
   ===================

   Added
   -----

   * Nothing in this release.

   Changed
   -------

   * The console log line for a completed request now includes the
     elapsed time in milliseconds, appended after the status code.

   Fixed
   -----

   * The console log formatter no longer double-escapes quote
     characters when a log line contains a quoted value.

   Packaging
   ---------

   * The source distribution now includes the ``docs/`` folder's
     RST sources, not just the rendered text, so downstream
     packagers can rebuild the docs offline.

A few conventions worth calling out explicitly:

- Bullet items use ``*``, not ``-``. This is opposite of the section
  underline character and that is fine — the underline is RST syntax,
  the bullet is a style choice, and mixing the two characters this
  way is what the Docs Guild settled on for legibility.
- If a subsection has nothing to report, either omit it entirely
  (preferred) or, if you want to explicitly record that nothing
  changed in that category for a release users might expect it in,
  write a single item reading exactly ``Nothing in this release.``
  Do not leave an empty subsection with no bullet under it — that
  renders oddly and has broken the docs build twice.
- Each bullet is one sentence or a short run-on describing a single
  change. Do not bundle two unrelated changes into one bullet joined
  by "and" or a semicolon — split them.
- Bullets should be user-facing in phrasing even when the change is
  internal. Write "the console log formatter no longer
  double-escapes quote characters" rather than naming which internal
  routine changed.
- Past tense throughout: "added," "changed," "fixed," not "add,"
  "change," "fix."

Line-Item Wording Patterns
============================

Owner: Docs Guild (Sasha Perlman).

To keep the changelog scannable, use one of these sentence openings
depending on the subsection:

.. list-table:: Preferred Opening Patterns by Subsection
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 20 40 40

   * - Subsection
     - Preferred opening
     - Example
   * - Added
     - "Added ..." or "The package now ..."
     - "Added a plain-text summary line at the end of every console
       log."
   * - Changed
     - "Changed ..." or "The ... now ..."
     - "The default console log format now includes a timestamp with
       millisecond precision."
   * - Deprecated
     - "Deprecated ..."
     - "Deprecated the short command-line flags in favor of their
       long forms; the short forms will be removed in a future
       release."
   * - Fixed
     - "Fixed ..." or "The ... no longer ..."
     - "Fixed a formatting defect where the command help text
       wrapped mid-word on narrow terminals."
   * - Removed
     - "Removed ..."
     - "Removed the legacy console log format from 2024."
   * - Packaging
     - "The source distribution now ..." or "Packaging changed so
       that ..."
     - "The source distribution now excludes editor swap files."
   * - Docs
     - "Documented ..." or "Clarified ..."
     - "Clarified the wording of the command help text for the
       startup flags."

Avoid vague openers like "Improved ..." or "Updated ..." with no
object — say what was improved or updated. "Improved logging" tells
the reader nothing; "the console log line for a request now includes
elapsed time" does.

Attribution Line
==================

Owner: Release Engineering (Devon Ruiz).

At the end of each version's subsections, before the next version
heading, add a single attribution line in italics naming who
prepared the release:

.. code-block:: text

   *Prepared by Devon Ruiz.*

This line is optional for patch releases cut by the same person who
owns the release calendar, but it is required for any release cut by
someone filling in, so there's a record of who to ask about that
specific entry later.

Worked Example: A Full Entry
==============================

Below is a complete, realistic entry following every rule above.
This is the kind of entry that should pass review without comment:

.. code-block:: text

   1.4.0 - 2026-01-14
   ===================

   Added
   -----

   * Nothing in this release.

   Changed
   -------

   * The console log format for a completed request now writes the
     elapsed time in milliseconds as the last field on the line,
     instead of omitting it.
   * The command help text for the top-level command now lists
     global flags before per-command flags, matching the order they
     must be given on the command line.

   Deprecated
   ----------

   * Deprecated the two-letter short forms of the startup flags.
     They continue to work in this release and will be removed no
     earlier than version 2.0.

   Fixed
   -----

   * Fixed a defect where the console log line for a failed request
     omitted the status code when the failure happened before the
     status was known, writing a blank field instead.

   Removed
   -------

   * Nothing removed in this release.

   Packaging
   ---------

   * The source distribution now includes ``CHANGELOG.rst`` at the
     top level so it is visible without unpacking into a subfolder.

   Docs
   ----

   * Documented the new elapsed-time field in the console log format
     reference page.

   *Prepared by Devon Ruiz.*

Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
=====================================

Owner: Docs Guild (Sasha Perlman).

- **Mixing present and past tense in the same entry.** Read the
  whole entry aloud before submitting; every bullet should sound
  like something that already happened.
- **Putting a packaging change under "Changed."** If the change is
  only visible to someone building or unpacking the source
  distribution, it belongs under ``Packaging``, even if it feels
  minor enough to lump in elsewhere.
- **Writing "various fixes" or "minor cleanup."** Every bullet names
  the specific thing that changed. If there truly were many tiny
  unrelated fixes, list them as separate bullets rather than
  summarizing.
- **Forgetting the attribution line on a release cut by a stand-in.**
  This has happened twice, both times when Sasha covered a release
  for Devon; check the bottom of the entry before merging.
- **Using a version heading that does not match the tag.** The
  heading has no ``v`` prefix; double-check this specifically because
  it is easy to copy the tag name straight into the heading by habit.
- **Nesting bullets.** Keep each subsection flat — one level of
  bullets. If a change genuinely needs elaboration, put the detail in
  the same bullet as a second sentence rather than an indented
  sub-bullet.

Checklist Before Merging a Changelog Entry
=============================================

- [ ] Version heading has no ``v`` prefix and the correct release
  date.
- [ ] Subsections appear in the order: Added, Changed, Deprecated,
  Fixed, Removed, Packaging, Docs.
- [ ] Empty subsections are omitted or contain exactly one
  "Nothing in this release." bullet.
- [ ] Bullets use ``*`` and are in past tense.
- [ ] No bullet bundles two unrelated changes.
- [ ] Attribution line present if someone other than the calendar
  owner prepared the release.
- [ ] Entry is at the top of ``CHANGELOG.rst``, immediately below the
  file's own title, above the previous newest entry.

Past Releases as Format Examples
===================================

The releases below are useful as format references because each one
covers a narrow, single-flavor set of changes, which makes it easy to
see one subsection style in isolation without the noise of a large
multi-area release.

.. list-table:: Format Reference Releases
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 15 15 15 55

   * - Version
     - Date
     - Flavor
     - What to look at
   * - 1.0.0
     - 2024-03-02
     - Docs only
     - A ``Docs``-only entry with every other subsection omitted.
   * - 1.1.0
     - 2024-06-28

       distribution wording.
   * - 1.2.0

       without naming a specific flag's underlying variable.
   * - 2.0
     - 2025-01-30
     - Console log format
     - A larger console log format overhaul; shows how to split one
       big change into several distinct bullets rather than one
       run-on paragraph.
   * - 2.1
     - 2025-05-14
     - Speed
     - Shows acceptable wording for a speed-only entry without
       promising specific numbers that later prove wrong.
   * - 2.2
     - 2025-09-02
     - Docs and packaging combined
     - Shows correct subsection ordering when both ``Packaging`` and
       ``Docs`` are present in the same entry.

Terminology
=============

**Changelog entry**
    The block of text under one version heading in
    ``CHANGELOG.rst``, from that heading down to (but not including)
    the next version heading.

**Version heading**
    The RST section title naming the version number and release date
    for one changelog entry.

**Subsection**
    One of the eight categories (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Fixed,
    Removed, Packaging, Docs) that group bullets within an entry.

**Bullet item**
    A single ``*``-prefixed line describing one discrete change.

**Attribution line**
    The italicized "Prepared by ..." line at the end of an entry
    naming who assembled it.

**Flavor**
    Informal shorthand used on this page for a release whose changes
    fall almost entirely into one category, such as a docs-only or
    packaging-only release.

**Cut**
    The act of finalizing a version's source distribution and
    uploading it; "cut time" means the point in the process when the
    changelog heading's stand-in date gets replaced with the real
    date.

**Source distribution**
    The packaged, distributable form of accountsvc produced from the
    repository for a given release; its exact contents are described
    on the packaging page, not here.

**Running file**
    A single file that accumulates entries over time rather than
    being split into one file per release; used here to describe how
    ``CHANGELOG.rst`` is organized.

1	# Release Notes for 2.2
2	
3	**Version:** 2.2
4	**Owner:** Docs Guild (Sasha Perlman)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-09-15
6	
7	## Summary
8	
9	This page records what changed in accountsvc 2.2 and recaps the release process that produced it. The 2.2 build touched command help text and fixed a series of stale links across the internal documentation tree. It did not change the package's console log format, its packaging layout, or its speed profile — those areas last moved in 2.1 and 2.0 respectively, and this page notes them here for continuity even though nothing in them shifted this time around.
10	
11	As with every accountsvc release, 2.2 stayed inside the areas this project's release notes have always covered: documentation wording, packaging mechanics, command help text, console log format, and speed. Nothing else changes hands in these notes, and nothing else is tracked here.
12	
13	## Release Process Overview
14	
15	**Section owner:** Devon Ruiz, Release Engineering
16	
17	At a high level, cutting an accountsvc release means:
18	
19	1. Confirm the working copy is clean and every intended change is merged to the main line.
20	2. Pick the next version number per the numbering scheme (see below).
21	3. Update the root `CHANGELOG.md` with a dated entry.
22	4. Walk the release checklist end to end.
23	5. Build the source distribution and verify its contents.
24	6. Tag the commit, push the tag, and drop the built file on the internal share.
25	7. Update this folder's release notes page for the new version.
26	
27	Small releases like 2.2 — reworked help text and doc link fixes — still go through all seven steps. There is no shortcut path for "documentation-only" releases; the checklist doesn't distinguish between a wording fix and a larger change, and the team has decided that's fine because the checklist itself is short.
28	
29	## Version Numbering
30	
31	**Section owner:** Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
32	
33	accountsvc uses a two-part `MAJOR.MINOR` number for its ordinary releases — 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, and so on — with an older three-part `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` style used for everything before 2.0 (1.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.2.0). The switch to the shorter two-part form happened at 2.0 and has held since.
34	
35	A few working rules, as practiced day to day:
36	
37	- The MAJOR number moves only when the command-line or the loopback service's observable behavior changes in a way that a caller would need to adjust for.
38	- The MINOR number moves for everything else that ships in a release: wording changes, packaging adjustments, console output formatting, or speed improvements.
39	- There is presently no PATCH number in active use under the 2.x line. If a fix is urgent enough to ship between planned MINOR releases, the team bumps MINOR anyway rather than introducing a third number back in — this keeps the numbering simple, if a little wasteful.
40	- Version numbers are never reused, and they are never skipped on purpose, though 2.2 followed 2.1 by about four months, which is a bit longer than the usual release rhythm.
41	
42	The detailed numbering scheme, including how pre-2.0 numbers were assigned, lives in its own page (see Related Pages). This section is a recap, not the full picture, and the two should agree — check the sibling page's current number if you're unsure which one is authoritative for a given detail.
43	
44	## Changelog Conventions
45	
46	**Section owner:** Sasha Perlman, Docs Guild
47	
48	The root `CHANGELOG.md` is the single record of what shipped, in order, across every accountsvc version. Each release gets one heading and a short list under it. The format the team has settled on:
49	
50	```
51	## 2.2 - 2025-09-15
52	- Reworded command help text for clarity and consistent tone.
53	- Fixed sixteen stale internal documentation links.
54	```
55	
56	A few conventions worth calling out:
57	
58	* Headings use the bare version number, not a "v" prefix, for anything 2.0 and later. Versions before 2.0 keep their "v" prefix (v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v1.2.0) because that's how they were originally written and nobody has gone back to change them.
59	* Entries are written in the past tense, one line each, starting with a verb.
60	* The date on a changelog heading is the date the tag was pushed, not the date the checklist started. For 2.2 those were two days apart — the checklist started 2025-09-13 and the tag went out 2025-09-15.
61	* Entries that touch only wording or documentation are still logged. There's no separate "documentation changelog" — everything goes in the one file.
62	* The changelog does not carry a separate "unreleased" heading between releases; changes accumulate as commits and only get written up when a release is actually cut.
63	
64	## Release Checklist
65	
66	**Section owner:** Devon Ruiz, Release Engineering
67	
68	The checklist below is what was walked for 2.2. It matches the shape of the standing checklist page, reproduced here for convenience:
69	
70	1. Confirm the working copy builds cleanly from a fresh checkout.
71	2. Confirm the changelog entry is written and dated.
72	3. Confirm command help text (the output shown when a command is asked for its own usage) reads correctly for every command the package exposes.
73	4. Confirm documentation links inside `docs/` resolve to real files.
74	5. Confirm the console log format sample in `docs/release-notes/samples/` still matches what the package prints on a plain run.
75	6. Confirm the source distribution builds and its file listing matches expectations.
76	7. Confirm someone other than the person cutting the release has looked over the diff.
77	8. Tag, push, and record the tag name in the changelog entry.
78	
79	For 2.2, steps 5 and 6 were confirmations that nothing had changed rather than new work — the console log format sample from 2.1 still matched, and the source distribution layout was untouched. Steps 3 and 4 were where the actual work happened.
80	
81	A note on freeze timing: the checklist calls for a short freeze on the main line — no unrelated merges — starting once step 1 passes and lasting until the tag is pushed. This has been the practice since 2.0. For 2.2 the freeze ran from the morning of 2025-09-13 through the afternoon of 2025-09-15, roughly two and a half working days.
82	
83	## Packaging the Source Distribution
84	
85	**Section owner:** Elliot Fenwick, Core Services
86	
87	accountsvc ships as a source distribution — a single distribution file built from the package directory, `accountsvc/`, plus the root `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, and packaging metadata. There is no wheel built for internal distribution; the source distribution is the only file placed on the internal share.
88	
89	The build for 2.2 followed the usual steps:
90	
91	```
92	git status
93	git tag -l "2.2"
94	python -m build --sdist
95	tar -tzf dist/accountsvc-2.2.tar.gz | sort
96	sha256sum dist/accountsvc-2.2.tar.gz > dist/accountsvc-2.2.tar.gz.sha256
97	```
98	
99	After the build, the file listing gets a manual look-through against `MANIFEST.in` to confirm nothing extra crept in and nothing expected is missing. For 2.2 the listing was identical to 2.1's, which is expected since neither release touched packaging metadata:
100	
101	| Path in distribution | Included since |
102	|---|---|
103	| accountsvc/ (package directory contents) | 1.0.0 |
104	| README.md | 1.0.0 |
105	| CHANGELOG.md | 1.0.0 |
106	| pyproject.toml | 1.2.0 |
107	| MANIFEST.in | 1.2.0 |
108	
109	Once the listing checks out, the file and its checksum go to the internal share and the tag gets pushed:
110	
111	```
112	git tag -a 2.2 -m "accountsvc 2.2"
113	git push origin 2.2
114	```
115	
116	Nothing about packaging changed in 2.2. The full packaging procedure, including how MANIFEST.in entries are chosen, is written up on its own page (see Related Pages) — this section is only a walk-through of the steps as they were actually run for this build.
117	
118	## What Changed in 2.2
119	
120	### Command Help Text
121	
122	The wording shown when a command is asked for its own usage was reworked across the board. The prior wording had accumulated small inconsistencies over several releases — some commands described their options in full sentences, others used sentence fragments, and capitalization of option names was uneven. For 2.2:
123	
124	- Every command's short usage summary was rewritten to a single sentence fragment starting with a verb.
125	- Option descriptions were shortened and made consistent in tense.
126	- A handful of options that had no description at all (left over from when they were added, in 1.2.0 and 2.0) got one.
127	- Capitalization of option names was made consistent — lowercase with hyphens throughout, matching how they're actually typed.
128	
129	This was purely a wording change. No option was added, removed, or renamed, and no command's actual behavior shifted. Anyone with scripts that check help text output for specific wording (rather than just checking that a command exits without error) should expect those checks to need updating.
130	
131	### Documentation Link Fixes
132	
133	Sixteen internal links across `docs/` were pointing at files that had since been renamed or moved — mostly a result of the release-notes folder's own file naming settling down over the last few versions (the shift from `release-notes-vX.Y.Z.md` to `release-notes-X.Y.md` at 2.0 left a number of older links unfixed). All sixteen were corrected in place. No page content beyond the links themselves was touched, and no new pages were added or removed as part of this fix.

136	
137	The table below shows which of the five areas this project's release notes track — documentation, packaging, command help text, console log format, and speed — were actually touched in each of the last several releases. A blank cell means that release didn't touch that area at all.

139	| Release | Documentation | Packaging | Help Text | Console Log Format | Speed |
140	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
141	| 1.0.0 | X | X | | | |

150	## Console Log Format Notes
151	
152	The console log format has not changed since 2.0 and 2.2 does not touch it. For reference, the current format is: a single line per event, a level name in capitals, then the message, with no timestamp shown by default and no separator character between the level name and the message beyond a single space. A sample of current output is kept at `docs/release-notes/samples/2.1-console-output.txt` — the sample file's name still carries the 2.1 label since that's the release that last changed the format, and nobody has renamed it since.
153	
154	## Speed Notes
155	
156	2.2 made no changes aimed at speed. The last release to touch this area was 2.1, which reduced the time the command line takes to start up for common operations and shortened the typical time before a loopback call returns for the more frequently used calls. Those improvements carried forward unchanged into 2.2; nothing in this release added or removed any of that work.
157	
158	## Manual Verification Performed for 2.2
159	
160	Before the tag was pushed, the following manual checks were run against a fresh checkout:
161	
162	* Ran every command with its usage flag and read the output line by line against the reworked wording.
163	* Spot-checked a sample of the sixteen fixed links by opening each target file directly.
164	* Compared the console output of a plain run against the sample file noted above, confirming no drift.
165	* Confirmed the source distribution file listing against the table in the Packaging section.
166	* Had a second person from the Docs Guild read the diff for wording consistency before the freeze ended.
167	
168	No automated checks are run as part of this process; verification for a release like this one is entirely manual, done by reading output and comparing it to what's expected.
169	
170	## Known Follow-ups
171	
172	- A few option descriptions added in this pass are longer than the rest and may need trimming in a later release for consistency.
173	- Two of the sixteen fixed links point at files that are themselves due for a rename in an upcoming pass; those links will need touching again once that happens.
174	- The console output sample file's name (`2.1-console-output.txt`) should probably be renamed to something version-neutral so it stops needing updates every time the format changes, but that's a small enough job that it's been carried forward from 2.1's own follow-up list without anyone picking it up yet.

176	## Terminology
177	
178	**Source distribution (sdist):** The single distribution file built from the package directory and its top-level metadata files, used to install or move accountsvc between machines without a separate build step for a wheel.
179	
180	**Command help text:** The wording printed when a command is asked to describe its own usage — its summary line and its option descriptions.
181	
182	**Console log format:** The visible shape of the lines the package prints to the console during a plain run — level name, message, and spacing, independent of what the messages actually say.
183	
184	**Change log:** The single dated record in the root `CHANGELOG.md` of what shipped in each release, in order, from 1.0.0 forward.
185	
186	**Version number:** The two-part (or, before 2.0, three-part) number identifying a release, assigned per the numbering rules in Version Numbering above.
187	
188	**Freeze:** The period between the start of a release's checklist and the pushed tag during which no unrelated changes are merged to the main line.

190	**Working copy:** A local checkout of the repository against which the checklist steps and the source distribution build are run.
191	
192	**Loopback service:** The HTTP service accountsvc runs for local calls only; referenced here only insofar as its help text and startup speed are covered by these notes, not how it handles any given call.
193	
194	**Manifest file:** `MANIFEST.in`, the file listing which non-package files are included when the source distribution is built.
195	
196	**Sample file:** A saved copy of console output, kept under `docs/release-notes/samples/`, used to confirm the console log format hasn't drifted between releases.

# Release Notes for 2.2

**Version:** 2.2
**Owner:** Docs Guild (Sasha Perlman)
**Last updated:** 2025-09-15

## Summary

This page records what changed in accountsvc 2.2 and recaps the release process that produced it. The 2.2 build touched command help text and fixed a series of stale links across the internal documentation tree. It did not change the package's console log format, its packaging layout, or its speed profile — those areas last moved in 2.1 and 2.0 respectively, and this page notes them here for continuity even though nothing in them shifted this time around.

As with every accountsvc release, 2.2 stayed inside the areas this project's release notes have always covered: documentation wording, packaging mechanics, command help text, console log format, and speed. Nothing else changes hands in these notes, and nothing else is tracked here.

## Release Process Overview

**Section owner:** Devon Ruiz, Release Engineering

At a high level, cutting an accountsvc release means:

1. Confirm the working copy is clean and every intended change is merged to the main line.
2. Pick the next version number per the numbering scheme (see below).
3. Update the root `CHANGELOG.md` with a dated entry.
4. Walk the release checklist end to end.
5. Build the source distribution and verify its contents.
6. Tag the commit, push the tag, and drop the built file on the internal share.
7. Update this folder's release notes page for the new version.

Small releases like 2.2 — reworked help text and doc link fixes — still go through all seven steps. There is no shortcut path for "documentation-only" releases; the checklist doesn't distinguish between a wording fix and a larger change, and the team has decided that's fine because the checklist itself is short.

## Version Numbering

**Section owner:** Mara Olsen, Platform Tools

accountsvc uses a two-part `MAJOR.MINOR` number for its ordinary releases — 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, and so on — with an older three-part `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` style used for everything before 2.0 (1.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.2.0). The switch to the shorter two-part form happened at 2.0 and has held since.

A few working rules, as practiced day to day:

- The MAJOR number moves only when the command-line or the loopback service's observable behavior changes in a way that a caller would need to adjust for.
- The MINOR number moves for everything else that ships in a release: wording changes, packaging adjustments, console output formatting, or speed improvements.
- There is presently no PATCH number in active use under the 2.x line. If a fix is urgent enough to ship between planned MINOR releases, the team bumps MINOR anyway rather than introducing a third number back in — this keeps the numbering simple, if a little wasteful.
- Version numbers are never reused, and they are never skipped on purpose, though 2.2 followed 2.1 by about four months, which is a bit longer than the usual release rhythm.

The detailed numbering scheme, including how pre-2.0 numbers were assigned, lives in its own page (see Related Pages). This section is a recap, not the full picture, and the two should agree — check the sibling page's current number if you're unsure which one is authoritative for a given detail.

## Changelog Conventions

**Section owner:** Sasha Perlman, Docs Guild

The root `CHANGELOG.md` is the single record of what shipped, in order, across every accountsvc version. Each release gets one heading and a short list under it. The format the team has settled on:

```
## 2.2 - 2025-09-15
- Reworded command help text for clarity and consistent tone.
- Fixed sixteen stale internal documentation links.
```

A few conventions worth calling out:

* Headings use the bare version number, not a "v" prefix, for anything 2.0 and later. Versions before 2.0 keep their "v" prefix (v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v1.2.0) because that's how they were originally written and nobody has gone back to change them.
* Entries are written in the past tense, one line each, starting with a verb.
* The date on a changelog heading is the date the tag was pushed, not the date the checklist started. For 2.2 those were two days apart — the checklist started 2025-09-13 and the tag went out 2025-09-15.
* Entries that touch only wording or documentation are still logged. There's no separate "documentation changelog" — everything goes in the one file.
* The changelog does not carry a separate "unreleased" heading between releases; changes accumulate as commits and only get written up when a release is actually cut.

## Release Checklist

**Section owner:** Devon Ruiz, Release Engineering

The checklist below is what was walked for 2.2. It matches the shape of the standing checklist page, reproduced here for convenience:

1. Confirm the working copy builds cleanly from a fresh checkout.
2. Confirm the changelog entry is written and dated.
3. Confirm command help text (the output shown when a command is asked for its own usage) reads correctly for every command the package exposes.
4. Confirm documentation links inside `docs/` resolve to real files.
5. Confirm the console log format sample in `docs/release-notes/samples/` still matches what the package prints on a plain run.
6. Confirm the source distribution builds and its file listing matches expectations.
7. Confirm someone other than the person cutting the release has looked over the diff.
8. Tag, push, and record the tag name in the changelog entry.

For 2.2, steps 5 and 6 were confirmations that nothing had changed rather than new work — the console log format sample from 2.1 still matched, and the source distribution layout was untouched. Steps 3 and 4 were where the actual work happened.

A note on freeze timing: the checklist calls for a short freeze on the main line — no unrelated merges — starting once step 1 passes and lasting until the tag is pushed. This has been the practice since 2.0. For 2.2 the freeze ran from the morning of 2025-09-13 through the afternoon of 2025-09-15, roughly two and a half working days.

## Packaging the Source Distribution

**Section owner:** Elliot Fenwick, Core Services

accountsvc ships as a source distribution — a single distribution file built from the package directory, `accountsvc/`, plus the root `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, and packaging metadata. There is no wheel built for internal distribution; the source distribution is the only file placed on the internal share.

The build for 2.2 followed the usual steps:

```
git status
git tag -l "2.2"
python -m build --sdist
tar -tzf dist/accountsvc-2.2.tar.gz | sort
sha256sum dist/accountsvc-2.2.tar.gz > dist/accountsvc-2.2.tar.gz.sha256
```

After the build, the file listing gets a manual look-through against `MANIFEST.in` to confirm nothing extra crept in and nothing expected is missing. For 2.2 the listing was identical to 2.1's, which is expected since neither release touched packaging metadata:

| Path in distribution | Included since |
|---|---|
| accountsvc/ (package directory contents) | 1.0.0 |
| README.md | 1.0.0 |
| CHANGELOG.md | 1.0.0 |
| pyproject.toml | 1.2.0 |
| MANIFEST.in | 1.2.0 |

Once the listing checks out, the file and its checksum go to the internal share and the tag gets pushed:

```
git tag -a 2.2 -m "accountsvc 2.2"
git push origin 2.2
```

Nothing about packaging changed in 2.2. The full packaging procedure, including how MANIFEST.in entries are chosen, is written up on its own page (see Related Pages) — this section is only a walk-through of the steps as they were actually run for this build.

## What Changed in 2.2

### Command Help Text

The wording shown when a command is asked for its own usage was reworked across the board. The prior wording had accumulated small inconsistencies over several releases — some commands described their options in full sentences, others used sentence fragments, and capitalization of option names was uneven. For 2.2:

- Every command's short usage summary was rewritten to a single sentence fragment starting with a verb.
- Option descriptions were shortened and made consistent in tense.
- A handful of options that had no description at all (left over from when they were added, in 1.2.0 and 2.0) got one.
- Capitalization of option names was made consistent — lowercase with hyphens throughout, matching how they're actually typed.

This was purely a wording change. No option was added, removed, or renamed, and no command's actual behavior shifted. Anyone with scripts that check help text output for specific wording (rather than just checking that a command exits without error) should expect those checks to need updating.

### Documentation Link Fixes

Sixteen internal links across `docs/` were pointing at files that had since been renamed or moved — mostly a result of the release-notes folder's own file naming settling down over the last few versions (the shift from `release-notes-vX.Y.Z.md` to `release-notes-X.Y.md` at 2.0 left a number of older links unfixed). All sixteen were corrected in place. No page content beyond the links themselves was touched, and no new pages were added or removed as part of this fix.

## Coverage Across Recent Releases

The table below shows which of the five areas this project's release notes track — documentation, packaging, command help text, console log format, and speed — were actually touched in each of the last several releases. A blank cell means that release didn't touch that area at all.

| Release | Documentation | Packaging | Help Text | Console Log Format | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0.0 | X | X | | | |
| 1.1.0 | X | | X | | |
| 1.2.0 | | X | | | |
| 2.0 | X | | X | X | |
| 2.1 | | | | X | X |
| 2.2 | X | | X | | |

This table is maintained by whoever writes each release's notes page; it's copied forward and one row added each time, so if a past row looks wrong the fix belongs on that release's own page rather than here.

## Console Log Format Notes

The console log format has not changed since 2.0 and 2.2 does not touch it. For reference, the current format is: a single line per event, a level name in capitals, then the message, with no timestamp shown by default and no separator character between the level name and the message beyond a single space. A sample of current output is kept at `docs/release-notes/samples/2.1-console-output.txt` — the sample file's name still carries the 2.1 label since that's the release that last changed the format, and nobody has renamed it since.

## Speed Notes

2.2 made no changes aimed at speed. The last release to touch this area was 2.1, which reduced the time the command line takes to start up for common operations and shortened the typical time before a loopback call returns for the more frequently used calls. Those improvements carried forward unchanged into 2.2; nothing in this release added or removed any of that work.

## Manual Verification Performed for 2.2

Before the tag was pushed, the following manual checks were run against a fresh checkout:

* Ran every command with its usage flag and read the output line by line against the reworked wording.
* Spot-checked a sample of the sixteen fixed links by opening each target file directly.
* Compared the console output of a plain run against the sample file noted above, confirming no drift.
* Confirmed the source distribution file listing against the table in the Packaging section.
* Had a second person from the Docs Guild read the diff for wording consistency before the freeze ended.

No automated checks are run as part of this process; verification for a release like this one is entirely manual, done by reading output and comparing it to what's expected.

## Known Follow-ups

- A few option descriptions added in this pass are longer than the rest and may need trimming in a later release for consistency.
- Two of the sixteen fixed links point at files that are themselves due for a rename in an upcoming pass; those links will need touching again once that happens.
- The console output sample file's name (`2.1-console-output.txt`) should probably be renamed to something version-neutral so it stops needing updates every time the format changes, but that's a small enough job that it's been carried forward from 2.1's own follow-up list without anyone picking it up yet.

## Terminology

**Source distribution (sdist):** The single distribution file built from the package directory and its top-level metadata files, used to install or move accountsvc between machines without a separate build step for a wheel.

**Command help text:** The wording printed when a command is asked to describe its own usage — its summary line and its option descriptions.

**Console log format:** The visible shape of the lines the package prints to the console during a plain run — level name, message, and spacing, independent of what the messages actually say.

**Change log:** The single dated record in the root `CHANGELOG.md` of what shipped in each release, in order, from 1.0.0 forward.

**Version number:** The two-part (or, before 2.0, three-part) number identifying a release, assigned per the numbering rules in Version Numbering above.

**Freeze:** The period between the start of a release's checklist and the pushed tag during which no unrelated changes are merged to the main line.

**Working copy:** A local checkout of the repository against which the checklist steps and the source distribution build are run.

**Loopback service:** The HTTP service accountsvc runs for local calls only; referenced here only insofar as its help text and startup speed are covered by these notes, not how it handles any given call.

**Manifest file:** `MANIFEST.in`, the file listing which non-package files are included when the source distribution is built.

**Sample file:** A saved copy of console output, kept under `docs/release-notes/samples/`, used to confirm the console log format hasn't drifted between releases.

## Files and Paths Referenced

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `accountsvc/` | The package directory; its contents make up the bulk of the source distribution. |
| `README.md` | Root-level project overview; included in every source distribution. |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | The project's single dated change log, updated with every release. |
| `pyproject.toml` | Packaging metadata used when building the source distribution. |
| `MANIFEST.in` | Lists non-package files to include when building the source distribution. |
| `docs/release-notes/` | This folder; holds the release checklist, numbering scheme, changelog conventions, packaging guide, and per-version release notes. |
| `docs/release-notes/release-notes-2.2.md` | This page. |
| `docs/release-notes/samples/2.1-console-output.txt` | Saved console output used to confirm the console log format is unchanged. |
| `dist/` | Local build output folder for the source distribution and its checksum file; not checked into the repository. |
| `scripts/` | Holds small shell helpers used around release time, including link-checking helpers used for the documentation fixes in this release. |

## Tools and Libraries

| Tool / library | Version used for 2.2 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.9 | accountsvc itself uses only the standard library; this is the build and packaging interpreter. |
| build | 1.2.1 | Used to produce the source distribution. |
| setuptools | 69.5.1 | Backend used by `build` for the source distribution. |
| git | 2.45.1 | Tagging and diff review. |
| sha256sum (coreutils) | 9.4 | Checksum generation for the built distribution file. |
| tar | 1.35 | Listing and inspecting the built distribution file. |

## Change Log

*(This is the change log for this page, not for accountsvc itself — see the root `CHANGELOG.md` for that.)*

- **2025-09-15** — Sasha Perlman — Wrote this page for the 2.2 release; recorded command help text and documentation link fixes.
- **2025-09-13** — Sasha Perlman — Drafted the coverage table and confirmed console log format and speed were untouched for this build.
- **2025-05-27** — Sasha Perlman — Wrote the sibling page for 2.1, which introduced the console log format and speed changes referenced here.
- **2025-02-11** — Mara Olsen — Wrote the sibling page for 2.0, marking the switch to the two-part version numbering scheme.
- **2024-10-22** — Mara Olsen — Wrote the sibling page for 1.2.0, covering the packaging changes that added `pyproject.toml` and `MANIFEST.in`.
- **2024-07-05** — Priya Nandakumar — Wrote the sibling page for 1.1.0, covering the first help text pass.
- **2024-03-18** — Priya Nandakumar — Wrote the sibling page for v1.0.0, the first release notes page in this folder.

## Related Pages

- Release Notes Folder Guide
- Version Numbering Scheme
- Changelog Conventions
- Release Checklist
- Packaging the Source Distribution
- Source Distribution Notes
- Changelog Entry Format
- Release Schedule
- Release Notes for 2.1
- Release Notes for 2.0
- Release Notes for v1.2.0
- Release Notes for v1.1.0
- Release Notes for v1.0.0

# docs/release-notes/release-schedule.yaml
#
# Release Schedule — internal documentation for accountsvc
# This file is hand-maintained. Keep entries dated and keep the
# terminology section current when new shorthand creeps into review
# comments.

title: Release Schedule
version: "2.5"
owner: Core Services (Elliot Fenwick)
last_updated: 2026-04-08
summary: >
  This page lists the planned cadence and target dates for upcoming
  builds of accountsvc, the steps each build passes through on its way
  out the door, and a compact record of what shipped in past versions.
  It is the page to check when someone asks "when's the next build"
  or "did 2.3 ever actually go out."

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# PURPOSE AND COVERAGE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
purpose: >
  accountsvc ships on an irregular but roughly quarterly cadence. Because
  the package has no external dependencies beyond the standard library,
  a build is mostly a documentation, packaging, and wording exercise —
  there is rarely a large functional change driving the calendar. This
  page exists so that the four or five people who touch the release
  process don't have to reconstruct the schedule from git tags and old
  chat threads every time.

what_this_page_covers:
  owner: Core Services (Elliot Fenwick)
  notes: >
    This page owns four things: the target-date table for upcoming
    builds, a short recap of the version numbering approach as it
    applies to scheduling, a condensed checklist for what has to happen
    before a build goes out, and a compact table of what shipped in
    past versions so nobody has to open six separate files to answer
    "did we already fix the help text wording in 2.2 or was that 2.3."
    Full write-ups of the numbering scheme, the changelog conventions,
    the checklist, and the packaging steps each live in their own page;
    this page summarizes them only as far as scheduling requires.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# VERSION NUMBERING (summary — full scheme lives in its own page)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
version_numbering:
  owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
  summary: >
    accountsvc uses a two-part version number, MAJOR.MINOR, for every
    build that goes out the door — 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, and so on. A third
    number is added only for an unplanned fix between scheduled builds
    (2.4.1, for example), and that third number is dropped again on the
    next scheduled MINOR bump. The version string lives in the packaging
    config file and in the top line of the changelog entry; both have to
    match before a build is tagged.
  bump_rules:
    - "MAJOR bumps only when the console log format or the on-disk database file layout changes in a way that would surprise someone who hasn't read the changelog first."
    - "MINOR bumps for everything else that ships in a scheduled build — documentation reorganizations, packaging fixes, command help text wording, and speed work all count as MINOR."
    - "The unplanned third number is reserved for a single narrow fix and is never carried forward; the next scheduled build resets to MAJOR.MINOR."
  cross_reference: >
    See Version Numbering Scheme (Platform Tools, v2.2) for the full
    reasoning behind the two-part approach and for how the number is
    stamped into the source distribution's file name.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHANGELOG CONVENTIONS (summary — full conventions live in their own page)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
changelog_conventions:
  owner: Docs Guild (Sasha Perlman)
  summary: >
    Every scheduled build gets one dated entry at the top of the
    changelog file, newest first. The entry names the version, the
    date the build was tagged (not the date the entry was written,
    which are sometimes a day or two apart), and a short bulleted list
    of what changed grouped under Documentation, Packaging, Command
    Help Text, Console Log Format, and Speed — whichever of those
    apply. Entries that don't fit one of those five buckets get flagged
    for the Release Checklist owner to sort out before the build is
    tagged, because a build with an unclassified change usually means
    someone forgot to update a heading.
  worked_example: |
    ## 2.5.0 — 2026-04-22
    ### Documentation
    - Reworded the quick-start section of the top-level README to match
      the current command help text.
    ### Packaging
    - Trimmed two stale example files out of the source distribution.
    ### Command Help Text
    - Shortened the summary line shown for the account-lookup command.
    ### Console Log Format
    - No change this build.
    ### Speed
    - Reduced local database file open time on first run by caching the
      pragma check from the previous run.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# RELEASE CHECKLIST (summary — full checklist lives in its own page)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
release_checklist:
  owner: Release Engineering (Devon Ruiz)
  summary: >
    The full checklist lives on its own page and is the one to follow
    step by step; the list below is the condensed version kept here so
    the schedule page can note which step corresponds to which target
    date without sending someone away to look it up.
  steps:
    - step: 1
      what: "Confirm the working tree is clean and the branch is up to date."
      how: "git status; git pull --ff-only"
    - step: 2
      what: "Confirm the changelog file has a dated entry for the new version, filed under the five buckets."
      how: "manual review against Changelog Conventions"
    - step: 3
      what: "Confirm the version string in the packaging config file matches the changelog entry."
      how: "grep -n \"version\" pyproject.toml"
    - step: 4
      what: "Open a local copy of the database file and confirm its schema pragma is the one expected for this build."
      how: "sqlite3 accounts.db \"PRAGMA user_version;\""
    - step: 5
      what: "Build the source distribution."
      how: "see Packaging the Source Distribution section below"
    - step: 6
      what: "Confirm the distribution's file listing matches what's expected — no stray files, no missing ones."
      how: "tar -tzf dist/accountsvc-2.5.0.tar.gz"
    - step: 7
      what: "Tag the build in git and push the tag."
      how: "git tag -a v2.5.0 -m \"accountsvc 2.5.0\"; git push origin v2.5.0"
    - step: 8
      what: "Publish the per-version release notes page and cross-link it from this schedule."
      how: "add docs/release-notes/release-notes-2.5.md; update related_pages below"
  cross_reference: >
    Full step-by-step detail, including who confirms each step and what
    to do when a step fails partway through, is on the Release
    Checklist page.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# PACKAGING THE SOURCE DISTRIBUTION (summary)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
packaging_source_distribution:
  owner: Core Services (Elliot Fenwick)
  summary: >
    accountsvc ships as a source distribution only — no wheel is
    published, since the package has no compiled parts and installing
    from source is fast enough that a wheel wouldn't save much. The
    build tool reads the packaging config file at the repository root
    and the MANIFEST.in file for any extra files (documentation
    fragments, the changelog file itself) that should be folded into
    the distribution beyond what the packaging backend includes by
    default.
  worked_example: |
    # from the repository root, with a clean working tree
    python -m build --sdist
    ls dist/
    #   accountsvc-2.5.0.tar.gz
    twine check dist/*
    tar -tzf dist/accountsvc-2.5.0.tar.gz | sort
  common_mistakes:
    - "Forgetting to add a newly created documentation file to MANIFEST.in, so it silently drops out of the distribution."
    - "Building from a working tree that still has an unstaged wording fix in the command help text — the build tool doesn't care about unstaged changes, it just packages whatever's on disk."
    - "Running the build twice without clearing the dist/ folder first and then not seeing that there are two tarballs with different sizes."
  note: >
    The full walkthrough, including the edge cases around the changelog
    file's line endings on Windows build hosts, was last revised around
    July 2024 and lives on its own page.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# UPCOMING BUILD SCHEDULE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
upcoming_schedule:
  owner: Core Services (Elliot Fenwick)
  notes: >
    Freeze date is when no further changes are accepted for that
    build except a fix to something the checklist itself turns up;
    target date is when the tag is expected to be pushed and the
    source distribution built. Both dates slip a few days more often
    than not — treat them as the current best guess, not a commitment.
  builds:
    - version: "2.5.0"
      focus: "Documentation wording pass, command help text shortening"
      freeze_date: 2026-04-15
      target_date: 2026-04-22
      owner: Elliot Fenwick
      status: in progress
    - version: "2.6.0"
      focus: "Console log format cleanup, remaining command help text edits"
      freeze_date: 2026-06-01
      target_date: 2026-06-10
      owner: Devon Ruiz
      status: planned
    - version: "2.7.0"
      focus: "Speed work on local database file access at startup, packaging trim"
      freeze_date: 2026-07-27
      target_date: 2026-08-05
      owner: Elliot Fenwick
      status: planned
    - version: "2.8.0"
      focus: "Documentation folder reorganization (tentative)"
      freeze_date: 2026-09-28
      target_date: 2026-10-14
      owner: unassigned
      status: tentative

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# PAST RELEASES AT A GLANCE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
past_releases:
  owner: Developer Experience (Priya Nandakumar)
  notes: >
    Every past build of accountsvc has touched only documentation,
    packaging, command help text, console log format, or speed —
    nothing else has ever gone into a changelog entry. The table below
    is the condensed version of that record kept for scheduling
    purposes; the full per-version write-ups are their own pages where
    they exist. Not every version got its own write-up page — 2.3.0 in
    particular was small enough that the changelog entry was judged
    sufficient at the time.
  releases:
    - version: "1.0.0"
      date: 2024-03-18
      focus: "Documentation, Packaging"
      summary: "First source distribution built; initial docs/ folder laid out; initial console log format established as plain single-line text."
    - version: "1.1.0"
      date: 2024-07-05
      focus: "Command Help Text, Documentation"
      summary: "Clarified wording across the command line's help text; minor documentation fixes carried over from the 1.0.0 write-up."
    - version: "1.2.0"
      date: 2024-10-22
      focus: "Packaging, Speed"
      summary: "Corrected a source distribution manifest gap that had been dropping a documentation fragment; sped up the local database file's first open on a cold start."
    - version: "2.0.0"
      date: 2025-02-11
      focus: "Documentation, Console Log Format"
      summary: "Reorganized the docs/ folder into its current shape; console log format changed to include a timestamp on every line."
    - version: "2.1.0"
      date: 2025-05-27
      focus: "Console Log Format, Documentation"
      summary: "Console log format switched from timestamp-plus-text to key-value pairs; documentation updated with examples of the new line format."
    - version: "2.2.0"
      date: 2025-09-15
      focus: "Speed, Command Help Text"
      summary: "Reduced loopback service start-up time; corrected two command help text strings that had gone stale after the 2.1.0 log format change."
    - version: "2.3.0"
      date: 2025-12-08
      focus: "Packaging, Documentation, Command Help Text"
      summary: "Trimmed the source distribution to drop a handful of stale example files; updated command help text wording; small documentation fixes across the changelog conventions and writeup pages. No dedicated release-notes page was written for this one — see the changelog file directly."
    - version: "2.4.0"
      date: 2026-02-20
      focus: "Speed, Console Log Format"
      summary: "Tightened the console log format's key ordering for readability; measurable load speed improvement when the local database file has accumulated a large number of records."

26	## Semantic Versioning Rules (Section Owner: Platform Tools)

33	- The loopback HTTP service changes request or response formats in ways that break existing functionality
34	- The database file format or initialization changes in an incompatible way
35	- A widely used feature is deprecated or removed

39	1. Renaming a flag from `--account-id` to `--id`
40	2. Changing the HTTP service from port 9000 to a configurable port with different defaults
41	3. Altering the database schema structure such that existing deployments cannot upgrade safely
42

220	## Terminology
221	
222	**Source Package**: A compressed `.tar.gz` file containing the complete package source code and documentation, ready for distribution to users.
223	
224	**Backward-compatible**: A change that does not break existing code using the package's command-line or HTTP interface; old code continues to work with new versions.

236	**Semantic versioning**: A versioning scheme using three numeric components (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`) to communicate the nature and breadth of changes between releases.

---

## Overview

The accountsvc package uses semantic versioning with a three-part version number: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.

* **Major releases** indicate significant feature additions or breaking API changes to the command line or loopback HTTP service.
* **Minor releases** add new functionality or change existing behavior in backward-compatible ways.
* **Patch releases** fix bugs, improve performance, update help text, or refine console output formatting without changing the service's functional behavior.

All release numbers are recorded in the `setup.cfg` file at the repository root, in the `[metadata]` section under `version =`. Tags in the version control system follow the pattern `v{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH}` (for example, `v2.2.0` or `v1.0.1`).

Release announcements and migration guides live in the `release-notes/` directory at the repository root as individual Markdown files. Naming conventions have evolved over time; you may encounter both `release-notes-v{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH}.md` and `release-notes-{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.md` depending on when each page was published.

---

## Semantic Versioning Rules (Section Owner: Platform Tools)

### Major Version Increments

Increment `MAJOR` when:

- The command-line interface adds, removes, or substantially alters argument names or behavior
- The loopback HTTP service changes request or response formats in ways that break existing functionality
- The database file format or initialization changes in an incompatible way
- A widely used feature is deprecated or removed

Examples of changes that warrant major version bumps:

1. Renaming a flag from `--account-id` to `--id`
2. Changing the HTTP service from port 9000 to a configurable port with different defaults
3. Altering the database schema structure such that existing deployments cannot upgrade safely

### Minor Version Increments

Increment `MINOR` when:

- New command-line flags or options are added
- The HTTP service gains new request paths or response fields (as long as existing requests still work unchanged)
- Help text is substantially rewritten, expanded, or reorganized
- Console log output adds new fields or columns while preserving existing ones
- Performance improvements are made that do not alter external behavior

Do not increment `MINOR` for documentation-only changes unless the documentation is bundled in the package distribution itself (such as a `CHANGELOG.md` file in the root).

### Patch Version Increments

Increment `PATCH` when:

- Bug fixes are made to the core service or CLI
- Help text is corrected or slightly improved
- Console log format is adjusted (e.g., timestamp precision, field spacing)
- Performance regressions are fixed
- Dependencies or packaging metadata are updated

## Release Workflow

### Planning and Preparation

Before beginning work on a release, consult the `release-schedule.yaml` file in the `release-notes/` directory to confirm the next scheduled release date and target version number. This file is maintained by Core Services (Elliot Fenwick).

Create a new branch with the naming pattern `release/{VERSION}`, for example `release/2.3.0`. This branch diverges from `main` at the point where development for that release stabilizes.

### Updating Version Numbers

1. Open `setup.cfg` in a text editor.
2. Locate the `version =` line under `[metadata]`.

   ```

1. Review all uncommitted or recently merged changes that affect user-visible behavior

- Verification that all documentation pages are current
- Confirmation that help text output matches documentation

Past releases of the package are documented in the `release-notes/` folder. Documentation-focused releases emphasize changes to:

- Command help text and error messages  
- Console log output format and verbosity
- Performance improvements in startup time or database query speed
- Packaging and distribution changes

### Structure of Release Notes

Each release notes file follows this pattern:

- **Release heading** with version and date

- **Changes to Documentation** or **Command Help Updates**

- **Performance Notes**
- **Packaging or Distribution Changes**
- **Migration Guide** (included if breaking changes exist)

The complete release notes for each version appear in separate files in the `release-notes/` directory.

---

## Source Distribution Packaging

When packaging the source distribution for release, follow the procedures in `packaging-source-distribution.rst` (v1.2.0, Core Services, Elliot Fenwick, last updated 2024-06-14).

### Required Distribution Components

The source distribution must contain:

- The `accountsvc/` package directory at the repository root
- The `README.md` file from the repository root  
- A `setup.cfg` file with correct version metadata
- The `docs/` folder with all documentation and changelog files

```
