If you hit anything weird during clone or first checkout (odd line endings,
access errors on scripts/, slow clone over VPN), Troubleshooting
Workstation Setup has a running list of known issues and fixes — check there
before contacting the IT team.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 2 — SUPPORTED PYTHON VERSIONS (owner: Runtime Infra, Yusuf Demir)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

accountsvc targets the standard library only — there is no dependency
resolution to fight — but the interpreter version still matters for
supported language features and for what the loopback service and CLI are
verified against in CI.

As of this writing, supported versions are:

  Python 3.11   — minimum supported, still common in older images
  Python 3.12   — primary target, what most of the team runs day to day
  Python 3.13   — supported, some contributors are early adopters here

Python 3.10 and earlier are not supported. Python 3.9 support was dropped
some time back; if you find a stray reference to 3.9 in an old branch or a
comment, it's leftover and not authoritative — Supported Python Versions is
the source of truth, not this checklist.

To check what you have installed:

     python3 --version

If you manage multiple interpreter versions, a version manager keeps things
sane. Example using a common one:

     pyenv install 3.12.4
     pyenv local 3.12.4

Confirm the local pin took effect:

     python --version
     # should print 3.12.4, not your system default

Virtual environment, standard library only, nothing exotic:

     python3 -m venv .venv
     source .venv/bin/activate        # macOS/Linux
     .venv\Scripts\activate           # Windows PowerShell

Because accountsvc has no third-party runtime dependencies, "installing
dependencies" mostly means installing the development tooling (formatter,
linter, docs builder) rather than anything the package needs to run. See the
Tools and Versions table below and Dependency Management for the fuller
story on how that tooling is pinned.

     python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip
     python3 -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 3 — EDITOR CONFIGURATION (owner: Developer Experience, Theo Banks)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full page: Editor Configuration (v1.2). The short version most people need
on day one:

- Formatting and linting should run automatically on save. If you're
  fighting the formatter manually, your editor isn't configured yet — stop
  and fix that first, don't hand-format.
- Shared indentation, encoding, and whitespace rules are checked into the
  repo root as an editor-config file; most editors pick this up
  automatically with no plugin required. Confirm yours does.
- A shared settings file for VS Code users lives alongside the editor
  config; if you use VS Code, copy it into your workspace settings rather
  than starting from scratch.
- Set your editor's rulers/column guides to match the line-length limit in
  the coding style guide (see below) — the formatter enforces it, but a
  visible ruler saves you a reformat-and-rereview cycle.
- Enable "format on save" and "organize imports on save" if your editor
  supports it. Nearly everyone on the team runs this way; reviewers will
  occasionally comment if a diff shows unformatted or unsorted imports.

Quick sanity check once configured: open any file under accountsvc/, make a
trivial whitespace edit, save, and confirm the formatter didn't rewrite
unrelated lines. If it rewrites the whole file, your formatter version
likely doesn't match the pinned version (see the tools table) — reinstall
the dev dependencies rather than a global copy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 4 — LOCAL DEVELOPMENT WORKFLOW (owner: Developer Experience, Theo Banks)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Detailed page: Local Development Workflow (v2.5). What you need for
onboarding purposes: run through it once, end to end, before you write any
real change. This gets your environment exercised and surfaces setup
problems early, while they're still cheap to fix.

Typical first-week flow:

  1. Activate your virtual environment.
  2. Format the whole tree once to confirm your formatter matches the
     team's pinned version (this should produce zero diffs on a clean
     checkout — if it doesn't, your formatter version is off).
  3. Make a trivial, throwaway local edit (add a blank line somewhere under
     scripts/, then revert it) just to confirm your editor's format-on-save
     and the CLI-invoked formatter agree with each other.
  4. Check the log output location the local service writes to during
     manual runs — new contributors often don't know where to look. Ask
     your onboarding buddy if it's not obvious from Local Development
     Workflow; the exact path has moved more than once.

If any of this doesn't work cleanly, this is exactly the kind of thing
Troubleshooting Workstation Setup exists for.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 5 — CODE REVIEW CONVENTIONS (owner: Core Services, Priya Chandran)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full page: Code Review Conventions (v3.1). Highlights for your first PR:

- Keep PRs small. A first PR that touches more than a couple hundred lines
  will usually get sent back for splitting, not reviewed as-is.
- Every PR needs a one- or two-sentence summary of *why*, not just *what* —
  the diff already says what.
- Two confirmations are the norm for changes inside accountsvc/; one confirmation
  is enough for docs-only or scripts/-only changes.
- Reviewers are expected to respond within one business day. If you haven't
  heard anything in two, it's fine to nudge the reviewer directly.
- Handle every comment with either a code change or a reply — don't,
  silently resolve threads. Reviewers see and it slows things down, not
  speeds them up.
- Rebase rather than merge when bringing your branch up to date, unless the
  reviewer asks for a merge commit for some specific reason.

Worked example of a review-ready PR description:

     Summary:
     Adjust how the loopback service logs slow requests so the
     threshold is configurable instead of hardcoded.

     Why:
     Ops asked for this after the last on-call cycle; the fixed
     threshold was too noisy on the staging host.

     Verification:
     Ran the local development workflow manually against a local
     copy of the database file; confirmed log output reflects the
     new threshold.

Note: as of the last review of this checklist, one confirmation was standard
for all changes under a certain size — that guidance has since tightened to
two confirmations for package changes, so trust Code Review Conventions over
the older wording if you see it repeated elsewhere.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 6 — COMMIT MESSAGE STYLE (owner: Core Services, Priya Chandran)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full page: Commit Message Style (v2.0.1). Format in brief:

     <area>: <short imperative summary, under ~65 chars>

     <optional body — wrap around 72 columns, explain why not what>

     <optional footer — issue references, one per line>

"Area" is a short lowercase tag for the part of the repo you touched —
common ones are cli, service, storage, docs, scripts. Examples:

     cli: add --verbose flag to the account lookup command
     service: tighten timeout handling on the loopback listener
     storage: reindex the local database file on startup
     docs: fix broken link in workstation setup page

Bad example (too vague, no area, past tense):

     Fixed bug

Good rewrite:

     storage: fix incorrect row count after a failed write

A few conventions people forget in week one:
  - imperative mood ("add", not "added" or "adds")
  - no trailing period on the summary line
  - one logical change per commit — if your commit message needs "and" to
    describe it, it's probably two commits
  - squash your throwaway "wip" and "fix typo" commits before opening the
    PR; reviewers see the squashed commits, not your local mess

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 7 — CODING STYLE (owner: Language Tooling, Owen Fitzgerald)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full page: Coding Style Guide (v4.0), with a condensed cheat-sheet at Style
Quick Reference (v1.3) — print the quick reference, it's one page and
covers 90% of what reviewers actually comment on.

Highlights:

  - Line length: 88 columns. The formatter enforces this; don't argue with
    it in review, argue with Owen's team if you think it's wrong.
  - Naming: snake_case for functions and variables, PascalCase for classes,
    UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for module-level constants.
  - Imports: standard library only for accountsvc's runtime code, grouped
    and sorted automatically on save (see editor configuration above).
    Development-only tooling imports (formatter, linter configs) don't
    count against this — they're not shipped.
  - Docstrings: every public function and class gets one-line summary docs
    at minimum; longer explanations are welcome but a summary is not
    optional.
  - Avoid deep nesting — if you're four levels of indentation in, look for
    an early return or a helper instead of adding a fifth.
  - Prefer explicit over clever. Reviewers will ask you to unwind a
    one-liner more often than they'll ask you to compress one.

Worked before/after (illustrative, not from the real package):

     Before:
     Function f with parameter x and optional y
       if y==None:y=[]
       for i in range(len(x)):
         if x[i]>0:y.append(x[i])
       return y

     After:
     Function keep_positive with parameters values and result
         """Return a new list containing only the positive values."""
         if result is None:
             result = []
         for value in values:
             if value > 0:
                 result.append(value)
         return result

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GLOSSARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

area tag
    The short lowercase prefix in a commit summary line identifying which
    part of the repo the commit touches (cli, service, storage, docs,
    scripts).

database file
    The local SQLite file the service and CLI use to hold customer account
    state. Onboarding does not require understanding its internal layout,
    only where it lives on your workstation.

dev dependency
    A tool needed to develop accountsvc (formatter, linter, docs builder)
    but not needed at runtime, since the package itself uses only the
    standard library.

editor config file
    The shared, editor-agnostic file at the repo root that defines
    indentation, encoding, and whitespace rules picked up automatically by
    most editors.

format on save
    An editor setting that runs the team's pinned formatter automatically
    each time a file is saved, keeping diffs free of incidental formatting
    changes.

loopback service
    The HTTP service accountsvc runs, bound to the local machine rather
    than exposed to the network, used for local development and manual
    checks.

onboarding buddy
    An existing team member informally paired with a new contributor for
    their first one to two weeks, mainly for unblocking setup issues fast.

pinned version
    The exact version of a tool (formatter, linter, interpreter) that CI
    and the team agree to use, recorded in requirements-dev.txt, so that
    "works on my machine" differences don't creep in.

quick reference
    The condensed, single-page version of the coding style guide, meant to
    sit next to your keyboard rather than be read cover to cover.

virtual environment
    An isolated Python environment created per-checkout so that development
    tooling versions don't collide with anything else installed on your
    machine.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
REPOSITORY FILES AND PATHS REFERENCED BY THIS PAGE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  accountsvc/                 Package directory; the CLI and loopback
                               service code live here.
  README.md                   Repository root readme; brief project
                               summary and links into docs/.
  docs/developer-handbook/     Folder holding this checklist and its sibling
                               pages.
  docs/developer-handbook/README.md
                               Index page for the developer handbook folder.
  requirements-dev.txt         Pinned versions of development-only tooling
                               (formatter, linter, docs builder).
  .editorconfig                Shared indentation/encoding/whitespace rules
                               picked up by most editors automatically.
  editor-settings.yaml          Shared VS Code workspace settings file
                               referenced from Editor Configuration.
  scripts/                     Small helper scripts for local development;
                               a common place for a first, low-risk PR.
  scripts/format_check.sh      Runs the pinned formatter in check-only mode
                               across the tree; used in step 4 above.
  docs/developer-handbook/troubleshooting-setup.md
                               Known issues and fixes for workstation setup
                               problems, referenced repeatedly above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TOOLS AND VERSIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Tool / Package          Pinned Version     Purpose
  ----------------------  -----------------  --------------------------------
  Python                  3.12.4             Primary target interpreter
  Python (minimum)        3.11.9             Oldest supported interpreter
  git                     2.43+              Version control
  pyenv                   2.3.x              Optional interpreter version
                                              manager
  black                   24.4.2             Code formatter, runs on save
                                              and in CI
  ruff                    0.5.0               Linter, runs in CI and
                                              optionally on save
  mypy                    1.10.0             Static type checking (advisory
                                              in CI, not yet blocking)
  sphinx                  7.3.7               Docs builder for docs/
  pre-commit              3.7.1               Local hook runner wrapping
                                              black/ruff before commit
  VS Code                 1.90+ (any recent)  Primary supported editor;
                                              others work but are less
                                              exercised by the team

Note that mypy is currently advisory rather than a hard gate in review —
this has been proposed to change; if you see it blocking a PR, that's
ahead of what's documented here, ask in #accountsvc-dev to confirm current
status.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
FIRST-WEEK FAQ
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Q: I have Python 3.10 installed system-wide, can I just use that?
A: No — use a version manager to get 3.11 or later per the Supported
   Python Versions page, and pin it locally to this checkout rather than
   changing your system Python.

Q: Do I need to install anything beyond the dev dependencies file?
A: Usually not. accountsvc's runtime code has no third-party dependencies;
   almost everything you install in week one is developer tooling.

Q: My formatter reformats the whole file instead of just my change.
A: Your local formatter version doesn't match the pinned version. Reinstall
   from requirements-dev.txt rather than using a globally installed copy.

Q: Who do I ask about editor problems specific to VS Code extensions?
A: Developer Experience owns editor configuration generally; Runtime Infra
   (Yusuf Demir) currently maintains the shared VS Code settings file
   specifically, since it also encodes some interpreter-path assumptions.

Q: How big should my first PR be?
A: Small. A docs fix or a one-line change under scripts/ is a completely
   normal and encouraged first contribution — see the checklist above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

                      status.

10	## Purpose
11	
12	*Section owner: Mara Olsen*
13	
14	This page is the front door to the `developer-handbook/` folder for the accountsvc repository. It doesn't try to teach you anything about accountsvc itself — for that, start with the repository root `README.md` and then come back here. What this page does is tell you what pages exist, who owns each one, when it was last touched, and roughly what order to read them in if you're new to the team.
15	
16	The handbook covers workstation setup, editor configuration, supported Python versions, code review conventions, commit message style, and coding style, plus a few supporting pages on repository layout, dependency management, and troubleshooting. If you're looking for something and it's not indexed below, it probably doesn't exist yet — open an issue against Platform Tools rather than guessing.
17	
18	As of this writing the handbook has thirteen pages, including this index. A few of the entries below lag a little behind the pages themselves; if the version number here disagrees with the header block on the actual page, trust the page, not the index. We try to keep this synced but it slips.
19	
20	## How This Index Works
21	
22	Each page in the folder carries its own header block (title, version, owner, last-updated date) at the top, matching the format used on this page. The index below restates those fields so you can scan the whole handbook without opening every file. Pages are grouped loosely by when you'd need them — getting-started material first, then day-to-day editor and workflow references, then the conventions you'll be held to during review, then troubleshooting.
23	
24	Formats are mixed on purpose. Most pages are Markdown, one is reStructuredText (`local-development-workflow.rst`), a couple are plain text (`onboarding-checklist.txt`, `style-quick-reference.txt`), and one is YAML (`editor-settings.yaml`) because it's meant to be copied directly into an editor config rather than read as prose. Don't assume `.md` everywhere.
25	
26	## Getting Started
27	
28	Read these in roughly this order during your first week.
29	
30	1. **Workstation Setup** — version 2.3 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2025-01-20 — [workstation-setup.md](./workstation-setup.md)
31	2. **Supported Python Versions** — version v1.3.0 — owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir) — updated 2026-02-03 — [supported-python-versions.md](./supported-python-versions.md)
32	3. **Repository Layout** — version 1.1 — owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) — updated 2024-04-10 — [repository-layout.md](./repository-layout.md)
33	4. **Onboarding Checklist** — version 1.0 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2024-06-14 — [onboarding-checklist.txt](./onboarding-checklist.txt)
34	
35	The Onboarding Checklist is a plain-text tick list, intentionally terse — it points at the other pages rather than repeating them, so treat it as a table of contents for your first day rather than a stand-alone guide.

37	## Editor and Local Workflow
38	
39	* **Editor Configuration** — version 1.2 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2024-11-15 — [editor-configuration.md](./editor-configuration.md)
40	* **Shared Editor Settings** — version v1.0.1 — owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir) — updated 2026-04-08 — [editor-settings.yaml](./editor-settings.yaml)
41	* **Local Development Workflow** — version 2.5 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2025-03-27 — [local-development-workflow.rst](./local-development-workflow.rst)
42	* **Dependency Management** — version v1.1.3 — owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir) — updated 2026-01-18 — [dependency-management.md](./dependency-management.md)

44	Editor Configuration explains the reasoning behind our settings; editor-settings.yaml is the file you actually import. Owen Fitzgerald keeps asking us to merge these two, and honestly he's right, but nobody's gotten around to it.

48	These are the pages reviewers will point you at when they leave a comment on your change.

53	- **Style Quick Reference**, version 1.3, owner Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald), updated 2025-12-29. [style-quick-reference.txt](./style-quick-reference.txt)
54	
55	Style Quick Reference is a cheat sheet — it exists so you don't have to reopen the full Coding Style Guide every time you forget the line-length limit. It is not a substitute for reading the guide once, in full, before your first review.

107	## Terminology
108	
109	Terms used loosely and inconsistently across the handbook are defined here once, so individual pages don't have to keep re-explaining them.
110	
111	- **Handbook page** — Any file directly under `developer-handbook/`, regardless of its format (Markdown, reStructuredText, plain text, or YAML).
112	- **Header block** — The small table or list at the top of a handbook page giving its title, version, owner, and last-updated date. Every page in this folder is expected to have one.
113	- **Section owner** — The person named as responsible for a particular section of a page, noted inline as *Section owner: Name*. Not every section has one; sections without a named owner default to the page's overall owner.
114	- **Folder index** — This page. The single entry point that links out to every other page in `developer-handbook/`.
115	- **Sibling page** — Any other page in the same `developer-handbook/` folder, referenced from a Related Pages section.
116	- **Workstation** — The laptop or desktop machine a developer uses for day-to-day work on accountsvc, as distinct from any shared or hosted machine.
117	- **Loopback service** — The locally-bound HTTP service that accountsvc runs during development, reachable only from the same machine.
118	- **Standard library** — The set of modules that ship with Python itself; accountsvc is built entirely on top of these, with no third-party runtime dependencies.
119	- **Local development workflow** — The repeating cycle of editing the package, running it locally against its database file, and iterating, described in `local-development-workflow.rst`.
120	- **Quick reference** — A condensed, cheat-sheet version of a longer page, meant for glancing at rather than reading start to finone.
121	- **Glossary** — This section. A list of terms defined once so other pages don't repeat the definitions.

123	## Contributing to the Handbook
124	
125	*Section owner: Theo Banks*
126	
127	If you're adding a new page or making a meaningful change to an existing one, follow this loop:
128	
129	1. Update the page itself first — content, header block (bump the version, update the date, confirm the owner), and its terminology or file-listing sections if anything changed.
130	2. Come back to this index and update the corresponding row: title, version, owner, and date should match what you just wrote on the page.
131	3. If you're adding a brand-new page, pick a heading above that fits it, or propose a new heading in review if none of the existing ones make sense.
132	4. Add a line to the Change Log below describing what changed and why, and name a release the same way the rest of the log does.
133	5. Open a normal review following Code Review Conventions — handbook changes go through the same process as code changes, just with a lighter bar for sign-off since there's no code being run.
134	
135	A few conventions specific to this folder:
136	
137	* Keep the terminology section on each page in alphabetical order where practical; it's easier to scan.
138	* Don't remove a page's header block fields even if they seem redundant with the index — pages get read outside the context of the index all the time, especially when someone's linked directly to a section.
139	* If you rename a page's title without renaming the file, or vice versa, please update this index in the same change. We've fallen behind on this before (see the Coding Style Guide owner listed above, which is stale relative to the page itself) and it causes confusion during onboarding.
140	* Plain-text pages (`.txt`) should stay short. If a `.txt` page is growing past a page or two, it's probably time to convert it to Markdown and give it real section structure.

# Developer Handbook Index

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Title | Developer Handbook Index |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Owner | Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) |
| Last updated | 2026-05-12 |

## Purpose

*Section owner: Mara Olsen*

This page is the front door to the `developer-handbook/` folder for the accountsvc repository. It doesn't try to teach you anything about accountsvc itself — for that, start with the repository root `README.md` and then come back here. What this page does is tell you what pages exist, who owns each one, when it was last touched, and roughly what order to read them in if you're new to the team.

The handbook covers workstation setup, editor configuration, supported Python versions, code review conventions, commit message style, and coding style, plus a few supporting pages on repository layout, dependency management, and troubleshooting. If you're looking for something and it's not indexed below, it probably doesn't exist yet — open an issue against Platform Tools rather than guessing.

As of this writing the handbook has thirteen pages, including this index. A few of the entries below lag a little behind the pages themselves; if the version number here disagrees with the header block on the actual page, trust the page, not the index. We try to keep this synced but it slips.

## How This Index Works

Each page in the folder carries its own header block (title, version, owner, last-updated date) at the top, matching the format used on this page. The index below restates those fields so you can scan the whole handbook without opening every file. Pages are grouped loosely by when you'd need them — getting-started material first, then day-to-day editor and workflow references, then the conventions you'll be held to during review, then troubleshooting.

Formats are mixed on purpose. Most pages are Markdown, one is reStructuredText (`local-development-workflow.rst`), a couple are plain text (`onboarding-checklist.txt`, `style-quick-reference.txt`), and one is YAML (`editor-settings.yaml`) because it's meant to be copied directly into an editor config rather than read as prose. Don't assume `.md` everywhere.

## Getting Started

Read these in roughly this order during your first week.

1. **Workstation Setup** — version 2.3 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2025-01-20 — [workstation-setup.md](./workstation-setup.md)
2. **Supported Python Versions** — version v1.3.0 — owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir) — updated 2026-02-03 — [supported-python-versions.md](./supported-python-versions.md)
3. **Repository Layout** — version 1.1 — owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) — updated 2024-04-10 — [repository-layout.md](./repository-layout.md)
4. **Onboarding Checklist** — version 1.0 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2024-06-14 — [onboarding-checklist.txt](./onboarding-checklist.txt)

The Onboarding Checklist is a plain-text tick list, intentionally terse — it points at the other pages rather than repeating them, so treat it as a table of contents for your first day rather than a stand-alone guide.

## Editor and Local Workflow

* **Editor Configuration** — version 1.2 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2024-11-15 — [editor-configuration.md](./editor-configuration.md)
* **Shared Editor Settings** — version v1.0.1 — owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir) — updated 2026-04-08 — [editor-settings.yaml](./editor-settings.yaml)
* **Local Development Workflow** — version 2.5 — owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks) — updated 2025-03-27 — [local-development-workflow.rst](./local-development-workflow.rst)
* **Dependency Management** — version v1.1.3 — owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir) — updated 2026-01-18 — [dependency-management.md](./dependency-management.md)

Editor Configuration explains the reasoning behind our settings; editor-settings.yaml is the file you actually import. Owen Fitzgerald keeps asking us to merge these two, and honestly he's right, but nobody's gotten around to it.

## Contribution Conventions

These are the pages reviewers will point you at when they leave a comment on your change.

- **Code Review Conventions**, version 3.1, owner Core Services (Priya Chandran), updated 2025-06-30. [code-review-conventions.md](./code-review-conventions.md)
- **Commit Message Style**, version v2.0.1, owner Core Services (Priya Chandran), updated 2024-08-22. [commit-message-style.md](./commit-message-style.md)
- **Coding Style Guide**, version 4.0, owner Developer Experience (Theo Banks), updated 2025-09-04. [coding-style-guide.md](./coding-style-guide.md)
- **Style Quick Reference**, version 1.3, owner Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald), updated 2025-12-29. [style-quick-reference.txt](./style-quick-reference.txt)

Style Quick Reference is a cheat sheet — it exists so you don't have to reopen the full Coding Style Guide every time you forget the line-length limit. It is not a substitute for reading the guide once, in full, before your first review.

## Reference and Troubleshooting

- **Troubleshooting Setup**, version v3.1.0, owner Platform Tools (Mara Olsen), updated 2025-11-05. [troubleshooting-setup.md](./troubleshooting-setup.md)

This is the smallest section in the handbook and it's usually the one people search for first. If your workstation setup is failing partway through, this page has more specific remedies than Workstation Setup does — that page assumes things go smoothly.

## Repository and Host Paths Referenced by This Handbook

The handbook as a whole points at the following paths, either as things to open, edit, or run. This index page doesn't use most of these directly, but since it's the entry point to the folder, it's worth collecting them here once.

| Path | Function |
|---|---|
| `README.md` (repository root) | Top-level description of accountsvc; the first thing anyone should read before this handbook |
| `accountsvc/` | The package directory itself; the handbook describes how to work in this repository, not what's inside this directory |
| `developer-handbook/` | This folder; contains every page listed on this index |
| `developer-handbook/README.md` | This page, the folder index |
| `developer-handbook/workstation-setup.md` | Workstation provisioning steps |
| `developer-handbook/supported-python-versions.md` | Which Python versions the team builds and runs against |
| `developer-handbook/editor-configuration.md` | Narrative guidance for configuring an editor |
| `developer-handbook/editor-settings.yaml` | Machine-readable settings file meant to be imported into an editor |
| `developer-handbook/code-review-conventions.md` | How reviews are run and what reviewers look for |
| `developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md` | Commit message formatting rules |
| `developer-handbook/coding-style-guide.md` | Full coding style reference |
| `developer-handbook/style-quick-reference.txt` | Condensed style cheat sheet |
| `developer-handbook/repository-layout.md` | Tour of the top-level folders and what lives in each |
| `developer-handbook/dependency-management.md` | How the team tracks and updates dependencies |
| `developer-handbook/local-development-workflow.rst` | Day-to-day loop of running and iterating on the package locally |
| `developer-handbook/troubleshooting-setup.md` | Fixes for common workstation setup failures |
| `developer-handbook/onboarding-checklist.txt` | First-week tick list for new developers |
| `docs/` | General project documentation outside the developer handbook; referenced but not owned by this folder |
| `scripts/` | Small helper scripts referenced from a few handbook pages, mostly around workstation setup |

## Tooling Referenced Across the Handbook

This is a rollup, not a definitive inventory — each page may pin a slightly different point version depending on when it was last edited. If a page and this table disagree, the page wins for its own topic.

| Tool / Package | Version referenced | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.9 (minimum), 3.12.6 (recommended) | Supported Python Versions, Workstation Setup |
| pip | 24.0 | Dependency Management, Workstation Setup |
| venv (standard library) | bundled with Python 3.11/3.12 | Workstation Setup, Local Development Workflow |
| git | 2.43.0 | Workstation Setup, Commit Message Style |
| Visual Studio Code | 1.94 | Editor Configuration, Shared Editor Settings |
| black | 24.3.0 | Coding Style Guide, Style Quick Reference |
| flake8 | 7.0.0 | Coding Style Guide, Editor Configuration |
| PowerShell | 7.4 | Workstation Setup, Troubleshooting Setup |
| SQLite command-line shell | 3.45 | Local Development Workflow, Repository Layout |

Note that black and flake8 are development-time tools used to keep the codebase consistent; they are not runtime dependencies of the package, since accountsvc itself only uses the Python standard library.

## Terminology

Terms used loosely and inconsistently across the handbook are defined here once, so individual pages don't have to keep re-explaining them.

- **Handbook page** — Any file directly under `developer-handbook/`, regardless of its format (Markdown, reStructuredText, plain text, or YAML).
- **Header block** — The small table or list at the top of a handbook page giving its title, version, owner, and last-updated date. Every page in this folder is expected to have one.
- **Section owner** — The person named as responsible for a particular section of a page, noted inline as *Section owner: Name*. Not every section has one; sections without a named owner default to the page's overall owner.
- **Folder index** — This page. The single entry point that links out to every other page in `developer-handbook/`.
- **Sibling page** — Any other page in the same `developer-handbook/` folder, referenced from a Related Pages section.
- **Workstation** — The laptop or desktop machine a developer uses for day-to-day work on accountsvc, as distinct from any shared or hosted machine.
- **Loopback service** — The locally-bound HTTP service that accountsvc runs during development, reachable only from the same machine.
- **Standard library** — The set of modules that ship with Python itself; accountsvc is built entirely on top of these, with no third-party runtime dependencies.
- **Local development workflow** — The repeating cycle of editing the package, running it locally against its database file, and iterating, described in `local-development-workflow.rst`.
- **Quick reference** — A condensed, cheat-sheet version of a longer page, meant for glancing at rather than reading start to finone.
- **Glossary** — This section. A list of terms defined once so other pages don't repeat the definitions.

## Contributing to the Handbook

*Section owner: Theo Banks*

If you're adding a new page or making a meaningful change to an existing one, follow this loop:

1. Update the page itself first — content, header block (bump the version, update the date, confirm the owner), and its terminology or file-listing sections if anything changed.
2. Come back to this index and update the corresponding row: title, version, owner, and date should match what you just wrote on the page.
3. If you're adding a brand-new page, pick a heading above that fits it, or propose a new heading in review if none of the existing ones make sense.
4. Add a line to the Change Log below describing what changed and why, and name a release the same way the rest of the log does.
5. Open a normal review following Code Review Conventions — handbook changes go through the same process as code changes, just with a lighter bar for sign-off since there's no code being run.

A few conventions specific to this folder:

* Keep the terminology section on each page in alphabetical order where practical; it's easier to scan.
* Don't remove a page's header block fields even if they seem redundant with the index — pages get read outside the context of the index all the time, especially when someone's linked directly to a section.
* If you rename a page's title without renaming the file, or vice versa, please update this index in the same change. We've fallen behind on this before (see the Coding Style Guide owner listed above, which is stale relative to the page itself) and it causes confusion during onboarding.
* Plain-text pages (`.txt`) should stay short. If a `.txt` page is growing past a page or two, it's probably time to convert it to Markdown and give it real section structure.

1	# Troubleshooting Workstation Setup
2	
3	**Version:** v3.2.0
4	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-11-05
6	
7	## Coverage of this page
8	
9	This page is a running log of workstation problems that have actually tripped up contributors setting up `accountsvc` for the first time (or after a long absence), along with the steps that resolved them. It is meant to be read alongside `workstation-setup.md` and `supported-python-versions.md` rather than as a replacement for either — those pages describe what a correct setup looks like; this one describes what to do when your setup doesn't match that description.
10	
11	A few ground rules for this page:
12	
13	- Entries are added by whoever solved the problem, so the tone and level of detail vary. That's fine.
14	- If you hit something new, add it here rather than only mentioning it in chat. Three different people fixed the same virtual-environment problem in 2025 before anyone wrote it down.
15	- Entries that stop being relevant (old toolchain versions, retired scripts) should be trimmed during the yearly handbook review, not left to rot indefinitely. In practice this doesn't always happen on schedule.
16	
17	`accountsvc` itself is a small standard-library-only package — a command line tool plus a loopback HTTP service for customer accounts, backed by a local SQLite state file. None of that internal behavior is covered here; this page is strictly about getting a workstation into a state where you can build, run, and edit the project at all.
18	
19	## Terminology
20	
21	**Virtual environment** — an isolated Python installation directory (created with the `venv` module) that keeps project dependencies separate from whatever else is installed on the machine. Almost every problem on this page traces back to a missing, stale, or wrongly-activated virtual environment.
22	
23	**Editable install** — installing a package so that changes to the working tree take effect immediately, without reinstalling. Contributors sometimes install `accountsvc` as a regular (non-editable) package by mistake and then can't understand why their edits aren't showing up.
24	
25	**Loopback service** — the part of `accountsvc` that listens on the local loopback interface only. It is not reachable from other machines on the network, which is deliberate and unrelated to anything covered on this page.
26	
27	**State file** — the local SQLite file the service reads from and writes to. Referred to here only as a file on disk that can be locked, moved, or missing; its internal layout is out of coverage for this page.
28	
29	**Entry point** — the console-script hook that lets you invoke the package's command line tool by name from a shell, once the package is installed into the active virtual environment.
30	
31	**Pre-commit hook** — a script that runs automatically before a commit is recorded, configured through `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. Most "my commit was rejected" issues on this page are pre-commit hook issues, not git issues.
32	
33	**Linter / formatter** — static tools that flag or rewrite code style issues before a change is committed. `accountsvc` uses both; version drift between the tool installed locally and the version pinned in the repo is a recurring source of confusion.
34	
35	**Working tree** — your local checkout of the repository, as distinct from the remote. Several entries below start with "the working tree was in a state where..." because that's usually the actual root cause.
36	
37	**Shim** — a small stand-in executable (for example, the one created by the Python launcher on Windows, or by a version manager like `pyenv`) that forwards a command to the real interpreter. Shim confusion is the single most common cause of "wrong Python version" complaints.
38	
39	**Loopback interface** — the local-only network interface (`127.0.0.1` on most systems) that the service binds to. Mentioned here only because "something else is already listening on that interface" is a common startup failure.
40	
41	## Quick diagnostic checklist
42	
43	Before filing an issue with Platform Tools, work through this list. It resolves roughly two-thirds of onboarding problems on its own.
44	
45	| # | Check | How |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| 1 | Is a virtual environment actually active? | Look for the `(venv)` or `(.venv)` prefix in your shell prompt. |
48	| 2 | Is the active interpreter the one you think it is? | Run `python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"` and compare the printed path against your project's `.venv` folder. |
49	| 3 | Is the package installed in editable mode? | Run `pip show accountsvc` and check the `Location` line points at your working tree, not a site-packages copy. |
50	| 4 | Are dev tool versions pinned versions? | Compare `pip freeze` output against `requirements-dev.txt`. |
51	| 5 | Is another copy of the service already running? | Check for a stray process holding the loopback port or the state file open. |
52	| 6 | Is the working tree clean? | `git status` — a half-merged rebase or stray untracked file causes more confusion than people expect. |
53	| 7 | Are pre-commit hooks installed for this checkout? | `pre-commit run --all-files` should not fail with "hook not found." |
54	
55	## Interpreter and version problems — Section owner: Yusuf Demir (Runtime Infra)
56	
57	The most common workstation problem, by a wide margin, is contributors building against the wrong Python interpreter. This happens more on Windows than elsewhere because of how the Python launcher and PATH resolution interact.
58	
59	**Symptom: `python` resolves to a much older or newer interpreter than expected, even inside an activated virtual environment.**
60	
61	This is almost always a shim ordering problem. On Windows, if the Python launcher's shim directory appears earlier on PATH than your virtual environment's `Scripts` folder, commands can silently resolve to the wrong interpreter even with the environment "active" in the prompt.
62	
63	Steps that have resolved this in the past:
64	
65	1. Open a fresh shell (don't reuse one that's had multiple environments activated in it — PATH entries accumulate).
66	2. Confirm the interpreter used to create the virtual environment:
67	   ```
68	   py -0p
69	   ```
70	   This lists every interpreter the launcher knows about and its path. Compare against the minimum version required — see `supported-python-versions.md` (v1.4.0) for the current matrix.
71	3. Recreate the virtual environment explicitly against the correct interpreter rather than trying to repair PATH ordering:
72	   ```
73	   py -3.11 -m venv .venv
74	   ```
75	4. Re-activate and re-check `sys.executable` as in the diagnostic checklist above.
76	
77	Marta Ilic hit a variant of this on 2025-04-02 where a system-wide install from a Windows Store package took priority over the launcher entirely; removing the Store package and reinstalling from python.org fixed it permanently.
78	
79	**Symptom: `pip install -e .` fails with a message about an unsupported Python version.**
80	
81	Check the minor version, not just the major version. As of this writing the project's floor is Python 3.11.4 — a point release matters here because a change in how the standard library's `sqlite3` module reports lock states landed mid-3.11, and older 3.11.0–3.11.2 builds have occasionally caused confusing behavior around the state file during local development.
82	
83	| Interpreter reported | Outcome |
84	|---|---|
85	| 3.9.x | Install refuses outright. |
86	| 3.10.x | Not currently supported for this repository; upgrade before continuing. |
87	| 3.11.0–3.11.2 | Installs, but avoid — known state-file locking oddities. |
88	| 3.11.4+ | Supported baseline. |
89	| 3.12.x | Supported, used by most of the team's own workstations. |
90	| 3.13.x | Works in practice; not yet the team default. |
91	
92	## Virtual environment problems
93	
94	**Symptom: activation script runs with no error, but nothing changes.**
95	
96	On Windows, this is nearly always someone using `cmd.exe` conventions inside PowerShell or vice versa. The two activation scripts are not interchangeable:
97	
98	- PowerShell: `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`
99	- cmd.exe: `.venv\Scripts\activate.bat`
100	- bash / zsh (macOS, Linux, WSL): `source .venv/bin/activate`
101	
102	If running the `.ps1` script produces no visible error but also no prompt change, script execution is likely being silently blocked by the shell's default restriction on unsigned scripts. Rather than changing machine-wide settings, most contributors just run the equivalent `.bat` script from an old-style `cmd.exe` window, or invoke PowerShell with an explicit unblock flag for that single session. Ask Runtime Infra if you're unsure which approach your machine's baseline allows.
103	
104	**Symptom: `pip install -e .` appears to succeed, but edits to the working tree aren't picked up.**
105	
106	Usually one of:
107	
108	- The package got installed non-editable at some point earlier (check `pip show accountsvc`'s `Location` field — if it points into `site-packages` rather than your checkout, that's the problem).
109	- Two virtual environments exist and you're editing files under one checkout while running from an environment tied to a different, older checkout on disk (this happens after cloning the repo twice under different folder names, which is more common than it sounds).
110	
111	Fix: remove the stale `.venv` folder, recreate it, and reinstall.
112	
113	```
114	Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .venv
115	py -3.11 -m venv .venv
116	.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
117	pip install --upgrade pip
118	pip install -e .
119	```
120	
121	**Symptom: `.venv` folder is enormous (several hundred MB) compared to teammates' environments.**
122	
123	Usually caused by installing unrelated packages into the project's virtual environment instead of a separate scratch environment, or by an old build cache directory getting swept in accidentally. There's no supported repair for this beyond recreating the environment from `requirements-dev.txt`.
124	
125	## Editor and tooling problems — Section owner: Theo Banks (Developer Experience)
126	
127	Most editor problems come down to one of: the editor isn't reading the shared settings baseline, the editor's own interpreter selector points somewhere other than `.venv`, or an extension version has drifted out of step with what the repo's config expects.
128	
129	**Symptom: on-save formatting doesn't match what CI (or a teammate's machine) produces.**
130	
131	1. Confirm your editor picked up the shared baseline in `editor-settings.yaml` (v1.4, maintained by Developer Experience) rather than only your personal user settings. Workspace-level `.vscode/settings.json` should extend, not fully override, that baseline.
132	2. Confirm the formatter version installed in `.venv` matches the pinned version in `requirements-dev.txt`. A formatter installed globally, outside the project's environment, is a frequent cause — VS Code will happily use whichever one it finds first on PATH if the interpreter selector isn't pointed at `.venv`.
133	3. Reload the editor window after switching interpreters; some extensions cache the interpreter path until restart.
134	
135	**Symptom: the editor's Python interpreter selector shows no environments, or the wrong one, after creating `.venv`.**
136	
137	This is common right after a fresh clone, before the folder has been opened once with the environment already present. Close and reopen the folder (not just reload window) after `.venv` exists, so the editor's environment discovery re-scans the folder.
138	
139	**Symptom: inline linter warnings in the editor don't match what running the linter from the shell shows.**
140	
141	The editor extension and the shell command are two separate installs of the same tool and can drift independently. Check both versions:
142	
143	```
144	python -m ruff --version
145	```
146	against the extension's reported version (usually visible in the extension's own output panel). If they differ, reinstall the extension's bundled tool or point it explicitly at the `.venv` copy — see `editor-configuration.md` (v1.4) for the exact setting name, under the interpreter override section.
147	
148	## Git and commit hook problems — Section owner: Priya Chandran (Core Services)
149	
150	**Symptom: `pre-commit run --all-files` reports "hook not found" or hangs indefinitely on first run.**
151	
152	The hooks defined in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` build their own isolated environments the first time they run, which requires network access and can take a couple of minutes on a slow connection — it isn't actually hung, just slow. If it genuinely fails:
153	
154	1. Clear the pre-commit cache: `pre-commit clean`
155	2. Reinstall the hook environments: `pre-commit install-hooks`
156	3. Re-run against the whole tree.
157	
158	**Symptom: commit is rejected with formatting complaints even though the editor showed no warnings.**
159	
160	This almost always means the editor's on-save formatter and the pre-commit hook's pinned formatter version disagree — see the editor section above. Run the formatter manually from the shell (not the editor) before committing, so you're checking against the same version the hook will use:
161	
162	```
163	python -m black --check accountsvc
164	```
165	
166	**Symptom: commit message rejected by hook with a message about the subject line format.**
167	
168	The expected style is documented in `commit-message-style.md` (v2.0.1, owner Theo Banks) — imperative mood, subject under about 72 characters, no trailing period. A worked example:
169	
170	```
171	Fix stale lock check on state file open
172	
173	Previously the open helper assumed a fresh file every time, which
174	caused a false "in use" warning after an unclean shutdown. Check the
175	lock flag before raising.
176	```
177	
178	Jordan Petrakis ran into the rejection hook firing on an otherwise fine message on 2025-09-11 because the subject line included a trailing period; removing it was enough.
179	
180	## Coding style and linter/formatter problems — Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald (Language Tooling)
181	
182	Most style-related setup problems are version drift, not actual disagreement about style rules — the rules themselves are in `coding-style-guide.md` (v4.0) and summarized in `style-quick-reference.txt` (v1.3), neither of which this page repeats.
183	
184	**Symptom: linter flags things locally that don't get flagged in CI, or vice versa.**
185	
186	1. Check the pinned linter version in `requirements-dev.txt` against your local install:
187	   ```
188	   pip show ruff | findstr Version
189	   ```
190	2. If they differ, reinstall from the pinned requirements file rather than upgrading independently:
191	   ```
192	   pip install -r requirements-dev.txt --force-reinstall
193	   ```
194	3. Confirm there isn't a second config file shadowing the repo's `pyproject.toml` — a stray personal config in your home directory can override project settings for some tools.
195	
196	**Symptom: line-length or indentation warnings appear only in one editor.**
197	
198	Check `.editorconfig` at the repository root is actually being read — some editors need a dedicated extension for this, and without it they'll silently fall back to whatever their own default indentation setting is, which can conflict with the repo's four-space, no-tab convention.
199	
200	## Database state file problems — Section owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)
201	
202	The state file is a plain file on disk, and most problems here are file-system problems rather than anything specific to the service.
203	
204	**Symptom: starting the service fails with a message that the state file is locked or unavailable.**
205	
206	Almost always caused by a previous run of the service (or a leftover shell) still holding the file open. Rather than removing the file:
207	
208	1. Check for a running instance:
209	   ```
210	   Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -match "python" }
211	   ```
212	2. End the stray process if one is found.
213	3. If no process is found but the file still reports as locked, open it briefly with the `sqlite3` shell and use the `.open` meta-command to confirm it isn't held by something outside your session (an antivirus scanner and a sync app — OneDrive folders are a repeat offender here — are the two most common culprits on Windows workstations).
214	4. If the working folder is inside a synced cloud folder, move the checkout out of it. Syncing tools reopening the file mid-write has caused this more than once.
215	
216	**Symptom: state file grows unexpectedly large during local development.**
217	
218	Not typically something to act on for local development; it's expected that repeated runs against the same file accumulate size over ordinary use. If disk space is actually a concern, remove the local file and let the service recreate a fresh one on next start — this only affects your own local copy, not anything shared.
219	
220	## Loopback service startup problems
221	
222	**Symptom: service fails to start with a message that the network location is already in use.**
223	
224	Something else on the workstation is already bound to the loopback port the service tries to use by default — often a leftover instance from an earlier session, occasionally an unrelated local tool (some editor extensions and local proxy tools default to nearby ports). 225	
226	```

228	```
229	
230	Match the PID in the last column against Task Manager (or `Get-Process -Id`) and end that process if it's a stray copy of the service, or reconfigure whichever local tool is squatting on the port.
231	
232	**Symptom: service appears to start (no error printed) but nothing responds on the loopback interface.**
233	
234	Confirm you're actually looking at the right interface and port combination — a surprising number of these reports turn out to be someone pointing a browser or an HTTP tool at the wrong port after copying an old command from a previous conversation. Double-check against whatever the current default is before assuming the service itself is broken.
235	
236	## Command line entry point problems
237	
238	**Symptom: the command isn't found on PATH after installing.**
239	
240	This means the virtual environment's `Scripts` (Windows) or `bin` (macOS/Linux) folder isn't on PATH for the current shell session, even though the package installed fine. 244	```

247	
248	Check the install is editable (see the virtual environment section above). Non-editable installs are the almost universal cause here.

# Troubleshooting Workstation Setup

**Version:** v3.2.0
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
**Last updated:** 2025-11-05

## Coverage of this page

This page is a running log of workstation problems that have actually tripped up contributors setting up `accountsvc` for the first time (or after a long absence), along with the steps that resolved them. It is meant to be read alongside `workstation-setup.md` and `supported-python-versions.md` rather than as a replacement for either — those pages describe what a correct setup looks like; this one describes what to do when your setup doesn't match that description.

A few ground rules for this page:

- Entries are added by whoever solved the problem, so the tone and level of detail vary. That's fine.
- If you hit something new, add it here rather than only mentioning it in chat. Three different people fixed the same virtual-environment problem in 2025 before anyone wrote it down.
- Entries that stop being relevant (old toolchain versions, retired scripts) should be trimmed during the yearly handbook review, not left to rot indefinitely. In practice this doesn't always happen on schedule.

`accountsvc` itself is a small standard-library-only package — a command line tool plus a loopback HTTP service for customer accounts, backed by a local SQLite state file. None of that internal behavior is covered here; this page is strictly about getting a workstation into a state where you can build, run, and edit the project at all.

## Terminology

**Virtual environment** — an isolated Python installation directory (created with the `venv` module) that keeps project dependencies separate from whatever else is installed on the machine. Almost every problem on this page traces back to a missing, stale, or wrongly-activated virtual environment.

**Editable install** — installing a package so that changes to the working tree take effect immediately, without reinstalling. Contributors sometimes install `accountsvc` as a regular (non-editable) package by mistake and then can't understand why their edits aren't showing up.

**Loopback service** — the part of `accountsvc` that listens on the local loopback interface only. It is not reachable from other machines on the network, which is deliberate and unrelated to anything covered on this page.

**State file** — the local SQLite file the service reads from and writes to. Referred to here only as a file on disk that can be locked, moved, or missing; its internal layout is out of coverage for this page.

**Entry point** — the console-script hook that lets you invoke the package's command line tool by name from a shell, once the package is installed into the active virtual environment.

**Pre-commit hook** — a script that runs automatically before a commit is recorded, configured through `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. Most "my commit was rejected" issues on this page are pre-commit hook issues, not git issues.

**Linter / formatter** — static tools that flag or rewrite code style issues before a change is committed. `accountsvc` uses both; version drift between the tool installed locally and the version pinned in the repo is a recurring source of confusion.

**Working tree** — your local checkout of the repository, as distinct from the remote. Several entries below start with "the working tree was in a state where..." because that's usually the actual root cause.

**Shim** — a small stand-in executable (for example, the one created by the Python launcher on Windows, or by a version manager like `pyenv`) that forwards a command to the real interpreter. Shim confusion is the single most common cause of "wrong Python version" complaints.

**Loopback interface** — the local-only network interface (`127.0.0.1` on most systems) that the service binds to. Mentioned here only because "something else is already listening on that interface" is a common startup failure.

## Quick diagnostic checklist

Before filing an issue with Platform Tools, work through this list. It resolves roughly two-thirds of onboarding problems on its own.

| # | Check | How |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is a virtual environment actually active? | Look for the `(venv)` or `(.venv)` prefix in your shell prompt. |
| 2 | Is the active interpreter the one you think it is? | Run `python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"` and compare the printed path against your project's `.venv` folder. |
| 3 | Is the package installed in editable mode? | Run `pip show accountsvc` and check the `Location` line points at your working tree, not a site-packages copy. |
| 4 | Are dev tool versions pinned versions? | Compare `pip freeze` output against `requirements-dev.txt`. |
| 5 | Is another copy of the service already running? | Check for a stray process holding the loopback port or the state file open. |
| 6 | Is the working tree clean? | `git status` — a half-merged rebase or stray untracked file causes more confusion than people expect. |
| 7 | Are pre-commit hooks installed for this checkout? | `pre-commit run --all-files` should not fail with "hook not found." |

## Interpreter and version problems — Section owner: Yusuf Demir (Runtime Infra)

The most common workstation problem, by a wide margin, is contributors building against the wrong Python interpreter. This happens more on Windows than elsewhere because of how the Python launcher and PATH resolution interact.

**Symptom: `python` resolves to a much older or newer interpreter than expected, even inside an activated virtual environment.**

This is almost always a shim ordering problem. On Windows, if the Python launcher's shim directory appears earlier on PATH than your virtual environment's `Scripts` folder, commands can silently resolve to the wrong interpreter even with the environment "active" in the prompt.

Steps that have resolved this in the past:

1. Open a fresh shell (don't reuse one that's had multiple environments activated in it — PATH entries accumulate).
2. Confirm the interpreter used to create the virtual environment:
   ```
   py -0p
   ```
   This lists every interpreter the launcher knows about and its path. Compare against the minimum version required — see `supported-python-versions.md` (v1.4.0) for the current matrix.
3. Recreate the virtual environment explicitly against the correct interpreter rather than trying to repair PATH ordering:
   ```
   py -3.11 -m venv .venv
   ```
4. Re-activate and re-check `sys.executable` as in the diagnostic checklist above.

Marta Ilic hit a variant of this on 2025-04-02 where a system-wide install from a Windows Store package took priority over the launcher entirely; removing the Store package and reinstalling from python.org fixed it permanently.

**Symptom: `pip install -e .` fails with a message about an unsupported Python version.**

Check the minor version, not just the major version. As of this writing the project's floor is Python 3.11.4 — a point release matters here because a change in how the standard library's `sqlite3` module reports lock states landed mid-3.11, and older 3.11.0–3.11.2 builds have occasionally caused confusing behavior around the state file during local development.

| Interpreter reported | Outcome |
|---|---|
| 3.9.x | Install refuses outright. |
| 3.10.x | Not currently supported for this repository; upgrade before continuing. |
| 3.11.0–3.11.2 | Installs, but avoid — known state-file locking oddities. |
| 3.11.4+ | Supported baseline. |
| 3.12.x | Supported, used by most of the team's own workstations. |
| 3.13.x | Works in practice; not yet the team default. |

## Virtual environment problems

**Symptom: activation script runs with no error, but nothing changes.**

On Windows, this is nearly always someone using `cmd.exe` conventions inside PowerShell or vice versa. The two activation scripts are not interchangeable:

- PowerShell: `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`
- cmd.exe: `.venv\Scripts\activate.bat`
- bash / zsh (macOS, Linux, WSL): `source .venv/bin/activate`

If running the `.ps1` script produces no visible error but also no prompt change, script execution is likely being silently blocked by the shell's default restriction on unsigned scripts. Rather than changing machine-wide settings, most contributors just run the equivalent `.bat` script from an old-style `cmd.exe` window, or invoke PowerShell with an explicit unblock flag for that single session. Ask Runtime Infra if you're unsure which approach your machine's baseline allows.

**Symptom: `pip install -e .` appears to succeed, but edits to the working tree aren't picked up.**

Usually one of:

- The package got installed non-editable at some point earlier (check `pip show accountsvc`'s `Location` field — if it points into `site-packages` rather than your checkout, that's the problem).
- Two virtual environments exist and you're editing files under one checkout while running from an environment tied to a different, older checkout on disk (this happens after cloning the repo twice under different folder names, which is more common than it sounds).

Fix: remove the stale `.venv` folder, recreate it, and reinstall.

```
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .venv
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -e .
```

**Symptom: `.venv` folder is enormous (several hundred MB) compared to teammates' environments.**

Usually caused by installing unrelated packages into the project's virtual environment instead of a separate scratch environment, or by an old build cache directory getting swept in accidentally. There's no supported repair for this beyond recreating the environment from `requirements-dev.txt`.

## Editor and tooling problems — Section owner: Theo Banks (Developer Experience)

Most editor problems come down to one of: the editor isn't reading the shared settings baseline, the editor's own interpreter selector points somewhere other than `.venv`, or an extension version has drifted out of step with what the repo's config expects.

**Symptom: on-save formatting doesn't match what CI (or a teammate's machine) produces.**

1. Confirm your editor picked up the shared baseline in `editor-settings.yaml` (v1.4, maintained by Developer Experience) rather than only your personal user settings. Workspace-level `.vscode/settings.json` should extend, not fully override, that baseline.
2. Confirm the formatter version installed in `.venv` matches the pinned version in `requirements-dev.txt`. A formatter installed globally, outside the project's environment, is a frequent cause — VS Code will happily use whichever one it finds first on PATH if the interpreter selector isn't pointed at `.venv`.
3. Reload the editor window after switching interpreters; some extensions cache the interpreter path until restart.

**Symptom: the editor's Python interpreter selector shows no environments, or the wrong one, after creating `.venv`.**

This is common right after a fresh clone, before the folder has been opened once with the environment already present. Close and reopen the folder (not just reload window) after `.venv` exists, so the editor's environment discovery re-scans the folder.

**Symptom: inline linter warnings in the editor don't match what running the linter from the shell shows.**

The editor extension and the shell command are two separate installs of the same tool and can drift independently. Check both versions:

```
python -m ruff --version
```
against the extension's reported version (usually visible in the extension's own output panel). If they differ, reinstall the extension's bundled tool or point it explicitly at the `.venv` copy — see `editor-configuration.md` (v1.4) for the exact setting name, under the interpreter override section.

## Git and commit hook problems — Section owner: Priya Chandran (Core Services)

**Symptom: `pre-commit run --all-files` reports "hook not found" or hangs indefinitely on first run.**

The hooks defined in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` build their own isolated environments the first time they run, which requires network access and can take a couple of minutes on a slow connection — it isn't actually hung, just slow. If it genuinely fails:

1. Clear the pre-commit cache: `pre-commit clean`
2. Reinstall the hook environments: `pre-commit install-hooks`
3. Re-run against the whole tree.

**Symptom: commit is rejected with formatting complaints even though the editor showed no warnings.**

This almost always means the editor's on-save formatter and the pre-commit hook's pinned formatter version disagree — see the editor section above. Run the formatter manually from the shell (not the editor) before committing, so you're checking against the same version the hook will use:

```
python -m black --check accountsvc
```

**Symptom: commit message rejected by hook with a message about the subject line format.**

The expected style is documented in `commit-message-style.md` (v2.0.1, owner Theo Banks) — imperative mood, subject under about 72 characters, no trailing period. A worked example:

```
Fix stale lock check on state file open

Previously the open helper assumed a fresh file every time, which
caused a false "in use" warning after an unclean shutdown. Check the
lock flag before raising.
```

Jordan Petrakis ran into the rejection hook firing on an otherwise fine message on 2025-09-11 because the subject line included a trailing period; removing it was enough.

## Coding style and linter/formatter problems — Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald (Language Tooling)

Most style-related setup problems are version drift, not actual disagreement about style rules — the rules themselves are in `coding-style-guide.md` (v4.0) and summarized in `style-quick-reference.txt` (v1.3), neither of which this page repeats.

**Symptom: linter flags things locally that don't get flagged in CI, or vice versa.**

1. Check the pinned linter version in `requirements-dev.txt` against your local install:

   ```
2. If they differ, reinstall from the pinned requirements file rather than upgrading independently:

   ```
3. Confirm there isn't a second config file shadowing the repo's `pyproject.toml` — a stray personal config in your home directory can override project settings for some tools.

**Symptom: line-length or indentation warnings appear only in one editor.**

Check `.editorconfig` at the repository root is actually being read — some editors need a dedicated extension for this, and without it they'll silently fall back to whatever their own default indentation setting is, which can conflict with the repo's four-space, no-tab convention.

## Database state file problems — Section owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)

The state file is a plain file on disk, and most problems here are file-system problems rather than anything specific to the service.

**Symptom: starting the service fails with a message that the state file is locked or unavailable.**

Almost always caused by a previous run of the service (or a leftover shell) still holding the file open. Rather than removing the file:

1. Check for a running instance:

   ```

3. If no process is found but the file still reports as locked, open it briefly with the `sqlite3` shell and use the `.open` meta-command to confirm it isn't held by something outside your session (an antivirus scanner and a sync app — OneDrive folders are a repeat offender here — are the two most common culprits on Windows workstations).
4. If the working folder is inside a synced cloud folder, move the checkout out of it. Syncing tools reopening the file mid-write has caused this more than once.

If disk space is actually a concern, remove the local file and let the service recreate a fresh one on next start — this only affects your own local copy, not anything shared.

## Loopback service startup problems

Check what's holding the port:

```

```

Match the PID in the last column against Task Manager (or `Get-Process -Id`) and end that process if it's a stray copy of the service, or reconfigure whichever local tool is squatting on the port.

**Symptom: service appears to start (no error printed) but nothing responds on the loopback interface.**

Confirm you're actually looking at the right interface and port combination — a surprising number of these reports turn out to be someone pointing a browser or an HTTP tool at the wrong port after copying an old command from a previous conversation. Double-check against whatever the current default is before assuming the service itself is broken.

## Command line entry point problems

**Symptom: the command isn't found on PATH after installing.**

This means the virtual environment's `Scripts` (Windows) or `bin` (macOS/Linux) folder isn't on PATH for the current shell session, even though the package installed fine. Re-activating the virtual environment in the current shell (not a different one) resolves this in nearly every case. If it doesn't, confirm the install actually succeeded by checking:

```
pip show accountsvc
```

**Symptom: the command runs, but appears to be an older cached copy of behavior you just changed.**

Check the install is editable (see the virtual environment section above). Non-editable installs are the almost universal cause here.
