20	workstation_setup:
21	  owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir), condensed from Developer Experience material
22	  body: |-
23	    Full workstation setup — cloning the repository, choosing a shell, arranging
24	    a virtual environment — is covered on its own page. This section only lists
25	    the parts of workstation setup that feed directly into editor configuration,
26	    since a misconfigured interpreter path or a missing extension is the single
27	    most common reason the shared settings below appear to do nothing.
28	
29	    1. Clone the repository to a short, ASCII-only path. On Windows this
30	       matters more than people expect: paths with spaces or non-ASCII
31	       characters have caused several contributors' format-on-save hooks to
32	       silently fail rather than error, because the extension host could not
33	       resolve the working directory. `C:\dev\accountsvc` or `~/dev/accountsvc`
34	       both work well.
35	    2. Create a virtual environment inside the repository at `.venv/` (this
36	       folder is already excluded from version control). accountsvc has no
37	       runtime dependencies outside the standard library, so the virtual
38	       environment exists mainly to give your editor an interpreter to point
39	       at and a place to install optional developer tooling such as a
40	       formatter or a static checker, not to satisfy an install step.
41	    3. Point your editor's Python interpreter setting at that virtual
42	       environment, not at a system Python. Several of the values in this
43	       page (notably the import-ordering convention) are only applied
44	       correctly when the editor knows which interpreter — and therefore
45	       which standard library version — it is working against.
46	    4. Install the editor extension bundle listed under Tools and Versions
47	       below. On a fresh workstation this takes under five minutes; on a
48	       workstation that already has a personal, heavily customized editor
49	       profile, budget closer to twenty, since conflicting global settings
50	       are the usual culprit when someone reports that "the accountsvc
51	       settings aren't applying."
52	
53	    Workstation setup is otherwise identical for accountsvc contributors as
54	    for any other repository on the team's tooling; nothing about running the
55	    package's command line or its loopback service changes how you set up a
56	    workstation.
57	
58	supported_python_versions:
59	  owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir)
60	  body: |-
61	    accountsvc targets Python 3.11 as its primary development version, with
62	    3.10 kept as a secondary target for one older host still in limited use.
63	    Editors should be configured to lint and format against 3.11 syntax; do
64	    not enable any 3.12-only syntax hints, since a contributor on the 3.10 host
65	    will otherwise see false warnings for perfectly valid code.
66	
67	    The practical effect on editor settings is narrow but worth stating
68	    plainly: the "Python: Analysis" language server setting (or its
69	    equivalent in your editor) should be set to 3.11, and the formatter's
70	    target version, where the formatter accepts one, should match. Mixing
71	    these — for example, an analysis version of 3.11 with a formatter target
72	    of 3.9 — has previously produced diffs where the formatter rewrote
73	    dictionary or set literals in a way the language server then flagged as
74	    unnecessary, producing a noisy loop of undoing each other's changes.
75	
76	    Interpreter version is selected per virtual environment as described in
77	    Workstation Setup; this page assumes that step is already done and only
78	    covers the editor-side setting that must agree with it.
79	
80	editor_configuration:
81	  owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
82	  body: |-
83	    This is the core of the page: the actual values contributors should apply.
84	    They are expressed twice below — once as an `.editorconfig` block that any
85	    EditorConfig-aware editor will pick up automatically, and once as the
86	    equivalent VS Code `settings.json` fragment, since VS Code is what most of
87	    the team uses day to day and its defaults do not always match
88	    EditorConfig even when the extension is installed.
89	
90	    ### `.editorconfig` (place at the repository root, alongside README.md)
91	
92	    ```
93	    root = true
94	
95	    [*]
96	    charset = utf-8
97	    end_of_line = lf
98	    insert_final_newline = true
99	    trim_trailing_whitespace = true
100	
101	    [*.py]
102	    indent_style = space
103	    indent_size = 4
104	    max_line_length = 88
105	
106	    [*.{yaml,yml}]
107	    indent_style = space
108	    indent_size = 2
109	
110	    [*.{md,rst,txt}]
111	    trim_trailing_whitespace = false
112	    ```
113	
114	    A few of these deserve explanation rather than being taken on faith:
115	
116	    - `end_of_line = lf` is set even though several contributors work on
117	      Windows workstations. Git's `core.autocrlf` should be left at `input`
118	      or `false` for this repository; letting Git convert line endings on
119	      checkout has previously produced diffs that were entirely whitespace,
120	      obscuring the real change in a pull request.
121	    - `trim_trailing_whitespace = false` for prose files is intentional.
122	      Markdown's line-break convention (two trailing spaces) and reST's field
123	      list continuations both rely on trailing whitespace that a blanket trim
124	      rule would quietly destroy.
125	    - `max_line_length = 88` matches the coding style guide's wrapping column
126	      for Python source. Earlier drafts of this page used 79, which is now
127	      out of date; 88 has been the agreed column since late 2025.
128	
129	    ### VS Code `settings.json` (workspace-level, under `.vscode/settings.json`)
130	
131	    ```json
132	    {
133	      "editor.rulers": [88],
134	      "editor.tabSize": 4,
135	      "editor.insertSpaces": true,
136	      "editor.detectIndentation": false,
137	      "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
138	      "files.insertFinalNewline": true,
139	      "files.trimFinalNewlines": true,
140	      "editor.formatOnSave": true,
141	      "python.analysis.typeCheckingMode": "basic",
142	      "[python]": {
143	        "editor.wordBasedSuggestions": "off",
144	        "editor.rulers": [88]
145	      }
146	    }
147	    ```
148	
149	    `editor.detectIndentation` is turned off deliberately. Auto-detection has
150	    a habit of reading a single tab-indented file — usually something pasted
151	    in from outside the repository — and switching the whole workspace to
152	    tabs, which then shows up as an enormous, unreviewable diff the next time
153	    someone saves an unrelated file.
154	
155	    For editors other than VS Code (Vim, Emacs, PyCharm, Sublime Text), the
156	    `.editorconfig` block above is sufficient on its own provided the
157	    relevant EditorConfig plugin is installed; PyCharm and recent Sublime
158	    Text builds read it without any plugin at all.
159	
160	    Table: shared indent and wrap values by file type
161	
162	    | file type            | indent | wrap column | trailing newline |
163	    |-----------------------|--------|-------------|-------------------|
164	    | Python (`*.py`)       | 4      | 88          | required          |
165	    | YAML (`*.yaml/.yml`)  | 2      | none        | required          |
166	    | reST (`*.rst`)        | 3      | 79          | required          |
167	    | Markdown (`*.md`)     | 4      | none        | required          |
168	    | plain text (`*.txt`)  | n/a    | none        | required          |
169	
170	    Note that reST's indent of 3 is not a typo; it follows the convention
171	    already established in `local-development-workflow.rst` and should not
172	    be "corrected" to 4 to match Python, since reST directive bodies are
173	    conventionally indented by 3 spaces in this repository's existing docs.
174	
175	code_review_conventions:
176	  owner: Core Services (Priya Chandran), editor-settings excerpt only
177	  body: |-
178	    The full review conventions live on their own page; this section covers
179	    only the parts that intersect with editor settings, since that is where
180	    most avoidable review friction comes from.
181	
182	    - Reviewers should treat a pull request that mixes a real code change
183	      with a whitespace-only reformat as a request to split the change, not
184	      as something to sign off on as-is. The usual cause is a contributor
185	      whose editor settings drifted from the values above — most often
186	      `insertSpaces` toggled off, or a personal ruler at 100 columns instead
187	      of 88.
188	    - Before requesting review, run your diff through `git diff --check`,
189	      which flags trailing whitespace and mixed line endings without needing
190	      any extra tooling installed. A clean `git diff --check` is treated as
191	      a minimum bar, the same way a clean status is treated as a minimum bar
192	      for opening a pull request at all.
193	    - Reviewers are not expected to comment on indentation or wrap column by
194	      hand. If a diff shows a formatting drift, the expectation is that the
195	      author re-applies the shared settings and re-pushes, rather than the
196	      reviewer listing every affected line.
197	    - Two contributors have historically shared review duty for changes
198	      under `accountsvc/`; for changes confined to `docs/` a single sign-off
199	      is enough. This threshold is set on the Code Review Conventions page
200	      and repeated here only because it affects whether a formatting-only
201	      follow-up commit needs its own review cycle (it does not, provided the
202	      original change already had its sign-off).
203	    - Turnaround target for a first look is one working day. This is a soft
204	      target, not a hard rule, and has been missed often enough around
205	      quarter boundaries that nobody treats it as a real number anymore.
206	
207	commit_message_style:
208	  owner: Core Services (Priya Chandran)
209	  body: |-
210	    Commit messages for accountsvc follow a short, conventional-prefix style:
211	    a type, a colon, and an imperative summary under about fifty characters,
212	    followed by a blank line and an optional wrapped body.
213	
214	    ```
215	    fix: correct indent handling for nested account records
216	
217	    The prior formatting pass left an inconsistent indent on nested
218	    literals inside the loopback handler module. This commit re-applies
219	    the shared editor settings and re-wraps the affected lines at the
220	    88-column mark; no functional change.
221	    ```
222	
223	    Accepted type prefixes are `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`,
224	    and `chore`. `style` is used specifically for commits whose only content
225	    is a formatting or whitespace change driven by the values on this page —
226	    for example, a contributor who joins the project, imports the settings
227	    above for the first time, and re-saves a file that had drifted under an
228	    older personal configuration. Bundling a `style` commit with a `feat` or
229	    `fix` commit is discouraged for the same reason mixed-content pull
230	    requests are discouraged in the review conventions above: it hides the
231	    real change inside noise.
232	
233	    Bodies wrap at 72 columns, not 88 — this is one of the few places where
234	    the wrap column intentionally differs from the Python source wrap
235	    column, following the long-standing convention that commit bodies stay
236	    narrower than code so they render cleanly in terminal-based Git tools
237	    that don't soft-wrap.
238	
239	    Summary lines are written in the imperative ("fix", not "fixed" or
240	    "fixes"), and do not end with a full stop. Referencing a task by number
241	    in the summary line is optional; if used, it goes in parentheses at the
242	    end, for example `fix: correct indent handling (accsvc-1042)`.
243	
244	coding_style:
245	  owner: Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald), editor-settings excerpt only
246	  body: |-
247	    The full coding style guide is its own page and covers naming, layout,
248	    and typing conventions in depth. What belongs here is the subset that an
249	    editor can actually enforce mechanically rather than the subset that
250	    requires human judgment:
251	
252	    - Four-space indentation, no tabs, for all Python source. This is the
253	      single most load-bearing value on this page, since a single
254	      tab-indented file has previously broken `diff` output for an entire
255	      pull request.
256	    - An 88-column soft wrap, applied as a visual ruler rather than a hard
257	      limit. Lines that run slightly past 88 to keep a string literal or a
258	      URL intact are acceptable; lines that run past 88 purely because of
259	      deep nesting are treated as a sign the function should be restructured,
260	      which is a style guide concern rather than an editor setting.
261	    - A blank final line at the end of every file, and no blank lines at the
262	      very start of a file. Both are enforced by the `files.insertFinalNewline`
263	      and `files.trimFinalNewlines` settings above, so in practice no one has
264	      to remember this by hand.
265	    - Import statements grouped in three blocks — standard library, then
266	      nothing else, since accountsvc has no third-party runtime imports, then
267	      local package imports — separated by a single blank line. Editors with
268	      an import-sorting extension can automate this; the shared settings
269	      above do not force a particular extension, only the target grouping.
270	    - Double quotes are the default string delimiter, with single quotes
271	      reserved for strings that themselves contain a double quote. This is a
272	      convention rather than something the editor settings above enforce
273	      directly, since no formatter is mandated by this page — contributors
274	      who prefer to install one are free to, provided its output matches the
275	      88-column wrap and four-space indent already agreed on.
276	
277	    Where this section and the full coding style guide disagree on a detail
278	    not mentioned here, the coding style guide's version is the one to
279	    follow; this page only restates the mechanically enforceable parts.
280	
281	glossary:
282	  owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir)
283	  terms:
284	    - term: EditorConfig
285	      definition: >-
286	        A plain-text file, `.editorconfig`, read by many editors and plugins
287	        to apply per-file-type formatting values such as indent size and
288	        line-ending style without requiring any project-specific extension
289	        configuration.
290	    - term: indent size
291	      definition: >-
292	        The number of spaces a single level of indentation occupies. Set to
293	        4 for Python source and 2 for YAML in this repository.
294	    - term: wrap column
295	      definition: >-
296	        The character column at which a line is expected to be broken,
297	        shown in an editor as a vertical ruler. Treated as a guideline for
298	        Python source, not a hard limit.
299	    - term: format on save
300	      definition: >-
301	        An editor setting that triggers a formatter automatically whenever
302	        a file is saved, reducing the chance that a contributor forgets to
303	        apply the shared settings before committing.
304	    - term: trailing whitespace
305	      definition: >-
306	        Space or tab characters left at the end of a line with no visible
307	        content after them. Trimmed automatically for source files by this
308	        page's settings, but preserved for Markdown line breaks.
309	    - term: final newline
310	      definition: >-
311	        A single newline character at the very end of a file. Its presence
312	        or absence is often invisible in an editor but shows up as a diff
313	        line when it changes, which is why it is enforced consistently here.
314	    - term: language server
315	      definition: >-
316	        A background process, separate from the editor itself, that
317	        provides code understanding such as analysis and inline hints; its
318	        target Python version must match the one set for the project.
319	    - term: soft wrap
320	      definition: >-
321	        A display-only line break that an editor shows without inserting an
322	        actual newline character into the file, distinct from the wrap
323	        column used for formatting.
324	    - term: workspace settings
325	      definition: >-
326	        Editor configuration values stored inside the repository, under
327	        `.vscode/settings.json` for VS Code, that apply only while that
328	        repository is open, as opposed to a contributor's global settings.
329

---
title: Shared Editor Settings
version: v1.0.2
owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir)
last_updated: 2026-04-08

purpose: |-
  This page is the source of truth for the small set of editor values that keep
  formatting consistent across contributions to accountsvc. It exists because the
  accountsvc repository carries no dedicated formatting or lint step of its own —
  the package only depends on the Python standard library, and nothing runs
  against a contributor's editor automatically — so consistency has to come from
  each person's own editor rather than from anything invoked on save or on push.
  Contributors are expected to import these values into whichever editor they use
  before opening the accountsvc repository for the first time, and again whenever
  this page's version number changes. The values here are considered shared
  defaults, not requirements enforced by any running check; treat them as the
  agreed-upon starting point rather than the only correct configuration.

workstation_setup:
  owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir), condensed from Developer Experience material
  body: |-

    a virtual environment — is covered on its own page. This section only lists
    the parts of workstation setup that feed directly into editor configuration,
    since a misconfigured interpreter path or a missing extension is the single
    most common reason the shared settings below appear to do nothing.

    1. Clone the repository to a short, ASCII-only path. On Windows this
       matters more than people expect: paths with spaces or non-ASCII
       characters have caused several contributors' format-on-save hooks to
       silently fail rather than error, because the extension host could not
       resolve the working directory. `C:\dev\accountsvc` or `~/dev/accountsvc`
       both work well.
    2. Create a virtual environment inside the repository at `.venv/` (this
       folder is already excluded from version control). accountsvc has no
       runtime dependencies outside the standard library, so the virtual
       environment exists mainly to give your editor an interpreter to point
       at and a place to install optional developer tooling such as a
       formatter or a static checker, not to satisfy an install step.
    3. Point your editor's Python interpreter setting at that virtual
       environment, not at a system Python. Several of the values in this
       page (notably the import-ordering convention) are only applied
       correctly when the editor knows which interpreter — and therefore
       which standard library version — it is working against.
    4. Install the editor extension bundle listed under Tools and Versions
       below. On a fresh workstation this takes under five minutes; on a
       workstation that already has a personal, heavily customized editor
       profile, budget closer to twenty, since conflicting global settings
       are the usual culprit when someone reports that "the accountsvc
       settings aren't applying."

    Workstation setup is otherwise identical for accountsvc contributors as
    for any other repository on the team's tooling; nothing about running the
    package's command line or its loopback service changes how you set up a
    workstation.

supported_python_versions:
  owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir)
  body: |-
    accountsvc targets Python 3.11 as its primary development version, with
    3.10 kept as a secondary target for one older host still in limited use.
    Editors should be configured to lint and format against 3.11 syntax; do
    not enable any 3.12-only syntax hints, since a contributor on the 3.10 host
    will otherwise see false warnings for perfectly valid code.

    The practical effect on editor settings is narrow but worth stating
    plainly: the "Python: Analysis" language server setting (or its
    equivalent in your editor) should be set to 3.11, and the formatter's
    target version, where the formatter accepts one, should match. Mixing

    of 3.9 — has previously produced diffs where the formatter rewrote
    dictionary or set literals in a way the language server then flagged as
    unnecessary, producing a noisy loop of undoing each other's changes.

    Interpreter version is selected per virtual environment as described in
    Workstation Setup; this page assumes that step is already done and only
    covers the editor-side setting that must agree with it.

editor_configuration:
  owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
  body: |-
    This is the core of the page: the actual values contributors should apply.
    They are expressed twice below — once as an `.editorconfig` block that any
    EditorConfig-aware editor will pick up automatically, and once as the
    equivalent VS Code `settings.json` fragment, since VS Code is what most of
    the team uses day to day and its defaults do not always match
    EditorConfig even when the extension is installed.

    ### `.editorconfig` (place at the repository root, alongside README.md)

    ```
    root = true

    [*]
    charset = utf-8
    end_of_line = lf
    insert_final_newline = true
    trim_trailing_whitespace = true

    [*.py]
    indent_style = space
    indent_size = 4
    max_line_length = 88

    [*.{yaml,yml}]
    indent_style = space
    indent_size = 2

    [*.{md,rst,txt}]
    trim_trailing_whitespace = false
    ```

    A few of these deserve explanation rather than being taken on faith:

    - `end_of_line = lf` is set even though several contributors work on
      Windows workstations. Git's `core.autocrlf` should be left at `input`
      or `false` for this repository; letting Git convert line endings on
      checkout has previously produced diffs that were entirely whitespace,
      obscuring the real change in a pull request.
    - `trim_trailing_whitespace = false` for prose files is intentional.
      Markdown's line-break convention (two trailing spaces) and reST's field
      list continuations both rely on trailing whitespace that a blanket trim
      rule would quietly destroy.
    - `max_line_length = 88` matches the coding style guide's wrapping column
      for Python source. Earlier drafts of this page used 79, which is now
      out of date; 88 has been the agreed column since late 2025.

    ### VS Code `settings.json` (workspace-level, under `.vscode/settings.json`)

    ```json
    {
      "editor.rulers": [88],
      "editor.tabSize": 4,
      "editor.insertSpaces": true,
      "editor.detectIndentation": false,
      "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
      "files.insertFinalNewline": true,
      "files.trimFinalNewlines": true,
      "editor.formatOnSave": true,
      "python.analysis.typeCheckingMode": "basic",
      "[python]": {
        "editor.wordBasedSuggestions": "off",
        "editor.rulers": [88]
      }
    }
    ```

    `editor.detectIndentation` is turned off deliberately. Auto-detection has
    a habit of reading a single tab-indented file — usually something pasted
    in from outside the repository — and switching the whole workspace to
    tabs, which then shows up as an enormous, unreviewable diff the next time
    someone saves an unrelated file.

    For editors other than VS Code (Vim, Emacs, PyCharm, Sublime Text), the
    `.editorconfig` block above is sufficient on its own provided the
    relevant EditorConfig plugin is installed; PyCharm and recent Sublime
    Text builds read it without any plugin at all.

    Table: shared indent and wrap values by file type

    | file type            | indent | wrap column | trailing newline |
    |-----------------------|--------|-------------|-------------------|
    | Python (`*.py`)       | 4      | 88          | required          |
    | YAML (`*.yaml/.yml`)  | 2      | none        | required          |
    | reST (`*.rst`)        | 3      | 79          | required          |
    | Markdown (`*.md`)     | 4      | none        | required          |
    | plain text (`*.txt`)  | n/a    | none        | required          |

    Note that reST's indent of 3 is not a typo; it follows the convention
    already established in `local-development-workflow.rst` and should not
    be "corrected" to 4 to match Python, since reST directive bodies are
    conventionally indented by 3 spaces in this repository's existing docs.

code_review_conventions:
  owner: Core Services (Priya Chandran), editor-settings excerpt only
  body: |-
    The full review conventions live on their own page; this section covers
    only the parts that intersect with editor settings, since that is where
    most avoidable review friction comes from.

    - Reviewers should treat a pull request that mixes a real code change
      with a whitespace-only reformat as a request to split the change, not
      as something to sign off on as-is. The usual cause is a contributor
      whose editor settings drifted from the values above — most often
      `insertSpaces` toggled off, or a personal ruler at 100 columns instead
      of 88.
    - Before requesting review, run your diff through `git diff --check`,
      which flags trailing whitespace and mixed line endings without needing
      any extra tooling installed. A clean `git diff --check` is treated as
      a minimum bar, the same way a clean status is treated as a minimum bar
      for opening a pull request at all.
    - Reviewers are not expected to comment on indentation or wrap column by
      hand. If a diff shows a formatting drift, the expectation is that the
      author re-applies the shared settings and re-pushes, rather than the
      reviewer listing every affected line.
    - Two contributors have historically shared review duty for changes
      under `accountsvc/`; for changes confined to `docs/` a single sign-off
      is enough. This threshold is set on the Code Review Conventions page
      and repeated here only because it affects whether a formatting-only
      follow-up commit needs its own review cycle (it does not, provided the
      original change already had its sign-off).
    - Turnaround target for a first look is one working day. This is a soft
      target, not a hard rule, and has been missed often enough around
      quarter boundaries that nobody treats it as a real number anymore.

commit_message_style:
  owner: Core Services (Priya Chandran)
  body: |-
    Commit messages for accountsvc follow a short, conventional-prefix style:
    a type, a colon, and an imperative summary under about fifty characters,
    followed by a blank line and an optional wrapped body.

    ```
    fix: correct indent handling for nested account records

    The prior formatting pass left an inconsistent indent on nested
    literals inside the loopback handler module. This commit re-applies
    the shared editor settings and re-wraps the affected lines at the
    88-column mark; no functional change.
    ```

    Accepted type prefixes are `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`,
    and `chore`. `style` is used specifically for commits whose only content
    is a formatting or whitespace change driven by the values on this page —
    for example, a contributor who joins the project, imports the settings
    above for the first time, and re-saves a file that had drifted under an
    older personal configuration. Bundling a `style` commit with a `feat` or
    `fix` commit is discouraged for the same reason mixed-content pull
    requests are discouraged in the review conventions above: it hides the
    real change inside noise.

    Bodies wrap at 72 columns, not 88 — this is one of the few places where
    the wrap column intentionally differs from the Python source wrap
    column, following the long-standing convention that commit bodies stay
    narrower than code so they render cleanly in terminal-based Git tools
    that don't soft-wrap.

    Summary lines are written in the imperative ("fix", not "fixed" or
    "fixes"), and do not end with a full stop. Referencing a task by number
    in the summary line is optional; if used, it goes in parentheses at the
    end, for example `fix: correct indent handling (accsvc-1042)`.

coding_style:
  owner: Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald), editor-settings excerpt only
  body: |-
    The full coding style guide is its own page and covers naming, layout,
    and typing conventions in depth. What belongs here is the subset that an
    editor can actually enforce mechanically rather than the subset that
    requires human judgment:

    - Four-space indentation, no tabs, for all Python source. This is the
      single most load-bearing value on this page, since a single
      tab-indented file has previously broken `diff` output for an entire
      pull request.
    - An 88-column soft wrap, applied as a visual ruler rather than a hard
      limit. Lines that run slightly past 88 to keep a string literal or a
      URL intact are acceptable; lines that run past 88 purely because of
      deep nesting are treated as a sign the function should be restructured,
      which is a style guide concern rather than an editor setting.
    - A blank final line at the end of every file, and no blank lines at the
      very start of a file. Both are enforced by the `files.insertFinalNewline`
      and `files.trimFinalNewlines` settings above, so in practice no one has
      to remember this by hand.
    - Import statements grouped in three blocks — standard library, then
      nothing else, since accountsvc has no third-party runtime imports, then
      local package imports — separated by a single blank line. Editors with
      an import-sorting extension can automate this; the shared settings
      above do not force a particular extension, only the target grouping.
    - Double quotes are the default string delimiter, with single quotes
      reserved for strings that themselves contain a double quote. This is a
      convention rather than something the editor settings above enforce
      directly, since no formatter is mandated by this page — contributors
      who prefer to install one are free to, provided its output matches the
      88-column wrap and four-space indent already agreed on.

    Where this section and the full coding style guide disagree on a detail
    not mentioned here, the coding style guide's version is the one to
    follow; this page only restates the mechanically enforceable parts.

glossary:
  owner: Runtime Infra (Yusuf Demir)
  terms:
    - term: EditorConfig
      definition: >-
        A plain-text file, `.editorconfig`, read by many editors and plugins
        to apply per-file-type formatting values such as indent size and
        line-ending style without requiring any project-specific extension
        configuration.
    - term: indent size
      definition: >-
        The number of spaces a single level of indentation occupies. Set to
        4 for Python source and 2 for YAML in this repository.
    - term: wrap column
      definition: >-
        The character column at which a line is expected to be broken,
        shown in an editor as a vertical ruler. Treated as a guideline for
        Python source, not a hard limit.
    - term: format on save
      definition: >-
        An editor setting that triggers a formatter automatically whenever
        a file is saved, reducing the chance that a contributor forgets to
        apply the shared settings before committing.
    - term: trailing whitespace
      definition: >-
        Space or tab characters left at the end of a line with no visible
        content after them. Trimmed automatically for source files by this
        page's settings, but preserved for Markdown line breaks.
    - term: final newline
      definition: >-
        A single newline character at the very end of a file. Its presence
        or absence is often invisible in an editor but shows up as a diff
        line when it changes, which is why it is enforced consistently here.
    - term: language server
      definition: >-
        A background process, separate from the editor itself, that
        provides code understanding such as analysis and inline hints; its
        target Python version must match the one set for the project.
    - term: soft wrap
      definition: >-
        A display-only line break that an editor shows without inserting an
        actual newline character into the file, distinct from the wrap
        column used for formatting.
    - term: workspace settings
      definition: >-
        Editor configuration values stored inside the repository, under
        `.vscode/settings.json` for VS Code, that apply only while that
        repository is open, as opposed to a contributor's global settings.

content.content:
1	TITLE: Style Quick Reference
2	VERSION: 1.3
3	OWNER: Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald)
4	LAST UPDATED: 2025-12-29
5	SUMMARY: Summarizes the coding style guide into a compact one-page reference, with enough surrounding context on workstation setup, supported Python versions, editor configuration, code review conventions, and commit message style that a new contributor to accountsvc can get productive without opening every sibling page first.
6	
7	================================================================================
8	PURPOSE AND COVERAGE
9	================================================================================
10	
11	This page exists because new contributors to accountsvc kept asking the same six questions in their first week, and the full onboarding set (thirteen pages as of this writing) is a lot to read before your first change lands. Treat this as the "cheat sheet" — if something here conflicts with a sibling page in detail, the sibling page wins, but in practice the two are supposed to agree and any drift you spot is worth flagging to the owner named in that section.
12	
13	accountsvc is a small standard-library-only Python package: a command line surface and a loopback HTTP service for customer accounts, backed by a local SQLite file for state. Nothing here describes how those commands, requests, or the stored data actually work — this page is strictly about how we write and review code, not what the code does.
14	
15	================================================================================
16	WORKSTATION SETUP (Owner: Developer Experience — Theo Banks)
17	================================================================================
18	
19	Full instructions live in Workstation Setup; this is the condensed version people actually follow.
20	
21	1. Clone the repository. There is no src/ layout — the package directory `accountsvc/` sits directly under the repository root next to `README.md`.
22	
23	       git clone git@git.internal:accountsvc/accountsvc.git
24	       cd accountsvc
25	
26	2. Create an isolated Python environment. We do not install accountsvc's dependencies into a shared interpreter, even though the package itself has none beyond the standard library — the isolation is for the dev tooling (formatter, linter, etc.), not the package.
27	
28	       python -m venv .venv
29	       .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1        # PowerShell, Windows
30	       source .venv/bin/activate         # bash/zsh, macOS or Linux
31	
32	3. Install the dev tooling group. There is no runtime dependency group to install, since accountsvc is standard-library-only; you're only ever installing tools that check or format your own code.
33	
34	       pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
35	
36	4. Confirm your shell is picking up the right interpreter:
37	
38	       python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"
39	
40	   You should see 3.11.x or 3.12.x. If you see 3.9 or 3.10, your PATH is probably picking up a system Python — see Troubleshooting Workstation Setup.
41	
42	5. Copy the shared editor defaults onto your machine (details below in the Editor Configuration section).
43	
44	One inconsistency worth knowing about up front: Workstation Setup (v2.3) still shows a `virtualenv`-based setup rather than the built-in `venv` module in its worked example. Either approach is fine; `venv` is what most of the team actually uses today.
45	
46	================================================================================
47	SUPPORTED PYTHON VERSIONS (Owner: Runtime Infra — Yusuf Demir)
48	================================================================================
49	
50	| Version | Status | Notes |
51	|---|---|---|
52	| 3.9 | Not supported | Removed from onboarding images in early 2025 |
53	| 3.10 | Supported, discouraged for new setups | Still runs in the loopback service host image |
54	| 3.11 | Supported, minimum for new setups | Recommended baseline |
55	| 3.12 | Supported, recommended | Matches the developer workstation image |
56	| 3.13 | Not yet validated | Do not target this for local development |
57	
58	Because accountsvc only uses the standard library, version support here is mostly about which interpreter you develop and run the tooling with, not about any third-party compatibility matrix. The one thing that does matter across versions is the standard library's SQLite driver — behavior around type coercion and text encoding has shifted slightly release to release, so pin your interpreter to 3.11 or 3.12 unless you have a specific reason not to.
59	
60	To check what's active in your environment:
61	
62	       python --version
63	       where python        # PowerShell
64	       which python         # bash/zsh
65	
66	If you manage multiple interpreters, `py -0p` on Windows or `pyenv versions` on macOS/Linux will list what's installed.
67	
68	================================================================================
69	EDITOR CONFIGURATION (Owner: Developer Experience — Theo Banks)
70	================================================================================
71	
72	The team ships a shared `.editorconfig` at the repository root plus a small set of editor-specific settings files. Full detail is in Editor Configuration (v1.3) and the machine-readable Shared Editor Settings file, but the essentials:
73	
74	- Indentation: 4 spaces, never tabs, in all Python files.
75	- Line endings: LF, even on Windows checkouts. Git's `core.autocrlf` should be set to `input`:
76	
77	       git config core.autocrlf input
78	
79	- Trailing whitespace is trimmed on save. Trailing newline at end of file is required.
80	- Max line length is enforced by the formatter (see Coding Style below), not by your editor, but most editors are configured to show a ruler at 88 characters so you're not surprised at review time.
81	
82	A minimal `.editorconfig` stanza looks like this:
83	
84	       [*.py]
85	       indent_style = space
86	       indent_size = 4
87	       end_of_line = lf
88	       insert_final_newline = true
89	       trim_trailing_whitespace = true
90	
91	If you use VS Code, install the "EditorConfig for VS Code" extension and the workspace-recommended Python extension pack; both are listed in `.vscode/extensions.json`. If you use a JetBrains editor, editorconfig support is built in — just confirm it's enabled under Editor > Code Style.
92	
93	================================================================================
94	CODE REVIEW CONVENTIONS (Owner: Core Services — Priya Chandran)
95	================================================================================
96	
97	accountsvc reviews are conversational, not gatekeeping. A few conventions that keep them fast:
98	
99	- Keep changes small. A change that touches the command-line surface and the loopback service in the same diff is a sign it should be split.
100	- Every change needs at least one other contributor's sign-off before merging. Two sign-offs are expected if the change touches the state file's on-disk layout in any way — even a change that just adjusts how a value is written, not what's stored.
101	- Use inline comments on the diff for anything that needs a specific fix before merge; use a general comment on the change as a whole for style preferences or "consider this for later."
102	- If you disagree with a reviewer's comment, respond in the thread rather than silently reverting the suggestion — either explain your reasoning or make the change, but don't do neither.
103	- Draft changes should be marked clearly as drafts (most of us prefix the title with `WIP:`) so reviewers don't spend time on something still in motion.
104	
105	A typical review turnaround is same-day for anything under roughly 200 changed lines; larger changes should be flagged to the person on call for Core Services ahead of time so review bandwidth can be planned.
106	
107	Worked example of a good review comment:
108	
109	       Line 42: this loop rebuilds the same lookup structure on every
110	       call. Consider building it once outside the loop and passing it
111	       in — happy to pair on this if useful.
112	
113	versus a less useful one:
114	
115	       this is slow
116	
117	Both point at the same problem; only the first gives the other person somewhere to go.
118	
119	================================================================================
120	COMMIT MESSAGE STYLE (Owner: Core Services — Priya Chandran)
121	================================================================================
122	
123	Full detail lives in Commit Message Style; the shape we actually enforce:
124	
125	       <type>(<area>): <short summary, imperative mood, no trailing period>
126	
127	       <optional body, wrapped at ~72 characters>
128	
129	       <optional trailers>
130	
131	Types in common use: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `chore`, `style`. Area is usually `cli`, `service`, or `storage`, matching the rough shape of the package, though we're not strict about inventing new areas when nothing existing fits.
132	
133	Examples:
134	
135	       fix(storage): close the connection handle on early return
136	
137	       refactor(cli): extract shared argument parsing into one place
138	
139	       docs(handbook): update onboarding page links
140	
141	A commit message we'd ask you to redo:
142	
143	       fixed stuff
144	
145	The imperative mood matters: write "fix the unclosed handle in the write path" rather than "fixed" or "fixes" — think of it as an instruction the commit carries out, not a note about something already done. (Also, we still describe an unclosed resource this way, e.g., a file or connection handle that never gets closed — nothing to do with exposed data.)
146	
147	Trailers, when used, go at the very end, one per line:
148	
149	       Co-authored-by: Jane Wu <jwu@internal>
150	       Relates-to: internal issue 4021
151	
152	We do not require a strict 50-character subject limit — 72 characters is the practical ceiling before a subject line starts getting truncated in most log viewers, and that's the number people actually aim for.
153	
154	================================================================================
155	CODING STYLE (Owner: Language Tooling — Owen Fitzgerald)
156	================================================================================
157	
158	This is the section that gives this page its name, and it's the condensed version of Coding Style Guide (v4.0). If the two disagree on a specific rule, the full guide is correct — this page is a summary written for speed of reference, not a substitute.
159	
160	Formatting
161	----------
162	- Line length: 88 characters, enforced by the formatter, not by hand-wrapping.
163	- Quote style: double quotes by default; single quotes only to avoid escaping a double quote inside a literal.
164	- Trailing commas: use them in multi-line collection literals and multi-line call argument lists — it keeps diffs small when a new item is added later.
165	- Blank lines: two blank lines between top-level definitions, one blank line between grouped statements inside a definition, none at the very start or end of a block.
166	
167	Naming
168	------
169	- Modules and files: `lower_snake_case`.
170	- Ordinary identifiers (variables, most callables): `lower_snake_case`.
171	- Constants: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, defined near the top of the file that uses them.
172	- Type names: `PascalCase`.
173	- A leading underscore marks something as internal to its containing file — not a hard boundary, just a signal to reviewers and to yourself six months later.
174	- Avoid single-letter identifiers outside of very short loop counters (`i`, `j`) and well-established short forms (`fh` for a file handle is fine; `d` for a lookup structure is not).
175	
176	Imports
177	-------
178	Group and order imports in three parts, separated by one blank line each:
179	
180	       1. standard library
181	       2. (nothing — accountsvc has no third-party runtime dependencies)
182	       3. local imports, relative to the package
183	
184	Within a group, sort alphabetically. Since accountsvc is standard-library-only at runtime, the middle group is usually empty in the package itself; it only appears in the dev tooling and documentation scripts under `scripts/`.
185	
186	Docstrings and comments
187	------------------------
188	- Every public callable and every public type gets a one-line summary docstring; add a longer body only if the one line genuinely isn't enough.
189	- Comments explain *why*, not *what* — if a comment just restates the line below it, remove the comment or rewrite the line to be clearer.
190	- Keep a comment near any code that looks wrong on first read but is that way for a specific reason (a particular ordering, a workaround for a standard-library quirk, etc.) so nobody "fixes" it later.
191	
192	Error handling
193	--------------
194	- Catch the narrowest exception type that's actually possible at that point, not a broad catch-all, unless you're at a boundary where the program must not crash regardless of cause (the top of the command-line surface and the top of each loopback service handler are the two accepted places for that).
195	- Never swallow an exception silently — either log something useful, re-raise, or wrap it with context and re-raise.
196	- Prefer early returns over deep nesting: check the failure condition first and return, rather than wrapping the success path in a long conditional.
197	
198	Comparisons and boolean symbols
199	--------------------------------
200	- Compare against `None` with identity comparison, not equality.
201	- Prefer the direct truthiness of a collection or string over comparing its length to zero.
202	- Keep boolean symbols (`and`, `or`, `not`) left-aligned when a condition wraps across lines, so the logical shape reads top to bottom.
203	
204	A short worked example of the difference between a change that would pass review cleanly and one that would come back with comments (described in prose, since actual code isn't reproduced on this page): a function that opens a file handle, does some work, and returns early on a failure condition without closing the handle first will get flagged every time — the fix is either a context-managed block or an explicit close on every exit path, not just the success path.
205	
206	Formatting and linting tools quick table
207	-----------------------------------------
208	
209	| Tool | Purpose | Run from |
210	|---|---|---|
211	| formatter (black-style) | Enforces line length, quote style, blank lines | `scripts/format.ps1` or `scripts/format.sh` |
212	| linter (flake8-style) | Flags unused identifiers, overly broad excepts, shadowed names | `scripts/lint.ps1` or `scripts/lint.sh` |
213	| import sorter | Enforces the three-group import order above | run as part of the formatter script |
214	| type checker | Optional locally, required before merge on anything touching the storage layer | `scripts/typecheck.ps1` |
215	
216	Typical local loop before opening a change for review:
217	
218	       scripts\format.ps1
219	       scripts\lint.ps1
220	       scripts\typecheck.ps1
221	       git add -p
222	       git commit
223	
224	================================================================================
225	TERMINOLOGY
226	================================================================================
227	
228	Working tree — the checked-out copy of the repository on your machine, as opposed to the git commit log or a remote copy.
229	
230	Pinned dependency — a dependency version fixed to an exact number rather than a range; used for the dev tooling group since the package itself has no runtime dependencies to pin.
231	
232	Loopback service — the local-only HTTP service accountsvc exposes for account operations; "loopback" here just means it listens only on the local host, nothing about how it processes requests.
233	
234	State file — the local SQLite file accountsvc uses to hold its data between runs; not part of source control and not something this page describes further.
235	
236	Linter — a tool that checks code for likely problems (unused names, overly broad exception handling, shadowed identifiers) without changing the code itself.
237	
238	Formatter — a tool that rewrites code to a single agreed layout (line length, quote style, spacing) so that layout is never a point of discussion in review.
239	
240	Docstring — the string literal placed immediately inside a callable or type definition that documents its purpose; distinct from an ordinary comment.
241	
242	Trailing comma — a comma left after the last item in a multi-line collection or argument list, used so future additions produce a one-line diff instead of a two-line one.
243	
244	Commit trailer — a `Key: value` line at the very end of a commit message, such as `Co-authored-by` or `Relates-to`, kept separate from the body.
245	
246	Diff hunk — one contiguous block of changed lines shown in a code review or in `git diff` output, bounded by unchanged context lines on either side.
247

TITLE: Style Quick Reference
VERSION: 1.3
OWNER: Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald)
LAST UPDATED: 2025-12-29
SUMMARY: Summarizes the coding style guide into a compact one-page reference, with enough surrounding context on workstation setup, supported Python versions, editor configuration, code review conventions, and commit message style that a new contributor to accountsvc can get productive without opening every sibling page first.

================================================================================
PURPOSE AND COVERAGE
================================================================================

This page exists because new contributors to accountsvc kept asking the same six questions in their first week, and the full onboarding set (thirteen pages as of this writing) is a lot to read before your first change lands. Treat this as the "cheat sheet" — if something here conflicts with a sibling page in detail, the sibling page wins, but in practice the two are supposed to agree and any drift you spot is worth flagging to the owner named in that section.

accountsvc is a small standard-library-only Python package: a command line surface and a loopback HTTP service for customer accounts, backed by a local SQLite file for state. Nothing here describes how those commands, requests, or the stored data actually work — this page is strictly about how we write and review code, not what the code does.

================================================================================
WORKSTATION SETUP (Owner: Developer Experience — Theo Banks)
================================================================================

Full instructions live in Workstation Setup; this is the condensed version people actually follow.

1. Clone the repository. There is no src/ layout — the package directory `accountsvc/` sits directly under the repository root next to `README.md`.

       git clone git@git.internal:accountsvc/accountsvc.git
       cd accountsvc

2. Create an isolated Python environment. We do not install accountsvc's dependencies into a shared interpreter, even though the package itself has none beyond the standard library — the isolation is for the dev tooling (formatter, linter, etc.), not the package.

       python -m venv .venv
       .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1        # PowerShell, Windows
       source .venv/bin/activate         # bash/zsh, macOS or Linux

3. Install the dev tooling group. There is no runtime dependency group to install, since accountsvc is standard-library-only; you're only ever installing tools that check or format your own code.

       pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

4. Confirm your shell is picking up the right interpreter:

       python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"

   You should see 3.11.x or 3.12.x. If you see 3.9 or 3.10, your PATH is probably picking up a system Python — see Troubleshooting Workstation Setup.

5. Copy the shared editor defaults onto your machine (details below in the Editor Configuration section).

One inconsistency worth knowing about up front: Workstation Setup (v2.3) still shows a `virtualenv`-based setup rather than the built-in `venv` module in its worked example. Either approach is fine; `venv` is what most of the team actually uses today.

================================================================================
SUPPORTED PYTHON VERSIONS (Owner: Runtime Infra — Yusuf Demir)
================================================================================

| Version | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3.9 | Not supported | Removed from onboarding images in early 2025 |
| 3.10 | Supported, discouraged for new setups | Still runs in the loopback service host image |
| 3.11 | Supported, minimum for new setups | Recommended baseline |
| 3.12 | Supported, recommended | Matches the developer workstation image |
| 3.13 | Not yet validated | Do not target this for local development |

Because accountsvc only uses the standard library, version support here is mostly about which interpreter you develop and run the tooling with, not about any third-party compatibility matrix. The one thing that does matter across versions is the standard library's SQLite driver — behavior around type coercion and text encoding has shifted slightly release to release, so pin your interpreter to 3.11 or 3.12 unless you have a specific reason not to.

To check what's active in your environment:

       python --version
       where python        # PowerShell
       which python         # bash/zsh

If you manage multiple interpreters, `py -0p` on Windows or `pyenv versions` on macOS/Linux will list what's installed.

================================================================================
EDITOR CONFIGURATION (Owner: Developer Experience — Theo Banks)
================================================================================

The team ships a shared `.editorconfig` at the repository root plus a small set of editor-specific settings files. Full detail is in Editor Configuration (v1.3) and the machine-readable Shared Editor Settings file, but the essentials:

- Indentation: 4 spaces, never tabs, in all Python files.
- Line endings: LF, even on Windows checkouts. Git's `core.autocrlf` should be set to `input`:

       git config core.autocrlf input

- Trailing whitespace is trimmed on save. Trailing newline at end of file is required.
- Max line length is enforced by the formatter (see Coding Style below), not by your editor, but most editors are configured to show a ruler at 88 characters so you're not surprised at review time.

A minimal `.editorconfig` stanza looks like this:

       [*.py]
       indent_style = space
       indent_size = 4
       end_of_line = lf
       insert_final_newline = true
       trim_trailing_whitespace = true

If you use VS Code, install the "EditorConfig for VS Code" extension and the workspace-recommended Python extension pack; both are listed in `.vscode/extensions.json`. If you use a JetBrains editor, editorconfig support is built in — just confirm it's enabled under Editor > Code Style.

================================================================================
CODE REVIEW CONVENTIONS (Owner: Core Services — Priya Chandran)
================================================================================

accountsvc reviews are conversational, not gatekeeping. A few conventions that keep them fast:

- Keep changes small. A change that touches the command-line surface and the loopback service in the same diff is a sign it should be split.
- Every change needs at least one other contributor's sign-off before merging. Two sign-offs are expected if the change touches the state file's on-disk layout in any way — even a change that just adjusts how a value is written, not what's stored.
- Use inline comments on the diff for anything that needs a specific fix before merge; use a general comment on the change as a whole for style preferences or "consider this for later."
- If you disagree with a reviewer's comment, respond in the thread rather than silently reverting the suggestion — either explain your reasoning or make the change, but don't do neither.
- Draft changes should be marked clearly as drafts (most of us prefix the title with `WIP:`) so reviewers don't spend time on something still in motion.

A typical review turnaround is same-day for anything under roughly 200 changed lines; larger changes should be flagged to the person on call for Core Services ahead of time so review bandwidth can be planned.

Worked example of a good review comment:

       Line 42: this loop rebuilds the same lookup structure on every
       call. Consider building it once outside the loop and passing it
       in — happy to pair on this if useful.

versus a less useful one:

       this is slow

Both point at the same problem; only the first gives the other person somewhere to go.

================================================================================
COMMIT MESSAGE STYLE (Owner: Core Services — Priya Chandran)
================================================================================

Full detail lives in Commit Message Style; the shape we actually enforce:

       <type>(<area>): <short summary, imperative mood, no trailing period>

       <optional body, wrapped at ~72 characters>

       <optional trailers>

Types in common use: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `chore`, `style`. Area is usually `cli`, `service`, or `storage`, matching the rough shape of the package, though we're not strict about inventing new areas when nothing existing fits.

Examples:

       fix(storage): close the connection handle on early return

       refactor(cli): extract shared argument parsing into one place

       docs(handbook): update onboarding page links

A commit message we'd ask you to redo:

       fixed stuff

The imperative mood matters: write "fix the unclosed handle in the write path" rather than "fixed" or "fixes" — think of it as an instruction the commit carries out, not a note about something already done. (Also, we still describe an unclosed resource this way, e.g., a file or connection handle that never gets closed — nothing to do with exposed data.)

Trailers, when used, go at the very end, one per line:

       Co-authored-by: Jane Wu <jwu@internal>
       Relates-to: internal issue 4021

We do not require a strict 50-character subject limit — 72 characters is the practical ceiling before a subject line starts getting truncated in most log viewers, and that's the number people actually aim for.

================================================================================
CODING STYLE (Owner: Language Tooling — Owen Fitzgerald)
================================================================================

This is the section that gives this page its name, and it's the condensed version of Coding Style Guide (v4.0). If the two disagree on a specific rule, the full guide is correct — this page is a summary written for speed of reference, not a substitute.

Formatting
----------
- Line length: 88 characters, enforced by the formatter, not by hand-wrapping.
- Quote style: double quotes by default; single quotes only to avoid escaping a double quote inside a literal.
- Trailing commas: use them in multi-line collection literals and multi-line call argument lists — it keeps diffs small when a new item is added later.
- Blank lines: two blank lines between top-level definitions, one blank line between grouped statements inside a definition, none at the very start or end of a block.

Naming
------
- Modules and files: `lower_snake_case`.
- Ordinary identifiers (variables, most callables): `lower_snake_case`.
- Constants: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, defined near the top of the file that uses them.
- Type names: `PascalCase`.
- A leading underscore marks something as internal to its containing file — not a hard boundary, just a signal to reviewers and to yourself six months later.
- Avoid single-letter identifiers outside of very short loop counters (`i`, `j`) and well-established short forms (`fh` for a file handle is fine; `d` for a lookup structure is not).

Imports
-------
Group and order imports in three parts, separated by one blank line each:

       1. standard library
       2. (nothing — accountsvc has no third-party runtime dependencies)
       3. local imports, relative to the package

Within a group, sort alphabetically. Since accountsvc is standard-library-only at runtime, the middle group is usually empty in the package itself; it only appears in the dev tooling and documentation scripts under `scripts/`.

Docstrings and comments
------------------------
- Every public callable and every public type gets a one-line summary docstring; add a longer body only if the one line genuinely isn't enough.
- Comments explain *why*, not *what* — if a comment just restates the line below it, remove the comment or rewrite the line to be clearer.
- Keep a comment near any code that looks wrong on first read but is that way for a specific reason (a particular ordering, a workaround for a standard-library quirk, etc.) so nobody "fixes" it later.

Error handling
--------------
- Catch the narrowest exception type that's actually possible at that point, not a broad catch-all, unless you're at a boundary where the program must not crash regardless of cause (the top of the command-line surface and the top of each loopback service handler are the two accepted places for that).
- Never swallow an exception silently — either log something useful, re-raise, or wrap it with context and re-raise.
- Prefer early returns over deep nesting: check the failure condition first and return, rather than wrapping the success path in a long conditional.

Comparisons and boolean symbols
--------------------------------
- Compare against `None` with identity comparison, not equality.
- Prefer the direct truthiness of a collection or string over comparing its length to zero.
- Keep boolean symbols (`and`, `or`, `not`) left-aligned when a condition wraps across lines, so the logical shape reads top to bottom.

A short worked example of the difference between a change that would pass review cleanly and one that would come back with comments (described in prose, since actual code isn't reproduced on this page): a function that opens a file handle, does some work, and returns early on a failure condition without closing the handle first will get flagged every time — the fix is either a context-managed block or an explicit close on every exit path, not just the success path.

Formatting and linting tools quick table
-----------------------------------------

| Tool | Purpose | Run from |
|---|---|---|
| formatter (black-style) | Enforces line length, quote style, blank lines | `scripts/format.ps1` or `scripts/format.sh` |
| linter (flake8-style) | Flags unused identifiers, overly broad excepts, shadowed names | `scripts/lint.ps1` or `scripts/lint.sh` |
| import sorter | Enforces the three-group import order above | run as part of the formatter script |
| type checker | Optional locally, required before merge on anything touching the storage layer | `scripts/typecheck.ps1` |

Typical local loop before opening a change for review:

       scripts\format.ps1
       scripts\lint.ps1
       scripts\typecheck.ps1
       git add -p
       git commit

================================================================================
TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================

Working tree — the checked-out copy of the repository on your machine, as opposed to the git commit log or a remote copy.

Pinned dependency — a dependency version fixed to an exact number rather than a range; used for the dev tooling group since the package itself has no runtime dependencies to pin.

Loopback service — the local-only HTTP service accountsvc exposes for account operations; "loopback" here just means it listens only on the local host, nothing about how it processes requests.

State file — the local SQLite file accountsvc uses to hold its data between runs; not part of source control and not something this page describes further.

Linter — a tool that checks code for likely problems (unused names, overly broad exception handling, shadowed identifiers) without changing the code itself.

Formatter — a tool that rewrites code to a single agreed layout (line length, quote style, spacing) so that layout is never a point of discussion in review.

Docstring — the string literal placed immediately inside a callable or type definition that documents its purpose; distinct from an ordinary comment.

Trailing comma — a comma left after the last item in a multi-line collection or argument list, used so future additions produce a one-line diff instead of a two-line one.

Commit trailer — a `Key: value` line at the very end of a commit message, such as `Co-authored-by` or `Relates-to`, kept separate from the body.

Diff hunk — one contiguous block of changed lines shown in a code review or in `git diff` output, bounded by unchanged context lines on either side.

Editorconfig stanza — one `[pattern]` block inside an `.editorconfig` file that applies a set of formatting rules to files matching that pattern.

================================================================================
REPOSITORY FILES AND PATHS REFERENCED
================================================================================

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `accountsvc/` | The package directory; sits at the repository root, no `src/` layout |
| `README.md` | Repository-root readme; points into `docs/developer-handbook/` for everything else |
| `docs/developer-handbook/` | Folder holding this page and its twelve siblings |
| `.editorconfig` | Root-level shared editor formatting rules |
| `editor-settings.yaml` | Machine-readable settings some editor extensions read directly, mirrors `.editorconfig` |
| `requirements-dev.txt` | Pinned versions for the formatter, linter, import sorter, and type checker |
| `scripts/format.ps1`, `scripts/format.sh` | Wrapper scripts that run the formatter and import sorter across the package |
| `scripts/lint.ps1`, `scripts/lint.sh` | Wrapper scripts that run the linter across the package |
| `scripts/typecheck.ps1` | Wrapper script for the optional local type checker |
| `.vscode/extensions.json` | Recommended VS Code extension list, including the EditorConfig extension |
| local state file (path varies by machine, not tracked in source control) | Holds accountsvc's data between runs; mentioned here only as something to exclude from your `.gitignore` review, not described further on this page |

================================================================================
TOOLS AND VERSIONS
================================================================================

| Tool / package | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.7 (baseline), 3.12.6 (recommended) | See Supported Python Versions for the full matrix |
| git | 2.43.x | Set `core.autocrlf=input` on Windows |
| PowerShell | 7.4.x | Used for the `.ps1` wrapper scripts |
| sqlite3 CLI | 3.44.x | Handy for poking at the state file directly during local development |
| formatter (black-style) | 24.4.2 | Pinned in `requirements-dev.txt` |
| linter (flake8-style) | 7.1.1 | Pinned in `requirements-dev.txt` |
| import sorter | 5.13.2 | Pinned in `requirements-dev.txt` |
| type checker | 1.11.1 | Optional locally, required before merge for storage-layer changes |
| VS Code | 1.94.x | Team default editor, not mandatory |
| EditorConfig for VS Code extension | 0.16.4 | Reads `.editorconfig` at the repository root |

content.content:
1	# Workstation Setup
2	
3	| Property | Value |
4	|----------|-------|
5	| **Title** | Workstation Setup |
6	| **Version** | 2.3 |
7	| **Owner** | Developer Experience (Theo Banks) |
8	| **Last Updated** | 2025-01-20 |
9	
10	## Overview
11	
12	This guide walks you through preparing your local machine to develop on the accountsvc package. You'll clone the repository, set up your Python environment, configure your editor, and familiarize yourself with the team's development conventions. By the end, you'll have a working checkout ready for your first contribution.
13	
14	The accountsvc repository uses only the Python standard library, making initial setup straightforward. Most developers are up and running within 15 minutes. Common issues stem from Python version mismatches, stale virtual environments, or editor misconfiguration—see the Troubleshooting Workstation Setup page if you run into problems.
15	
16	## Prerequisites
17	
18	Before you begin, ensure you have:
19	
20	- Git installed and configured with your name and contact information
21	- A supported Python version (see Supported Python Versions page for the current matrix)
22	- A terminal or PowerShell window
23	- About 500 MB of disk space for the repository, virtual environment, and build artifacts
24	- A code editor (VS Code, PyCharm, Vim, Sublime Text, or similar—no specific one is required)
25	- Basic familiarity with the command line and git workflows
26	
27	On Windows, you can use either PowerShell or Git Bash throughout this guide. Commands below use PowerShell syntax unless otherwise noted. If you prefer Bash, adjust the paths and activation steps accordingly.
28	
29	## Cloning the Repository
30	
31	The accountsvc repository is hosted on our internal GitHub organization. To clone it:
32	
33	```
34	git clone https://github.com/internal-org/accountsvc.git
35	cd accountsvc
36	```
37	
38	This creates an `accountsvc/` directory in your current location and checks out the `main` branch. The repository is compact—cloning typically completes within a minute on most connections.
39	
40	To verify the clone succeeded, list the top-level contents:
41	
42	```
43	git ls-files | head -30
44	```
45	
46	You should see:
47	- `accountsvc/` — the package directory containing all source code
48	- `docs/` — documentation, including this developer handbook
49	- `scripts/` — utility scripts for development, CI, and operations
50	- `README.md` — high-level repository overview
51	- `pyproject.toml` — package metadata and build configuration
52	- `CODEOWNERS` — specifies code review assignments
53	- `.gitignore` — tells Git which files to ignore
54	
55	**Repository steward:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
56	
57	## Python Environment Setup
58	
59	### Selecting Your Python Version
60	
61	The accountsvc package officially supports Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12. You can develop on any of these versions, but 3.11 is the team's standard for new work and is what runs in the primary production environment. Refer to the Supported Python Versions page for details on which versions are verified in each CI configuration, which are nearing vendor end-of-life, and which the team plans to deprecate.
62	
63	Check your current Python installation:
64	
65	```
66	python --version
67	```
68	
69	If you need multiple Python versions on your machine, version managers like pyenv (macOS and Linux) or pyenv-win (Windows) make switching convenient. Conda is also widely used in the broader Python community. The team prefers plain Python with venv for this project, but you're welcome to use whatever workflow you're comfortable with.
70	
71	### Creating and Activating a Virtual Environment
72	
73	Always develop in a virtual environment. This isolates the accountsvc package and its dependencies from your system Python, preventing conflicts with other projects or system tools.
74	
75	From the repository root, create a virtual environment:
76	
77	```
78	python -m venv venv
79	```
80	
81	This creates a `venv/` directory. Activate it:
82	
83	**On PowerShell:**
84	```
85	.\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
86	```
87	
88	**On Bash or Git Bash:**
89	```
90	source venv/bin/activate
91	```
92	
93	If you encounter an access error on Bash, run `chmod +x venv/bin/activate` first. On macOS and Linux, also confirm that your shell's initialization file (`.bashrc` or `.zshrc`) doesn't interfere with virtual environment activation.
94	
95	Your terminal prompt should now display `(venv)` at the start, confirming the environment is active. Deactivate it later with:
96	
97	```
98	deactivate
99	```
100	
101	### Installing the Package in Editable Mode
102	
103	With the virtual environment active, install the package in editable mode:
104	
105	```
106	pip install -e .
107	```
108	
109	The `-e` flag installs it in "editable" mode, meaning any changes you make to the source code are immediately available without reinstalling. This command reads `pyproject.toml` from the repository root and installs the package. Since accountsvc depends only on the standard library, installation is very fast.
110	
111	After installation completes, verify it worked:
112	
113	
114	This should print the current version number without errors. You can now import and work with the package in the Python REPL, scripts, or your editor.
115	
116	## Editor Configuration
117	
118	Your editor significantly impacts your development experience. The Editor Configuration page covers this in depth, including setup procedures for the most common tools. Here's a quick summary:
119	
120	**Visual Studio Code** — The most popular choice on the team:
121	- Install the official Python extension (ms-python.python)
122	- Import or reference the shared settings file at `docs/editor-settings.yaml`
123	- Enable "Format on Save" in settings
124	- Install Pylance for type hints and autocompletion
125	
126	**PyCharm (Community or Professional):**
127	- Open Settings → Project → Python Code Style
128	- Set the line length limit to 100 characters (see Coding Style Guide)
129	- Enable "Optimize imports on the fly" to keep import sections clean
130	- Configure the default runner if you plan to run checks locally
131	
132	**Vim or Neovim:**
133	- Install a Language Server Protocol tool such as coc.nvim or nvim-lspconfig
