1	# Code Review Conventions
2	
3	**Version:** 3.1
4	**Owner:** Core Services (Priya Chandran)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-06-30
6	
7	**Summary:** This page describes how contributors open, discuss, and merge changes to the package and the service. It covers what a change should look like before it is opened for review, how reviewers are picked, what reviewers check, how comments are written and settled, and how a change is merged once it is ready. It also touches on the parts of commit message style and coding style that reviewers apply directly during a review, since those two areas show up in almost every comment thread on this repository.
8	
9	## Overview
10	
11	accountsvc is small enough that most changes touch either the package directory or a handful of files in docs/ or scripts/, and the review process reflects that. There is no formal review board and no scheduled review window — a contributor opens a pull request, a reviewer is picked from the small pool of people who know the package and the service well, and the two of them work through the change in comments until it is ready to merge. The goal of this page is to make that back-and-forth predictable: what size a change should be, who looks at it, what they're looking for, how comments are phrased, and what "ready to merge" actually means on this repository.
12	
13	Because the package keeps its state in a local database file and exposes both a command line and a loopback HTTP service, changes tend to fall into a few recognizable shapes: changes to the command line surface, changes to the service's local behavior, changes to how the database file is read or written, and changes to documentation or scripts that don't touch the package at all. Reviewers are chosen, in part, based on which of these shapes a change fits, and the checklist a reviewer works through shifts slightly depending on the shape too. That's covered in more detail under **Choosing Reviewers** and **What Reviewers Check** below.
14	
15	A note on tone: this repository has always leaned toward short, direct review comments rather than long discussions in the pull request description. If a comment thread runs past four or five exchanges without resolving, the convention is to pick up a short call instead of continuing in text — see **Responding to Feedback**.
16	
17	## Terminology
18	
19	- **Change** — the full set of commits proposed for merge in a single pull request. Sometimes called a "change set" in older comment threads on this repository, though the shorter term is preferred now.
20	- **Pull request (PR)** — the mechanism used to open a change, attach a description, and start a review thread. On this repository, pull requests are opened against the internal git host at `git.corp.internal/accountsvc`.
21	- **Author** — the person who wrote the change and opened the pull request.
22	- **Reviewer** — the person asked to look at the change before it merges. On accountsvc there is normally one reviewer per change; two are asked for changes that touch the database file directly.
23	- **Blocking comment** — a comment that must be resolved before the change can merge. Blocking comments are written as plain sentences with no prefix.
24	- **Nit** — a small, non-blocking comment, usually about naming, spacing, or wording, prefixed with `nit:` so the author knows it can be left as-is if they disagree.
25	- **Sign-off** — a reviewer's mark, given as a short comment such as "looks good" or a thumbs-up reaction on the pull request, that the change is ready to merge from their side. accountsvc does not use a separate formal sign-off step beyond this.
26	- **Squash merge** — combining every commit in a pull request into a single commit at merge time. This is the default merge method on accountsvc; see **Merge Conventions**.
27	- **Fast-forward merge** — a merge that moves the target branch pointer forward without creating a merge commit. Used only for small documentation-only changes on this repository.
28	- **Stale change** — a pull request whose branch has drifted far enough from the main branch that it needs a rebase or merge-in before a reviewer can safely look at it again.
29	- **Working copy** — a contributor's local checkout of the repository, as set up in Workstation Setup.
30	- **Formatting pass** — running the formatter across a change before opening it, described under **Style and Formatting Checks During Review**.
31	
32	## Before You Open a Change (Owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services)
33	
34	A change is ready to open once it clears a short list of checks. These aren't enforced by any tool on this repository — they're checked by hand, by the author, before asking anyone to look:
35	
36	1. The formatter has been run across every file touched by the change (see **Style and Formatting Checks During Review** for the exact command).
37	2. The style check script runs clean, or any remaining warnings are ones the reviewer has already agreed to leave in place.
38	3. Commits are organized into logical steps rather than left as a raw log of every edit made while working — see **Commit Messages During Review**.
39	4. If the change touches the command line surface or the service's local behavior, the README at the repository root has been updated to match.
40	5. If the change touches the database file, the author has run a manual check against a local copy of the file rather than the one used for day-to-day work.
41	
42	Contributors sometimes ask whether a change needs to be "complete" before it's opened. The answer on accountsvc has always been no — a change that's still being worked through design questions can be opened as a draft pull request, which signals to reviewers that comments are welcome but a sign-off isn't being requested yet. Mark a draft clearly in the pull request title, for example `[draft] rework local check output for the service`.
43	
44	## Opening a Pull Request
45	
46	Branches are named `initials/short-description`, for example `bg/loopback-timeout-cleanup`. Once a branch is pushed, the pull request description should follow this shape:
47	
48	```
49	## What this changes
50	One or two sentences on what the change does and why.
51	
52	## How it was checked
53	What you ran locally to confirm the change works — the formatter,
54	the style check, and a manual check of the command line or the
55	service if either was touched.
56	
57	## Notes for the reviewer
58	Anything you want a second pair of eyes on specifically, or any
59	part of the change you're not fully happy with yet.
60	```
61	
62	Not every field needs a long answer — a one-line "how it was checked" is fine for a documentation-only change. What matters is that the field exists; pull requests opened without a "how it was checked" section are routinely sent back with a comment asking for one before review starts.
63	
64	Once the pull request is open, post a short line in the `#accountsvc-dev` channel in the internal chat tool if the change is larger than roughly 150 lines, or if it touches the database file. Small changes don't need a chat message — the reviewer picked in the pull request itself is enough.
65	
66	## Choosing Reviewers
67	
68	accountsvc has four people who regularly review changes: Priya Chandran, Owen Fitzgerald, Yusuf Demir, and Theo Banks. There's no strict reviewer order — the convention is to pick whoever last touched the part of the package the change is closest to, which usually means checking the commit log for the files being changed and asking whoever shows up most.
69	
70	A rough guide, since "closest to" isn't always obvious:
71	
72	| Change touches… | Ask first |
73	|---|---|
74	| the command line surface | Priya Chandran |
75	| the service's local behavior | Priya Chandran or Theo Banks |
76	| the database file directly | Yusuf Demir, plus a second reviewer |
77	| style, formatting, or the coding style guide itself | Owen Fitzgerald |
78	| workstation or editor setup | Theo Banks |
79	| documentation only | whoever owns the page being changed |
80	
81	If the obvious reviewer is out, ask in `#accountsvc-dev` rather than picking at random — small as the pool is, the wrong reviewer for a database-file change has sent more than one bug back through a second round.
82	
83	## Review Size Guidelines
84	
85	Large changes take longer to review and are more likely to hide a problem in the middle of an otherwise fine diff. The rough guideline on this repository:
86	
87	- Under 150 lines changed: normal review, usually turned around same day.
88	- 150–400 lines: fine, but the author should call out in the description which parts are mechanical (renames, formatting) versus which parts carry the actual change.
89	- Over 400 lines: the reviewer can ask the author to split the change before starting review. This isn't a hard rule, but it's been invoked often enough that it's worth planning around.
90	
91	Changes that are mostly generated by the formatter (for example, a repository-wide line-length fix) are the one exception — line count doesn't matter much there since the diff is mechanical, but the author should say so plainly in the description so the reviewer doesn't read every line by hand.
92	
93	## What Reviewers Check
94	
95	A reviewer on accountsvc is checking four things, roughly in this order:
96	
97	* **Correctness of intent** — does the change do what the description says it does? This is checked by reading the diff against the description, not by re-deriving the whole design from scratch.
98	* **Fit with the rest of the package** — does the change follow the shape of the surrounding code? Naming, structure, and the general layout described in Repository Layout all come up here.
99	* **Manual behavior check** — for anything touching the command line or the service, the reviewer runs the change locally against a fresh copy of the database file and confirms it behaves the way the description says. This is a manual check, not an automated one, and it's expected to take a few minutes rather than being skipped.
100	* **Style and formatting** — covered in detail below, but this is usually the fastest part of the review since the formatter and style check catch most of it before the reviewer ever opens the diff.
101	
102	Reviewers are asked to leave at least one substantive comment on every non-trivial change, even a positive one, so the author knows the diff was actually read rather than skimmed. "Looks good" with nothing else attached is discouraged for anything over roughly 50 lines.
103	
104	## Comment Conventions (Owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services)
105	
106	Comments on accountsvc pull requests follow a small set of conventions that have built up over the last couple of years:
107	
108	1. Blocking comments are phrased as plain statements or questions: "This will read the database file before it's opened for writing — is that intentional?"
109	2. Nits are prefixed: "nit: this name reads oddly next to the other names nearby, consider something closer to the existing pattern."
110	3. Comments that are purely stylistic and already covered by the formatter or the style check are not worth leaving — if the tool didn't catch it, it's probably a judgment call worth raising as a nit rather than a blocking comment.
111	4. When a reviewer disagrees with an approach but the author has a reasonable case for it, the convention is to say so plainly rather than let a blocking comment sit unresolved: "I'd have done this differently, but I don't think it's worth blocking on — go ahead."
112	5. Comments referencing a specific line should quote the smallest relevant piece of the diff rather than the whole function or block, so the thread stays easy to follow later.
113	
114	A short worked example, as it would appear in the pull request thread:
115	
116	```
117	> reviewer: nit: "tmp_val" is a little terse next to the naming used
118	> elsewhere in this file — maybe something more descriptive?
119	
120	> author: fair, renamed in the latest push.
121	
122	> reviewer: This closes the database file before the last write
123	> finishes in the case where the command exits early. Blocking —
124	> can you confirm the order there?
125	
126	> author: good catch, moved the close to the end. Ready for another look.
127	
128	> reviewer: looks good, thanks.
129	```
130	
131	## Responding to Feedback
132	
133	Authors are expected to resolve each comment thread individually rather than pushing a large follow-up commit and leaving every thread open. The convention is:
134	
135	- Push a small commit (or amend, if the branch hasn't been shared elsewhere) that responds to one or two related comments.
136	- Reply on the thread with what changed, even briefly — "moved this to the end of the function" is enough.
137	- Leave the thread open for the reviewer to close, rather than closing it yourself. This has been the convention since early 2024 and occasionally trips up new contributors who are used to closing their own threads elsewhere.
138	
139	If a thread runs past four or five exchanges without settling, stop and set up a short call instead of continuing in text — this has saved more than one review from turning into a multi-day back-and-forth over something that would have taken two minutes to sort out out loud. Note the outcome of the call as a short comment on the thread afterward so there's a record for anyone reading the pull request later.
140	
141	Changes that sit open for more than a few days without activity are considered stale rather than abandoned — ping the reviewer directly in `#accountsvc-dev` rather than opening a second pull request.
142	
143	## Sign-off and Merge Conventions (Owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services)
144	
145	A change is ready to merge once:
146	
147	- Every blocking comment is resolved (nits can be left open at the author's discretion).
148	- The reviewer has left a sign-off, either a short comment or a thumbs-up reaction on the pull request.
149	- The branch is not stale — if the main branch has moved on significantly, rebase or merge it in before merging, and give the reviewer a quick second look if the rebase touched anything non-mechanical.
150	
151	The default merge method on accountsvc is a squash merge, so the many small commits made while working through review comments collapse into one commit on the main branch. The one exception is documentation-only changes with a single clean commit already, which use a fast-forward merge to keep the commit log easy to read for pages that don't touch the package at all.
152	
153	Only the author merges their own change once sign-off is given — reviewers don't merge on someone else's behalf, even for small changes, since it keeps the merge log a reliable record of who actually decided a change was ready to go out.
154	
155	## Style and Formatting Checks During Review
156	
157	Reviewers on accountsvc expect the formatter and the style check to have already been run before a change is opened. Both are wired up as small shell scripts at the repository root:
158	
159	```
160	scripts/format.sh
161	scripts/style-check.sh
162	```
163	
164	`scripts/format.sh` runs the formatter across every file changed against the main branch. `scripts/style-check.sh` runs the linter and prints any remaining issues, including anything the formatter can't fix on its own (unused names, overly long lines in comments, that sort of thing). Contributors who use the shared editor settings described in Shared Editor Settings usually see very few style check issues by the time they open a change, since the editor catches most of it as they type.
165	
166	A short worked example of the local check, run against a working copy before opening a change:
167	
168	```
169	$ scripts/format.sh
170	formatted 3 files, 0 unchanged
171	$ scripts/style-check.sh
172	no issues found
173	```
174	
175	If `scripts/style-check.sh` reports something the author disagrees with, that's a fine thing to raise as a comment on the pull request rather than argue about in the shell — the reviewer has the last call on whether a style check warning needs fixing before merge. In practice this comes up maybe once every few changes, usually around line length in a comment or a name that's a little too close to an existing one elsewhere in the package.
176	
177	Reviewers are also expected to glance over the general shape of the code even after the tools run clean — nesting depth, how far a piece of logic sits from where it's used, and whether a new piece of the command line or the service reads like the rest of the package. None of that is enforced by a script, and it's the part of a review that takes a human reviewer's judgment rather than a tool's output.
178	
179	## Commit Messages During Review
180	
181	A short summary of what reviewers check on commit messages, since this comes up in nearly every review thread:
182	
183	* The first line is a short summary under about 70 characters, written in the imperative ("fix the local check timeout" rather than "fixed" or "fixes").
184	* A body paragraph explains why the change was made if it isn't obvious from the summary alone — reviewers ask for this on anything non-trivial.
185	* Commits within a single pull request should each stand on their own where practical — a reviewer should be able to read commit by commit and follow the logic, rather than needing to read the whole diff at once to make sense of any individual step.
186	* A commit that only exists to fix something from two commits earlier in the same pull request is fine to leave as-is before merge, since the squash merge collapses it anyway — no need to go back and rewrite the branch's commit log by hand unless the reviewer specifically asks for it.
187	
188	Setting up the commit template locally makes this easier to keep consistent:
189	
190	```
191	git config commit.template .gitmessage
192	```
193	
194	Full detail on commit message wording, capitalization, and the summary-line convention is its own topic — reviewers on accountsvc apply it during review but the wording rules themselves live in Commit Message Style (v2.0, Priya Chandran).
195	
196	## Handling Stale Changes
197	
198	A change is considered stale once the main branch has moved on enough that a rebase would touch more than a handful of lines outside the original change, or once a pull request has sat without a reply for more than about a week. Reviewers aren't expected to keep a stale change in mind — it's on the author to bring it back up to date and ping again in `#accountsvc-dev` before asking for another look. If the underlying reason for the change no longer applies (the part of the package it touched has since been reworked by someone else), close the pull request with a short note rather than letting it sit open indefinitely.
199	
200	## Files and Paths Referenced
201	
202	| Path | Purpose |
203	|---|---|
204	| `accountsvc/` | the package directory; reviewers check every changed file here against the conventions on this page |
205	| `README.md` (repository root) | setup and usage instructions; kept in sync with any change to the command line or the service |
206	| `docs/developer-handbook/code-review-conventions.md` | this page |
207	| `docs/developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md` | commit summary and body wording that reviewers apply during comment threads |
208	| `docs/developer-handbook/coding-style-guide.md` | formatting and layout guidance behind most style comments |
209	| `docs/developer-handbook/style-quick-reference.txt` | short version of the style guide reviewers sometimes link directly in a nit |
210	| `docs/developer-handbook/repository-layout.md` | where package pieces are expected to live, checked when a change adds a new file |
211	| `.gitmessage` (repository root) | commit template installed with `git config commit.template` |
212	| `.editorconfig` (repository root) | shared indentation and line-ending settings, reducing formatting noise in review diffs |

# Code Review Conventions

**Version:** 3.1
**Owner:** Core Services (Priya Chandran)
**Last updated:** 2025-06-30

**Summary:** This page describes how contributors open, discuss, and merge changes to the package and the service. It covers what a change should look like before it is opened for review, how reviewers are picked, what reviewers check, how comments are written and settled, and how a change is merged once it is ready. It also touches on the parts of commit message style and coding style that reviewers apply directly during a review, since those two areas show up in almost every comment thread on this repository.

## Overview

accountsvc is small enough that most changes touch either the package directory or a handful of files in docs/ or scripts/, and the review process reflects that. There is no formal review board and no scheduled review window — a contributor opens a pull request, a reviewer is picked from the small pool of people who know the package and the service well, and the two of them work through the change in comments until it is ready to merge. The goal of this page is to make that back-and-forth predictable: what size a change should be, who looks at it, what they're looking for, how comments are phrased, and what "ready to merge" actually means on this repository.

Because the package keeps its state in a local database file and exposes both a command line and a loopback HTTP service, changes tend to fall into a few recognizable shapes: changes to the command line surface, changes to the service's local behavior, changes to how the database file is read or written, and changes to documentation or scripts that don't touch the package at all. Reviewers are chosen, in part, based on which of these shapes a change fits, and the checklist a reviewer works through shifts slightly depending on the shape too. That's covered in more detail under **Choosing Reviewers** and **What Reviewers Check** below.

A note on tone: this repository has always leaned toward short, direct review comments rather than long discussions in the pull request description. If a comment thread runs past four or five exchanges without resolving, the convention is to pick up a short call instead of continuing in text — see **Responding to Feedback**.

## Terminology

- **Change** — the full set of commits proposed for merge in a single pull request. Sometimes called a "change set" in older comment threads on this repository, though the shorter term is preferred now.
- **Pull request (PR)** — the mechanism used to open a change, attach a description, and start a review thread. On this repository, pull requests are opened against the internal git host at `git.corp.internal/accountsvc`.
- **Author** — the person who wrote the change and opened the pull request.
- **Reviewer** — the person asked to look at the change before it merges. On accountsvc there is normally one reviewer per change; two are asked for changes that touch the database file directly.
- **Blocking comment** — a comment that must be resolved before the change can merge. Blocking comments are written as plain sentences with no prefix.
- **Nit** — a small, non-blocking comment, usually about naming, spacing, or wording, prefixed with `nit:` so the author knows it can be left as-is if they disagree.
- **Sign-off** — a reviewer's mark, given as a short comment such as "looks good" or a thumbs-up reaction on the pull request, that the change is ready to merge from their side. accountsvc does not use a separate formal sign-off step beyond this.
- **Squash merge** — combining every commit in a pull request into a single commit at merge time. This is the default merge method on accountsvc; see **Merge Conventions**.
- **Fast-forward merge** — a merge that moves the target branch pointer forward without creating a merge commit. Used only for small documentation-only changes on this repository.
- **Stale change** — a pull request whose branch has drifted far enough from the main branch that it needs a rebase or merge-in before a reviewer can safely look at it again.
- **Working copy** — a contributor's local checkout of the repository, as set up in Workstation Setup.
- **Formatting pass** — running the formatter across a change before opening it, described under **Style and Formatting Checks During Review**.

## Before You Open a Change (Owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services)

A change is ready to open once it clears a short list of checks. These aren't enforced by any tool on this repository — they're checked by hand, by the author, before asking anyone to look:

1. The formatter has been run across every file touched by the change (see **Style and Formatting Checks During Review** for the exact command).
2. The style check script runs clean, or any remaining warnings are ones the reviewer has already agreed to leave in place.
3. Commits are organized into logical steps rather than left as a raw log of every edit made while working — see **Commit Messages During Review**.
4. If the change touches the command line surface or the service's local behavior, the README at the repository root has been updated to match.
5. If the change touches the database file, the author has run a manual check against a local copy of the file rather than the one used for day-to-day work.

Contributors sometimes ask whether a change needs to be "complete" before it's opened. The answer on accountsvc has always been no — a change that's still being worked through design questions can be opened as a draft pull request, which signals to reviewers that comments are welcome but a sign-off isn't being requested yet. Mark a draft clearly in the pull request title, for example `[draft] rework local check output for the service`.

## Opening a Pull Request

Branches are named `initials/short-description`, for example `bg/loopback-timeout-cleanup`. Once a branch is pushed, the pull request description should follow this shape:

```
## What this changes
One or two sentences on what the change does and why.

## How it was checked
What you ran locally to confirm the change works — the formatter,
the style check, and a manual check of the command line or the
service if either was touched.

## Notes for the reviewer
Anything you want a second pair of eyes on specifically, or any
part of the change you're not fully happy with yet.
```

Not every field needs a long answer — a one-line "how it was checked" is fine for a documentation-only change. What matters is that the field exists; pull requests opened without a "how it was checked" section are routinely sent back with a comment asking for one before review starts.

Once the pull request is open, post a short line in the `#accountsvc-dev` channel in the internal chat tool if the change is larger than roughly 150 lines, or if it touches the database file. Small changes don't need a chat message — the reviewer picked in the pull request itself is enough.

## Choosing Reviewers

accountsvc has four people who regularly review changes: Priya Chandran, Owen Fitzgerald, Yusuf Demir, and Theo Banks. There's no strict reviewer order — the convention is to pick whoever last touched the part of the package the change is closest to, which usually means checking the commit log for the files being changed and asking whoever shows up most.

A rough guide, since "closest to" isn't always obvious:

| Change touches… | Ask first |
|---|---|
| the command line surface | Priya Chandran |
| the service's local behavior | Priya Chandran or Theo Banks |
| the database file directly | Yusuf Demir, plus a second reviewer |
| style, formatting, or the coding style guide itself | Owen Fitzgerald |
| workstation or editor setup | Theo Banks |
| documentation only | whoever owns the page being changed |

If the obvious reviewer is out, ask in `#accountsvc-dev` rather than picking at random — small as the pool is, the wrong reviewer for a database-file change has sent more than one bug back through a second round.

## Review Size Guidelines

Large changes take longer to review and are more likely to hide a problem in the middle of an otherwise fine diff. The rough guideline on this repository:

- Under 150 lines changed: normal review, usually turned around same day.
- 150–400 lines: fine, but the author should call out in the description which parts are mechanical (renames, formatting) versus which parts carry the actual change.
- Over 400 lines: the reviewer can ask the author to split the change before starting review. This isn't a hard rule, but it's been invoked often enough that it's worth planning around.

Changes that are mostly generated by the formatter (for example, a repository-wide line-length fix) are the one exception — line count doesn't matter much there since the diff is mechanical, but the author should say so plainly in the description so the reviewer doesn't read every line by hand.

## What Reviewers Check

A reviewer on accountsvc is checking four things, roughly in this order:

* **Correctness of intent** — does the change do what the description says it does? This is checked by reading the diff against the description, not by re-deriving the whole design from scratch.
* **Fit with the rest of the package** — does the change follow the shape of the surrounding code? Naming, structure, and the general layout described in Repository Layout all come up here.
* **Manual behavior check** — for anything touching the command line or the service, the reviewer runs the change locally against a fresh copy of the database file and confirms it behaves the way the description says. This is a manual check, not an automated one, and it's expected to take a few minutes rather than being skipped.
* **Style and formatting** — covered in detail below, but this is usually the fastest part of the review since the formatter and style check catch most of it before the reviewer ever opens the diff.

Reviewers are asked to leave at least one substantive comment on every non-trivial change, even a positive one, so the author knows the diff was actually read rather than skimmed. "Looks good" with nothing else attached is discouraged for anything over roughly 50 lines.

## Comment Conventions (Owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services)

Comments on accountsvc pull requests follow a small set of conventions that have built up over the last couple of years:

1. Blocking comments are phrased as plain statements or questions: "This will read the database file before it's opened for writing — is that intentional?"
2. Nits are prefixed: "nit: this name reads oddly next to the other names nearby, consider something closer to the existing pattern."
3. Comments that are purely stylistic and already covered by the formatter or the style check are not worth leaving — if the tool didn't catch it, it's probably a judgment call worth raising as a nit rather than a blocking comment.
4. When a reviewer disagrees with an approach but the author has a reasonable case for it, the convention is to say so plainly rather than let a blocking comment sit unresolved: "I'd have done this differently, but I don't think it's worth blocking on — go ahead."
5. Comments referencing a specific line should quote the smallest relevant piece of the diff rather than the whole function or block, so the thread stays easy to follow later.

A short worked example, as it would appear in the pull request thread:

```
> reviewer: nit: "tmp_val" is a little terse next to the naming used
> elsewhere in this file — maybe something more descriptive?

> author: fair, renamed in the latest push.

> reviewer: This closes the database file before the last write
> finishes in the case where the command exits early. Blocking —
> can you confirm the order there?

> author: good catch, moved the close to the end. Ready for another look.

> reviewer: looks good, thanks.
```

## Responding to Feedback

Authors are expected to resolve each comment thread individually rather than pushing a large follow-up commit and leaving every thread open. The convention is:

- Push a small commit (or amend, if the branch hasn't been shared elsewhere) that responds to one or two related comments.
- Reply on the thread with what changed, even briefly — "moved this to the end of the function" is enough.
- Leave the thread open for the reviewer to close, rather than closing it yourself. This has been the convention since early 2024 and occasionally trips up new contributors who are used to closing their own threads elsewhere.

If a thread runs past four or five exchanges without settling, stop and set up a short call instead of continuing in text — this has saved more than one review from turning into a multi-day back-and-forth over something that would have taken two minutes to sort out out loud. Note the outcome of the call as a short comment on the thread afterward so there's a record for anyone reading the pull request later.

Changes that sit open for more than a few days without activity are considered stale rather than abandoned — ping the reviewer directly in `#accountsvc-dev` rather than opening a second pull request.

## Sign-off and Merge Conventions (Owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services)

A change is ready to merge once:

- Every blocking comment is resolved (nits can be left open at the author's discretion).
- The reviewer has left a sign-off, either a short comment or a thumbs-up reaction on the pull request.
- The branch is not stale — if the main branch has moved on significantly, rebase or merge it in before merging, and give the reviewer a quick second look if the rebase touched anything non-mechanical.

The default merge method on accountsvc is a squash merge, so the many small commits made while working through review comments collapse into one commit on the main branch. The one exception is documentation-only changes with a single clean commit already, which use a fast-forward merge to keep the commit log easy to read for pages that don't touch the package at all.

Only the author merges their own change once sign-off is given — reviewers don't merge on someone else's behalf, even for small changes, since it keeps the merge log a reliable record of who actually decided a change was ready to go out.

## Style and Formatting Checks During Review

Reviewers on accountsvc expect the formatter and the style check to have already been run before a change is opened. Both are wired up as small shell scripts at the repository root:

```
scripts/format.sh
scripts/style-check.sh
```

`scripts/format.sh` runs the formatter across every file changed against the main branch. `scripts/style-check.sh` runs the linter and prints any remaining issues, including anything the formatter can't fix on its own (unused names, overly long lines in comments, that sort of thing). Contributors who use the shared editor settings described in Shared Editor Settings usually see very few style check issues by the time they open a change, since the editor catches most of it as they type.

A short worked example of the local check, run against a working copy before opening a change:

```
$ scripts/format.sh
formatted 3 files, 0 unchanged
$ scripts/style-check.sh
no issues found
```

If `scripts/style-check.sh` reports something the author disagrees with, that's a fine thing to raise as a comment on the pull request rather than argue about in the shell — the reviewer has the last call on whether a style check warning needs fixing before merge. In practice this comes up maybe once every few changes, usually around line length in a comment or a name that's a little too close to an existing one elsewhere in the package.

Reviewers are also expected to glance over the general shape of the code even after the tools run clean — nesting depth, how far a piece of logic sits from where it's used, and whether a new piece of the command line or the service reads like the rest of the package. None of that is enforced by a script, and it's the part of a review that takes a human reviewer's judgment rather than a tool's output.

## Commit Messages During Review

A short summary of what reviewers check on commit messages, since this comes up in nearly every review thread:

* The first line is a short summary under about 70 characters, written in the imperative ("fix the local check timeout" rather than "fixed" or "fixes").
* A body paragraph explains why the change was made if it isn't obvious from the summary alone — reviewers ask for this on anything non-trivial.
* Commits within a single pull request should each stand on their own where practical — a reviewer should be able to read commit by commit and follow the logic, rather than needing to read the whole diff at once to make sense of any individual step.
* A commit that only exists to fix something from two commits earlier in the same pull request is fine to leave as-is before merge, since the squash merge collapses it anyway — no need to go back and rewrite the branch's commit log by hand unless the reviewer specifically asks for it.

Setting up the commit template locally makes this easier to keep consistent:

```
git config commit.template .gitmessage
```

Full detail on commit message wording, capitalization, and the summary-line convention is its own topic — reviewers on accountsvc apply it during review but the wording rules themselves live in Commit Message Style (v2.0, Priya Chandran).

## Handling Stale Changes

A change is considered stale once the main branch has moved on enough that a rebase would touch more than a handful of lines outside the original change, or once a pull request has sat without a reply for more than about a week. Reviewers aren't expected to keep a stale change in mind — it's on the author to bring it back up to date and ping again in `#accountsvc-dev` before asking for another look. If the underlying reason for the change no longer applies (the part of the package it touched has since been reworked by someone else), close the pull request with a short note rather than letting it sit open indefinitely.

## Files and Paths Referenced

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `accountsvc/` | the package directory; reviewers check every changed file here against the conventions on this page |
| `README.md` (repository root) | setup and usage instructions; kept in sync with any change to the command line or the service |
| `docs/developer-handbook/code-review-conventions.md` | this page |
| `docs/developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md` | commit summary and body wording that reviewers apply during comment threads |
| `docs/developer-handbook/coding-style-guide.md` | formatting and layout guidance behind most style comments |
| `docs/developer-handbook/style-quick-reference.txt` | short version of the style guide reviewers sometimes link directly in a nit |
| `docs/developer-handbook/repository-layout.md` | where package pieces are expected to live, checked when a change adds a new file |
| `.gitmessage` (repository root) | commit template installed with `git config commit.template` |
| `.editorconfig` (repository root) | shared indentation and line-ending settings, reducing formatting noise in review diffs |
| `scripts/format.sh` | formatting pass run before a change is opened |
| `scripts/style-check.sh` | style check run before a change is opened and referenced when a warning comes up in review |
| local console output from a manual check | the output a reviewer captures while running the command line or the service against a copy of the database file, often pasted directly into a comment thread |

## Tools and Library Versions

| git | 2.44.0 or newer | branching, commits, and the pull request workflow |

- **3.0** — 2025-02-14 — moved from a two-reviewer default to a single reviewer for most changes, with a second reviewer kept only for changes touching the database file directly.

1	# Commit Message Style
2	
3	**Version:** v2.0.1
4	**Owner:** Core Services (Priya Chandran)
5	**Last updated:** 2024-08-22
6	
7	## Purpose and Coverage
8	
9	This page sets out the expected structure and wording for commit messages across the accountsvc repository. It applies to every commit merged into `main`, including squash-merges from pull requests, direct pushes made by maintainers during a release, and the occasional revert. It does not apply to tags or to text written in pull request descriptions, though the two often echo each other.
10	
11	The rules here exist so that `git log`, `git blame`, and the changelog generator scripts under `scripts/` can produce useful output without a human re-reading every diff. A consistent commit log is also what lets the on-call engineer (there is no formal on-call schedule — see Code Review Conventions for how review load is currently shared) figure out what shipped between two dates without opening a browser.
12	
13	Section owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services.
14	
15	## Commit Message Anatomy
16	
17	Every commit message has three parts, only the first of which is required:
18	
19	1. **Subject line** — one line, imperative mood, no trailing period.
20	2. **Body** — optional but expected for anything non-trivial; wrapped at 72 columns.
21	3. **Footer** — optional metadata lines (issue references, co-authors, breaking-change markers).
22	
23	A blank line must separate the subject from the body, and another blank line separates the body from the footer. Git itself will complain (mildly, via `git log --oneline` looking wrong) if you skip this.
24	
25	### Subject Line Format
26	
27	```
28	<type>(<area>): <short summary>
29	```
30	
31	- `<type>` — one of the categories in the table below.
32	- `<area>` — the part of the package touched, usually a directory or subsystem name under `accountsvc/`. Optional for repository-wide changes (tooling, docs).
33	- `<short summary>` — imperative, lower-case after the colon, no period, ideally under 50 characters, hard cap 72.
34	
35	Examples:
36	
37	```
38	feat(cli): add --format flag to output command
39	fix(storage): correct off-by-one in row iteration
40	docs(handbook): clarify commit footer rules
41	chore(deps): bump ruff to 0.6.1
42	```
43	
44	Area naming is somewhat informal in practice — some contributors write `feat(http)`, others write `feat(server)` for the same subsystem. Try to match whatever area name appears most recently in `git log -- accountsvc/<dir>` for that part rather than inventing a new one.
45	
46	### Commit Types
47	
48	| Type | When to use it | Shows up in changelog? |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| `feat` | New capability or behavior | Yes |
51	| `fix` | Bug fix | Yes |
52	| `docs` | Documentation only, including this handbook | No |
53	| `style` | Formatting, whitespace, import order — no logic change | No |
54	| `refactor` | Code restructuring with no behavior change | No |
55	| `perf` | Performance improvement | Yes |
56	| `chore` | Build scripts, dependency bumps, repo housekeeping | No |
57	| `revert` | Reverting a prior commit | Yes |
58	
59	Note that `qa` is deliberately not in this list; commits touching that area should use `chore` or `refactor` depending on intent.
60	
61	### Body
62	
63	The body explains *why*, not *what* — the diff already shows what. Wrap lines at 72 columns (most editors, including the shared VS Code settings, do this automatically once `editor.rulers` is set — see Editor Configuration). Use full sentences. Bullet points are acceptable for enumerating multiple related changes within one commit, though a commit that needs more than three bullets is usually a sign it should have been split.
64	
65	Example body:
66	
67	```
68	fix(storage): correct off-by-one in row iteration
69	
70	The row cursor advanced twice per loop when a filter clause was
71	present, causing the last row of any filtered result to be silently
72	skipped. This only manifested once result sets exceeded one page,
73	which is why it went unnoticed until the 1.9 release.
74	
75	Added a guard so the cursor only advances once per iteration
76	regardless of filter state.
77	```
78	
79	### Footer
80	
81	Footer lines use `key: value` pairs, one per line, in this order when more than one applies:
82	
83	1. `Refs:` — issue or tracking reference (internal tracker IDs only, e.g. `ACC-441`)
84	2. `Breaking:` — one-line description of a breaking change, if any
85	3. `Co-authored-by:` — for pair-written commits, standard Git trailer format
86	
87	Example:
88	
89	```
90	feat(cli): add --format flag to output command
91	
92	Supports plain, json, and tsv. Default remains plain to avoid
93	surprising existing scripts.
94	
95	Refs: ACC-318
96	Co-authored-by: Priya Chandran <bgigurtsis@gmail.com>
97	```
98	
99	(Priya's own commits use the standard `Co-authored-by` trailer when a change was genuinely worked on jointly at a shared terminal — this is uncommon for accountsvc given the small team, but happened during the 1.9 storage rewrite.)
100	
101	## Worked Examples
102	
103	Below are three full examples that a new contributor can use as templates.
104	
105	### Example 1 — small bug fix, no body needed
106	
107	```
108	fix(cli): handle empty argument list without traceback
109	```
110	
111	A one-line fix genuinely doesn't need a body if the subject fully explains the change and there's no "why" beyond "it crashed."
112	
113	### Example 2 — feature with body and footer
114	
115	```
116	feat(http): add pagination to listing responses
117	
118	Large account lists were being returned in a single response,
119	which was slow for anything over a few thousand rows. Responses
120	now include a cursor value that the caller passes back to get
121	the next slice.
122	
123	Existing callers that don't pass a cursor continue to get the
124	full first slice, so this is not a breaking change for current
125	integrations.
126	
127	Refs: ACC-402
128	```
129	
130	### Example 3 — chore with multiple bullets
131	
132	```
133	chore(deps): bump standard tooling to Q3 versions
134	
135	- ruff 0.5.0 -> 0.6.1
136	- black 24.4.2 -> 24.8.0
137	- mypy 1.10.0 -> 1.11.1
138	
139	No source changes required; only a handful of import-order
140	warnings surfaced and were auto-fixed by ruff.
141	```
142	
143	## Amending, Squashing, and Reverting
144	
145	**Amending.** `git commit --amend` is fine for fixing a typo in your own subject line before pushing. Never amend a commit that's already been pushed to a shared branch unless the branch is yours alone and nobody else has based work on it.
146	
147	**Squashing.** Pull requests are merged with "squash and merge" by default (see Code Review Conventions for the review process itself). The squash commit message should be rewritten by hand to follow this page's format — GitHub's auto-generated squash message, which just concatenates all commit subjects, is not acceptable as a final message. Rewrite it into one clean subject and a body summarizing the whole change.
148	
149	**Reverting.** Use `git revert`, not `git reset`, on shared branches. The generated revert message starts with `Revert "..."` — leave that prefix in place, but add a body explaining why:
150	
151	```
152	revert(storage): revert "fix(storage): correct off-by-one in row
153	iteration"
154	
155	The fix introduced a regression where non-filtered result sets
156	lost their last row instead of filtered ones. Reverting until a
157	combined fix is ready.
158

171	- Don't bundle an unrelated dependency bump into a feature commit just because you happened to touch `requirements.txt` at the same time. Split it into its own `chore(deps)` commit.

174	
175	Contributors are expected to clean up their branch commits before requesting review, not after. A typical local sequence:
176	
177	```
178	git fetch origin

186	```

188	`--force-with-lease` rather than `--force` is required practice here — it fails safely if someone else pushed to your branch (rare, but has happened when a reviewer pushed a small fix directly).

192	- Write in the imperative: "add," "fix," "remove" — not "added," "fixes," "removes."
193	- Avoid vague summaries like "misc changes" or "updates." If you can't summarize the change in one line, it's probably more than one commit.
194	- Don't reference people by name in the subject line ("fix Theo's bug") — put attribution, if relevant, in the body.

196	- Non-English text is fine in code comments where relevant but commit messages are written in English for consistency across the small team.

# Commit Message Style

**Version:** v2.0.1
**Owner:** Core Services (Priya Chandran)
**Last updated:** 2024-08-22

## Purpose and Coverage

This page sets out the expected structure and wording for commit messages across the accountsvc repository. It applies to every commit merged into `main`, including squash-merges from pull requests, direct pushes made by maintainers during a release, and the occasional revert. It does not apply to tags or to text written in pull request descriptions, though the two often echo each other.

The rules here exist so that `git log`, `git blame`, and the changelog generator scripts under `scripts/` can produce useful output without a human re-reading every diff. A consistent commit log is also what lets the on-call engineer (there is no formal on-call schedule — see Code Review Conventions for how review load is currently shared) figure out what shipped between two dates without opening a browser.

Section owner: Priya Chandran, Core Services.

## Commit Message Anatomy

Every commit message has three parts, only the first of which is required:

1. **Subject line** — one line, imperative mood, no trailing period.
2. **Body** — optional but expected for anything non-trivial; wrapped at 72 columns.
3. **Footer** — optional metadata lines (issue references, co-authors, breaking-change markers).

A blank line must separate the subject from the body, and another blank line separates the body from the footer. Git itself will complain (mildly, via `git log --oneline` looking wrong) if you skip this.

### Subject Line Format

```
<type>(<area>): <short summary>
```

- `<type>` — one of the categories in the table below.
- `<area>` — the part of the package touched, usually a directory or subsystem name under `accountsvc/`. Optional for repository-wide changes (tooling, docs).
- `<short summary>` — imperative, lower-case after the colon, no period, ideally under 50 characters, hard cap 72.

Examples:

```
feat(cli): add --format flag to output command
fix(storage): correct off-by-one in row iteration
docs(handbook): clarify commit footer rules
chore(deps): bump ruff to 0.6.1
```

Area naming is somewhat informal in practice — some contributors write `feat(http)`, others write `feat(server)` for the same subsystem. Try to match whatever area name appears most recently in `git log -- accountsvc/<dir>` for that part rather than inventing a new one.

### Commit Types

| Type | When to use it | Shows up in changelog? |
|---|---|---|
| `feat` | New capability or behavior | Yes |
| `fix` | Bug fix | Yes |
| `docs` | Documentation only, including this handbook | No |
| `style` | Formatting, whitespace, import order — no logic change | No |
| `refactor` | Code restructuring with no behavior change | No |
| `perf` | Performance improvement | Yes |
| `chore` | Build scripts, dependency bumps, repo housekeeping | No |
| `revert` | Reverting a prior commit | Yes |

Note that `qa` is deliberately not in this list; commits touching that area should use `chore` or `refactor` depending on intent.

### Body

The body explains *why*, not *what* — the diff already shows what. Wrap lines at 72 columns (most editors, including the shared VS Code settings, do this automatically once `editor.rulers` is set — see Editor Configuration). Use full sentences. Bullet points are acceptable for enumerating multiple related changes within one commit, though a commit that needs more than three bullets is usually a sign it should have been split.

Example body:

```
fix(storage): correct off-by-one in row iteration

The row cursor advanced twice per loop when a filter clause was
present, causing the last row of any filtered result to be silently
skipped. This only manifested once result sets exceeded one page,
which is why it went unnoticed until the 1.9 release.

Added a guard so the cursor only advances once per iteration
regardless of filter state.
```

### Footer

Footer lines use `key: value` pairs, one per line, in this order when more than one applies:

1. `Refs:` — issue or tracking reference (internal tracker IDs only, e.g. `ACC-441`)
2. `Breaking:` — one-line description of a breaking change, if any
3. `Co-authored-by:` — for pair-written commits, standard Git trailer format

Example:

```
feat(cli): add --format flag to output command

Supports plain, json, and tsv. Default remains plain to avoid
surprising existing scripts.

Refs: ACC-318
Co-authored-by: Priya Chandran <bgigurtsis@gmail.com>
```

(Priya's own commits use the standard `Co-authored-by` trailer when a change was genuinely worked on jointly at a shared terminal — this is uncommon for accountsvc given the small team, but happened during the 1.9 storage rewrite.)

## Worked Examples

Below are three full examples that a new contributor can use as templates.

### Example 1 — small bug fix, no body needed

```
fix(cli): handle empty argument list without traceback
```

A one-line fix genuinely doesn't need a body if the subject fully explains the change and there's no "why" beyond "it crashed."

### Example 2 — feature with body and footer

```
feat(http): add pagination to listing responses

Large account lists were being returned in a single response,
which was slow for anything over a few thousand rows. Responses
now include a cursor value that the caller passes back to get
the next slice.

Existing callers that don't pass a cursor continue to get the
full first slice, so this is not a breaking change for current
integrations.

Refs: ACC-402
```

### Example 3 — chore with multiple bullets

```
chore(deps): bump standard tooling to Q3 versions

- ruff 0.5.0 -> 0.6.1
- black 24.4.2 -> 24.8.0
- mypy 1.10.0 -> 1.11.1

No source changes required; only a handful of import-order
warnings surfaced and were auto-fixed by ruff.
```

## Amending, Squashing, and Reverting

**Amending.** `git commit --amend` is fine for fixing a typo in your own subject line before pushing. Never amend a commit that's already been pushed to a shared branch unless the branch is yours alone and nobody else has based work on it.

**Squashing.** Pull requests are merged with "squash and merge" by default (see Code Review Conventions for the review process itself). The squash commit message should be rewritten by hand to follow this page's format — GitHub's auto-generated squash message, which just concatenates all commit subjects, is not acceptable as a final message. Rewrite it into one clean subject and a body summarizing the whole change.

**Reverting.** Use `git revert`, not `git reset`, on shared branches. The generated revert message starts with `Revert "..."` — leave that prefix in place, but add a body explaining why:

```
revert(storage): revert "fix(storage): correct off-by-one in row
iteration"

The fix introduced a regression where non-filtered result sets
lost their last row instead of filtered ones. Reverting until a
combined fix is ready.

Refs: ACC-441
```

## Commit Granularity

Section owner: Priya Chandran.

Rules of thumb, not laws:

- One logical change per commit. "Logical" is doing a lot of work in that sentence — use judgment.
- A commit should leave the repository in a state where the package still imports and the command-line entry point still runs. Don't commit half a rename.
- It's fine, even encouraged, to have a commit that only moves code and a separate commit that changes behavior in that moved code. Reviewers can then diff the behavior change in isolation.
- Don't bundle an unrelated dependency bump into a feature commit just because you happened to touch `requirements.txt` at the same time. Split it into its own `chore(deps)` commit.

## Interactive Rebase Before Opening a Pull Request

Contributors are expected to clean up their branch commits before requesting review, not after. A typical local sequence:

```
git fetch origin
git rebase -i origin/main
```

In the interactive editor, `squash` or `fixup` any "oops" commits (typo fixes, half-finished attempts) into the commit they belong with, then rewrite subject lines to match the format in this page. Force-push the cleaned branch:

```
git push --force-with-lease
```

`--force-with-lease` rather than `--force` is required practice here — it fails safely if someone else pushed to your branch (rare, but has happened when a reviewer pushed a small fix directly).

## Language and Tone Conventions

- Write in the imperative: "add," "fix," "remove" — not "added," "fixes," "removes."
- Avoid vague summaries like "misc changes" or "updates." If you can't summarize the change in one line, it's probably more than one commit.
- Don't reference people by name in the subject line ("fix Theo's bug") — put attribution, if relevant, in the body.
- Emoji are not used in this repository's commit messages. This is a stylistic choice, not a hard rule enforced by anything, but nobody does it and reviewers will ask about it if you start.
- Non-English text is fine in code comments where relevant but commit messages are written in English for consistency across the small team.

## Common Mistakes Seen in This Repository

| Mistake | Example | Preferred form |
|---|---|---|
| Past tense subject | `fixed bug in output` | `fix(cli): correct output formatting` |
| Vague summary | `updates` | `refactor(storage): simplify connection setup` |
| Missing type prefix | `add pagination` | `feat(http): add pagination to listing responses` |
| Trailing period | `fix(cli): correct flag parsing.` | `fix(cli): correct flag parsing` |
| Body explaining "what" instead of "why" | "Changed line 42 to use a for loop" | "Switched to a for loop because the generator held the file open longer than needed" |
| Multiple unrelated changes in one commit | `feat(cli): add flag and bump deps` | Split into two commits |

## Tooling Support

There is no commit-msg git hook enforced server-side today. The repository briefly had a local `commit-msg` hook shipped via `scripts/install-hooks.sh` (added around version 1.7 of the package), but it was removed in early 2025 when it started rejecting valid revert commits due to a regex bug, and nobody has reinstated it since. Reviewers currently enforce this page by eye during pull request review.

| Tool / Package | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Git | 2.43+ | Version control, all workflows on this page assume this or newer |
| commitizen | 3.27.0 | Optional local helper for building conformant messages (`cz commit`) |
| GitHub | n/a (SaaS) | Hosts pull requests and performs squash-merge |
| ruff | 0.6.1 | Referenced in dependency-bump commit examples above |
| Python | 3.11 | Runtime the package targets; irrelevant to message format but shows up in commit bodies constantly |

`commitizen` is optional and not everyone on the team uses it. Priya uses it; Yusuf does not and writes messages by hand; both produce conformant output, which is really the only check that matters here.

## Repository Files Referenced

| Path | Function |
|---|---|
| `docs/developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md` | This page |
| `docs/developer-handbook/code-review-conventions.md` | Describes how pull requests carrying these commits get reviewed and merged |
| `docs/developer-handbook/coding-style-guide.md` | Covers formatting of the code itself, separate from the message describing it |
| `scripts/install-hooks.sh` | Formerly installed a local commit-msg hook; currently unused, left in place for reference |
| `scripts/generate-changelog.py` | Reads commit subjects by type prefix to assemble the release changelog |
| `.gitmessage` | Optional commit template a contributor can point Git at via `git config commit.template .gitmessage` |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | Repository-root file populated from `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, and `revert` commit subjects |

## Terminology

- **Subject line** — the single required first line of a commit message, summarizing the change.
- **Body** — the optional free-text paragraph(s) following the subject, explaining rationale.
- **Footer** — trailing `key: value` lines carrying structured metadata such as issue references.
- **Area** — the parenthesized part of the subject line naming the affected part of the package.
- **Type prefix** — the word before the area (`feat`, `fix`, `chore`, etc.) categorizing the commit.
- **Squash-merge** — a GitHub merge strategy that collapses all commits in a pull request into one.
- **Trailer** — a Git-recognized `key: value` line at the end of a commit message, such as `Co-authored-by`.
- **Fixup commit** — a small local commit intended to be squashed into an earlier one before review, never merged standalone.
- **Force-with-lease** — a safer variant of `git push --force` that aborts if the remote branch changed unexpectedly.
- **Breaking change** — a change that alters existing caller-visible behavior in a way that requires callers to adapt.

## Change Log

| 2023-02-10 | v1.0.0 | Initial page: subject line format and basic type list. |
| 2023-06-19 | v1.1.0 | Added footer conventions and `Refs:` field. |

| 2024-03-15 | v1.3.0 | Added interactive rebase section and `--force-with-lease` guidance. |
| 2024-05-28 | v1.4.0 | Removed `qa` from the type table; folded qa-related commits into `chore`/`refactor` per team discussion. |
| 2024-07-02 | v2.0.0 | Major rewrite: added worked examples, common-mistakes table, and tooling section covering commitizen. |
| 2024-08-22 | v2.0.1 | Corrected commit-msg hook status after its removal; clarified that enforcement is currently manual during review. |

1	# Coding Style Guide
2	
3	**Title:** Coding Style Guide  
4	**Version:** 4.0  
5	**Owner:** Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald)  
6	**Last Updated:** 2025-09-04  
7	**Summary:** Covers naming, formatting, and structural conventions expected in Python contributed to the package.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Overview
12	
13	This guide establishes the coding conventions and style standards for all contributions to the accountsvc package. All code merged into the repository must comply with these standards. We maintain consistency across the codebase to improve readability, reduce cognitive load during review, and make onboarding smoother for new contributors.
14	
15	The standards in this guide apply to source files, configuration modules, utility scripts, and documentation code examples. For environment setup and Python version support, see the companion pages [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md) and [Workstation Setup](workstation-setup.md). For automated formatting validation and editor setup, see [Editor Configuration](editor-configuration.md) and [Shared Editor Settings](editor-settings.yaml).
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Naming Conventions
20	
21	**Section Owner:** Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald)
22	
23	### Variables and Functions
24	
25	Use lowercase with underscores for variable and function names. This applies to module-level constants that are not intended for external use.
26	
27	- Prefer descriptive names over single characters, except in loop counters and mathematical contexts.
28	- Avoid abbreviations unless they are universally understood in your domain (e.g., `conn` for database connection is acceptable; `dbcx` is not).
29	- Use plural names for collections: `results`, `user_ids`, `configuration_items`.
30	- Prefix private or internal functions with a single underscore: `_helper_function()`.
31	
32	### Classes and Types
33	
34	Use PascalCase for class names. Base exception classes should end with `Error` or `Exception`.
35	
36	- One class per file unless closely related helper classes are required.
37	- Name exception classes to describe the error condition: `ValidationError`, `ConnectionError`, `ConfigurationError`.
38	
39	### Constants and Enumerations
40	
41	Use UPPER_CASE with underscores for module-level constants. Constant values should appear near the top of the module after imports.
42	
43	- Database timeout limits, default configuration values, and string literals used in multiple places belong in the constants section.
44	- Define related constants in logical groups.
45	
46	### Modules
47	
48	Module file names use lowercase with underscores. A module name should reflect its primary responsibility.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Code Formatting and Structure
53	
54	**Section Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
55	
56	### Line Length
57	
58	Keep lines to a maximum of 100 characters. This applies to all Python source files and inline comments.
59	
60	Lines exceeding 100 characters are difficult to review on standard displays and split-screen editors. The trade-off between readability and strict line length is resolved in favor of the limit; use implicit line continuation for long expressions and function definitions.
61	
62	### Indentation
63	
64	Use 4 spaces per indentation level. Never use tabs. Configure your editor to convert tabs to spaces automatically (see [Editor Configuration](editor-configuration.md)).
65	
66	### Blank Lines
67	
68	- Separate top-level definitions (functions, classes) with two blank lines.
69	- Separate methods within a class with one blank line.
70	- Use one blank line sparingly within functions to group logical sections, but prefer extracting such sections into helper functions.
71	
72	### Imports
73	
74	Organize imports in three groups, separated by a blank line:
75	
76	1. standard library modules
77	2. third-party modules
78	3. local package imports
79	
80	Within each group, sort names alphabetically. Import entire modules rather than specific names from modules, except where the module is primarily a collection (e.g., `from collections import defaultdict` is acceptable; `from os import path` should be `import os`).
81	
82	Group long import statements using implicit line continuation:
83	
84	
85	Do not use `from module import *`.
86	
87	### Whitespace
88	
89	- One space around binary operation symbols (`=`, `+`, `==`, `and`, `or`, etc.).
90	- No space immediately inside parentheses or brackets.
91	- One space after commas in sequences.
92	- One space after colons in dictionary literals, but not in type hints (actually, we're now doing `key: value` in dicts and `name: str` in type hints—check the recent PRs).
93	
94	---
95	
96	## Type Hints and Documentation
97	
98	**Section Owner:** Language Tooling (Owen Fitzgerald)
99	
100	### Type Hints
101	
102	Use type hints for function definitions and class attributes. The package targets Python 3.9 and later, so modern type syntax is available. Do not use `typing.Optional` where `None` is a possible return value; use the union syntax with `None`.
103	
104	All public-facing functions must include return type hints. For internal functions, hints are strongly encouraged but not strictly required if the context is entirely clear.
105	
106	
107	### Docstrings
108	
109	Write docstrings for all public functions, classes, and modules. Use the multi-line docstring format for anything longer than one line.
110	
111	A docstring should state what the function or class does, list parameters and their types (even though hints exist), describe the return value, and document any exceptions that are raised intentionally.
112	
113	Module-level docstrings should appear at the very top of the file and briefly describe the module's purpose and main contents.
114	
115	### Comments
116	
117	Inline comments explain the "why" rather than the "what." The code itself should be clear enough that the "what" is self-evident.
118	
119	- Use full sentences starting with a capital letter.
120	- Keep comments concise and on the same line as code when possible.
121	- For multi-line explanations, use a comment block before the code rather than trailing comments.
122	
123	---
124	
125	## Structural Patterns
126	
127	### Function and Method Size
128	
129	Keep functions focused and reasonably short. A function longer than 50 lines is a signal to refactor. Extract helper functions rather than nesting complex logic.
130	
131	### Conditional Complexity
132	
133	Avoid deep nesting. Prefer early returns and guard clauses. A function body should not exceed 3 levels of nesting without refactoring.
134	
135	### Error Handling
136	
137	Catch specific exceptions, never bare `except:` clauses. Log exceptions with full context rather than silently swallowing errors. The service uses the standard library logging module; see the package for current logging configuration.
138	
139	### Database Interactions
140	
141	All database operations go through the dedicated data access layer. Do not construct database queries in multiple places. Centralize query logic to reduce duplication and improve maintainability.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Commit and Review Standards
146	
147	For detailed commit message formatting, see [Commit Message Style](commit-message-style.md).
148	
149	For code review expectations and feedback conventions, see [Code Review Conventions](code-review-conventions.md).
150	
151	### Pre-Commit Checks
152	
153	Before opening a pull request:
154	
155	1. Verify your changes comply with this guide using the linting script located at `scripts/lint.sh`.
156	2. Run any available local validation tools (configured in your editor; see [Shared Editor Settings](editor-settings.yaml)).
157	3. Ensure imports are organized and sorted.
158	4. Check line lengths and indentation visually or with editor tools.
159	
160	### Pull Request Extent
161	
162	- One logical change per pull request. If your work spans multiple unrelated concerns, split into separate PRs.
163	- Keep PRs small enough to review thoroughly in under 30 minutes. Reviewers are more likely to catch issues and provide useful feedback on focused changes.
164	- Include a clear description of the change and the motivation behind it.
165	
166	---
