1	# operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-thresholds.yaml
2	#
3	# =============================================================================
4	# HEADER BLOCK
5	# =============================================================================
6	# Title:         Host Monitoring Threshold Settings
7	# Version:       1.2
8	# Owner:         Reliability (Priya Nair)
9	# Last updated:  2025-08-19
10	#
11	# Summary:
12	#   This page holds the numeric threshold values that host monitoring checks
13	#   read when they decide whether accountsvc's host is in a warn or critical
14	#   state. It covers disk space, memory, the size of the service's own
15	#   console log files, loopback port conflicts, SQLite file locking, and the
16	#   copying of the database file for backup. The values here are the ones
17	#   currently wired into the monitoring checks that run on a workstation or a
18	#   small host running accountsvc; they are not aspirational targets, they
19	#   are what the checks actually compare against today.
20	#
21	#   accountsvc itself has no monitoring of its own — it is a small package
22	#   built on the standard library, with a command line and a loopback HTTP
23	#   service, that keeps its state in a local SQLite file. All of the
24	#   thresholds below live in host-level tooling (cron jobs, Scheduled Tasks,
25	#   a small watcher script in scripts/) that watches the host the package
26	#   runs on.
27	#
28	# =============================================================================
29	# PURPOSE AND COVERAGE
30	# =============================================================================
31	# This page is the single place where the numeric knobs for host monitoring
32	# live. Other pages in this folder describe *why* a given area matters and
33	# *how* to act on an alert; this page is meant to answer "what number did we
34	# actually set, and who decided it." If you change a number here, also check
35	# whether the matching narrative page (disk-space-monitoring.md,
36	# console-log-files.md, log-file-growth.md, sqlite-file-locking.md,
37	# database-file-backup-copy.md, port-conflicts.md) needs a companion update,
38	# though in practice those pages tend to lag this one by a few weeks.
39	#
40	# Each section below is owned by the team most likely to be paged when that
41	# threshold fires, not necessarily the team that last edited the number.
42	# Threshold changes should go through the section owner even if someone else
43	# makes the edit.
44	#
45	# =============================================================================
46	# TERMINOLOGY
47	# =============================================================================
48	# Warn threshold:
49	#   The value at which a check should raise a low-severity alert — someone
50	#   should look at it during business hours, but nothing is actively broken.
51	#
52	# Critical threshold:
53	#   The value at which a check should raise a high-severity alert — the host
54	#   is close to, or already in, a bad state and should be looked at promptly.
55	#
56	# Check interval:
57	#   How often the host monitoring loop re-evaluates a given threshold, in
58	#   seconds. Shorter intervals catch problems faster but cost more CPU and
59	#   more log lines.
60	#
61	# Loopback port:
62	#   The local TCP port the service's HTTP interface binds to on 127.0.0.1.
63	#   Because it is loopback-only, conflicts are almost always with something
64	#   else on the same workstation, not with another host on the network.
65	#
66	# Bind attempt:
67	#   A single try by the service to acquire its loopback port at startup.
68	#   The monitoring checks count these separately from ordinary startup time.
69	#
70	# Busy timeout:
71	#   The amount of time SQLite's own driver will wait for a lock on the
72	#   database file to clear before giving up and returning a lock error.
73	#   This is a setting on the SQLite connection, not a host monitoring value,
74	#   but the thresholds below are tuned around it.
75	#
76	# Console log file:
77	#   The plain-text file the service writes its own startup, shutdown, and
78	#   request-handling lines to. On this host it is distinct from the
79	#   database file and from any OS-level system log.
80	#
81	# Working copy:
82	#   A copy of the database file made for backup purposes while the service
83	#   may still be running. It is not a live file the service reads from.
84	#
85	# Free space:
86	#   Disk space on the host volume that holds accountsvc's data directory,
87	#   reported in megabytes and as a percentage of total volume size.
88	#
89	# Watcher script:
90	#   The small standalone script (not part of the accountsvc package) that
91	#   reads this file, checks the host, and raises alerts. It lives in
92	#   scripts/ and is described briefly under Referenced Files below.
93	#
94	# Size delta:
95	#   The percentage difference in file size between a newly made backup copy
96	#   of the database file and the previous copy. Large jumps usually mean
97	#   something changed about how the service is being used, not that the
98	#   copy failed.
99	#
100	# =============================================================================
101	# DISK SPACE THRESHOLDS
102	# Section owner: Reliability (Priya Nair)
103	# =============================================================================
104	# These apply to the volume holding accountsvc's data directory (see
105	# filesystem-layout.md for exactly where that is on a given host type). The
106	# warn threshold is meant to give a comfortable few days of runway on a
107	# workstation; the critical threshold assumes the database file and console
108	# log files are the only things that will keep growing without a person
109	# stepping in.
110	disk_space:
111	  warn_percent_used: 80
112	  critical_percent_used: 92
113	  warn_free_megabytes: 2048
114	  critical_free_megabytes: 512
115	  check_interval_seconds: 300
116	  # Small-host note: on the shared small hosts (see
117	  # workstation-vs-small-host.md) several other things may share the volume,
118	  # so the critical free-space number is sometimes hit well before
119	  # accountsvc's own files look large. Host Operations occasionally lowers
120	  # warn_free_megabytes to 3072 on those hosts without changing this file,
121	  # which is why the two don't always line up — check the local override
122	  # file mentioned under Referenced Files before assuming this page is wrong.
123	
124	# =============================================================================
125	# MEMORY THRESHOLDS
126	# Section owner: Reliability (Priya Nair)
127	# =============================================================================
128	# accountsvc's own memory footprint is small and steady under normal load;
129	# these thresholds exist mainly to catch a host-wide memory problem (another
130	# process, a workstation left with too many browser tabs open, and so on)
131	# rather than anything specific to the package.
132	memory:
133	  warn_percent_used: 75
134	  critical_percent_used: 90
135	  warn_free_megabytes: 512
136	  critical_free_megabytes: 256
137	  check_interval_seconds: 300
138	  # These numbers assume a workstation with at least 8 GB of RAM. On the
139	  # smaller hosts described in workstation-vs-small-host.md, Devon's team has
140	  # sometimes run with warn_percent_used at 85 instead, since 75% is reached
141	  # almost immediately on a 2 GB host just from the OS and a desktop shell.
142	
143	# =============================================================================
144	# CONSOLE LOG FILE SIZE THRESHOLDS
145	# Section owner: Systems Support (Callum Reyes)
146	# =============================================================================
147	# These thresholds watch the size of the service's own console log file(s),
148	# not any OS system log. A single console log file growing past the warn
149	# size is usually fine; past the critical size it starts to slow down
150	# anything that tails or greps it, and on a small host it can start eating
151	# into the disk space thresholds above.
152	console_log_file:
153	  warn_size_megabytes: 100
154	  critical_size_megabytes: 250
155	  max_size_megabytes: 300
156	  check_interval_seconds: 600
157	  # max_size_megabytes is the point past which the watcher script expects a
158	  # new console log file to have been started already; if the current file
159	  # is still growing past this size, that is treated as its own alert
160	  # separate from the plain critical threshold, because it usually means the
161	  # log-growth handling described in log-file-growth.md (v1.4) didn't run.
162	  #
163	  # Cross-reference note: console-log-files.md (currently v1.1) describes
164	  # where these files live and how they're named; log-file-growth.md
165	  # describes what happens once a file crosses max_size_megabytes.
166	
167	# =============================================================================
168	# PORT CONFLICT CHECK THRESHOLDS
169	# Section owner: Host Operations (Devon Price)
170	# =============================================================================
171	# The service's HTTP interface binds a single loopback port at startup.
172	# These thresholds control how the watcher script decides that repeated
173	# bind failures at that port mean a real conflict rather than a slow
174	# startup or a previous copy of the service still shutting down.
175	port_conflict:
176	  check_interval_seconds: 60
177	  max_bind_attempts: 3
178	  bind_attempt_backoff_seconds: 2
179	  warn_after_conflicts_per_hour: 2
180	  critical_after_conflicts_per_hour: 5
181	  # A "conflict" here means the watcher script observed the configured port
182	  # already bound by a process it did not recognize as accountsvc itself at
183	  # the moment a start was attempted. One conflict right after a host restart
184	  # is common (something else grabbed the port before accountsvc could) and
185	  # is not counted toward the hourly figures above.
186	
187	# =============================================================================
188	# SQLITE FILE LOCKING THRESHOLDS
189	# Section owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
190	# =============================================================================
191	# These numbers exist because the database file is a single SQLite file on
192	# local disk with no separate lock manager. On a workstation with one user
193	# running the command line and the HTTP interface side by side, brief lock
194	# waits are normal; the thresholds below are for catching waits that go on
195	# long enough to suggest something is holding the file open longer than it
196	# should.
197	sqlite_locking:
198	  warn_busy_timeout_milliseconds: 5000
199	  critical_busy_timeout_milliseconds: 15000
200	  warn_wait_seconds: 5
201	  critical_wait_seconds: 15
202	  max_concurrent_writers: 1
203	  check_interval_seconds: 120
204	  # warn/critical_busy_timeout_milliseconds describe the busy-timeout value
205	  # the service's own SQLite connection is expected to be configured with,
206	  # not a value the watcher script sets itself. If you check the current
207	  # setting by hand, the equivalent sqlite3 command-line check is:
208	  #
209	  #   sqlite3 /path/to/accountsvc.db "PRAGMA busy_timeout;"
210	  #
211	  # max_concurrent_writers is always 1 for a local SQLite file used this way;
212	  # it is included here mainly as a documented constant so nobody "fixes" it
213	  # upward later while chasing a lock-wait alert.
214	
215	# =============================================================================
216	# DATABASE FILE BACKUP COPY THRESHOLDS
217	# Section owner: Infrastructure (Wren Ashby)
218	# =============================================================================
219	# These thresholds watch the recurring job that copies the database file out
220	# to a backup location. They are about the copy operation itself — its age,
221	# its size compared to the previous copy, and how long it took — not about
222	# what is stored inside the file.
223	database_backup_copy:
224	  warn_age_hours: 26
225	  critical_age_hours: 50
226	  warn_size_delta_percent: 15
227	  critical_size_delta_percent: 40
228	  copy_duration_warn_seconds: 30
229	  copy_duration_critical_seconds: 90
230	  check_interval_seconds: 900
231	  # warn_age_hours/critical_age_hours assume the backup copy job is meant to
232	  # run roughly once every 24 hours; the extra couple of hours of headroom
233	  # is there for hosts where the job is tied to a workstation being powered
234	  # on rather than a fixed daily job. If the copy job on a given host runs
235	  # more often than daily, Wren's team recommends tightening both numbers
236	  # rather than leaving the defaults, though as of this writing most hosts
237	  # still run the daily schedule and use the defaults above unchanged.
238	
239	# =============================================================================
240	# WORKED EXAMPLES AND PROCEDURES
241	# =============================================================================
242	#
243	# --- Example 1: Manually checking disk space against the thresholds above
244	#
245	#   On a Linux workstation or small host:
246	#
247	#     df -h /var/lib/accountsvc
248	#
249	#   Compare the "Use%" column against warn_percent_used (80) and
250	#   critical_percent_used (92) above. To get a size for accountsvc's own
251	#   files specifically (database file plus console logs), rather than the
252	#   whole volume:
253	#
254	#     du -sh /var/lib/accountsvc/*.db /var/log/accountsvc/*.log
255	#
256	#   On a Windows host running the small-host layout, the rough equivalent
257	#   is checking free space on the drive holding the data directory from
258	#   File Explorer's drive properties, or from a shell:
259	#
260	#     Get-PSDrive C | Select-Object Used,Free
261	#
262	# --- Example 2: Checking console log file size by hand
263	#
264	#   The watcher script does this automatically every ten minutes per the
265	#   check_interval_seconds value above, but to check by hand:
266	#
267	#     ls -lh /var/log/accountsvc/console.log
268	#
269	#   If the size is over 100 MB (warn_size_megabytes) but under 250 MB, this
270	#   is a warn-level condition and does not need immediate action beyond
271	#   confirming the log-growth handling from log-file-growth.md has run
272	#   recently. Past 300 MB (max_size_megabytes), open console-log-files.md
273	#   and confirm a new log file has actually been started.
274	#
275	# --- Example 3: Diagnosing a suspected port conflict before it hits
276	#     the critical threshold
277	#
278	#   Find whatever currently holds the loopback port the service expects:
279	#
280	#     # Linux / macOS
281	#     lsof -i :8080
282	#
283	#     # Windows
284	#     netstat -ano | findstr :8080
285	#
286	#   If the same unrelated process shows up across several checks within an
287	#   hour, that will push past warn_after_conflicts_per_hour (2) on its own;
288	#   see port-conflicts.md for what to do once you've identified the
289	#   process holding the port.
290	#
291	# --- Example 4: Checking SQLite lock wait behavior
292	#
293	#   Confirm the current busy-timeout setting the service's connection is
294	#   using (see sqlite-file-locking.md v2.1 for background on why this
295	#   matters):
296	#
297	#     sqlite3 /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db "PRAGMA busy_timeout;"
298	#
299	#   To reproduce a lock wait on purpose for a check, open a second
300	#   interactive sqlite3 session against the same file and start a
301	#   transaction that holds a write lock:
302	#
303	#     sqlite3 /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db
304	#     sqlite> BEGIN IMMEDIATE;
305	#     -- leave this session open, then try to use the service normally --
306	#
307	#   A wait under 5 seconds (warn_wait_seconds) before the lock clears is
308	#   normal contention. A wait past 15 seconds (critical_wait_seconds)
309	#   usually means the second session (or another copy of the service) was
310	#   left open by accident.
311	#
312	# --- Example 5: Making a backup copy of the database file and checking
313	#     it against the thresholds
314	#
315	#   The simplest safe copy, since SQLite's own file format tolerates a
316	#   straight file copy as long as nothing is mid-write:
317	#
318	#     sqlite3 /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db ".backup '/backups/accountsvc-2026-09-27.db'"
319	#
320	#   Then compare the new copy's size against the previous one:
321	#
322	#     ls -l /backups/accountsvc-2026-09-26.db /backups/accountsvc-2026-09-27.db
323	#
324	#   A difference under 15% (warn_size_delta_percent) is unremarkable day to
325	#   day. A jump past 40% (critical_size_delta_percent) in either direction
326	#   is worth a look — usually it means unusually heavy use of the service
327	#   the prior day, not a problem with the copy step itself. Timing the copy
328	#   with `time` on Linux or Measure-Command on Windows and comparing the
329	#   result against copy_duration_warn_seconds (30) / copy_duration_critical_seconds
330	#   (90) is described further in database-file-backup-copy.md.
331	#
332	# =============================================================================
333	# HOW THESE THRESHOLDS ARE USED BY HOST MONITORING
334	# Section owner: Reliability (Priya Nair)
335	# =============================================================================
336	# The watcher script (scripts/host_monitor_check on most hosts) reads this
337	# file once at startup and re-reads it if the file's modification time
338	# changes, so an edit here takes effect without restarting the host
339	# monitoring loop itself. Each of the six blocks above maps to one check
340	# function inside that script; the check_interval_seconds value under each
341	# block controls how often that particular check runs, independent of the
342	# others — disk space is checked every five minutes while SQLite locking is
343	# checked every two, for instance.
344	#
345	# On workstations where the watcher script is run under a user's own account
346	# session rather than a system-level Scheduled Task or cron entry, checks
347	# only run while that session is active — see workstation-vs-small-host.md
348	# for how this affects coverage overnight or over a weekend.
349	#
350	# =============================================================================
351	# REFERENCED FILES AND HOST PATHS
352	# =============================================================================
353	referenced_files:
354	  - path: operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-thresholds.yaml
355	    purpose: This page; the source of truth for the numeric values above.
356	  - path: operations-runbooks/host-monitoring.md
357	    purpose: Narrative page describing what host monitoring watches and why; does not itself hold numbers.
358	  - path: operations-runbooks/disk-space-monitoring.md
359	    purpose: Procedures for freeing disk space once a threshold from this page fires.
360	  - path: operations-runbooks/console-log-files.md
361	    purpose: Describes where console log files live and how they are named.
362	  - path: operations-runbooks/log-file-growth.md
363	    purpose: Describes what happens once a console log file crosses max_size_megabytes.
364	  - path: operations-runbooks/sqlite-file-locking.md
365	    purpose: Background on why SQLite locking behaves the way it does on this host.
366	  - path: operations-runbooks/database-file-backup-copy.md
367	    purpose: Full procedure for making and verifying a backup copy of the database file.
368	  - path: operations-runbooks/port-conflicts.md
369	    purpose: Diagnosis steps for a loopback port already in use.
370	  - path: operations-runbooks/filesystem-layout.md
371	    purpose: Where accountsvc's data directory and console log directory sit on a given host type.
372	  - path: operations-runbooks/workstation-vs-small-host.md
373	    purpose: How coverage and scheduling of these checks differ between a personal workstation and a small shared host.
374	  - path: scripts/host_monitor_check
375	    purpose: The watcher script that reads this file and raises alerts against it.
376	  - path: scripts/host_monitor_overrides.yaml
377	    purpose: Optional per-host override file some small hosts use to adjust a handful of values from this page locally.
378	  - path: /var/log/accountsvc/console.log
379	    purpose: Example console log file path referenced in the log-size examples above.
380	  - path: /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db
381	    purpose: Example database file path referenced in the SQLite and backup-copy examples above.
382	
383	# =============================================================================
384	# TOOLS AND LIBRARIES
385	# =============================================================================
386	tools:
387	  - name: accountsvc
388	    version: "1.4"
389	    note: Standard-library-only Python package this page's checks all exist to support.
390	  - name: Python
391	    version: "3.11"
392	    note: Interpreter the watcher script itself runs under on most hosts.
393	  - name: sqlite3 (command-line tool)
394	    version: "3.44.0"
395	    note: Used for PRAGMA checks and the .backup command in the worked examples.
396	  - name: cron
397	    version: system-provided
398	    note: Schedules the watcher script on Linux small hosts.
399	  - name: Task Scheduler
400	    version: Windows 10/11 built-in
401	    note: Schedules the watcher script on Windows workstations.
402	  - name: lsof
403	    version: "4.95"
404	    note: Identifies what holds the loopback port during a conflict check.
405	  - name: PSDrive (PowerShell cmdlet)
406	    version: PowerShell 5.1 built-in
407	    note: Used for the Windows disk-space example above.
408	
409	# =============================================================================
410	# CHANGE LOG
411	# =============================================================================
412	change_log:
413	  - date: "2024-05-30"
414	    release: "1.0"
415	    change: >
416	      Initial version of this page; pulled the disk space and console log
417	      size numbers out of the old combined host-monitoring.md page into
418	      their own thresholds file so they could be edited without touching
419	      the narrative content.
420	  - date: "2024-10-14"
421	    release: "1.0.1"
422	    change: >
423	      Added the SQLite locking block after a workstation incident where a
424	      left-open interactive sqlite3 session held a write lock for over
425	      twenty minutes with no alert.
426	  - date: "2025-01-25"
427	    release: "1.1"
428	    change: >
429	      Added the port conflict block, coordinated with Devon Price's port
430	      conflict diagnosis work; set initial bind attempt and hourly
431	      conflict thresholds.
432	  - date: "2025-03-18"
433	    release: "1.1.1"
434	    change: >
435	      Lowered warn_free_megabytes for disk space from 3072 to 2048 after
436	      confirming most workstations do not need the extra headroom.
437	  - date: "2025-07-20"
438	    release: "1.1.2"
439	    change: >
440	      Adjusted console log warn/critical sizes upward (from 60/150 MB to
441	      100/250 MB) to match the larger default log-growth handling
442	      thresholds in log-file-growth.md.
443	  - date: "2025-08-05"
444	    release: "1.1.3"
445	    change: >
446	      Added the database backup copy block at Wren Ashby's request, with
447	      initial age and size-delta thresholds.
448	  - date: "2025-08-19"
449	    release: "1.2"
450	    change: >
451	      Reworked the memory block to use separate free-megabytes and
452	      percent-used thresholds rather than percent-used alone; added the
453	      small-host notes under disk space and memory documenting where
454	      Host Operations runs different local numbers.
455	
456	# =============================================================================
457	# RELATED PAGES
458	# =============================================================================
459	# - Operations Runbooks Index
460	# - Monitoring Host Health Around accountsvc
461	# - Watching Disk Space on the Host
462	# - Managing the Service's Console Log Files
463	# - Keeping Console Log Files From Growing Too Large
464	# - Understanding SQLite File Locking on This Host
465	# - Copying the Database File for Backup
466	# - Diagnosing Loopback Port Conflicts
467	# - Filesystem Layout for accountsvc on a Host
468	# - Running accountsvc on a Workstation vs. a Small Host
469	# - Quick Troubleshooting Checklist

# operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-thresholds.yaml
#
# =============================================================================
# HEADER BLOCK
# =============================================================================
# Title:         Host Monitoring Threshold Settings
# Version:       1.2
# Owner:         Reliability (Priya Nair)
# Last updated:  2025-08-19
#
# Summary:
#   This page holds the numeric threshold values that host monitoring checks
#   read when they decide whether accountsvc's host is in a warn or critical
#   state. It covers disk space, memory, the size of the service's own
#   console log files, loopback port conflicts, SQLite file locking, and the
#   copying of the database file for backup. The values here are the ones
#   currently wired into the monitoring checks that run on a workstation or a
#   small host running accountsvc; they are not aspirational targets, they
#   are what the checks actually compare against today.
#
#   accountsvc itself has no monitoring of its own — it is a small package
#   built on the standard library, with a command line and a loopback HTTP
#   service, that keeps its state in a local SQLite file. All of the
#   thresholds below live in host-level tooling (cron jobs, Scheduled Tasks,
#   a small watcher script in scripts/) that watches the host the package
#   runs on.
#
# =============================================================================
# PURPOSE AND COVERAGE
# =============================================================================
# This page is the single place where the numeric knobs for host monitoring
# live. Other pages in this folder describe *why* a given area matters and
# *how* to act on an alert; this page is meant to answer "what number did we
# actually set, and who decided it." If you change a number here, also check
# whether the matching narrative page (disk-space-monitoring.md,
# console-log-files.md, log-file-growth.md, sqlite-file-locking.md,
# database-file-backup-copy.md, port-conflicts.md) needs a companion update,
# though in practice those pages tend to lag this one by a few weeks.
#
# Each section below is owned by the team most likely to be paged when that
# threshold fires, not necessarily the team that last edited the number.
# Threshold changes should go through the section owner even if someone else
# makes the edit.
#
# =============================================================================
# TERMINOLOGY
# =============================================================================
# Warn threshold:
#   The value at which a check should raise a low-severity alert — someone
#   should look at it during business hours, but nothing is actively broken.
#
# Critical threshold:
#   The value at which a check should raise a high-severity alert — the host
#   is close to, or already in, a bad state and should be looked at promptly.
#
# Check interval:
#   How often the host monitoring loop re-evaluates a given threshold, in
#   seconds. Shorter intervals catch problems faster but cost more CPU and
#   more log lines.
#
# Loopback port:
#   The local TCP port the service's HTTP interface binds to on 127.0.0.1.
#   Because it is loopback-only, conflicts are almost always with something
#   else on the same workstation, not with another host on the network.
#
# Bind attempt:
#   A single try by the service to acquire its loopback port at startup.
#   The monitoring checks count these separately from ordinary startup time.
#
# Busy timeout:
#   The amount of time SQLite's own driver will wait for a lock on the
#   database file to clear before giving up and returning a lock error.
#   This is a setting on the SQLite connection, not a host monitoring value,
#   but the thresholds below are tuned around it.
#
# Console log file:
#   The plain-text file the service writes its own startup, shutdown, and
#   request-handling lines to. On this host it is distinct from the
#   database file and from any OS-level system log.
#
# Working copy:
#   A copy of the database file made for backup purposes while the service
#   may still be running. It is not a live file the service reads from.
#
# Free space:
#   Disk space on the host volume that holds accountsvc's data directory,
#   reported in megabytes and as a percentage of total volume size.
#
# Watcher script:
#   The small standalone script (not part of the accountsvc package) that
#   reads this file, checks the host, and raises alerts. It lives in
#   scripts/ and is described briefly under Referenced Files below.
#
# Size delta:
#   The percentage difference in file size between a newly made backup copy
#   of the database file and the previous copy. Large jumps usually mean
#   something changed about how the service is being used, not that the
#   copy failed.
#
# =============================================================================
# DISK SPACE THRESHOLDS
# Section owner: Reliability (Priya Nair)
# =============================================================================
# These apply to the volume holding accountsvc's data directory (see
# filesystem-layout.md for exactly where that is on a given host type). The
# warn threshold is meant to give a comfortable few days of runway on a
# workstation; the critical threshold assumes the database file and console
# log files are the only things that will keep growing without a person
# stepping in.
disk_space:
  warn_percent_used: 80
  critical_percent_used: 92
  warn_free_megabytes: 2048
  critical_free_megabytes: 512
  check_interval_seconds: 300
  # Small-host note: on the shared small hosts (see
  # workstation-vs-small-host.md) several other things may share the volume,
  # so the critical free-space number is sometimes hit well before
  # accountsvc's own files look large. Host Operations occasionally lowers
  # warn_free_megabytes to 3072 on those hosts without changing this file,
  # which is why the two don't always line up — check the local override
  # file mentioned under Referenced Files before assuming this page is wrong.

# =============================================================================
# MEMORY THRESHOLDS
# Section owner: Reliability (Priya Nair)
# =============================================================================
# accountsvc's own memory footprint is small and steady under normal load;
# these thresholds exist mainly to catch a host-wide memory problem (another
# process, a workstation left with too many browser tabs open, and so on)
# rather than anything specific to the package.
memory:
  warn_percent_used: 75
  critical_percent_used: 90
  warn_free_megabytes: 512
  critical_free_megabytes: 256
  check_interval_seconds: 300
  # These numbers assume a workstation with at least 8 GB of RAM. On the
  # smaller hosts described in workstation-vs-small-host.md, Devon's team has
  # sometimes run with warn_percent_used at 85 instead, since 75% is reached
  # almost immediately on a 2 GB host just from the OS and a desktop shell.

# =============================================================================
# CONSOLE LOG FILE SIZE THRESHOLDS
# Section owner: Systems Support (Callum Reyes)
# =============================================================================
# These thresholds watch the size of the service's own console log file(s),
# not any OS system log. A single console log file growing past the warn
# size is usually fine; past the critical size it starts to slow down
# anything that tails or greps it, and on a small host it can start eating
# into the disk space thresholds above.
console_log_file:
  warn_size_megabytes: 100
  critical_size_megabytes: 250
  max_size_megabytes: 300
  check_interval_seconds: 600
  # max_size_megabytes is the point past which the watcher script expects a
  # new console log file to have been started already; if the current file
  # is still growing past this size, that is treated as its own alert
  # separate from the plain critical threshold, because it usually means the
  # log-growth handling described in log-file-growth.md (v1.4) didn't run.
  #
  # Cross-reference note: console-log-files.md (currently v1.1) describes
  # where these files live and how they're named; log-file-growth.md
  # describes what happens once a file crosses max_size_megabytes.

# =============================================================================
# PORT CONFLICT CHECK THRESHOLDS
# Section owner: Host Operations (Devon Price)
# =============================================================================
# The service's HTTP interface binds a single loopback port at startup.
# These thresholds control how the watcher script decides that repeated
# bind failures at that port mean a real conflict rather than a slow
# startup or a previous copy of the service still shutting down.
port_conflict:
  check_interval_seconds: 60
  max_bind_attempts: 3
  bind_attempt_backoff_seconds: 2
  warn_after_conflicts_per_hour: 2
  critical_after_conflicts_per_hour: 5
  # A "conflict" here means the watcher script observed the configured port
  # already bound by a process it did not recognize as accountsvc itself at
  # the moment a start was attempted. One conflict right after a host restart
  # is common (something else grabbed the port before accountsvc could) and
  # is not counted toward the hourly figures above.

# =============================================================================
# SQLITE FILE LOCKING THRESHOLDS
# Section owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
# =============================================================================
# These numbers exist because the database file is a single SQLite file on
# local disk with no separate lock manager. On a workstation with one user
# running the command line and the HTTP interface side by side, brief lock
# waits are normal; the thresholds below are for catching waits that go on
# long enough to suggest something is holding the file open longer than it
# should.
sqlite_locking:
  warn_busy_timeout_milliseconds: 5000
  critical_busy_timeout_milliseconds: 15000
  warn_wait_seconds: 5
  critical_wait_seconds: 15
  max_concurrent_writers: 1
  check_interval_seconds: 120
  # warn/critical_busy_timeout_milliseconds describe the busy-timeout value
  # the service's own SQLite connection is expected to be configured with,
  # not a value the watcher script sets itself. If you check the current
  # setting by hand, the equivalent sqlite3 command-line check is:
  #
  #   sqlite3 /path/to/accountsvc.db "PRAGMA busy_timeout;"
  #
  # max_concurrent_writers is always 1 for a local SQLite file used this way;
  # it is included here mainly as a documented constant so nobody "fixes" it
  # upward later while chasing a lock-wait alert.

# =============================================================================
# DATABASE FILE BACKUP COPY THRESHOLDS
# Section owner: Infrastructure (Wren Ashby)
# =============================================================================
# These thresholds watch the recurring job that copies the database file out
# to a backup location. They are about the copy operation itself — its age,
# its size compared to the previous copy, and how long it took — not about
# what is stored inside the file.
database_backup_copy:
  warn_age_hours: 26
  critical_age_hours: 50
  warn_size_delta_percent: 15
  critical_size_delta_percent: 40
  copy_duration_warn_seconds: 30
  copy_duration_critical_seconds: 90
  check_interval_seconds: 900
  # warn_age_hours/critical_age_hours assume the backup copy job is meant to
  # run roughly once every 24 hours; the extra couple of hours of headroom
  # is there for hosts where the job is tied to a workstation being powered
  # on rather than a fixed daily job. If the copy job on a given host runs
  # more often than daily, Wren's team recommends tightening both numbers
  # rather than leaving the defaults, though as of this writing most hosts
  # still run the daily schedule and use the defaults above unchanged.

# =============================================================================
# WORKED EXAMPLES AND PROCEDURES
# =============================================================================
#
# --- Example 1: Manually checking disk space against the thresholds above
#
#   On a Linux workstation or small host:
#
#     df -h /var/lib/accountsvc
#
#   Compare the "Use%" column against warn_percent_used (80) and
#   critical_percent_used (92) above. To get a size for accountsvc's own
#   files specifically (database file plus console logs), rather than the
#   whole volume:
#
#     du -sh /var/lib/accountsvc/*.db /var/log/accountsvc/*.log
#
#   On a Windows host running the small-host layout, the rough equivalent
#   is checking free space on the drive holding the data directory from
#   File Explorer's drive properties, or from a shell:
#
#     Get-PSDrive C | Select-Object Used,Free
#
# --- Example 2: Checking console log file size by hand
#
#   The watcher script does this automatically every ten minutes per the
#   check_interval_seconds value above, but to check by hand:
#
#     ls -lh /var/log/accountsvc/console.log
#
#   If the size is over 100 MB (warn_size_megabytes) but under 250 MB, this
#   is a warn-level condition and does not need immediate action beyond
#   confirming the log-growth handling from log-file-growth.md has run
#   recently. Past 300 MB (max_size_megabytes), open console-log-files.md
#   and confirm a new log file has actually been started.
#
# --- Example 3: Diagnosing a suspected port conflict before it hits
#     the critical threshold
#
#   Find whatever currently holds the loopback port the service expects:
#
#     # Linux / macOS
#     lsof -i :8080
#
#     # Windows
#     netstat -ano | findstr :8080
#
#   If the same unrelated process shows up across several checks within an
#   hour, that will push past warn_after_conflicts_per_hour (2) on its own;
#   see port-conflicts.md for what to do once you've identified the
#   process holding the port.
#
# --- Example 4: Checking SQLite lock wait behavior
#
#   Confirm the current busy-timeout setting the service's connection is
#   using (see sqlite-file-locking.md v2.1 for background on why this
#   matters):
#
#     sqlite3 /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db "PRAGMA busy_timeout;"
#
#   To reproduce a lock wait on purpose for a check, open a second
#   interactive sqlite3 session against the same file and start a
#   transaction that holds a write lock:
#
#     sqlite3 /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db
#     sqlite> BEGIN IMMEDIATE;
#     -- leave this session open, then try to use the service normally --
#
#   A wait under 5 seconds (warn_wait_seconds) before the lock clears is
#   normal contention. A wait past 15 seconds (critical_wait_seconds)
#   usually means the second session (or another copy of the service) was
#   left open by accident.
#
# --- Example 5: Making a backup copy of the database file and checking
#     it against the thresholds
#
#   The simplest safe copy, since SQLite's own file format tolerates a
#   straight file copy as long as nothing is mid-write:
#
#     sqlite3 /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db ".backup '/backups/accountsvc-2026-09-27.db'"
#
#   Then compare the new copy's size against the previous one:
#
#     ls -l /backups/accountsvc-2026-09-26.db /backups/accountsvc-2026-09-27.db
#
#   A difference under 15% (warn_size_delta_percent) is unremarkable day to
#   day. A jump past 40% (critical_size_delta_percent) in either direction
#   is worth a look — usually it means unusually heavy use of the service
#   the prior day, not a problem with the copy step itself. Timing the copy
#   with `time` on Linux or Measure-Command on Windows and comparing the
#   result against copy_duration_warn_seconds (30) / copy_duration_critical_seconds
#   (90) is described further in database-file-backup-copy.md.
#
# =============================================================================
# HOW THESE THRESHOLDS ARE USED BY HOST MONITORING
# Section owner: Reliability (Priya Nair)
# =============================================================================
# The watcher script (scripts/host_monitor_check on most hosts) reads this
# file once at startup and re-reads it if the file's modification time
# changes, so an edit here takes effect without restarting the host
# monitoring loop itself. Each of the six blocks above maps to one check
# function inside that script; the check_interval_seconds value under each
# block controls how often that particular check runs, independent of the
# others — disk space is checked every five minutes while SQLite locking is
# checked every two, for instance.
#
# On workstations where the watcher script is run under a user's own account
# session rather than a system-level Scheduled Task or cron entry, checks
# only run while that session is active — see workstation-vs-small-host.md
# for how this affects coverage overnight or over a weekend.
#
# =============================================================================
# REFERENCED FILES AND HOST PATHS
# =============================================================================
referenced_files:
  - path: operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-thresholds.yaml
    purpose: This page; the source of truth for the numeric values above.
  - path: operations-runbooks/host-monitoring.md
    purpose: Narrative page describing what host monitoring watches and why; does not itself hold numbers.
  - path: operations-runbooks/disk-space-monitoring.md
    purpose: Procedures for freeing disk space once a threshold from this page fires.
  - path: operations-runbooks/console-log-files.md
    purpose: Describes where console log files live and how they are named.
  - path: operations-runbooks/log-file-growth.md
    purpose: Describes what happens once a console log file crosses max_size_megabytes.
  - path: operations-runbooks/sqlite-file-locking.md
    purpose: Background on why SQLite locking behaves the way it does on this host.
  - path: operations-runbooks/database-file-backup-copy.md
    purpose: Full procedure for making and verifying a backup copy of the database file.
  - path: operations-runbooks/port-conflicts.md
    purpose: Diagnosis steps for a loopback port already in use.
  - path: operations-runbooks/filesystem-layout.md
    purpose: Where accountsvc's data directory and console log directory sit on a given host type.
  - path: operations-runbooks/workstation-vs-small-host.md
    purpose: How coverage and scheduling of these checks differ between a personal workstation and a small shared host.
  - path: scripts/host_monitor_check
    purpose: The watcher script that reads this file and raises alerts against it.
  - path: scripts/host_monitor_overrides.yaml
    purpose: Optional per-host override file some small hosts use to adjust a handful of values from this page locally.
  - path: /var/log/accountsvc/console.log
    purpose: Example console log file path referenced in the log-size examples above.
  - path: /var/lib/accountsvc/accountsvc.db
    purpose: Example database file path referenced in the SQLite and backup-copy examples above.

# =============================================================================
# TOOLS AND LIBRARIES
# =============================================================================
tools:
  - name: accountsvc
    version: "1.4"
    note: Standard-library-only Python package this page's checks all exist to support.
  - name: Python

    note: Identifies what holds the loopback port during a conflict check.
  - name: PSDrive (PowerShell cmdlet)

1	# Diagnosing Loopback Port Conflicts
2	
3	| Field | Value |
4	|-------|-------|
5	| **Title** | Diagnosing Loopback Port Conflicts |
6	| **Version** | 2.1 |
7	| **Owner** | Host Operations (Devon Price) |
8	| **Last Updated** | 2025-01-18 |
9	
10	## Overview
11	
12	When the accountsvc service fails to start with a "port already in use" error, or when the loopback HTTP listener crashes unexpectedly, a port conflict has occurred. Another process on the same workstation or small host is already bound to the port that accountsvc expects to listen on. This runbook walks you through finding the conflicting process, understanding why it's present, and resolving the conflict without disrupting normal service operation or other running applications.
13	
14	Port conflicts are among the most common operational issues on development workstations and small host deployments. Unlike larger infrastructure, a single machine running multiple services means shared network resources and a higher probability of collision.
15	
16	## Coverage
17	
18	This page covers loopback port conflicts specifically—conflicts on `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`. It does not cover network-facing (external) port bindings, firewall rules, or network interface configuration. For broader host health and monitoring context, see the host monitoring page.
19	
20	The procedures assume a Windows 10 workstation or a small single-machine host running Linux or Windows, where accountsvc is the primary service. Multi-machine deployments should consult your infrastructure team.
21	
22	## Finding the Conflicting Process
23	
24	### Windows Workstations (PowerShell)
25	
26	The most reliable method on Windows is the `netstat` command, which lists all active network connections and listening ports.
27	
28	```
29	netstat -anob
30	```
31	
32	The flags mean:
33	- `-a`: Show all connections and listening ports
34	- `-n`: Display host and port numbers in numerical form
35	- `-o`: Include the process identifier (PID) for each connection
36	- `-b`: Show the executable name associated with each connection
37	
38	Run this in PowerShell with elevated access. The output is verbose; filter for the port accountsvc uses (commonly port 8080) to find your conflict:
39	
40	```
41	netstat -anob | findstr :8080
42	```
43	
44	This returns one or more lines like:
45	
46	```
47	  TCP    127.0.0.1:8080         0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING       2944
48	  TCP    [::1]:8080             [::]:0                 LISTENING       2944
49	```
50	
51	The PID `2944` appears on the right. Cross-reference it with the task manager or use `Get-Process`:
52	
53	```
54	Get-Process -Id 2944
55	```
56	
57	Output example:
58	```
59	Handles  NPM(K)    PM(K)      WS(K)     CPU(s)     Id  SI ProcessName
60	-------  ------    -----      -----     ------     --  -- -----------
61	    120       8    15232      18404       0.05   2944   1 python
62	```
63	
64	The executable is `python` running as PID 2944. Open Task Manager (`Taskmgr.exe`) and locate this process to see its full command line and parent process. Note the working directory if visible.
65	
66	### Linux / Small Hosts (Bash)
67	
68	On Linux, use `lsof` (list open files) or `ss` (socket statistics), both showing process names and port bindings:
69	
70	```
71	sudo lsof -i :8080
72	```
73	
74	Output:
75	```
76	The output lists process command, process identifier, owning user, file descriptor, connection protocol type, network interface details, size metric, and node designation.
77	python3    5521   root   17u  IPv4   123456      0t0  TCP localhost:8080 (LISTEN)
78	python3    5521   root   18u  IPv6   123457      0t0  TCP [::1]:8080 (LISTEN)
79	```
80	
81	The PID is `5521`. Check its details:
82	
83	```
84	ps aux | grep 5521
85	```
86	
87	Or use `ss` for a more structured output:
88	
89	```
90	sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080
91	```
92	
93	This shows the listening socket, protocol (TCP), and the process PID and name.
94	
95	## Understanding the Cause
96	
97	Once you have identified the process, determine what it is and why it is running. Common scenarios:
98	
99	| Process | Likely Cause | Action |
100	|---------|--------------|--------|
101	| Another instance of accountsvc | Supervisor restarted it, or an old process did not terminate cleanly | Check supervisor logs; see *startup-and-shutdown.rst* |
102	| IDE development server (Flask, Django, etc.) | Developer left their local server running in the background | Contact the developer or close their IDE session |
103	| Node.js / npm dev server | JavaScript development tool left running | Check the working directory; alert the developer |
104	| Java application or build tool | Another service or CI tool on the machine | Coordinate with the team running that application |
105	| System service or daemon | OS-level service auto-started at boot | Verify it is necessary; disable if redundant |
106	| Verification process runner | Automated verification or monitoring process still running | Check scheduled tasks (Windows) or cron (Linux) |
107	
108	### Checking for Multiple accountsvc Instances
109	
110	The most common cause is that accountsvc has crashed or hung, but the supervisor process (if configured) has not yet restarted it, or two supervisors are managing the same service:
111	
112	On Windows, verify only one accountsvc instance is present:
113	
114	```
115	Get-Process python | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -eq "python" }
116	```
117	
118	On Linux:
119	
120	```
121	ps aux | grep accountsvc
122	```
123	
124	Look for duplicate processes or processes with identical command lines. If you see two running accountsvc services, one is likely the old crashed process and one is the new restart. Proceed to **Resolving the Conflict** below.
125	
126	If the conflicting process is unrelated to accountsvc, decide whether to terminate it, move it to a different port, or reconfigure accountsvc to use an alternate port.
127	
128	## Resolving the Conflict
129	
130	### Option 1: Terminate the Conflicting Process (Preferred if Safe)
131	
132	If the conflicting process is dead or extraneous, terminate it cleanly:
133	
134	**Windows (PowerShell):**
135	
136	```
137	Stop-Process -Id 2944
138	```
139	
140	Verify it has stopped:
141	
142	```
143	Get-Process -Id 2944 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
144	```
145	
146	If no output appears, the process has exited.
147	
148	**Linux:**
149	
150	```
151	sudo kill 5521
152	```
153	
154	Wait a few seconds and check:
155	
156	```
157	sudo lsof -i :8080
158	```
159	
160	If the port is now free, proceed to restart accountsvc via its supervisor. See *process-supervision.rst* for the correct restart procedure on your host.
161	
162	If the process does not respond to `SIGTERM`, use `kill -9`:
163	
164	```
165	sudo kill -9 5521
166	```
167	
168	### Option 2: Change the Service Port
169	
170	If the conflicting process is legitimate and in use, configure accountsvc to listen on a different loopback port. Configuration is typically stored in a local settings file or environment variable (consult your host's setup guide or the filesystem layout page). After reconfiguring the port, restart accountsvc and verify the new port is listening:
171	
172	**Windows:**
173	
174	```
175	netstat -anob | findstr :8081
176	```
177	
178	**Linux:**
179	
180	```
181	sudo lsof -i :8081
182	```
183	
184	If the port is now in use and accountsvc is listening, the conflict is resolved. Update any application code, monitoring scripts, or documentation that referenced the old port.
185	
186	### Option 3: Restart the Supervisor (Nuclear Option)
187	
188	If you cannot cleanly terminate the process or identify the conflict, restarting the supervisor process will kill all children and perform a full service restart:
189	
190	**Windows (if using a Windows Service or Task Scheduler):**
191	
192	Open Task Scheduler (`taskschd.msc`) and disable then re-enable the accountsvc task. Or, restart the service via Services (`services.msc`).
193	
194	**Linux (if using systemd):**
195	
196	```
197	sudo systemctl restart accountsvc
198	```
199	
200	This forcefully terminates all accountsvc processes and restarts the supervisor, clearing port bindings. Use only if other methods fail, as it may interrupt ongoing operations. Coordinate with accountsvc users beforehand.
201	
202	## Preventing Port Conflicts
203	
204	### Use a Non-Standard Port
205	
206	Development workstations often run multiple services. Consider configuring accountsvc to use port 8888 or 9090 rather than the common port 8080. Fewer applications bind to these ports, reducing collision probability.
207	
208	### Enable Socket Reuse
209	
210	Modern operating systems support the `SO_REUSEADDR` socket option, which allows a process to bind to a port shortly after the previous process releases it, avoiding a lingering `TIME_WAIT` state. The accountsvc service has this option enabled by default; no configuration is required.
211	
212	### Isolate Development Environments
213	
214	If running multiple accountsvc instances for different projects on the same workstation, use containers (Docker) or virtual machines to isolate each instance and its port bindings. See *workstation-vs-small-host.md* for guidance on multi-instance setups.
215	
216	### Regular Port Monitoring
217	
218	On shared hosts, periodically check port assignments to identify unexpected listeners:
219	
220	**Windows:**
221	
222	```
223	Execute netstat showing all connections in numerical format with associated process information, saving output to a file for review.
224	```
225	
226	**Linux:**
227	
228	```
229	Execute netstat with elevated access showing all listening connections in numerical format with process information, saving output to a file.
230	```
231	
232	Review the file for unfamiliar processes and investigate anomalies.
233	
234	## Related Operational Topics
235	
236	### Disk Space and Log File Growth
237	
238	When troubleshooting a crashed accountsvc service, check whether disk space exhaustion caused the failure. A full disk prevents the service from writing console log files, which may hide the root cause. See *disk-space-monitoring.md* and *console-log-files.md* for diagnostic and preventive steps.
239	
240	### SQLite File Locking
241	
242	If accountsvc terminates unexpectedly during a port conflict resolution or restart, the SQLite database file may remain locked by a zombie process. See *sqlite-file-locking.md* for diagnosing and clearing file locks before restarting the service.
243	
244	### Backup and Restoration
245	
246	After resolving a port conflict and restarting accountsvc, verify data consistency by checking the database file's modification time and size. A recent anomaly (such as sudden growth or a timestamp far in the past) may indicate corruption. See *database-file-backup-copy.md* for backup procedures and *host-monitoring.md* for continuous monitoring thresholds.
247	
248	## Terminology and Glossary
249	
250	**Loopback Interface**
251	The reserved loopback IP `127.0.0.1` (IPv4) or `[::1]` (IPv6) that refers to the local machine only. Traffic to loopback IPs does not traverse the network stack and is isolated to a single host. The service listens exclusively on loopback.
252	
253	**Port Binding**
254	The act of a process claiming exclusive use of a TCP port on a specific interface. Once a process binds to a port, other processes cannot bind to the same interface and port pair until the original process closes the socket.
255	
256	**Port Conflict (also Port Collision)**
257	A condition where two processes attempt to bind to the same loopback port simultaneously, or when a process tries to bind to a port already claimed by another process. The second process receives an error and cannot start.
258	
259	**TIME_WAIT State**
260	A TCP socket state that occurs after a connection is closed. The operating system holds the socket in this state briefly (typically 60 seconds on Linux, longer on Windows) to ensure delayed packets are not misdelivered to a new process on the same port. This can cause a "port in use" error if restarting a service quickly.
261	
262	**Process Identifier (PID)**
263	A unique numerical identifier assigned by the operating system to each running process. PIDs allow tools like `netstat`, `lsof`, and `ps` to correlate network bindings with specific executables.
264	
265	**Socket**
266	A connection point for network communication created by the operating system. A socket is identified by a protocol (TCP), a local interface, and a local port. Binding a socket reserves the port for exclusive use.
267	
268	**Listening Port**
269	A port on which a process is actively accepting incoming network connections. The port is said to be in the `LISTEN` state, and incoming connection requests on that port are routed to the listening process.
270	
271	**Netstat**
272	A command-line tool available on Windows and Linux that displays network connections, network configuration tables, and interface statistics. It is useful for identifying processes that are listening on or have open connections to specific ports.
273	
274	**lsof (list open files)**
275	A Unix and Linux command that lists all files and network sockets opened by running processes. With the `-i` flag, it filters for network connections and is the preferred tool for port diagnostics on Linux systems.
276	
277	## Referenced Files and Paths
278	
279	| Path | Purpose |
280	|------|------|
281	| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\` (Windows) or `/opt/accountsvc/` (Linux) | Working directory for the accountsvc service instance; contains configuration and state files. |
282	| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\accounts.db` (Windows) or `/opt/accountsvc/accounts.db` (Linux) | SQLite database file holding service state. Locking issues often occur here during restarts. |
283	| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\service.log` (Windows) or `/var/log/accountsvc.log` (Linux) | Primary console log file written by accountsvc. Check for startup errors or crash messages. |
284	| `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` (Windows) or `/etc/hosts` (Linux) | System host file; accountsvc resolves `localhost` using this file. Misconfiguration is rare but worth checking if loopback connectivity fails. |

# Diagnosing Loopback Port Conflicts

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Diagnosing Loopback Port Conflicts |
| **Version** | 2.1 |
| **Owner** | Host Operations (Devon Price) |
| **Last Updated** | 2025-01-18 |

## Overview

When the accountsvc service fails to start with a "port already in use" error, or when the loopback HTTP listener crashes unexpectedly, a port conflict has occurred. Another process on the same workstation or small host is already bound to the port that accountsvc expects to listen on. This runbook walks you through finding the conflicting process, understanding why it's present, and resolving the conflict without disrupting normal service operation or other running applications.

Port conflicts are among the most common operational issues on development workstations and small host deployments. Unlike larger infrastructure, a single machine running multiple services means shared network resources and a higher probability of collision.

## Coverage

This page covers loopback port conflicts specifically—conflicts on `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`. It does not cover network-facing (external) port bindings, firewall rules, or network interface configuration. For broader host health and monitoring context, see the host monitoring page.

The procedures assume a Windows 10 workstation or a small single-machine host running Linux or Windows, where accountsvc is the primary service. Multi-machine deployments should consult your infrastructure team.

## Finding the Conflicting Process

### Windows Workstations (PowerShell)

The most reliable method on Windows is the `netstat` command, which lists all active network connections and listening ports.

```
netstat -anob
```

The flags mean:
- `-a`: Show all connections and listening ports
- `-n`: Display host and port numbers in numerical form
- `-o`: Include the process identifier (PID) for each connection
- `-b`: Show the executable name associated with each connection

Run this in PowerShell with elevated access. The output is verbose; filter for the port accountsvc uses (commonly port 8080) to find your conflict:

```
netstat -anob | findstr :8080
```

This returns one or more lines like:

```
  TCP    127.0.0.1:8080         0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING       2944
  TCP    [::1]:8080             [::]:0                 LISTENING       2944
```

The PID `2944` appears on the right. Cross-reference it with the task manager or use `Get-Process`:

```
Get-Process -Id 2944
```

Output example:
```
Handles  NPM(K)    PM(K)      WS(K)     CPU(s)     Id  SI ProcessName
-------  ------    -----      -----     ------     --  -- -----------
    120       8    15232      18404       0.05   2944   1 python
```

The executable is `python` running as PID 2944. Open Task Manager (`Taskmgr.exe`) and locate this process to see its full command line and parent process. Note the working directory if visible.

### Linux / Small Hosts (Bash)

On Linux, use `lsof` (list open files) or `ss` (socket statistics), both showing process names and port bindings:

```
sudo lsof -i :8080
```

Output:
```
The output lists process command, process identifier, owning user, file descriptor, connection protocol type, network interface details, size metric, and node designation.
python3    5521   root   17u  IPv4   123456      0t0  TCP localhost:8080 (LISTEN)
python3    5521   root   18u  IPv6   123457      0t0  TCP [::1]:8080 (LISTEN)
```

The PID is `5521`. Check its details:

```
ps aux | grep 5521
```

Or use `ss` for a more structured output:

```
sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080
```

This shows the listening socket, protocol (TCP), and the process PID and name.

## Understanding the Cause

Once you have identified the process, determine what it is and why it is running. Common scenarios:

| Process | Likely Cause | Action |
|---------|--------------|--------|
| Another instance of accountsvc | Supervisor restarted it, or an old process did not terminate cleanly | Check supervisor logs; see *startup-and-shutdown.rst* |
| IDE development server (Flask, Django, etc.) | Developer left their local server running in the background | Contact the developer or close their IDE session |
| Node.js / npm dev server | JavaScript development tool left running | Check the working directory; alert the developer |
| Java application or build tool | Another service or CI tool on the machine | Coordinate with the team running that application |
| System service or daemon | OS-level service auto-started at boot | Verify it is necessary; disable if redundant |
| Verification process runner | Automated verification or monitoring process still running | Check scheduled tasks (Windows) or cron (Linux) |

### Checking for Multiple accountsvc Instances

The most common cause is that accountsvc has crashed or hung, but the supervisor process (if configured) has not yet restarted it, or two supervisors are managing the same service:

On Windows, verify only one accountsvc instance is present:

```
Get-Process python | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -eq "python" }
```

On Linux:

```
ps aux | grep accountsvc
```

Look for duplicate processes or processes with identical command lines. If you see two running accountsvc services, one is likely the old crashed process and one is the new restart. Proceed to **Resolving the Conflict** below.

If the conflicting process is unrelated to accountsvc, decide whether to terminate it, move it to a different port, or reconfigure accountsvc to use an alternate port.

## Resolving the Conflict

### Option 1: Terminate the Conflicting Process (Preferred if Safe)

If the conflicting process is dead or extraneous, terminate it cleanly:

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```
Stop-Process -Id 2944
```

Verify it has stopped:

```
Get-Process -Id 2944 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

If no output appears, the process has exited.

**Linux:**

```
sudo kill 5521
```

Wait a few seconds and check:

```
sudo lsof -i :8080
```

If the port is now free, proceed to restart accountsvc via its supervisor. See *process-supervision.rst* for the correct restart procedure on your host.

If the process does not respond to `SIGTERM`, use `kill -9`:

```
sudo kill -9 5521
```

### Option 2: Change the Service Port

If the conflicting process is legitimate and in use, configure accountsvc to listen on a different loopback port. Configuration is typically stored in a local settings file or environment variable (consult your host's setup guide or the filesystem layout page). After reconfiguring the port, restart accountsvc and verify the new port is listening:

**Windows:**

```
netstat -anob | findstr :8081
```

**Linux:**

```
sudo lsof -i :8081
```

If the port is now in use and accountsvc is listening, the conflict is resolved. Update any application code, monitoring scripts, or documentation that referenced the old port.

### Option 3: Restart the Supervisor (Nuclear Option)

If you cannot cleanly terminate the process or identify the conflict, restarting the supervisor process will kill all children and perform a full service restart:

**Windows (if using a Windows Service or Task Scheduler):**

Open Task Scheduler (`taskschd.msc`) and disable then re-enable the accountsvc task. Or, restart the service via Services (`services.msc`).

**Linux (if using systemd):**

```
sudo systemctl restart accountsvc
```

This forcefully terminates all accountsvc processes and restarts the supervisor, clearing port bindings. Use only if other methods fail, as it may interrupt ongoing operations. Coordinate with accountsvc users beforehand.

## Preventing Port Conflicts

### Use a Non-Standard Port

Development workstations often run multiple services. Consider configuring accountsvc to use port 8888 or 9090 rather than the common port 8080. Fewer applications bind to these ports, reducing collision probability.

### Enable Socket Reuse

Modern operating systems support the `SO_REUSEADDR` socket option, which allows a process to bind to a port shortly after the previous process releases it, avoiding a lingering `TIME_WAIT` state. The accountsvc service has this option enabled by default; no configuration is required.

### Isolate Development Environments

If running multiple accountsvc instances for different projects on the same workstation, use containers (Docker) or virtual machines to isolate each instance and its port bindings. See *workstation-vs-small-host.md* for guidance on multi-instance setups.

### Regular Port Monitoring

On shared hosts, periodically check port assignments to identify unexpected listeners:

**Windows:**

```
Execute netstat showing all connections in numerical format with associated process information, saving output to a file for review.
```

**Linux:**

```
Execute netstat with elevated access showing all listening connections in numerical format with process information, saving output to a file.
```

Review the file for unfamiliar processes and investigate anomalies.

## Related Operational Topics

### Disk Space and Log File Growth

When troubleshooting a crashed accountsvc service, check whether disk space exhaustion caused the failure. A full disk prevents the service from writing console log files, which may hide the root cause. See *disk-space-monitoring.md* and *console-log-files.md* for diagnostic and preventive steps.

### SQLite File Locking

If accountsvc terminates unexpectedly during a port conflict resolution or restart, the SQLite database file may remain locked by a zombie process. See *sqlite-file-locking.md* for diagnosing and clearing file locks before restarting the service.

### Backup and Restoration

After resolving a port conflict and restarting accountsvc, verify data consistency by checking the database file's modification time and size. A recent anomaly (such as sudden growth or a timestamp far in the past) may indicate corruption. See *database-file-backup-copy.md* for backup procedures and *host-monitoring.md* for continuous monitoring thresholds.

## Terminology and Glossary

**Loopback Interface**
The reserved loopback IP `127.0.0.1` (IPv4) or `[::1]` (IPv6) that refers to the local machine only. Traffic to loopback IPs does not traverse the network stack and is isolated to a single host. The service listens exclusively on loopback.

**Port Binding**
The act of a process claiming exclusive use of a TCP port on a specific interface. Once a process binds to a port, other processes cannot bind to the same interface and port pair until the original process closes the socket.

**Port Conflict (also Port Collision)**
A condition where two processes attempt to bind to the same loopback port simultaneously, or when a process tries to bind to a port already claimed by another process. The second process receives an error and cannot start.

**TIME_WAIT State**
A TCP socket state that occurs after a connection is closed. The operating system holds the socket in this state briefly (typically 60 seconds on Linux, longer on Windows) to ensure delayed packets are not misdelivered to a new process on the same port. This can cause a "port in use" error if restarting a service quickly.

**Process Identifier (PID)**
A unique numerical identifier assigned by the operating system to each running process. PIDs allow tools like `netstat`, `lsof`, and `ps` to correlate network bindings with specific executables.

**Socket**
A connection point for network communication created by the operating system. A socket is identified by a protocol (TCP), a local interface, and a local port. Binding a socket reserves the port for exclusive use.

**Listening Port**
A port on which a process is actively accepting incoming network connections. The port is said to be in the `LISTEN` state, and incoming connection requests on that port are routed to the listening process.

**Netstat**
A command-line tool available on Windows and Linux that displays network connections, network configuration tables, and interface statistics. It is useful for identifying processes that are listening on or have open connections to specific ports.

**lsof (list open files)**
A Unix and Linux command that lists all files and network sockets opened by running processes. With the `-i` flag, it filters for network connections and is the preferred tool for port diagnostics on Linux systems.

## Referenced Files and Paths

| Path | Purpose |
|------|------|
| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\` (Windows) or `/opt/accountsvc/` (Linux) | Working directory for the accountsvc service instance; contains configuration and state files. |
| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\accounts.db` (Windows) or `/opt/accountsvc/accounts.db` (Linux) | SQLite database file holding service state. Locking issues often occur here during restarts. |
| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\service.log` (Windows) or `/var/log/accountsvc.log` (Linux) | Primary console log file written by accountsvc. Check for startup errors or crash messages. |
| `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` (Windows) or `/etc/hosts` (Linux) | System host file; accountsvc resolves `localhost` using this file. Misconfiguration is rare but worth checking if loopback connectivity fails. |
| `docs/operations-runbooks/` | Documentation folder containing runbooks referenced by this page. |
| Helper scripts for port conflict detection | Optional monitoring tools for automated port binding conflict discovery; may exist in your repository. |

## Tools and Library Versions

| Tool / Command | Version | Platform | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| netstat | Built-in | Windows, Linux | List listening ports and identify processes by PID. |
| lsof | 4.94.0+ | Linux / macOS | List open files and network sockets; finer-grained filtering than netstat. |
| ss (socket statistics) | Built-in (iproute2) | Linux | Modern replacement for netstat; faster and more reliable. |
| Task Scheduler | Built-in | Windows | Schedule or manage supervisor tasks for accountsvc restarts. |
| systemd | 240+, typically pre-installed | Linux | System and service manager; restarts accountsvc services. |
| sqlite3 CLI | 3.32.0+ | Windows, Linux | Inspect and validate the SQLite database file; rarely needed for port conflicts but useful for follow-up diagnostics. |
| PowerShell | 5.1+ (Windows 10), 7.0+ (cross-platform) | Windows, Linux | System-level shell for process and service management. |
