1	# Keeping Console Log Files From Growing Too Large
2	
3	**Version:** 1.5
4	**Owner:** Systems Support (Callum Reyes)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-07-14
6	
7	> Covers moving, compressing, and trimming console log files on a schedule so they don't use up the host's disk over time.
8	
9	This page is the working guide for keeping accountsvc's own console log file from turning into a disk problem on a workstation or a small host. It sits next to several other operations runbooks — on port conflicts, disk space, the database file, host monitoring, and backup copying — and touches on each of those only where it bears directly on log growth. For the fuller treatment of any one of those topics, see the Related Pages section at the bottom.
10	
11	## Purpose and Coverage
12	
13	accountsvc writes a continuous console log while it's running — startup lines, request handling notes, and the occasional warning when something on the host isn't quite right (a busy port, a locked database file, low disk space). Left alone, that log file just keeps growing. On a workstation that might sit for months without anyone paying attention, or on a small host with a modest disk, an unattended console log can quietly use up space that the database file and the rest of the host need.
14	
15	This page covers:
16	
17	- how and why the console log file grows over time;
18	- how log growth shows up alongside other host issues (port conflicts, disk space, database file locking);
19	- the manual steps for moving the current log file aside and compressing older copies;
20	- the scheduled version of that same process, using cron on a small host or Task Scheduler on a workstation;
21	- how to confirm the schedule is actually keeping the log file's size in check;
22	- how log housekeeping fits around copying the database file for backup, so the two jobs don't collide.
23	
24	It does not cover the service's own startup or shutdown steps, or how the console log's individual lines are formatted — those live on their own pages.
25	
26	## Why the Console Log File Grows
27	
28	accountsvc writes to its console log continuously while it runs. New lines get added at the end; nothing in the service itself trims what's already there. That's a reasonable design for a small package that only uses the standard library — it keeps the writing logic simple — but it means the log file's size is entirely a host upkeep concern, not something the service manages on its own.
29	
30	A few things drive how fast the file grows:
31	
32	1. How long the service has been running without a restart. A process that's been up for three months on a workstation someone forgot about will have a much bigger log file than one restarted weekly.
33	2. How busy the loopback service is. More requests generally means more lines written.
34	3. Whether anything on the host is in a bad state that the service keeps noting — a port conflict on startup, a database file that's briefly locked, low disk headroom — each of these tends to produce repeated lines rather than one.
35	4. Whether the console output is being sent straight to a file, or through some other capture step that adds its own line each time (some small hosts wrap the service in a supervisor that timestamps every line it forwards, which roughly doubles the line length).
36	
37	None of this is unusual for a small standard-library service. It's the same shape of problem as any long-running process that writes to a console: the file is fine for a while, and then, if nobody's watching, it isn't.
38	
39	## Console Log Growth and Port Conflicts
40	
41	*(Section owner: Devon Price, Host Operations)*
42	
43	When accountsvc can't bind its loopback port on startup — because something else on the host already has it — it writes a line about that failure and then either exits or waits and tries again, depending on how it was started. On a host where the port conflict isn't fixed quickly, that produces a burst of near-identical lines in the console log every time the service (or its supervisor) tries to start it again.
44	
45	This matters for log growth in two ways:
46	
47	- A stuck port conflict during, say, an overnight window can add thousands of short, repeated lines to the log by morning — not enough on its own to fill a disk, but enough to throw off size estimates if you're eyeballing the file rather than checking it.
48	- If the port conflict is being caused by an old accountsvc process that never fully stopped, you can end up with two console log files being written to at once for a while, which is confusing when you go to move the current one aside.
49	
50	The practical upshot for log housekeeping: if you observe the console log growing unusually fast, check whether it's a genuine spike in service activity or a port conflict looping in the background. The diagnosis steps for the conflict itself are covered elsewhere; the point here is just that unexplained log growth is sometimes a port problem wearing a disk-space costume.
51	
52	## Console Log Growth and Disk Space
53	
54	*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Reliability)*
55	
56	Console log growth is one of a handful of things that eat into a host's free disk space, alongside the database file and whatever else lives on the same disk. On a small host, the database file usually grows slowly and predictably; the console log is the more likely thing to surprise you, especially if the roll-over schedule described later on this page has stopped running for some reason.
57	
58	A rough way to think about headroom: if the console log file and its compressed older copies together are taking up more than a few hundred megabytes on a host with a modest disk, it's worth checking why the roll-over schedule hasn't kept up. On most workstations and small hosts running accountsvc, a healthy console log setup keeps the *current* log file under a few tens of megabytes and the compressed older copies well under that each, because compression on plain text console lines usually gets you a large reduction in size.
59	
60	Watching disk space in general — thresholds, what else typically lives on the disk, how to check free space quickly — is its own page. What belongs here is narrower: when disk space gets tight, the console log is one of the first places to look, and it's usually the easiest one to fix, since older copies can simply be cleared out or moved somewhere else without touching the database file at all.
61	
62	## Console Log Growth and SQLite File Locking
63	
64	*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*
65	
66	The console log file and the database file are two completely separate files on disk, and moving or compressing the console log has no effect on the database file's own lock. That said, the two show up together often enough in this page's day-to-day use that it's worth being explicit about the boundary.
67	
68	When the database file is briefly locked — another process on the host has it open, or accountsvc itself is mid-write — the service sometimes writes a line to the console log noting that a write had to wait its turn. These lines are harmless and expected on a host with more than one thing touching the database file, but a host where they show up constantly is one where something is holding the file open longer than it should, and that's worth chasing down on its own terms.
69	
70	For log housekeeping purposes, the only thing to remember is: never try to move or compress the console log file *while* also trying to open the database file for a backup copy, if both are being scripted on the same schedule. There's no lock conflict between the two files, but running both jobs at the exact same minute on a small host with limited disk read/write capacity can make each one slower and occasionally causes a scheduled job to be skipped because the previous one hadn't finished. Space the two schedules apart by at least a few minutes.
71	
72	## Console Log Growth and Host Monitoring
73	
74	*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Reliability)*
75	
76	Most hosts running accountsvc have some form of general host monitoring in place — disk space thresholds, process presence, that kind of thing. Console log growth ties into that monitoring in one direct way: the disk space threshold that host monitoring watches doesn't distinguish between the database file, the console log, and anything else on the disk. If the console log's roll-over schedule silently stops working, the first sign is usually a disk space threshold being crossed weeks or months later, at which point the fix (clearing out old log copies) is trivial but the diagnosis takes longer than it should because nobody suspected the log file first.
77	
78	A small improvement worth making on any host where you're setting up monitoring from scratch: add a separate, lower threshold specifically on the size of the console log file's directory, well below the general disk space threshold. That way a stuck roll-over schedule shows up as its own flag rather than getting lost in a general "disk is getting full" alert that could mean several different things.
79	
80	The general host monitoring setup — what gets watched, how often, where the thresholds live — is covered on its own page. The log-specific threshold described here is a small addition on top of that general setup, not a replacement for it.
81	
82	## Copying the Database File for Backup — And Keeping Logs Out of the Way
83	
84	*(Section owner: Wren Ashby, Infrastructure)*
85	
86	Copying the database file for backup is a separate job from log housekeeping, but the two often get scheduled around the same time on a small host, because both are things you want done regularly and both benefit from a quiet moment when the service isn't under load. A few points worth being explicit about, from the log side of that overlap:
87	
88	- **Don't compress the console log and copy the database file in the same script step.** If one part fails partway — say, the disk fills up mid-copy — you don't want to be untangling which of two unrelated jobs caused it.
89	- **The console log's own size shouldn't be a reason to delay a backup copy.** If the disk is tight because the console log has grown too large, clear out old log copies first, confirm there's enough free space for the database file's copy, and then run the backup step. Don't skip a backup copy because of log clutter; fix the clutter.
90	- **Keep the two output locations separate.** Compressed older console log copies and database file copies for backup should not land in the same folder. It's a small thing, but on more than one small host someone has accidently included a week's worth of old console log copies in a folder that was meant to hold only database file copies, which makes it harder to see at a glance what's actually there.
91	
92	The step-by-step procedure for copying the database file itself — locking considerations, how to confirm the copy is usable, where copies should land — is its own page. What matters here is scheduling: give the two jobs separate windows, at least five minutes apart, on any host where both run automatically.
93	
94	## Manual Procedure: Moving and Compressing the Console Log File
95	
96	This is the by-hand version of log housekeeping — worth knowing even if you've set up the scheduled version below, because you'll want to run it by hand the first time on a new host, or any time the scheduled version needs a nudge.
97	
98	**Step 1 — Check the current size.**
99	
100	On a small host:
101	
102	```
103	du -h /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log
104	```
105	
106	On a workstation, the rough equivalent in PowerShell:
107	
108	```
109	Get-Item C:\ProgramData\accountsvc\var\console.log | Select-Object Length
110	```
111	
112	**Step 2 — Move the current log file aside.**
113	
114	The service keeps writing to whatever file descriptor it opened at startup, so simply renaming the file out from under it is safe on most setups — new lines keep going to the old inode until the service is next restarted, at which point it opens a fresh file at the same path. This is the one part of the manual procedure where a restart of accountsvc eventually matters, though the move itself doesn't require one.
115	
116	```
117	mv /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log.1
118	```
119	
120	**Step 3 — Compress the moved copy.**
121	
122	```
123	gzip /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log.1
124	```
125	
126	This leaves you with `console.log.1.gz` and, going forward, a fresh `console.log` collecting new output.
127	
128	**Step 4 — Confirm the fresh log file is being written to.**
129	
130	Wait a minute or two, then check the fresh file has grown past zero bytes. If accountsvc was started with an explicit file handle rather than being restarted, there's a chance the fresh file stays empty and the old, now-moved file keeps growing instead — in which case a restart of the service is needed to pick up the new path. Check with the person who owns the process supervision setup on that host before restarting anything outside a planned window.
131	
132	**Step 5 — Repeat for older copies as needed.**
133	
134	If a host has gone a while without attention, you may find several uncompressed copies sitting around from earlier by-hand moves. Compress each in turn:
135	
136	```
137	for f in /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log.*; do
138	  case "$f" in
139	    *.gz) ;;
140	    *) gzip "$f" ;;
141	  esac
142	done
143	```
144	
145	This loop skips anything already ending in `.gz` and compresses the rest — handy after a host has been left alone for a stretch and there's a mix of compressed and uncompressed copies sitting in the same folder.
146	
147	## Scheduled Procedure: Trimming Older Copies
148	
149	The manual steps above are fine for a one-off, but the point of this page is to make sure log housekeeping happens on a schedule without anyone needing to remember it. Two small scripts cover this: one that moves the current log aside and compresses it (the roll-over script), and one that clears out compressed copies past a set age (the trim script).
150	
151	### Setting the cut-off age
152	
153	Most hosts running accountsvc keep the last 14 days of compressed console log copies and clear out anything older. That's a starting point, not a fixed rule — a workstation that's rebooted often and generates comparatively little output can reasonably keep 30 days; a small host with limited disk and a busier loopback service might need to trim down to 7 days. Whatever the number, write it down on this page or in the script itself so the next person doesn't have to guess.
154	
155	### The roll-over script, scheduled
156	
157	On a small host, a cron entry:
158	
159	```
160	# /etc/cron.d/accountsvc-logs
161	15 2 * * * accountsvc /opt/accountsvc/scripts/roll-console-log.sh
162	```
163	
164	This runs the move-and-compress steps every night at 2:15 AM, under whatever host account owns accountsvc's files.
165	
166	### The trim script, scheduled
167	
168	A separate cron entry a few minutes later, so the two don't overlap:
169	
170	```
171	25 2 * * * accountsvc /opt/accountsvc/scripts/trim-old-logs.sh
172	```
173	
174	The trim script itself is a short wrapper around `find`, something like:
175	
176	```
177	find /opt/accountsvc/var -name 'console.log.*.gz' -mtime +14 -exec rm -f {} \;
178	```
179	
180	adjusted to whatever cut-off age the host has settled on.
181	
182	### The same idea on a workstation
183	
184	Task Scheduler doesn't use cron syntax, but the shape is identical: two scheduled tasks, one for roll-over and one for trimming, spaced a few minutes apart, both set to run daily during a quiet stretch (early morning is the usual choice, matching the small-host convention above so the two environments behave the same way even if the mechanics differ). Name the tasks clearly — `accountsvc-log-rollover` and `accountsvc-log-trim` — so anyone looking at the Task Scheduler library later can tell at a glance what they're for.
185	
186	### A worked example
187	
188	Say a small host has been running accountsvc for four months with no log housekeeping in place at all. The console log file has grown to just under 2 GB. Here's the sequence that gets it back under control without disrupting the service:
189	
190	1. Check free disk space first — you need enough headroom to hold both the uncompressed 2 GB file and its compressed copy briefly, before the uncompressed original is cleared out.
191	2. Run the manual move-and-compress steps once by hand rather than waiting for the schedule, since a file this size is worth watching directly rather than trusting a cron job you haven't confirmed works yet on this host.
192	3. Confirm the compressed copy is a reasonable fraction of the original — plain console text usually compresses down substantially, so a 2 GB file landing well under half a gigabyte compressed is typical; if it comes out much larger than that, something about the log's content (repeated binary-looking output, for instance) is worth a second look.
193	4. Set up the two cron entries above going forward, and pick a cut-off age — 14 days is the default, but on a host that had gone four months without attention, it's worth checking in again after the first week to make sure the schedule actually ran before trusting it long-term.
194	5. Note the date this was done somewhere on the host (a plain text file in the same folder works fine) so the next person who finds a large log file knows when housekeeping last happened.
195	
196	## verifying the schedule is doing its job
197	
198	Once a schedule is in place, don't just assume it's running. A few quick checks, worth doing after first setting things up and then every so often afterward:
199	
200	- Look for a compressed copy with today's or yesterday's date in the folder where they land. If the newest compressed copy is older than the cut-off age itself, the roll-over script has stopped running.
201	- Check that the current, uncompressed console log file's size resets roughly on schedule rather than growing without bound across many days.
202	- Confirm old compressed copies past the cut-off age are actually gone, not just old — a trim script that's silently failing (a typo in a path, most often) will leave copies piling up indefinitely even while the roll-over half of the schedule works fine.
203	- On a small host, check the cron log itself (usually under `/var/log/cron` or through the system's own log viewer) for any errors from either script's scheduled run.
204	- On a workstation, open Task Scheduler and check the "Last Run Result" column for both tasks — anything other than a clean success code is worth chasing down.
205	
206	If either script has stopped running, the manual procedure above is always available as a stopgap while you sort out why the schedule isn't working.
207	
208	## Terminology
209	
210	**Console log file** — the file accountsvc writes its running output to, one line at a time, for as long as the process is up.
211	
212	**Roll over / roll-over** — the act of moving the current console log file aside under a new name and letting the service (or the file handle it holds) start writing a fresh file in its place.
213	
214	**Loopback service** — the part of accountsvc that listens on a local-only port for requests; mentioned here only because its activity level is one of the things that drives console log growth.
215	
216	**Small host** — a lightly resourced machine, physical or virtual, dedicated mostly to running accountsvc and a handful of other small services, typically with a modest disk and no local desktop use.
217	
218	**Workstation** — a general-use machine, usually someone's own desktop or laptop, where accountsvc runs alongside other unrelated software and is more likely to go unattended for stretches.
219	
220	**Disk headroom** — the free space remaining on the disk that holds accountsvc's files, relative to what the host actually needs day to day; log growth is one of the main things that eats into it over time.
221	
222	**File lock** — the mechanism SQLite uses to make sure only one write to the database file happens at a time; unrelated to how the console log file is written, but the two sometimes show up in the same conversation because both live on the same disk.
223	
224	**Database file** — the single SQLite file that holds accountsvc's state; kept entirely separate from the console log file in both content and housekeeping.
225	
226	**Cut-off age** — the number of days a compressed console log copy is kept before the trim script clears it out.
227	
228	**Compression** — the step of shrinking a moved console log copy with a standard tool like gzip, usually reducing plain text console output to a fraction of its original size.
229	
230	## Files and Paths Referenced
231	
232	| Path | Purpose |
233	|---|---|
234	| `accountsvc/` | the package directory holding the service and its command line tool |
235	| `/opt/accountsvc/var/console.log` (small host) or `C:\ProgramData\accountsvc\var\console.log` (workstation) | the current, actively written console log file |
236	| `/opt/accountsvc/var/console.log.*.gz` | older console log copies, moved aside and compressed |
237	| `/opt/accountsvc/var/accountsvc.db` | the database file holding the service's state; kept separate from log housekeeping |
238	| `scripts/roll-console-log.sh` | the script that moves the current log file aside and compresses the moved copy |
239	| `scripts/trim-old-logs.sh` | the script that clears out compressed log copies past the cut-off age |
240	| `/etc/cron.d/accountsvc-logs` (small host) | the scheduled trigger for the two scripts above |
241	| Task Scheduler tasks `accountsvc-log-rollover` and `accountsvc-log-trim` (workstation) | the workstation equivalent of the cron entries |
242	| `docs/operations-runbooks/console-log-files.md` | sibling page covering the console log file's own upkeep in more general terms |
243	| `docs/operations-runbooks/disk-space-monitoring.md` | sibling page on watching disk space generally, beyond just the console log |
244	| `docs/operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-thresholds.yaml` | threshold settings used by host monitoring, including the log-folder-specific one described above |
245	
246	## Tools and Versions
247	
248	| Tool / Package | Version | Purpose |
249	|---|---|---|
250	| gzip | 1.12 | compresses console log copies after they're moved aside |
251	| GNU findutils (`find`) | 4.9.0 | locates and clears out log copies past the cut-off age |
252	| cron (vixie-cron) | 4.1 | triggers the roll-over and trim scripts on a small host |
253	| Task Scheduler | built into Windows 10/11 | triggers the equivalent tasks on a workstation |
254	| Python | 3.11.6 | interpreter that runs accountsvc and produces the console log's lines |
255	| sqlite3 (command-line tool) | 3.45.1 | used to confirm the database file is intact, separately from any log housekeeping |
256	| rsync | 3.2.7 | used when copying the database file to another location for backup |
257	| PowerShell | 7.4.2 | used for the equivalent log-handling steps on a workstation |
258	
259	## Change Log
260	
261	| Date | Release | Owner | Summary |
262	|---|---|---|---|
263	| 2025-07-14 | Release 1.5 | Callum Reyes | Clarified the cut-off age used by the trim script; added the section on how log growth interacts with host monitoring alerts. |
264	| 2025-05-02 | Release 1.4 | Callum Reyes | Added the worked example for compressing several uncompressed copies at once after a host went months without attention. |
265	| 2025-02-20 | Release 1.3 | Callum Reyes | Added guidance on copying the database file for backup separately from log housekeeping, after the two were confused during a small host clean-up. |

267	| 2024-10-03 | Release 1.1 | Dana Okafor | Added the terminology section and the disk headroom figures used in the worked examples. |
268	| 2024-08-19 | Release 1.0 | Callum Reyes | First version of the page, covering the manual move-and-compress steps only. |
269	
270	## Related Pages

# Keeping Console Log Files From Growing Too Large

**Version:** 1.5
**Owner:** Systems Support (Callum Reyes)
**Last updated:** 2025-07-14

> Covers moving, compressing, and trimming console log files on a schedule so they don't use up the host's disk over time.

This page is the working guide for keeping accountsvc's own console log file from turning into a disk problem on a workstation or a small host. It sits next to several other operations runbooks — on port conflicts, disk space, the database file, host monitoring, and backup copying — and touches on each of those only where it bears directly on log growth. For the fuller treatment of any one of those topics, see the Related Pages section at the bottom.

## Purpose and Coverage

accountsvc writes a continuous console log while it's running — startup lines, request handling notes, and the occasional warning when something on the host isn't quite right (a busy port, a locked database file, low disk space). Left alone, that log file just keeps growing. On a workstation that might sit for months without anyone paying attention, or on a small host with a modest disk, an unattended console log can quietly use up space that the database file and the rest of the host need.

This page covers:

- how and why the console log file grows over time;
- how log growth shows up alongside other host issues (port conflicts, disk space, database file locking);
- the manual steps for moving the current log file aside and compressing older copies;
- the scheduled version of that same process, using cron on a small host or Task Scheduler on a workstation;
- how to confirm the schedule is actually keeping the log file's size in check;
- how log housekeeping fits around copying the database file for backup, so the two jobs don't collide.

It does not cover the service's own startup or shutdown steps, or how the console log's individual lines are formatted — those live on their own pages.

## Why the Console Log File Grows

accountsvc writes to its console log continuously while it runs. New lines get added at the end; nothing in the service itself trims what's already there. That's a reasonable design for a small package that only uses the standard library — it keeps the writing logic simple — but it means the log file's size is entirely a host upkeep concern, not something the service manages on its own.

A few things drive how fast the file grows:

1. How long the service has been running without a restart. A process that's been up for three months on a workstation someone forgot about will have a much bigger log file than one restarted weekly.
2. How busy the loopback service is. More requests generally means more lines written.
3. Whether anything on the host is in a bad state that the service keeps noting — a port conflict on startup, a database file that's briefly locked, low disk headroom — each of these tends to produce repeated lines rather than one.
4. Whether the console output is being sent straight to a file, or through some other capture step that adds its own line each time (some small hosts wrap the service in a supervisor that timestamps every line it forwards, which roughly doubles the line length).

None of this is unusual for a small standard-library service. It's the same shape of problem as any long-running process that writes to a console: the file is fine for a while, and then, if nobody's watching, it isn't.

## Console Log Growth and Port Conflicts

*(Section owner: Devon Price, Host Operations)*

When accountsvc can't bind its loopback port on startup — because something else on the host already has it — it writes a line about that failure and then either exits or waits and tries again, depending on how it was started. On a host where the port conflict isn't fixed quickly, that produces a burst of near-identical lines in the console log every time the service (or its supervisor) tries to start it again.

This matters for log growth in two ways:

- A stuck port conflict during, say, an overnight window can add thousands of short, repeated lines to the log by morning — not enough on its own to fill a disk, but enough to throw off size estimates if you're eyeballing the file rather than checking it.
- If the port conflict is being caused by an old accountsvc process that never fully stopped, you can end up with two console log files being written to at once for a while, which is confusing when you go to move the current one aside.

The practical upshot for log housekeeping: if you observe the console log growing unusually fast, check whether it's a genuine spike in service activity or a port conflict looping in the background. The diagnosis steps for the conflict itself are covered elsewhere; the point here is just that unexplained log growth is sometimes a port problem wearing a disk-space costume.

## Console Log Growth and Disk Space

*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Reliability)*

Console log growth is one of a handful of things that eat into a host's free disk space, alongside the database file and whatever else lives on the same disk. On a small host, the database file usually grows slowly and predictably; the console log is the more likely thing to surprise you, especially if the roll-over schedule described later on this page has stopped running for some reason.

A rough way to think about headroom: if the console log file and its compressed older copies together are taking up more than a few hundred megabytes on a host with a modest disk, it's worth checking why the roll-over schedule hasn't kept up. On most workstations and small hosts running accountsvc, a healthy console log setup keeps the *current* log file under a few tens of megabytes and the compressed older copies well under that each, because compression on plain text console lines usually gets you a large reduction in size.

Watching disk space in general — thresholds, what else typically lives on the disk, how to check free space quickly — is its own page. What belongs here is narrower: when disk space gets tight, the console log is one of the first places to look, and it's usually the easiest one to fix, since older copies can simply be cleared out or moved somewhere else without touching the database file at all.

## Console Log Growth and SQLite File Locking

*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*

The console log file and the database file are two completely separate files on disk, and moving or compressing the console log has no effect on the database file's own lock. That said, the two show up together often enough in this page's day-to-day use that it's worth being explicit about the boundary.

When the database file is briefly locked — another process on the host has it open, or accountsvc itself is mid-write — the service sometimes writes a line to the console log noting that a write had to wait its turn. These lines are harmless and expected on a host with more than one thing touching the database file, but a host where they show up constantly is one where something is holding the file open longer than it should, and that's worth chasing down on its own terms.

For log housekeeping purposes, the only thing to remember is: never try to move or compress the console log file *while* also trying to open the database file for a backup copy, if both are being scripted on the same schedule. There's no lock conflict between the two files, but running both jobs at the exact same minute on a small host with limited disk read/write capacity can make each one slower and occasionally causes a scheduled job to be skipped because the previous one hadn't finished. Space the two schedules apart by at least a few minutes.

## Console Log Growth and Host Monitoring

*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Reliability)*

Most hosts running accountsvc have some form of general host monitoring in place — disk space thresholds, process presence, that kind of thing. Console log growth ties into that monitoring in one direct way: the disk space threshold that host monitoring watches doesn't distinguish between the database file, the console log, and anything else on the disk. If the console log's roll-over schedule silently stops working, the first sign is usually a disk space threshold being crossed weeks or months later, at which point the fix (clearing out old log copies) is trivial but the diagnosis takes longer than it should because nobody suspected the log file first.

A small improvement worth making on any host where you're setting up monitoring from scratch: add a separate, lower threshold specifically on the size of the console log file's directory, well below the general disk space threshold. That way a stuck roll-over schedule shows up as its own flag rather than getting lost in a general "disk is getting full" alert that could mean several different things.

The general host monitoring setup — what gets watched, how often, where the thresholds live — is covered on its own page. The log-specific threshold described here is a small addition on top of that general setup, not a replacement for it.

## Copying the Database File for Backup — And Keeping Logs Out of the Way

*(Section owner: Wren Ashby, Infrastructure)*

Copying the database file for backup is a separate job from log housekeeping, but the two often get scheduled around the same time on a small host, because both are things you want done regularly and both benefit from a quiet moment when the service isn't under load. A few points worth being explicit about, from the log side of that overlap:

- **Don't compress the console log and copy the database file in the same script step.** If one part fails partway — say, the disk fills up mid-copy — you don't want to be untangling which of two unrelated jobs caused it.
- **The console log's own size shouldn't be a reason to delay a backup copy.** If the disk is tight because the console log has grown too large, clear out old log copies first, confirm there's enough free space for the database file's copy, and then run the backup step. Don't skip a backup copy because of log clutter; fix the clutter.
- **Keep the two output locations separate.** Compressed older console log copies and database file copies for backup should not land in the same folder. It's a small thing, but on more than one small host someone has accidently included a week's worth of old console log copies in a folder that was meant to hold only database file copies, which makes it harder to see at a glance what's actually there.

The step-by-step procedure for copying the database file itself — locking considerations, how to confirm the copy is usable, where copies should land — is its own page. What matters here is scheduling: give the two jobs separate windows, at least five minutes apart, on any host where both run automatically.

## Manual Procedure: Moving and Compressing the Console Log File

This is the by-hand version of log housekeeping — worth knowing even if you've set up the scheduled version below, because you'll want to run it by hand the first time on a new host, or any time the scheduled version needs a nudge.

**Step 1 — Check the current size.**

On a small host:

```
du -h /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log
```

On a workstation, the rough equivalent in PowerShell:

```
Get-Item C:\ProgramData\accountsvc\var\console.log | Select-Object Length
```

**Step 2 — Move the current log file aside.**

The service keeps writing to whatever file descriptor it opened at startup, so simply renaming the file out from under it is safe on most setups — new lines keep going to the old inode until the service is next restarted, at which point it opens a fresh file at the same path. This is the one part of the manual procedure where a restart of accountsvc eventually matters, though the move itself doesn't require one.

```
mv /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log.1
```

**Step 3 — Compress the moved copy.**

```
gzip /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log.1
```

This leaves you with `console.log.1.gz` and, going forward, a fresh `console.log` collecting new output.

**Step 4 — Confirm the fresh log file is being written to.**

Wait a minute or two, then check the fresh file has grown past zero bytes. If accountsvc was started with an explicit file handle rather than being restarted, there's a chance the fresh file stays empty and the old, now-moved file keeps growing instead — in which case a restart of the service is needed to pick up the new path. Check with the person who owns the process supervision setup on that host before restarting anything outside a planned window.

**Step 5 — Repeat for older copies as needed.**

If a host has gone a while without attention, you may find several uncompressed copies sitting around from earlier by-hand moves. Compress each in turn:

```
for f in /opt/accountsvc/var/console.log.*; do
  case "$f" in
    *.gz) ;;
    *) gzip "$f" ;;
  esac
done
```

This loop skips anything already ending in `.gz` and compresses the rest — handy after a host has been left alone for a stretch and there's a mix of compressed and uncompressed copies sitting in the same folder.

## Scheduled Procedure: Trimming Older Copies

The manual steps above are fine for a one-off, but the point of this page is to make sure log housekeeping happens on a schedule without anyone needing to remember it. Two small scripts cover this: one that moves the current log aside and compresses it (the roll-over script), and one that clears out compressed copies past a set age (the trim script).

### Setting the cut-off age

Most hosts running accountsvc keep the last 14 days of compressed console log copies and clear out anything older. That's a starting point, not a fixed rule — a workstation that's rebooted often and generates comparatively little output can reasonably keep 30 days; a small host with limited disk and a busier loopback service might need to trim down to 7 days. Whatever the number, write it down on this page or in the script itself so the next person doesn't have to guess.

### The roll-over script, scheduled

On a small host, a cron entry:

```
# /etc/cron.d/accountsvc-logs
15 2 * * * accountsvc /opt/accountsvc/scripts/roll-console-log.sh
```

This runs the move-and-compress steps every night at 2:15 AM, under whatever host account owns accountsvc's files.

### The trim script, scheduled

A separate cron entry a few minutes later, so the two don't overlap:

```
25 2 * * * accountsvc /opt/accountsvc/scripts/trim-old-logs.sh
```

The trim script itself is a short wrapper around `find`, something like:

```
find /opt/accountsvc/var -name 'console.log.*.gz' -mtime +14 -exec rm -f {} \;
```

adjusted to whatever cut-off age the host has settled on.

### The same idea on a workstation

Task Scheduler doesn't use cron syntax, but the shape is identical: two scheduled tasks, one for roll-over and one for trimming, spaced a few minutes apart, both set to run daily during a quiet stretch (early morning is the usual choice, matching the small-host convention above so the two environments behave the same way even if the mechanics differ). Name the tasks clearly — `accountsvc-log-rollover` and `accountsvc-log-trim` — so anyone looking at the Task Scheduler library later can tell at a glance what they're for.

### A worked example

Say a small host has been running accountsvc for four months with no log housekeeping in place at all. The console log file has grown to just under 2 GB. Here's the sequence that gets it back under control without disrupting the service:

1. Check free disk space first — you need enough headroom to hold both the uncompressed 2 GB file and its compressed copy briefly, before the uncompressed original is cleared out.
2. Run the manual move-and-compress steps once by hand rather than waiting for the schedule, since a file this size is worth watching directly rather than trusting a cron job you haven't confirmed works yet on this host.
3. Confirm the compressed copy is a reasonable fraction of the original — plain console text usually compresses down substantially, so a 2 GB file landing well under half a gigabyte compressed is typical; if it comes out much larger than that, something about the log's content (repeated binary-looking output, for instance) is worth a second look.
4. Set up the two cron entries above going forward, and pick a cut-off age — 14 days is the default, but on a host that had gone four months without attention, it's worth checking in again after the first week to make sure the schedule actually ran before trusting it long-term.
5. Note the date this was done somewhere on the host (a plain text file in the same folder works fine) so the next person who finds a large log file knows when housekeeping last happened.

## verifying the schedule is doing its job

Once a schedule is in place, don't just assume it's running. A few quick checks, worth doing after first setting things up and then every so often afterward:

- Look for a compressed copy with today's or yesterday's date in the folder where they land. If the newest compressed copy is older than the cut-off age itself, the roll-over script has stopped running.
- Check that the current, uncompressed console log file's size resets roughly on schedule rather than growing without bound across many days.
- Confirm old compressed copies past the cut-off age are actually gone, not just old — a trim script that's silently failing (a typo in a path, most often) will leave copies piling up indefinitely even while the roll-over half of the schedule works fine.
- On a small host, check the cron log itself (usually under `/var/log/cron` or through the system's own log viewer) for any errors from either script's scheduled run.
- On a workstation, open Task Scheduler and check the "Last Run Result" column for both tasks — anything other than a clean success code is worth chasing down.

If either script has stopped running, the manual procedure above is always available as a stopgap while you sort out why the schedule isn't working.

## Terminology

**Console log file** — the file accountsvc writes its running output to, one line at a time, for as long as the process is up.

**Roll over / roll-over** — the act of moving the current console log file aside under a new name and letting the service (or the file handle it holds) start writing a fresh file in its place.

**Loopback service** — the part of accountsvc that listens on a local-only port for requests; mentioned here only because its activity level is one of the things that drives console log growth.

**Small host** — a lightly resourced machine, physical or virtual, dedicated mostly to running accountsvc and a handful of other small services, typically with a modest disk and no local desktop use.

**Workstation** — a general-use machine, usually someone's own desktop or laptop, where accountsvc runs alongside other unrelated software and is more likely to go unattended for stretches.

**Disk headroom** — the free space remaining on the disk that holds accountsvc's files, relative to what the host actually needs day to day; log growth is one of the main things that eats into it over time.

**File lock** — the mechanism SQLite uses to make sure only one write to the database file happens at a time; unrelated to how the console log file is written, but the two sometimes show up in the same conversation because both live on the same disk.

**Database file** — the single SQLite file that holds accountsvc's state; kept entirely separate from the console log file in both content and housekeeping.

**Cut-off age** — the number of days a compressed console log copy is kept before the trim script clears it out.

**Compression** — the step of shrinking a moved console log copy with a standard tool like gzip, usually reducing plain text console output to a fraction of its original size.

1	# Monitoring Host Health Around accountsvc
2	
3	**Version:** v1.6.1  
4	**Owner:** Reliability (Priya Nair)  
5	**Last updated:** 2026-02-20  
6	**Summary:** Lists the host-level checks, including CPU, memory, disk, and process presence, that the team watches to keep the service running smoothly.
7	
8	## Overview
9	
10	When accountsvc runs on a workstation or small host, the service's health depends not just on its own process but on the host environment itself. This page describes the key host-level metrics the team monitors and the procedures for spotting problems before they cascade into service downtime.
11	
12	The service is lightweight and places modest demands on a typical system, but host constraints—full disk, high memory pressure, or port conflicts—can degrade or halt it with the same impact as an application-level bug. Monitoring these boundaries is preventive work. Unlike cloud-based services with automatic scaling, a small host requires manual oversight of resources and must be tuned for your workload.
13	
14	The host also runs the operating system, system services, and possibly other applications. The service shares CPU, RAM, and disk with these other processes. A baseline understanding of your host's resource profile is the first step toward reliable monitoring.
15	
16	## Host Resource Monitoring: CPU, Memory, and Disk
17	
18	**Section owner:** Reliability (Priya Nair)
19	
20	The service runs a lightweight HTTP server and performs queries against a local SQLite database. In steady state on a small host (512 MB RAM, quad-core CPU), it typically uses:
21	
22	- **CPU:** 1–5% during idle request handling; spikes to 15–30% during active query bursts
23	- **Memory:** 40–80 MB resident (excluding the database file itself)
24	- **Disk I/O:** Minor activity during individual requests; larger spikes during bulk writes
25	
26	These baselines assume the host is otherwise quiet. If your host runs additional software—backup jobs, scheduled tasks, or other network services—the baseline will be higher.
27	
28	### CPU Usage
29	
30	Monitor CPU with `Get-Process accountsvc` on Windows or `ps aux | grep accountsvc` on Linux. Sustained CPU above 30% suggests:
31	
32	- A backlog of queued requests exceeding the service's ability to process them
33	- Inefficient query patterns against the database (e.g., full table scans)
34	- An issue with the host's other services contending for resources
35	- Misconfigured request handling parameters
36	
37	Use `top` (or Task Manager on Windows) to observe the service in context with system-wide load. If load average climbs above the core count, investigate whether the host is running unrelated processes that should be stopped or moved to another machine.
38	
39	**Example:** On a four-core host, load average over 4.5 for more than five minutes means accountsvc may be starved for CPU. Check for backup jobs running unexpectedly, scheduled maintenance tasks from the OS, or other services using the CPU. Query the service's own console log to see if it is logging timeout errors or slow responses.
40	
41	**Checking load on Linux:**
42	```
43	uptime
44	# Output: 14:22:35 up 45 days, 3:18, 2 users, load average: 2.1, 2.0, 1.9
45	```
46	The three numbers are 1-minute, 5-minute, and 15-minute averages. On a 4-core system, 2.0 is moderate usage; above 5.0 is overloaded.
47	
48	**Checking load on Windows:** Task Manager (Performance tab) shows CPU usage. Resource Monitor (Processes tab) displays per-process CPU. A sustained spike above 80% total CPU warrants investigation.
49	
50	### Memory Usage
51	
52	The service keeps some state in memory but does not grow unbounded over time; memory accumulation in this codebase is rare. However, host memory pressure—when free RAM drops below 10% of total—degrades database performance and triggers swapping to disk, which cascades into I/O thrashing and severe slowdowns.
53	
54	Check process memory with:
55	
56	**Windows:**
57	```
58	Get-Process -Name "python*" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | 
59	  Where-Object {$_.ProcessName -like "*accountsvc*"} | 
60	  Select-Object ProcessName, WorkingSet64, PrivateMemorySize64
61	```
62	Convert bytes to MB by dividing by 1048576. WorkingSet64 is resident memory; PrivateMemorySize64 includes virtual memory.
63	
64	**Linux:**
65	```
66	ps aux | grep accountsvc | grep -v grep
67	# Look at the 6th column (RSS in KB); divide by 1024 for MB
68	```
69	
70	Do not rely solely on the service's memory footprint; monitor host free memory:
71	
72	**Windows:** Use `Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object CsPhysicallyInstalledSystemMemory` (returns bytes) or open Resource Monitor GUI. Divide result by 1073741824 for GB.
73	
74	**Linux:**
75	```
76	free -h
77	# Output:
78	#               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
79	# Mem:          7.8Gi       2.1Gi       1.2Gi      128Mi       4.5Gi       5.5Gi
80	```
81	Watch the "available" column, which accounts for cache reclamation.
82	
83	When free memory dips below 256 MB on a small host, the kernel begins aggressive cache reclamation. If this coincides with database query slowness or the service reporting timeout errors, check `dmesg` (Linux) for memory pressure warnings or the Event Viewer (Windows) for memory-related events. Swap activity (disk paging) is a key sign of memory exhaustion.
84	
85	### Disk Space
86	
87	Full disk is a common failure mode. SQLite databases expand on write operations, and the service's console log file also grows continuously. The host needs headroom for both the database file, console logs, temporary files, and OS operations.
88	
89	Check disk with:
90	
91	**Windows:**
92	```
93	Get-Volume C: | Select-Object DriveLetter, SizeRemaining, Size, PercentFree
94	# Returns sizes in bytes
95	```
96	
97	**Linux:**
98	```
99	df -h
100	# Shows filesystems with used, available, and percent full
101	```
102	
103	Recommended thresholds:
104	
105	- **Keep at least 500 MB free.** Below this, the service and OS operations function but with reduced resilience.
106	- **Warning threshold: 250 MB free.** At this level, file operations may slow or experience temporary failures.
107	- **Critical threshold: 50 MB free.** Some file operations begin to fail; consider the host unavailable until space is freed.
108	
109	The database file on a small host typically ranges from 5–50 MB. The console log file can grow 10–50 MB per day depending on log level and request volume. Combined with OS needs and other applications, a 100 GB host should have 5–10 GB of working space available. See the disk-space-monitoring page for detailed guidance and automated checks.
110	
111	**Example:** If your host's C: drive is 50 GB and free space falls to 150 MB, the disk is 99.7% full. Stop the service if necessary, move or compress old log files, or remove temporary files to free space immediately.
112	
113	## Port Conflicts
114	
115	**Section owner:** Host Operations (Devon Price)
116	
117	The service listens on localhost (typically `127.0.0.1:8080` or `127.0.0.1:9080` depending on local configuration). If another process binds to that port, the service fails to start and logs an error.
118	
119	Check whether the configured port is already in use:
120	
121	**Windows:**
122	```
123	netstat -ano | findstr :<port>
124	# or
125	Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort <port> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
126	```
127	
128	**Linux:**
129	```
130	ss -tlnp | grep :<port>
131	# or
132	netstat -tlnp | grep :<port>
133	```
134	
135	Both commands show the process ID (PID) of the occupant. Look it up:
136	
137	**Windows:**
138	```
139	Get-Process -Id <pid>
140	tasklist /FI "PID eq <pid>"
141	```
142	
143	**Linux:**
144	```
145	ps -p <pid>
146	ps aux | grep <pid> | grep -v grep
147	```
148	
149	**Example output (Windows):**
150	```
151	netstat -ano | findstr :8080
152	  Proto  Local Location        Foreign Location       State           PID
153	  TCP    127.0.0.1:8080         0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING       3284
154	  
155	Get-Process -Id 3284
156	# Handles  NPM(K)    PM(K)      WS(K)     CPU(s)     Id  SI ProcessName
157	#    142      12     8420      14008       0.00   3284   1  python
158	```
159	
160	**Example output (Linux):**
161	```
162	ss -tlnp | grep :8080
163	LISTEN  0  128  127.0.0.1:8080  0.0.0.0:*  pid=3284,name=python3
164	
165	ps -p 3284
166	  PID TTY      STAT   TIME COMMAND
167	  3284 ?        S      0:02 /usr/bin/python3 /opt/services/old_service.py
168	```
169	
170	If the conflicting process is unrelated or dormant, stop it or reconfigure one of the services. The port-conflicts diagnostic page has detailed procedures. Do not simply change the service's port without understanding why the conflict occurred; a restarting process may reclaim the port and cause intermittent failures.
171	
172	Verify that the service's configured loopback port in the configuration file matches the actual monitoring setup. Mismatches (e.g., the service is configured for port 8080 but documentation or external monitoring checks port 9080) silently prevent external tools from reaching it. Check the service configuration file:
173	
174	- Windows: `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\config.ini`
175	- Linux: `~/.accountsvc/config.ini` or `/etc/accountsvc/config.ini`
176	
177	Search the configuration file for the port setting and confirm it is active (not commented out).

179	## Process Presence and Supervision
180	
181	**Section owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
182	
183	Confirm that the service process exists and is responsive. A running process does not guarantee responsiveness; the process may be hung or deadlocked.
184	
185	**Check process existence:**
186	
187	**Windows:**
188	```
189	Get-Process -Name "python*" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | 
190	  Where-Object {$_.ProcessName -like "*accountsvc*" -or $_.CommandLine -like "*accountsvc*"}
191	```
192	
193	**Linux:**
194	```
195	ps aux | grep accountsvc | grep -v grep
196	pgrep -f accountsvc
197	```
198	
199	If the process is absent but the service is supposed to be running, check:
200	
201	1. Whether a supervisor (such as systemd on Linux or a process manager on Windows) is configured and active
202	2. The console log file for crash messages or errors at shutdown
203	3. Whether the service was manually stopped via `systemctl stop` or similar commands
204	4. The system event log for OS-level errors during startup
205	
206	A responsive service will answer HTTP requests on its configured port. Use `curl` or a similar HTTP tool for a quick check:
207	
208	```
209	curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
210	# Expected output: HTTP/1.1 200 OK or similar
211	```
212	
213	Adjust the port and path to match the service's actual configuration. A 2xx or 3xx HTTP status indicates the process is alive and responding to requests. A connection timeout or "refused" error suggests the process is not listening.
214	
215	The process-supervision page describes how to configure persistent supervision (systemd, supervisord, or equivalent) so the service auto-restarts on crash without manual intervention.
216	
217	## Console Log Files
218	
219	**Section owner:** Systems Support (Callum Reyes)
220	
221	The service writes log entries to a console log file. The location varies by OS:
222	
223	- **Windows:** `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\logs\console.log`
224	- **Linux:** `/var/log/accountsvc/console.log` or `~/.accountsvc/logs/console.log` (depending on whether the service runs as root or a user)
225	
226	Log file size grows over time as the service logs requests, errors, and diagnostic messages. Unbounded growth will eventually fill disk space and degrade system performance. The console-log-files page covers cycling and truncation strategies in detail.
227	
228	For monitoring, check the log file's age and size:
229	
230	**Windows:**
231	```
232	Get-ChildItem "C:\Users\$env:USERNAME\AppData\Local\accountsvc\logs\console.log" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | 
233	  Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTime
234	
235	# Length is in bytes
236	```
237	
238	**Linux:**
239	```
240	ls -lah /var/log/accountsvc/console.log
241	stat /var/log/accountsvc/console.log
242	```
243	
244	Monitor these indicators:
245	
246	- **Log file size:** If console.log exceeds 500 MB, use the cycling procedures on the log-file-growth page to store and truncate it. Size can be checked via `du` (Linux) or PowerShell properties.
247	- **Write time:** If the log file's modification time is older than the last known request timestamp (check your request log if available), the service may be hung or deadlocked. Compare with the current time using `date` (Linux) or `Get-Date` (Windows).
248	- **Disk usage of logs directory:** If the logs directory takes up more than 1 GB, investigate and manage old files. Check with `du -sh /var/log/accountsvc` (Linux) or `(Get-ChildItem -Recurse | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum).Sum` (Windows PowerShell).
249	
250	High-frequency logging is normal during active periods; do not treat steady growth as an error unless it correlates with disk space problems or unexplained slowness. Review log entries periodically to spot warning or error messages that indicate underlying issues.
251	
252	## SQLite File Locking and Concurrent Access
253	
254	**Section owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
255	
256	The service stores state in a SQLite database file located at:
257	
258	- **Windows:** `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\data\accounts.db`
259	- **Linux:** `/var/lib/accountsvc/accounts.db` or `~/.accountsvc/data/accounts.db`
260	
261	SQLite uses file-level locking: only one writer at a time is allowed, but multiple readers can coexist. If a maintenance task (such as a backup copy or a manual database consistency check) opens the database for writing at the same time the service attempts to write, both operations block. The first to acquire the lock proceeds; the other waits up to 30 seconds (the default timeout) before aborting with a "database is locked" error.
262	
263	Monitor the database file for active locks:
264	
265	**Windows:** Determining which process has a file open is complex on Windows. Use Process Explorer (from Sysinternals) to search for open file handles. Or try a backup; if it fails with "database is locked," the service is actively using the database.
266	
267	**Linux:** Use `lsof` if available:
268	```
269	lsof /var/lib/accountsvc/accounts.db
270	# Output lists processes with the file open
271	```
272	
273	`lsof` is not installed by default on all Linux systems; check with `which lsof`.
274	
275	The sqlite-file-locking page has detailed guidance on WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode and journaling behavior. WAL mode improves concurrency by allowing readers while writes are in progress, reducing lock contention.
276	
277	**Best practice for maintenance tasks:**
278	
279	Before performing manual operations on the database (such as a backup, consistency check, or schema inspection), ensure the service is idle or stopped:
280	
281	1. Stop the service (or wait for a quiet period with no requests).
282	2. Verify the database file's modification time is at least 30 seconds old: `stat` (Linux) or `Get-Item | Select-Object LastWriteTime` (Windows).
283	3. Perform your operation (e.g., copy the file, run a read-only check).
284	4. Restart the service if stopped.
285	
286	If you regularly encounter locks during backups, coordinate scheduled backups with the service's off-peak windows (e.g., 02:00 UTC if your service is busiest during business hours).
287	
288	## Database File Backup and Copying
289	
290	**Section owner:** Infrastructure (Wren Ashby)
291	
292	The database file must be backed up regularly to protect against data loss due to corruption, hardware failure, or accidental removal. The simplest approach is to copy the file to a separate location when the service is idle or stopped.
293	
294	**Basic backup procedure:**
295	
296	1. **Verify idle state:** Check the database file's modification time to confirm the service has not written recently:
297	   ```
298	   # Linux
299	   stat /var/lib/accountsvc/accounts.db | grep Modify
300	   
301	   # Windows
302	   Get-Item "C:\Users\$env:USERNAME\AppData\Local\accountsvc\data\accounts.db" | Select-Object LastWriteTime
303	   ```
304	
305	2. **Stop the service** (if performing during peak hours or doing a consistency check):
306	   ```
307	   # Linux with systemd
308	   sudo systemctl stop accountsvc
309	   
310	   # Or wait for the next quiet period
311	   ```
312	
313	3. **Copy the database file:**
314	   ```
315	   # Linux
316	   cp /var/lib/accountsvc/accounts.db /backup/accounts.db.2026-02-20
317	   cp /var/lib/accountsvc/accounts.db /backup/accounts.db.latest
318	   
319	   # Windows PowerShell
320	   Copy-Item "C:\Users\$env:USERNAME\AppData\Local\accountsvc\data\accounts.db" `
321	Backup to: D:\backup\accounts.db.2026-02-20
322	   Copy-Item "C:\Users\$env:USERNAME\AppData\Local\accountsvc\data\accounts.db" `
323	Backup to: D:\backup\accounts.db.latest
324	   ```
325	
326	4. **Verify the backup:** Check that the backup file size matches the original:
327	   ```
328	   # Linux
329	   ls -l /var/lib/accountsvc/accounts.db /backup/accounts.db.2026-02-20 | awk '{print $9, $5}'
330	   
331	   # Windows
332	   Get-Item "C:\Users\$env:USERNAME\AppData\Local\accountsvc\data\accounts.db", `
333	     "D:\backup\accounts.db.2026-02-20" | Select-Object FullName, Length
334	   ```
335	
336	5. **Restart the service** (if stopped):
337	   ```
338	   sudo systemctl start accountsvc
339	   ```
340	
341	Backups should be taken daily or weekly depending on data criticality and change frequency. Store backups on a separate filesystem, external storage, or cloud storage to protect against local disk failure. The database-file-backup-copy page covers automated backup procedures using scripting.
342	
343	**Backup management:** Keep at least three recent backups to guard against data corruption being copied to all backups. Older backups may be removed after 30 days or according to your organization's data lifecycle guidelines. Label each backup with the date to simplify tracking.
344	
345	## Monitoring Schedule and Alerting
346	
347	Establish a routine monitoring schedule based on your host's criticality:
348	
349	- **Daily:** Check process presence, verify disk free space is above the warning threshold (250 MB), and scan recent log entries for errors.
350	- **Weekly:** Review CPU and memory trends, perform a manual database consistency check during a quiet window, and confirm backup completion and file size.
351	- **Monthly:** Analyze long-term resource trends, adjust monitoring thresholds if needed, and review log file growth rate to tune cycling frequency.
352	
353	Many small hosts benefit from automated checks run on a schedule. A cron job (Linux) or Task Scheduler task (Windows) can run status checks at regular intervals:
354	
355	**Linux cron example** (runs daily at 02:00):
356	```
357	0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/check_accountsvc_host.sh
358	```
359	
360	**Windows Task Scheduler PowerShell example** (runs every 6 hours):
361	```
362	$svc = Get-Process -Name "python*" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | 
363	  Where-Object {$_.CommandLine -like "*accountsvc*"}
364	if ($null -eq $svc) {
365	  Write-Host "Service not running at $(Get-Date)" | 
366	    Out-File -Append "C:\logs\alerts.log"
367	}
368	
369	# Check disk space
370	$vol = Get-Volume C:
371	if ($vol.SizeRemaining -lt 250MB) {
372	  Write-Host "Disk space critical: $(($vol.SizeRemaining)/1GB)GB free at $(Get-Date)" | 
373	    Out-File -Append "C:\logs\alerts.log"
374	}
375	```
376	
377	Log all checks to a file for later review. Alert the team if thresholds are exceeded so corrective action can be taken before the service fails.
378	
379	## Terminology
380	
381	**Loopback interface:** A reserved network location (`127.0.0.1` on IPv4, `::1` on IPv6) that refers only to the local host. Traffic to a loopback interface never leaves the machine and cannot be accessed remotely; it is used for local inter-process communication and diagnostics.
382	
383	**Port binding:** The act of a network service listening for incoming connections on a specific port number. A port can be bound by only one process at a time; the second attempt to bind fails unless the first process releases it.
384	
385	**Resident Set Size (RSS):** The portion of a process's memory that resides in physical RAM, as opposed to virtual memory or swap space. RSS varies with system memory pressure; a process holding 100 MB RSS may expand to 200 MB if the OS swaps other data out.
386	
387	**File locking:** A mechanism by which a process prevents other processes from modifying a file while it is in use. SQLite uses advisory locks at the filesystem level; they do not prevent access but signal to other processes that the file is busy.
388	
389	**Load average:** A Unix/Linux metric that reports the average number of processes in the run queue over the past 1, 5, and 15 minutes. On a four-core system, a load average of 4.0 means the system is fully utilized; above 4.0 indicates queuing and delays.
390	
391	**Console log:** A text file written to by the running service that records informational and diagnostic messages. Different from application-level data stored in the database; it captures the service's operational events.
392	
393	**WAL mode (Write-Ahead Logging):** A SQLite journaling mode in which writes are first added to a separate log file, then applied to the main database file at sync points. WAL improves concurrency over traditional rollback journaling at the cost of slightly increased disk usage.
394	
395	**Disk I/O:** Input/output operations on persistent storage (hard disk or SSD). High I/O correlates with slow application performance when the storage drive is overloaded; modern SSDs can sustain high I/O, but older spinning disks have lower IOPS limits.
396	
397	**Process hang (or deadlock):** A state in which a process is still running but does not respond to requests or make progress. Usually caused by waiting indefinitely on a resource (e.g., a file lock, network connection, or another process).
398	
399	## Referenced Files and Paths
400	
401	| Path or File | Purpose |
402	|---|---|
403	| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\config.ini` (Windows) or `~/.accountsvc/config.ini` (Linux) | Configuration file specifying the service's listening port, log level, database location, and other tuning parameters. Must be readable by the service process. |
404	| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\logs\console.log` (Windows) or `/var/log/accountsvc/console.log` (Linux) | Service console log file. Grows with each request and diagnostic message. Monitored for size and content. |
405	| `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\accountsvc\data\accounts.db` (Windows) or `/var/lib/accountsvc/accounts.db` (Linux) | SQLite database file storing service state and customer data. Subject to file locking during concurrent access. |
406	| `docs/operations-runbooks/` | Folder containing all operations runbooks, including this page and siblings. |
407	| `scripts/check_accountsvc_host.sh` | Example host monitoring shell script for Linux. Requires customization for your environment, paths, and thresholds. |
408	| `/tmp/accountsvc_backup/` (Linux) or `C:\temp\accountsvc_backup\` (Windows) | Typical temporary location for database backup copies during maintenance tasks. Must exist and be writable. |
409	| `host-monitoring-thresholds.yaml` | YAML configuration file defining numeric thresholds for disk, memory, and CPU alerts. Maintained by Reliability team; used by automated monitoring scripts. |
410	| `~/.bashrc` or `/etc/profile.d/accountsvc.sh` (Linux) | Shell startup files; may be used to set environment variables for the service such as database paths or log levels. |
411	
412	## Tools and Versions
413	
414	| Tool | Version | Purpose |
415	|---|---|---|
416	| PowerShell | 5.1 (Windows 10) or 7.x (Windows 11) | Windows command-line and scripting environment for process and resource monitoring. |
417	| `netstat` | OS-provided (Windows 8+, Linux 2.6+) | Network diagnostic utility to list active ports, connections, and socket states. Windows and Linux both include it. |
418	| `ss` (socket statistics) | 5.x+ | Linux alternative to `netstat` with improved performance and clearer output format. |
419	| `ps` (process status) | GNU coreutils 8.x+ | Unix/Linux utility to list running processes and their resource usage (CPU, memory, PID, command). |
420	| `top` | procps-ng 3.x+ (Linux) or built-in Task Manager (Windows) | Interactive process and resource monitor. Shows real-time CPU, memory, and disk I/O. |
421	| `Get-Process` | PowerShell 5.1+ | Windows cmdlet to enumerate and inspect running processes and their properties. |
422	| `Get-Volume` / `Get-Disk` | PowerShell 5.1+ | Windows cmdlets to query filesystem capacity and free space. |
423	| `df` | GNU coreutils 8.x+ | Linux utility to report filesystem capacity and free space in a summary table. |
424	| `du` | GNU coreutils 8.x+ | Linux utility to estimate disk usage of directories and files. Used to identify large log or database files. |
425	| `lsof` | 4.9x+ | Unix/Linux utility to list open files and network connections by process. Optional; may not be installed on minimal systems. |
426	| `curl` | 7.x+ | Command-line HTTP utility for verifying service connectivity and health. |
427	| SQLite 3 | 3.8+ (typically 3.37+) | Database engine; the service uses this format for the accounts database file. Included as a runtime dependency. |
428	| `stat` | GNU coreutils 8.x+ (Linux) | Unix/Linux utility to display detailed file metadata including modification time and size in bytes. |
429	
430	## Change Log
431	
432	| Date | Release | Change Summary |
433	|---|---|---|
434	| 2024-09-05 | v1.0 | Initial runbook documenting host CPU, memory, disk, and process monitoring. Section on SQLite file locking added. |
435	| 2024-11-02 | v1.1 | Disk space thresholds revised to 500 MB recommended, 250 MB warning, 50 MB critical. Port conflict section expanded with `netstat` and `ss` examples. |
436	| 2025-01-18 | v1.2 | Added console log file growth monitoring and procedures for checking log file age and size. Cross-referenced related pages. |
437	| 2025-06-30 | v1.3 | Clarified database file locations for Windows and Linux; added backup copying procedures and data management guidance. Monitoring schedule section expanded. |
438	| 2025-08-19 | v1.5 | Automated checking examples (cron and Task Scheduler) included. Terminology section expanded to nine terms. Tools and versions table updated. |
439	| 2026-02-20 | v1.6.1 | Updated log file path examples for consistency with console-log-files page v1.2.0. Removed outdated warning about database size limits. Verified all tool versions against current platform support. |
440	
441	## Related Pages
442	
443	- [Operations Runbooks Index](README.md) – Main entry point for operations documentation (v1.4.0, updated 2026-05-12).
444	- [Diagnosing Loopback Port Conflicts](port-conflicts.md) – Detailed procedures for resolving port binding issues and identifying conflicting processes (2.1, updated 2025-01-18).
445	- [Watching Disk Space on the Host](disk-space-monitoring.md) – Automated disk monitoring, threshold configuration, and alerting (1.3, updated 2024-11-02).
446	- [Managing the Service's Console Log Files](console-log-files.md) – Log file cycling, truncation, and storage procedures (v1.2.0, updated 2025-06-30).
447	- [Keeping Console Log Files From Growing Too Large](log-file-growth.md) – Strategies for managing log size and preventing disk exhaustion (1.5, updated 2025-07-14).
448	- [Understanding SQLite File Locking on This Host](sqlite-file-locking.md) – Detailed explanation of WAL mode, journaling, and lock contention scenarios (2.0, updated 2024-09-05).
449	- [Copying the Database File for Backup](database-file-backup-copy.md) – Automated and manual backup procedures with consistency verification (2.4, updated 2025-03-11).
450	- [Starting and Stopping the Host Process](startup-and-shutdown.rst) – Procedures for starting, stopping, and reloading the service (1.1, updated 2024-05-22).
451	- [Keeping the Service Running with a Supervisor](process-supervision.rst) – Configuring systemd, supervisord, or other process managers for automatic restart (v1.3.2, updated 2025-10-09).
452	- [Filesystem Layout for accountsvc on a Host](filesystem-layout.md) – Directory structure and recommended paths for configuration, logs, and data (1.0, updated 2024-04-30).
453	- [Running accountsvc on a Workstation vs. a Small Host](workstation-vs-small-host.md) – Resource requirements, deployment differences, and tuning guidance (1.4, updated 2025-12-01).
