      4. Last updated — an ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD) matching the date on the
         newest line in the changelog. If these two dates disagree, the
         page is not ready to publish.

      A minimal header block, in markdown, looks like this:

        # Page Title
        **Version:** 1.0
        **Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
        **Last updated:** 2025-06-01

      In YAML pages such as this one, the same four fields are top-level
      keys, written before any section content, in the same order. Do not
      reorder them for aesthetic reasons — several downstream scripts,
      including scripts/check_changelog_fields.py, read the header fields
      positionally in older page formats and will misread a page where
      the order has been changed.

  - heading: "Field Order For Dated Entries"
    owner: "Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)"
    body: |
      A single changelog line is built from five fields. Four are
      required and one is optional. The order below is fixed across every
      page format — markdown table row, YAML list item, or plain-text
      line — because readers and the checker script both rely on
      predictable ordering.

      | Position | Field       | Required | Notes                                                        |
      |----------|-------------|----------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
      | 1        | Date        | yes      | ISO format, YYYY-MM-DD, newest entry at the top of the log    |
      | 2        | Release tag | yes      | Names the accountsvc release or docs release the edit ties to |
      | 3        | Owner tag   | yes      | Two or three initials, see the Terminology section below      |
      | 4        | Summary     | yes      | One line, present tense, no trailing period                   |
      | 5        | File note   | optional | Path of the specific file the edit touched, if narrower than the page |

      Field 5, the file note, is used sparingly — mostly on pages that
      cover more than one file, such as the Files And Paths Referenced
      table further down this page, or a page that documents several
      scripts at once. Most entries stop at field 4.

      A markdown table row that follows this order:

        | 2025-06-30 | accountsvc 3.5.0 | mo | Added wrap-width note under Writing the Summary Line |

      The same entry as a YAML list item:

        - date: 2025-06-30
          release: accountsvc 3.5.0
          owner: mo
          summary: "Added wrap-width note under Writing the Summary Line"

      Note that field order in the YAML form follows the same sequence as
      the table columns — date first, release second, owner third,
      summary fourth — even though YAML keys don't strictly require an
      order. Writers who reorder the keys "because it reads better" make
      the two formats drift apart, and that drift is exactly what this
      page exists to prevent.

  - heading: "Naming a Release"
    owner: "Developer Experience (Priya Nair)"
    body: |
      The release tag is the field writers get wrong most often, so it
      gets its own section. There are two kinds of release a changelog
      entry can name, and only two:

      - An accountsvc package release, written as "accountsvc" followed by
        the three-part version number, for example accountsvc 3.5.0. Use
        this when the edit was made because the package's own version
        changed — a new flag on the command line, a new field returned by
        the loopback service, a change to what the database file stores.
      - A docs-only release, written as "Docs 1.x" where x is a short,
        informal count kept by Platform Tools, for example Docs 1.4. Use
        this when the edit has nothing to do with an accountsvc release —
        a reworded paragraph, a fixed link, a glossary term added.

      Do not invent a third kind of tag and do not leave the field blank.
      A blank release tag is one of the most common reasons an entry gets
      sent back during review (see review-cadence.md for how that review
      happens). If you genuinely don't know which accountsvc release an
      edit lines up with, ask Platform Tools before publishing rather than
      guessing — a wrong release tag is worse than a slightly late one
      because it misleads anyone cross-referencing the package's own
      release notes against the docs.

  - heading: "Writing the Summary Line"
    body: |
      The summary is the one field most readers actually look at, so it
      carries the most style weight. Four rules apply:

      1. Present tense, active voice. "Adds a field note column" not
         "Added a field note column was added."
      2. One clause. If you need "and" to join two separate changes, that's
         two changelog entries, not one.
      3. No trailing punctuation. Entries are short enough that a period
         only adds visual noise across a table of them.
      4. Name the thing that changed, not the fact that something changed.
         "Fixed the owner tag table" beats "Fixed a mistake."

      Writers coming from the general writing-style-guide.md page will
      recognize most of these rules — they're the same voice rules
      applied to a much smaller unit of text. The one place changelog
      style and general page style diverge is tense: body prose on most
      pages should stay in present tense throughout, but changelog
      summaries specifically favor a terse present-tense phrase over a
      full sentence, which body prose should generally avoid.

      A short, useful summary:

        Reorders owner tag ahead of summary in the field table

      A summary that will get flagged in review:

        Made some changes to how the fields work and fixed a typo too

  - heading: "Worked Examples"
    body: |
      Below are three changelog entries drawn from real edits to other
      pages in docs-style/, shown as they'd appear on those pages. They
      illustrate the three most common reasons an entry gets added: a new
      page, an edit to an existing page, and two pages being folded into
      one.

      New page created:

        | 2024-04-27 | accountsvc 2.0.0 | dw | Adds Docs Contributor Onboarding as a new page |

      Existing page edited because of a package release:

        | 2025-12-01 | accountsvc 3.8.0 | oc | Adds a row to the Docs Build Toolchain tool table for the new markdown checker |

      Two pages folded into one, or one split into two — always name both
      pages by title in the summary so the log stays searchable by page
      name later:

        | 2025-01-30 | Docs 1.2 | tb | Splits owner duties out of Writing Style Guide into Glossary Upkeep Guide |

      Observe the field order — date, release, owner tag, summary — holds
      across all three, even though the reasons behind each edit are
      different. That consistency is the entire point of this page: a
      reader scanning ten pages' change logs should be able to find the
      release tag in the same spot every time without reading the whole
      line first.

  - heading: "How Entries Move From Draft To Published"
    owner: "Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)"
    body: |
      Adding a changelog line is not the last step of an edit, it's a
      step in the middle of one. The full sequence:

      1. Make the content edit to the page.
      2. Add one dated entry at the top of the page's change log,
         following the field order above.
      3. Update the header block's "last updated" date to match the new
         entry's date, and bump the page's own version number if the
         style guide's rules for what counts as a version bump apply
         (writing-style-guide.md covers that threshold, not this page).
      4. Run the field checker from the repository root:

           python scripts\check_changelog_fields.py docs-style\changelog-format.yaml

         On a working setup this prints one line per page checked and
         exits quietly if every field is present and in order. If a field
         is missing or out of order it prints the line number and which
         field it expected next.
      5. Open the page for review following the cadence and reviewer
         list in review-cadence.md.
      6. Once reviewed, the page moves through the steps in
         publishing-workflow.md to go live.

      Writers sometimes skip step 4 because the script feels like extra
      friction for a one-line edit. Skipping it is how mis-ordered fields
      make it into published pages — the checker catches roughly a dozen
      ordering mistakes a month across the docs-style/ folder alone, most
      of them the owner tag and release tag swapped.

  - heading: "Common Mistakes And Fixes"
    owner: "Docs Guild (Theo Banks)"
    body: |
      A running list, added to as new mistakes show up in review:

      - Missing release tag. Fix: add either an accountsvc release tag or
        a Docs release tag, never leave the field blank.
      - Owner tag using a full name instead of initials. Fix: two or three
        lowercase initials only, matching the Terminology section below.
      - Entries not sorted newest-first. Fix: the newest dated entry
        always sits at the top of the log; older entries stay below it in
        order.
      - Vague summaries such as "various fixes" or "cleanup." Fix: name
        the specific thing that changed, even if it takes a few more
        words.
      - Header block "last updated" date not matching the newest
        changelog entry's date. Fix: these two dates must always agree;
        update whichever one is stale.
      - Using the page's own version number as the release tag. Fix: the
        release tag names an accountsvc package release or a Docs release
        count, never the page's own version field — those are two
        different numbers and mixing them up breaks cross-referencing.
      - Summary lines ending in a period, when the house convention is no
        trailing punctuation. This one is cosmetic but flagged
        consistently enough that it's worth listing.

  - heading: "Wrap Width And Line Length"
    body: |
      Changelog summary lines should stay under about seventy characters
      where the page format allows measuring it easily — this keeps a
      markdown table of entries from wrapping awkwardly in a narrow
      terminal or a side-by-side diff view. This is narrower than the
      general body-text wrap width used elsewhere on the page, since a
      changelog table has less horizontal room once the date, release,
      and owner columns are accounted for.

      If a summary genuinely needs more than seventy characters to say
      something useful, let it run long rather than cutting it awkwardly
      — a slightly long line is easier to read than one truncated
      mid-word. The seventy-character figure is a guideline, not a hard
      limit enforced by the checker script, which only checks field order
      and presence, not line length.

  - heading: "Terminology"
    body: |
      - Header block — the four required fields (title, version, owner,
        last updated) that open every page, kept separate from the
        changelog.
      - Field order — the fixed sequence date, release tag, owner tag,
        summary, optional file note, used for every changelog line on
        every page.
      - Release tag — the second field in a changelog line, naming either
        an accountsvc package release or a Docs release count.
      - Owner tag — two or three lowercase initials identifying who made
        the edit, standing in for the fuller name used in the header's
        owner field.
      - Docs release — an informal, sequential count (Docs 1.1, Docs 1.2,
        and so on) used as a release tag for edits unrelated to an
        accountsvc package release, tracked loosely by Platform Tools.
      - Dated entry — one full changelog line: date, release tag, owner
        tag, and summary together.
      - Summary line — the fourth field of a dated entry, a short present
        tense phrase describing the edit.
      - File note — the optional fifth field, naming a specific path when
        a page covers more than one file and the edit only touched one of
        them.
      - Field checker — the short name used around the team for
        scripts/check_changelog_fields.py, the script that reads a page's
        change log and confirms the fields are present and in order.
      - Block scalar — the YAML syntax (a line starting with a pipe
        character) used to hold multi-line body text inside a section
        entry on YAML-format pages like this one.

  - heading: "Files And Paths Referenced"
    body: |
      | Path                                          | Purpose                                                                 |
      |------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
      | docs-style/changelog-format.yaml                | This page — defines fields, order, and naming for every page's change log |
      | docs-style/writing-style-guide.md               | General voice, tense, and wrap-width rules that the summary-line rules on this page borrow from |
      | docs-style/page-template-catalog.md             | Shows the header block and change log placement inside each page template |
      | docs-style/review-cadence.md                    | Sets how often pages, including their change logs, get reviewed |
      | docs-style/publishing-workflow.md               | Covers what happens to a page after its change log entry is added and reviewed |
      | docs-style/terminology-reference.rst             | The broader glossary this page's Terminology section supplements for changelog-specific terms |
      | scripts/check_changelog_fields.py                | Reads a page's change log and reports missing or out-of-order fields |
      | docs/release-notes/                              | Holds the combined, per-release notes pulled together from individual page change logs |
      | README.md                                        | Repository root readme; links out to docs-style/ for anyone new to the docs set |

  - heading: "Tools And Libraries"
    body: |
      | Tool                    | Version   | Used for                                                        |
      |--------------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
      | Python                  | 3.11.9    | Running scripts/check_changelog_fields.py and other docs scripts |
      | PyYAML                  | 6.0.1     | Parsing YAML-format pages, including this one, for the field checker |
      | yamllint                | 1.35.1    | General YAML syntax checking before a page is reviewed |
      | markdownlint-cli        | 0.38.0    | Table and heading structure checks on markdown-format pages |
      | Vale                    | 3.4.1     | Prose-style checking, including summary-line tense and length hints |
      | git                     | 2.44.0    | Version control for the docs-style/ folder and the wider repository |

  - heading: "Change Log"
    body: |
      | Date       | Release            | Owner | Summary                                                        |
      |------------|---------------------|-------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
      | 2024-02-14 | accountsvc 2.1.0    | oc    | Drafts the first field list — date and summary only              |
      | 2024-05-02 | Docs 1.1            | mo    | Adds the owner tag as a required third field                     |
      | 2024-09-20 | accountsvc 2.6.0    | mo    | Reorders fields so release tag comes before owner tag             |
      | 2025-01-15 | Docs 1.3            | mo    | Standardizes the dated entry table and sets a six-entry minimum   |
      | 2025-03-11 | Docs 1.4            | tb    | Cross-checks glossary terms against terminology-reference.rst     |
      | 2025-05-30 | accountsvc 3.0.0    | pn    | Adds worked examples tied to the 3.0.0 release cycle              |
      | 2025-07-09 | Docs 1.5            | mo    | Adds the wrap width note and fixes the field order table          |

  - heading: "Related Pages"
    body: |
      - Docs Style Folder Overview
      - Writing Style Guide
      - Page Template Catalog
      - Glossary Upkeep Guide
      - Documentation Review Cadence
      - Docs Publishing Workflow
      - Terminology Reference

1	# Docs Contributor Onboarding
2	
3	**Version:** v1.1.0
4	**Owner:** Support Enablement (Dana Whitfield)
5	**Last updated:** 2024-04-27
6	
7	## Purpose and Coverage
8	
9	This page is the front door for anyone joining the small group of people who write and maintain internal documentation for accountsvc. It is aimed at a first-time contributor who has never touched the `docs-style/` folder before and just needs to get a local copy of the wiki working, understand the basic rules, and land one small, real edit without breaking anything.
10	
11	It does not try to replace the specialist pages that cover writing style, templates, the glossary, review cadence, or the publish pipeline in depth — those live in their own pages and are linked from the Related Pages section below. Instead, this page walks through the whole loop once, at a beginner's pace, so a new writer has a mental map before they go read the deeper material.
12	
13	If you are looking for the accountsvc package's own behavior — the command line, the loopback HTTP service, or the SQLite database file it keeps its state in — that is covered elsewhere in the wider documentation set, not on this docs-program page.
14	
15	## Who This Page Is For
16	
17	- Someone newly added to the Support Enablement or Docs Guild lineup who has been asked to "pick up a small docs task."
18	- A developer on Core Services or Platform Tools who is contributing one or two pages and doesn't plan to become a regular writer.
19	- Anyone returning to docs work after a long gap who wants an overview of current paths and tool versions.
20	
21	If you already know the wiki well, skip ahead to the Change Log to see what's new in this onboarding flow since your last visit.
22	
23	## Before You Start
24	
25	You'll need:
26	
27	1. A working checkout of the accountsvc repository on your machine.
28	2. A plain-text editor you're comfortable with (the team mostly uses VS Code, but any editor that handles Markdown and reStructuredText is fine).
29	3. Git installed locally — version 2.40 or newer is recommended, though anything from the last few years will work for the steps here.
30	4. Access to the internal wiki host where the built docs are published (ask your team lead if you don't already have this; setup for that access is outside this page).
31	
32	You do **not** need a Python interpreter, a build of the accountsvc package itself, or any special local service running to write or preview most docs pages. The one exception is the diagram preview step described later, which uses a small local script.
33	
34	## Setting Up Your Local Copy of the Wiki
35	
36	*Section owner: Owen Castillo, Core Services*
37	
38	The documentation lives inside the same repository as the package, under `docs/`. There is no separate docs repository and no `src/` folder — the package directory `accountsvc/` and the top-level `README.md` sit at the repository root alongside `docs/`.
39	
40	1. Clone the repository if you haven't already:
41	
42	   ```shell
43	   git clone <repository-url> accountsvc-repo
44	   cd accountsvc-repo
45	   ```
46	
47	2. Confirm the docs-style folder is present:
48	
49	   ```shell
50	   ls docs/docs-style
51	   ```
52	
53	   You should see the sibling pages listed later on this page (`README.md`, `writing-style-guide.md`, `page-template-catalog.md`, and so on).
54	
55	3. Create a working branch for your first edit. The convention on this team is `docs/<short-topic>-<your-initials>`:
56	
57	   ```shell
58	   git checkout -b docs/glossary-typo-fix-mv
59	   ```
60	
61	4. Open the folder in your editor. Most contributors keep two panes open: the page they're editing, and `writing-style-guide.md` for quick reference on voice, headings, and formatting.
62	
63	5. If you want to preview how a page renders before it goes through the publish pipeline, run the local preview helper from the `scripts/` folder:
64	
65	   ```shell
66	   scripts/build-docs.sh --preview docs/docs-style/contributor-onboarding.md
67	   ```
68	
69	   This produces a rendered copy under `docs-build/preview/` that you can open in a browser. It does not publish anything and does not touch the live wiki host.
70	
71	That's the whole local setup. There's no database to seed and no service to start — the docs program is just files in a folder plus a small shell-based build step.
72	
73	## Making Your First Small Edit
74	
75	A good first task is something small and low-risk: fixing a typo, adding a missing glossary term, correcting a broken internal link, or tightening a sentence that's grown awkward after several edits. Here is a worked example based on a real kind of first task.
76	
77	**Scenario:** You discovered that `docs/glossary.md` is missing an entry for "docs-style folder," a term this very page uses.
78	
79	1. Open `docs/glossary.md` and find the alphabetical spot for the new term.
80	2. Add a short, single-sentence definition, matching the existing entries' tone (plain, declarative, no marketing language).
81	3. Save the file and check the diff:
82	
83	   ```shell
84	   git diff docs/glossary.md
85	   ```
86	
87	4. Commit with a message that names the page and the kind of change:
88	
89	   ```shell
90	   git commit -am "docs: add glossary entry for docs-style folder"
91	   ```
92	
93	5. Push your branch and open a merge request against the main branch:
94	
95	   ```shell
96	   git push -u origin docs/glossary-typo-fix-mv
97	   ```
98	
99	6. Tag the section owner named on the page you touched (see the "Section owner" notes throughout this page and the header block of the page itself) so they can take a look before it merges.
100	
101	That's it — one small, complete loop. Once this feels natural, you're ready to take on a full new page using one of the templates described below.
102	
103	## Writing Style Basics for New Contributors
104	
105	*Section owner: Theo Banks, Docs Guild*
106	
107	The full rules live in `writing-style-guide.md` (currently v1.3.0), but the handful that trip up new writers most often are:
108	
109	- **Second person, present tense** for instructions: "Open the file," not "The user should open the file."
110	- **One sentence per idea** in step lists — long compound steps are a common review comment.
111	- **Sentence case** for headings, not Title Case, except for the top-level page title.
112	- **Name real paths and files**, not generic placeholders. If a page mentions a folder, it should mention the actual folder.
113	- **Keep a header block on every page** — title, version, owner, last-updated date — even for very short pages.
114	
115	New writers also tend to over-explain the accountsvc package's own internals inside a docs-program page. Keep this page, and pages like it, focused on the docs program itself: how pages are written, reviewed, and shipped — not on what the package does when it runs.
116	
117	## Choosing and Filling In a Page Template
118	
119	*Section owner: Priya Nair, Developer Experience*
120	
121	Before you start a new page from a blank file, check `page-template-catalog.md`. It holds ready-made skeletons for the common page shapes the team uses: a how-to page, a reference page, a concept page, and a short FAQ page.
122	
123	To start a new page from a template:
124	
125	1. Copy the relevant template file from `docs/templates/` into the target folder.
126	2. Rename it to match the topic, using lowercase words separated by hyphens (`docs-style/new-page-topic.md`).
127	3. Fill in the header block first — title, version (new pages start at `1.0`), owner, and today's date.
128	4. Work through the template's section headings in order; remove any that truly don't apply, but don't add unrelated sections just because you have material for them.
129	5. Add the new page's title to any sibling "Related Pages" sections that should now point to it, and add the sibling pages to your own.
130	
131	A quick anti-pattern worth naming: don't build a new page by copying an existing sibling page and editing around it. That's how header-block fields quietly go stale (an old version number, an owner who's since moved teams). Always start from the current template.
132	
133	## Glossary Upkeep for New Writers
134	
135	*Section owner: Theo Banks, Docs Guild*
136	
137	The docs program keeps two glossary-shaped things, and new writers sometimes conflate them:
138	
139	- `docs/glossary.md` — the working glossary of terms used across the whole wiki. This is the file you edit day to day.
140	- `glossary-upkeep.md` — a guide (not a glossary itself) describing how and when the glossary gets reviewed, who signs off on new terms, and how conflicting definitions get resolved.
141	
142	As a new contributor, your job with the glossary is small: if you introduce a term that isn't already defined, add a one-line entry to `docs/glossary.md` in the same pull request. Don't invent a new term for something that already has one — search the glossary first. If two terms seem to mean the same thing, flag it to the Docs Guild rather than picking one yourself; term consolidation is handled during the quarterly glossary review, not ad hoc.
143	
144	A short worked example: while writing a new page you use the phrase "build step." Check `docs/glossary.md` — it already has an entry for "build step," so you use it as written rather than introducing "docs build" as a fresh synonym.
145	
146	## Review Cadence: What to Expect on Your First Few Pages
147	
148	*Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools*
149	
150	New contributor pages get a closer look than the team's regular cadence, on the theory that early feedback saves everyone time later.
151	
152	| Stage | Who reviews | Typical turnaround |
153	|---|---|---|
154	| First edit (typo, glossary entry, small fix) | The section owner named on the page | 2–3 business days |
155	| First new page | Section owner + one Docs Guild member | Within ten business days |
156	| Anything touching the publish pipeline or build tooling | Platform Tools | Within one week |
157	
158	For your first three pages, expect a full line-by-line pass rather than a light skim — this is normal and not a sign that something's wrong. After that, you move onto the regular monthly cadence described in `review-cadence.md`, where most pages only get a full pass once a quarter unless they're flagged as high-traffic.
159	
160	If a reviewer hasn't responded within the windows above, it's fine to send a friendly follow-up message rather than waiting indefinitely.
161	
162	## The Publishing Workflow, Step by Step
163	
164	*Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools*
165	
166	Once a page has been reviewed and merged, it doesn't appear on the internal wiki host automatically — the merge and the publish step are separate on purpose, so a bad build doesn't take the live wiki down mid-review.
167	
168	1. Merging your branch into main triggers nothing by itself.
169	2. A member of Platform Tools (or, for small teams, whoever's on the lineup that week) runs the build:
170	
171	   ```shell
172	   scripts/build-docs.sh --publish
173	   ```
174	
175	3. The build step writes rendered output into `docs-build/site/` and drops a log of the run into `docs-build/logs/`.
176	4. If the build succeeds, the rendered site is copied to the internal wiki host. If it fails — usually a broken internal link or a malformed table — the person running the build checks `docs-build/logs/` for the failing page and either fixes it directly (for a one-line problem) or sends it back to the original writer.
177	5. Publishing typically happens twice a week, not on every merge, so don't expect your change to appear on the live wiki within minutes of merging.
178	
179	For the full detail on build tooling versions and how the site generator is configured, see `build-toolchain.rst`.
180	
181	## Common First-Timer Mistakes
182	
183	* Forgetting to update the header block's "last updated" date after making a real change to a page.
184	* Adding a brand-new heading structure to a page instead of following the matching template.
185	* Writing about how the accountsvc package itself behaves inside a docs-program page — keep those two things separate.
186	* Skipping the glossary check and re-defining an existing term under a slightly different name.
187	* Assuming a merge equals a publish — see the workflow section above.
188	* Copying an old sibling page's header block wholesale, which drags its stale version number and owner into a brand-new page.
189	
190	## Getting Help
191	
192	If you're stuck, the fastest paths are:
193	
194	- Message the section owner named for the part of this page you're stuck on.
195	- Post in the docs channel with a link to your branch or draft page.
196	- For anything about the build or publish step specifically, go straight to Platform Tools rather than the page's listed owner, since build issues usually aren't page-specific.
197	
198	## Terminology
199	
200	**Docs-style folder** — the `docs/docs-style/` directory that holds every page about how the documentation itself is written, reviewed, and shipped, as opposed to pages about the package.
201	
202	**Header block** — the small block of metadata (title, version, owner, last-updated date) required at the top of every page in this folder.
203	
204	**Section owner** — the individual named as responsible for keeping one section of a page accurate, noted inline under that section's heading.
205	
206	**Page template** — a ready-made skeleton of headings and structure for a common page shape, kept in `docs/templates/` and described in the Page Template Catalog.
207	
208	**Glossary entry** — a single short definition inside `docs/glossary.md`, kept separate from the guide describing how the glossary is maintained.
209	
210	**Review cadence** — the schedule and depth of feedback a page gets, which is closer and more frequent for new contributors than for established pages.
211	
212	**Publish step** — the separate action, run by Platform Tools, that turns a merged set of pages into the live copy on the internal wiki host.
213	
214	**Build log** — the record of a single run of the build step, written to `docs-build/logs/` and used to diagnose a failed publish.

# Docs Contributor Onboarding

**Version:** v1.1.0
**Owner:** Support Enablement (Dana Whitfield)
**Last updated:** 2024-04-27

## Purpose and Coverage

This page is the front door for anyone joining the small group of people who write and maintain internal documentation for accountsvc. It is aimed at a first-time contributor who has never touched the `docs-style/` folder before and just needs to get a local copy of the wiki working, understand the basic rules, and land one small, real edit without breaking anything.

It does not try to replace the specialist pages that cover writing style, templates, the glossary, review cadence, or the publish pipeline in depth — those live in their own pages and are linked from the Related Pages section below. Instead, this page walks through the whole loop once, at a beginner's pace, so a new writer has a mental map before they go read the deeper material.

If you are looking for the accountsvc package's own behavior — the command line, the loopback HTTP service, or the SQLite database file it keeps its state in — that is covered elsewhere in the wider documentation set, not on this docs-program page.

## Who This Page Is For

- Someone newly added to the Support Enablement or Docs Guild lineup who has been asked to "pick up a small docs task."
- A developer on Core Services or Platform Tools who is contributing one or two pages and doesn't plan to become a regular writer.
- Anyone returning to docs work after a long gap who wants an overview of current paths and tool versions.

If you already know the wiki well, skip ahead to the Change Log to see what's new in this onboarding flow since your last visit.

## Before You Start

You'll need:

1. A working checkout of the accountsvc repository on your machine.
2. A plain-text editor you're comfortable with (the team mostly uses VS Code, but any editor that handles Markdown and reStructuredText is fine).
3. Git installed locally — version 2.40 or newer is recommended, though anything from the last few years will work for the steps here.
4. Access to the internal wiki host where the built docs are published (ask your team lead if you don't already have this; setup for that access is outside this page).

You do **not** need a Python interpreter, a build of the accountsvc package itself, or any special local service running to write or preview most docs pages. The one exception is the diagram preview step described later, which uses a small local script.

## Setting Up Your Local Copy of the Wiki

*Section owner: Owen Castillo, Core Services*

The documentation lives inside the same repository as the package, under `docs/`. There is no separate docs repository and no `src/` folder — the package directory `accountsvc/` and the top-level `README.md` sit at the repository root alongside `docs/`.

1. Clone the repository if you haven't already:

   ```shell
   git clone <repository-url> accountsvc-repo
   cd accountsvc-repo
   ```

2. Confirm the docs-style folder is present:

   ```shell
   ls docs/docs-style
   ```

   You should see the sibling pages listed later on this page (`README.md`, `writing-style-guide.md`, `page-template-catalog.md`, and so on).

3. Create a working branch for your first edit. The convention on this team is `docs/<short-topic>-<your-initials>`:

   ```shell
   git checkout -b docs/glossary-typo-fix-mv
   ```

4. Open the folder in your editor. Most contributors keep two panes open: the page they're editing, and `writing-style-guide.md` for quick reference on voice, headings, and formatting.

5. If you want to preview how a page renders before it goes through the publish pipeline, run the local preview helper from the `scripts/` folder:

   ```shell
   scripts/build-docs.sh --preview docs/docs-style/contributor-onboarding.md
   ```

   This produces a rendered copy under `docs-build/preview/` that you can open in a browser. It does not publish anything and does not touch the live wiki host.

That's the whole local setup. There's no database to seed and no service to start — the docs program is just files in a folder plus a small shell-based build step.

## Making Your First Small Edit

A good first task is something small and low-risk: fixing a typo, adding a missing glossary term, correcting a broken internal link, or tightening a sentence that's grown awkward after several edits. Here is a worked example based on a real kind of first task.

**Scenario:** You discovered that `docs/glossary.md` is missing an entry for "docs-style folder," a term this very page uses.

1. Open `docs/glossary.md` and find the alphabetical spot for the new term.
2. Add a short, single-sentence definition, matching the existing entries' tone (plain, declarative, no marketing language).
3. Save the file and check the diff:

   ```shell
   git diff docs/glossary.md
   ```

4. Commit with a message that names the page and the kind of change:

   ```shell
   git commit -am "docs: add glossary entry for docs-style folder"
   ```

5. Push your branch and open a merge request against the main branch:

   ```shell
   git push -u origin docs/glossary-typo-fix-mv
   ```

6. Tag the section owner named on the page you touched (see the "Section owner" notes throughout this page and the header block of the page itself) so they can take a look before it merges.

That's it — one small, complete loop. Once this feels natural, you're ready to take on a full new page using one of the templates described below.

## Writing Style Basics for New Contributors

*Section owner: Theo Banks, Docs Guild*

The full rules live in `writing-style-guide.md` (currently v1.3.0), but the handful that trip up new writers most often are:

- **Second person, present tense** for instructions: "Open the file," not "The user should open the file."
- **One sentence per idea** in step lists — long compound steps are a common review comment.
- **Sentence case** for headings, not Title Case, except for the top-level page title.
- **Name real paths and files**, not generic placeholders. If a page mentions a folder, it should mention the actual folder.
- **Keep a header block on every page** — title, version, owner, last-updated date — even for very short pages.

New writers also tend to over-explain the accountsvc package's own internals inside a docs-program page. Keep this page, and pages like it, focused on the docs program itself: how pages are written, reviewed, and shipped — not on what the package does when it runs.

## Choosing and Filling In a Page Template

*Section owner: Priya Nair, Developer Experience*

Before you start a new page from a blank file, check `page-template-catalog.md`. It holds ready-made skeletons for the common page shapes the team uses: a how-to page, a reference page, a concept page, and a short FAQ page.

To start a new page from a template:

1. Copy the relevant template file from `docs/templates/` into the target folder.
2. Rename it to match the topic, using lowercase words separated by hyphens (`docs-style/new-page-topic.md`).
3. Fill in the header block first — title, version (new pages start at `1.0`), owner, and today's date.
4. Work through the template's section headings in order; remove any that truly don't apply, but don't add unrelated sections just because you have material for them.
5. Add the new page's title to any sibling "Related Pages" sections that should now point to it, and add the sibling pages to your own.

A quick anti-pattern worth naming: don't build a new page by copying an existing sibling page and editing around it. That's how header-block fields quietly go stale (an old version number, an owner who's since moved teams). Always start from the current template.

## Glossary Upkeep for New Writers

*Section owner: Theo Banks, Docs Guild*

The docs program keeps two glossary-shaped things, and new writers sometimes conflate them:

- `docs/glossary.md` — the working glossary of terms used across the whole wiki. This is the file you edit day to day.
- `glossary-upkeep.md` — a guide (not a glossary itself) describing how and when the glossary gets reviewed, who signs off on new terms, and how conflicting definitions get resolved.

As a new contributor, your job with the glossary is small: if you introduce a term that isn't already defined, add a one-line entry to `docs/glossary.md` in the same pull request. Don't invent a new term for something that already has one — search the glossary first. If two terms seem to mean the same thing, flag it to the Docs Guild rather than picking one yourself; term consolidation is handled during the quarterly glossary review, not ad hoc.

A short worked example: while writing a new page you use the phrase "build step." Check `docs/glossary.md` — it already has an entry for "build step," so you use it as written rather than introducing "docs build" as a fresh synonym.

## Review Cadence: What to Expect on Your First Few Pages

*Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools*

New contributor pages get a closer look than the team's regular cadence, on the theory that early feedback saves everyone time later.

| Stage | Who reviews | Typical turnaround |
|---|---|---|
| First edit (typo, glossary entry, small fix) | The section owner named on the page | 2–3 business days |
| First new page | Section owner + one Docs Guild member | Within ten business days |
| Anything touching the publish pipeline or build tooling | Platform Tools | Within one week |

For your first three pages, expect a full line-by-line pass rather than a light skim — this is normal and not a sign that something's wrong. After that, you move onto the regular monthly cadence described in `review-cadence.md`, where most pages only get a full pass once a quarter unless they're flagged as high-traffic.

If a reviewer hasn't responded within the windows above, it's fine to send a friendly follow-up message rather than waiting indefinitely.

## The Publishing Workflow, Step by Step

*Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools*

Once a page has been reviewed and merged, it doesn't appear on the internal wiki host automatically — the merge and the publish step are separate on purpose, so a bad build doesn't take the live wiki down mid-review.

1. Merging your branch into main triggers nothing by itself.
2. A member of Platform Tools (or, for small teams, whoever's on the lineup that week) runs the build:

   ```shell
   scripts/build-docs.sh --publish
   ```

3. The build step writes rendered output into `docs-build/site/` and drops a log of the run into `docs-build/logs/`.
4. If the build succeeds, the rendered site is copied to the internal wiki host. If it fails — usually a broken internal link or a malformed table — the person running the build checks `docs-build/logs/` for the failing page and either fixes it directly (for a one-line problem) or sends it back to the original writer.
5. Publishing typically happens twice a week, not on every merge, so don't expect your change to appear on the live wiki within minutes of merging.

For the full detail on build tooling versions and how the site generator is configured, see `build-toolchain.rst`.

## Common First-Timer Mistakes

* Forgetting to update the header block's "last updated" date after making a real change to a page.
* Adding a brand-new heading structure to a page instead of following the matching template.
* Writing about how the accountsvc package itself behaves inside a docs-program page — keep those two things separate.
* Skipping the glossary check and re-defining an existing term under a slightly different name.
* Assuming a merge equals a publish — see the workflow section above.
* Copying an old sibling page's header block wholesale, which drags its stale version number and owner into a brand-new page.

## Getting Help

If you're stuck, the fastest paths are:

- Message the section owner named for the part of this page you're stuck on.
- Post in the docs channel with a link to your branch or draft page.
- For anything about the build or publish step specifically, go straight to Platform Tools rather than the page's listed owner, since build issues usually aren't page-specific.

## Terminology

**Docs-style folder** — the `docs/docs-style/` directory that holds every page about how the documentation itself is written, reviewed, and shipped, as opposed to pages about the package.

**Header block** — the small block of metadata (title, version, owner, last-updated date) required at the top of every page in this folder.

**Section owner** — the individual named as responsible for keeping one section of a page accurate, noted inline under that section's heading.

**Page template** — a ready-made skeleton of headings and structure for a common page shape, kept in `docs/templates/` and described in the Page Template Catalog.

**Glossary entry** — a single short definition inside `docs/glossary.md`, kept separate from the guide describing how the glossary is maintained.

**Review cadence** — the schedule and depth of feedback a page gets, which is closer and more frequent for new contributors than for established pages.

**Publish step** — the separate action, run by Platform Tools, that turns a merged set of pages into the live copy on the internal wiki host.

**Build log** — the record of a single run of the build step, written to `docs-build/logs/` and used to diagnose a failed publish.

**Worked example** — a small, concrete, step-by-step illustration used inside a page to show a procedure rather than just describe it.

**Sibling page** — any other page in the same folder that a page's Related Pages section points to, and which usually points back.

1	Link Checking Notes
2	Version: 1.0
3	Owner: Support Enablement (Dana Whitfield)
4	Last updated: 2026-01-14
5	
6	Purpose and Coverage
7	-----------------
8	This page describes the manual steps a writer follows before publishing or re-publishing a page in docs-style/ (and, by extension, any page in docs/ that cross-references a docs-style page) to confirm that internal links still point somewhere real. It does not cover external links to outside sites — those are checked separately and much less often, since they change less and the payoff for chasing them down is lower. It also does not cover the mechanics of the publishing step itself; that belongs to Docs Publishing Workflow.
9	
10	"Link checking" here means the practice of walking through a page's cross-references — to sibling pages, to sections within the same page, and occasionally to files outside docs-style/ such as scripts/ or a log folder — and verifying each one resolves to something that still exists, under the name it currently has. As of version 1.2 of this page we stopped treating anchor checks as optional; see the Anchors section below for why.
11	
12	Section Owner for this page: Dana Whitfield. Section owners for individual parts are called out below where a different person on the team wrote or maintains that part.
13	
14	Why Manual, Not Automated
15	--------------------------
16	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
17	
18	The docs-style folder is small enough (thirteen pages as of this writing) that a full automated link-checking pipeline has never been built for it. There's a modest shell script in scripts/ that catches the easy cases (see Tools and Configuration, below), but it does not understand headings that have been reworded, section anchors that were renamed without updating callers, or the difference between "this page moved" and "this page was removed on purpose." Those require a human to read the target page and confirm the reference still says what the writer meant.
19	
20	We have talked about wiring the link check into the build step described in Docs Build Toolchain, and Owen Castillo has a draft for that, but it hasn't landed. Until it does, the process below is what actually runs before each publish.
21	
22	Where Links Live
23	-----------------
24	Section owner: Dana Whitfield
25	
26	Internal links in docs-style/ show up in a few places, and each has its own quirks:
27	
28	1. Markdown-style relative links inside .md pages — the most common case. Example: a related-pages section linking `(page-template-catalog.md)`.
29	2. Anchor links inside a single page, pointing at a heading — for example a table of contents at the top of a long page linking down to a section further below.
30	3. Cross-file anchor links, where a page links to a specific heading in another page rather than just the top of it. These are the ones that break most often, because headings get reworded far more often than filenames change.
31	4. RST-style references inside the two .rst pages (terminology-reference.rst and build-toolchain.rst), which use a different linking syntax entirely and are easy to miss if you're only grepping for markdown-style brackets.
32	5. Plain-text mentions of a page title with no link at all — these aren't technically links, but a writer doing a link pass should still flag them if the title they name has since changed, since that's the same failure mode wearing a different hat.
33	
34	A rule of thumb: if you can `Ctrl+click` it in a text editor and it goes somewhere, it's covered by this page. If it's just a name mentioned in prose, it's a softer case but still worth a glance.
35	
36	Manual Link-Checking Procedure
37	-------------------------------
38	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
39	
40	Follow this before publishing any change to a page in docs-style/, and again on the quarterly pass described in Documentation Review Cadence.
41	
42	Step 1 — Pull the current state of docs-style/ and open the page you're changing side by side with its rendered neighbors. If you're on a shared checkout, run:
43	
44	    git pull origin main
45	    cd docs-style
46	
47	Step 2 — List every internal reference the page makes. The fastest way is a targeted grep for the link syntax rather than trying to read every line by eye:
48	
49	    rg -n "\]\(" writing-style-guide.md
50	
51	This turns up every markdown-style link target in the file along with its line number, which you then work through one at a time.
52	
53	Step 3 — For each link target that is a bare filename (no anchor), confirm the file exists in the same folder:
54	
55	    ls docs-style/ | rg -F "page-template-catalog.md"
56	
57	If the file is not there, check whether it was renamed. A quick way to catch a rename is to look at recent commits touching docs-style/:
58	
59	    git log --oneline --follow -- docs-style/
60	
61	Step 4 — For each link target that includes an anchor (anything after a `#`), open the target page and confirm a heading exists that would generate that anchor slug. See the Anchors section below for how slugs are derived — this is the step people skip, and it's the one that actually catches the most breakage.
62	
63	Step 5 — For plain-text mentions of a page's title (no link, just a name in a sentence), confirm the title in the header block of the target page still matches what's written. Titles do drift — a page gets renamed for clarity and the old name lingers in three other pages' related-pages sections for months.
64	
65	Step 6 — Once every link and mention checks out, note the pass in your own working notes (not a formal log — just enough that if someone asks "did you check X" you can say when). If you find and fix something, that's when it's worth a changelog entry on the page you fixed, not on this page.
66	
67	Step 7 — If you touched more than two pages in a single pass, it's worth doing a second lightweight sweep afterward, because fixing one broken anchor sometimes reveals that the heading you "fixed" it to point at is itself about to be reworded by someone else's change in progress. Coordinate over the usual channel rather than guessing.
68	
69	Worked Example 1: Checking a Markdown Page
70	--------------------------------------------
71	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
72	
73	Say you're updating markdown-conventions.md and it contains this line in its related-pages section:
74	
75	    See also: Writing Style Guide (writing-style-guide.md), Page Template Catalog (page-template-catalog.md#required-sections)
76	
77	Two things to check here. First, does writing-style-guide.md exist — yes, in docs-style/, unchanged. Second, does page-template-catalog.md have a heading that produces the anchor `required-sections`? Open the file and look for a heading spelled close to "Required Sections." If the actual heading in the current version of that page reads "Required Page Sections" instead, the anchor slug would be `required-page-sections`, and the link as written is broken even though the file itself exists. This is the single most common failure mode in this folder: the file is fine, the anchor drifted.
78	
79	Fix: update the anchor in markdown-conventions.md to match the current heading, or — better, if you're the one who's about to touch page-template-catalog.md anyway — ask Priya Nair whether the heading can be renamed back, since three other pages reference the old anchor text and it's cheaper to preserve the anchor than to chase every caller.
80	
81	Worked Example 2: Checking an RST Page
82	----------------------------------------
83	Section owner: Owen Castillo (Core Services owns both .rst pages in this folder)
84	
85	terminology-reference.rst and build-toolchain.rst use a different cross-reference syntax, and a grep tuned for markdown brackets will silently miss it. A quick separate pass:
86	
87	    rg -n ":ref:" terminology-reference.rst
88	    rg -n "\`.*\`_" build-toolchain.rst
89	
90	RST inline references and markdown links look nothing alike, and because there are only two .rst pages in the folder it's easy to forget them entirely during a link pass — which is exactly what happened during the November 2025 sweep, when a rename in build-toolchain.rst's section on toolchain versions went unnoticed in terminology-reference.rst for about six weeks.
91	
92	Anchors, Headings, and Slugs
93	------------------------------
94	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
95	
96	Most of the markdown rendering used for docs-style/ derives an anchor slug from a heading by lowercasing it, replacing spaces with hyphens, and dropping punctuation. "Manual Link-Checking Procedure" becomes `manual-link-checking-procedure`. Two headings with the same text on the same page get a numeric suffix on the second one (`-1`, `-2`), which is a separate trap: if a page has two headings that render to the same slug and a link points at the second occurrence, renaming or reordering headings elsewhere on that page can silently shift which one the link resolves to.
97	
98	Practical implication: whenever you reword a heading, grep the whole docs-style/ folder for the old anchor text before you commit, not just the page you're editing:
99	
100	    rg -n "manual-link-checking" docs-style/
101	
102	This one command has caught more stale anchors than the entire scripted check described below, because the script only checks that a target file exists — it does not currently parse headings on the far side of a cross-file anchor link.
103	
104	Handling Moved or Renamed Pages
105	---------------------------------
106	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
107	
108	When a page in docs-style/ is renamed (filename change, not just a title change), the writer doing the rename is responsible for finding every other page that links to the old filename and updating it in the same change. This is different from a heading rename, which only breaks anchors — a filename rename breaks the link outright.
109	
110	    rg -l "old-file-name.md" docs-style/
111	
112	Update every hit before you commit the rename. If you can't update every hit in the same change (for example, a page owned by another team is mid-edit and you don't want to collide), leave a plain-text note at the top of the renamed page for one publish cycle: "formerly old-file-name.md" — this is the one case where a temporary pointer-style note earns its keep, since readers following stale bookmarks or old cross-references from outside docs-style/ will otherwise land nowhere.
113	
114	Common Link Breakage Patterns
115	-------------------------------
116	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
117	
118	| Pattern | What it looks like | How it's usually caught | Typical fix |
119	|---|---|---|---|
120	| Stale anchor, file intact | Link resolves to a real file, wrong section | Manual open-and-read (Step 4) | Update the anchor to match the current heading |
121	| Renamed file, old links untouched | grep for old filename turns up hits elsewhere | `rg -l` sweep after a rename | Update every caller in the same change |
122	| Reworded title, related-pages text unchanged | Title in prose no longer matches header block | Step 5, side-by-side read | Update the prose to the current title |
123	| Duplicate heading slug shift | Link now resolves to the wrong one of two same-named headings | Rare, usually reported by a reader | Rename one heading to disambiguate |
124	| RST reference missed by markdown-tuned grep | Broken :ref: went undetected for weeks | Separate rst-specific pass (Example 2) | Run the rst grep every time, not just when "something feels off" |
125	| Cross-file anchor into a page that was reorganized | Anchor used to be near the top, heading text changed during reorg | Full read of the target page, not just a grep | Point the anchor at the new heading text |
126	| link to a scripts/ file that was moved during a toolchain cleanup | 404 on what used to be a working link | Found during the quarterly pass, not before | Update the path, or point at the folder instead of the file if the exact name isn't stable |
127	
128	Cadence and Coordination
129	-------------------------
130	Section Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools sets the overall review cadence)
131	
132	This page's procedure runs at two cadences. First, per-change: whenever a writer edits a page in docs-style/, they run at least Steps 1 through 5 against that one page before publishing. Second, on the quarterly pass defined by Documentation Review Cadence, someone runs the full procedure against every page in the folder, not just the one being changed that week — this is the pass that catches drift accumulated from other people's small, individually-reasonable edits.
133	
134	The last full quarterly pass across docs-style/ was completed 2026-01-10, ahead of this page's own last-updated date, and turned up four stale anchors and one renamed-file miss (the build-toolchain.rst case described above). The next full pass is scheduled to align with the cadence described in Documentation Review Cadence, coordinated by Priya Nair since Developer Experience currently owns two of the pages most often touched between passes.
135	
136	Tools and Configuration
137	-------------------------
138	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
139	
140	The scripted half of link checking is a small shell script kept at scripts/check-links.sh. It is deliberately unambitious: it walks every markdown file in a given folder, extracts bracketed link targets, and confirms the target file exists relative to the linking page. It does not follow anchors, does not understand RST references, and does not check anything outside the folder you point it at.
141	
142	A representative invocation:
143	
144	    bash scripts/check-links.sh docs-style/
145	
146	Sample output from a clean run looks like:
147	
148	    checking docs-style/README.md ... 6 links, 0 broken
149	    checking docs-style/writing-style-guide.md ... 4 links, 0 broken
150	    checking docs-style/page-template-catalog.md ... 5 links, 0 broken
151	    checking docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md ... 3 links, 0 broken
152	    checking docs-style/review-cadence.md ... 2 links, 0 broken
153	    checking docs-style/publishing-workflow.md ... 7 links, 0 broken
154	    checking docs-style/terminology-reference.rst ... skipped (rst not supported)
155	    checking docs-style/build-toolchain.rst ... skipped (rst not supported)
156	    all checked files clean
157	
158	Note the two "skipped" lines — this is why Example 2 above exists as a separate manual step. The script's author (a contractor who moved off the team in mid-2025) left a comment in the script noting that RST support was "next," and it has stayed "next" since. If you're the one who finally adds it, update this page's changelog and the Tools table below.
159	
160	For the ad hoc greps used throughout this page, ripgrep is preferred over plain grep for speed on the full docs/ tree, but either works fine on a folder as small as docs-style/. On a Windows checkout without ripgrep installed, PowerShell's Select-String does the same job for a single file:
161	
162	    Select-String -Path .\docs-style\writing-style-guide.md -Pattern "\]\("
163	
164	There is also a hosted link checker (markdown-link-check) that some contributors run locally against a single page before opening a change; it is not wired into the shared workflow, so results from it are advisory only and should not be treated as equivalent to the manual procedure above.
165	
166	Coordination with Publishing
167	------------------------------
168	Section Owner: Mara Olsen
169	
170	Link checking happens before publishing, not as part of it. The publishing step itself, described in Docs Publishing Workflow, produces a build log that will surface a subset of broken links as warnings — specifically the ones where a linked file is entirely missing — but it does not catch anchor drift or reworded titles. Treat the build log as a backstop, not a substitute for the manual pass. Docs Publishing Workflow is currently maintained by Priya Nair, so if a build-log warning about a link doesn't make sense, that's who to ask.
171	
172	Build logs from recent publishes live in docs/build-logs/ and are worth a skim after any change that touched more than one page, since a warning there is the cheapest signal you'll get that something upstream broke.
173	
174	Known Gaps
175	-----------
176	Section Owner: Dana Whitfield
177	
178	- The scripted check does not understand anchors at all, cross-file or same-file.
179	- The scripted check does not run against the two .rst pages.
180	- There is no tooling that checks links from outside docs-style/ into docs-style/ — if a page in docs/ links into this folder and something here gets renamed, nothing will flag it automatically. This has bitten us at least twice; both times a reader reported the broken link rather than a writer catching it first.
181	- Plain-text title mentions (Step 5) are the easiest step to skip under time pressure, and it shows in how often they're the thing that's stale during a quarterly pass.
182	
183	Terminology
184	------------
185	Section Owner: Priya Nair (Developer Experience keeps the shared glossary; entries below are specific to link checking and may duplicate or slightly extend that shared list)
186	
187	Anchor — the portion of a link after a `#` that points at a specific heading within a page rather than the top of it.
188	
189	Slug — the lowercased, hyphenated form of a heading that a page renderer generates automatically and that anchors must match to resolve.
190	
191	Cross-file anchor — a link that includes both a different filename and an anchor, pointing at a specific section of another page.
192	
193	Broken link — any internal reference whose target file, heading, or title no longer matches what the reference expects.
194	
195	Quarterly pass — the full link-checking sweep across every page in docs-style/, run on the cadence set out in Documentation Review Cadence, as distinct from a per-change check limited to the page being edited.
196	
197	Related-pages section — the section, present on most pages in this folder, listing sibling pages by title; the primary place stale title mentions and stale filenames tend to surface.
198	
199	Header block — the title, version, owner, and last-updated fields required at the top of every page in docs-style/, used here as a quick way to confirm a linked page's stated title still matches how it's referenced elsewhere.
200	
201	Build log — the output produced during the publishing step, kept in docs/build-logs/, which surfaces a narrow subset of broken links (missing files only) as warnings.
202	
203	Rename sweep — the grep-based check for every reference to an old filename or old anchor text, run immediately after renaming a page or heading.
204

207	- docs-style/README.md — folder overview and index of the pages covered by this documentation program.
208	- docs-style/writing-style-guide.md — the style rules a link-checking pass assumes are already applied to prose (tone, tense, terminology choices).

213	- docs-style/terminology-reference.rst — one of the two RST-format pages that need a separate manual grep pass, as shown in Example 2.

Link Checking Notes
Version: 1.0
Owner: Support Enablement (Dana Whitfield)
Last updated: 2026-01-14

Purpose and Coverage
-----------------
This page describes the manual steps a writer follows before publishing or re-publishing a page in docs-style/ (and, by extension, any page in docs/ that cross-references a docs-style page) to confirm that internal links still point somewhere real. It does not cover external links to outside sites — those are checked separately and much less often, since they change less and the payoff for chasing them down is lower. It also does not cover the mechanics of the publishing step itself; that belongs to Docs Publishing Workflow.

"Link checking" here means the practice of walking through a page's cross-references — to sibling pages, to sections within the same page, and occasionally to files outside docs-style/ such as scripts/ or a log folder — and verifying each one resolves to something that still exists, under the name it currently has. As of version 1.2 of this page we stopped treating anchor checks as optional; see the Anchors section below for why.

Section Owner for this page: Dana Whitfield. Section owners for individual parts are called out below where a different person on the team wrote or maintains that part.

Why Manual, Not Automated
--------------------------
Section Owner: Dana Whitfield

The docs-style folder is small enough (thirteen pages as of this writing) that a full automated link-checking pipeline has never been built for it. There's a modest shell script in scripts/ that catches the easy cases (see Tools and Configuration, below), but it does not understand headings that have been reworded, section anchors that were renamed without updating callers, or the difference between "this page moved" and "this page was removed on purpose." Those require a human to read the target page and confirm the reference still says what the writer meant.

We have talked about wiring the link check into the build step described in Docs Build Toolchain, and Owen Castillo has a draft for that, but it hasn't landed. Until it does, the process below is what actually runs before each publish.

Where Links Live
-----------------
Section owner: Dana Whitfield

Internal links in docs-style/ show up in a few places, and each has its own quirks:

1. Markdown-style relative links inside .md pages — the most common case. Example: a related-pages section linking `(page-template-catalog.md)`.
2. Anchor links inside a single page, pointing at a heading — for example a table of contents at the top of a long page linking down to a section further below.
3. Cross-file anchor links, where a page links to a specific heading in another page rather than just the top of it. These are the ones that break most often, because headings get reworded far more often than filenames change.
4. RST-style references inside the two .rst pages (terminology-reference.rst and build-toolchain.rst), which use a different linking syntax entirely and are easy to miss if you're only grepping for markdown-style brackets.
5. Plain-text mentions of a page title with no link at all — these aren't technically links, but a writer doing a link pass should still flag them if the title they name has since changed, since that's the same failure mode wearing a different hat.

A rule of thumb: if you can `Ctrl+click` it in a text editor and it goes somewhere, it's covered by this page. If it's just a name mentioned in prose, it's a softer case but still worth a glance.

Manual Link-Checking Procedure
-------------------------------
Section Owner: Dana Whitfield

Follow this before publishing any change to a page in docs-style/, and again on the quarterly pass described in Documentation Review Cadence.

Step 1 — Pull the current state of docs-style/ and open the page you're changing side by side with its rendered neighbors. If you're on a shared checkout, run:

    git pull origin main
    cd docs-style

Step 2 — List every internal reference the page makes. The fastest way is a targeted grep for the link syntax rather than trying to read every line by eye:

    rg -n "\]\(" writing-style-guide.md

This turns up every markdown-style link target in the file along with its line number, which you then work through one at a time.

Step 3 — For each link target that is a bare filename (no anchor), confirm the file exists in the same folder:

    ls docs-style/ | rg -F "page-template-catalog.md"

If the file is not there, check whether it was renamed. A quick way to catch a rename is to look at recent commits touching docs-style/:

    git log --oneline --follow -- docs-style/

Step 4 — For each link target that includes an anchor (anything after a `#`), open the target page and confirm a heading exists that would generate that anchor slug. See the Anchors section below for how slugs are derived — this is the step people skip, and it's the one that actually catches the most breakage.

Step 5 — For plain-text mentions of a page's title (no link, just a name in a sentence), confirm the title in the header block of the target page still matches what's written. Titles do drift — a page gets renamed for clarity and the old name lingers in three other pages' related-pages sections for months.

Step 6 — Once every link and mention checks out, note the pass in your own working notes (not a formal log — just enough that if someone asks "did you check X" you can say when). If you find and fix something, that's when it's worth a changelog entry on the page you fixed, not on this page.

Step 7 — If you touched more than two pages in a single pass, it's worth doing a second lightweight sweep afterward, because fixing one broken anchor sometimes reveals that the heading you "fixed" it to point at is itself about to be reworded by someone else's change in progress. Coordinate over the usual channel rather than guessing.

Worked Example 1: Checking a Markdown Page
--------------------------------------------
Section Owner: Dana Whitfield

Say you're updating markdown-conventions.md and it contains this line in its related-pages section:

    See also: Writing Style Guide (writing-style-guide.md), Page Template Catalog (page-template-catalog.md#required-sections)

Two things to check here. First, does writing-style-guide.md exist — yes, in docs-style/, unchanged. Second, does page-template-catalog.md have a heading that produces the anchor `required-sections`? Open the file and look for a heading spelled close to "Required Sections." If the actual heading in the current version of that page reads "Required Page Sections" instead, the anchor slug would be `required-page-sections`, and the link as written is broken even though the file itself exists. This is the single most common failure mode in this folder: the file is fine, the anchor drifted.

Fix: update the anchor in markdown-conventions.md to match the current heading, or — better, if you're the one who's about to touch page-template-catalog.md anyway — ask Priya Nair whether the heading can be renamed back, since three other pages reference the old anchor text and it's cheaper to preserve the anchor than to chase every caller.

Worked Example 2: Checking an RST Page
----------------------------------------
Section owner: Owen Castillo (Core Services owns both .rst pages in this folder)

terminology-reference.rst and build-toolchain.rst use a different cross-reference syntax, and a grep tuned for markdown brackets will silently miss it. A quick separate pass:

    rg -n ":ref:" terminology-reference.rst
    rg -n "\`.*\`_" build-toolchain.rst

RST inline references and markdown links look nothing alike, and because there are only two .rst pages in the folder it's easy to forget them entirely during a link pass — which is exactly what happened during the November 2025 sweep, when a rename in build-toolchain.rst's section on toolchain versions went unnoticed in terminology-reference.rst for about six weeks.

Section Owner: Dana Whitfield

| link to a scripts/ file that was moved during a toolchain cleanup | 404 on what used to be a working link | Found during the quarterly pass, not before | Update the path, or point at the folder instead of the file if the exact name isn't stable |

-------------------------
Section Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools sets the overall review cadence)

    checking docs-style/writing-style-guide.md ... 4 links, 0 broken
    checking docs-style/page-template-catalog.md ... 5 links, 0 broken
    checking docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md ... 3 links, 0 broken
    checking docs-style/review-cadence.md ... 2 links, 0 broken

------------

Header block — the title, version, owner, and last-updated fields required at the top of every page in docs-style/, used here as a quick way to confirm a linked page's stated title still matches how it's referenced elsewhere.

Build log — the output produced during the publishing step, kept in docs/build-logs/, which surfaces a narrow subset of broken links (missing files only) as warnings.

Rename sweep — the grep-based check for every reference to an old filename or old anchor text, run immediately after renaming a page or heading.

Files and Paths Referenced
-----------------------------
- docs-style/README.md — folder overview and index of the pages covered by this documentation program.
- docs-style/writing-style-guide.md — the style rules a link-checking pass assumes are already applied to prose (tone, tense, terminology choices).
- docs-style/page-template-catalog.md — defines the section structure each page type is expected to follow, referenced when confirming a linked anchor should exist under a given template.
- docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md — the process for keeping the shared glossary current; referenced when a term used in this page's Terminology section might already be defined centrally.
- docs-style/review-cadence.md — sets the quarterly cadence this page's full sweep is timed against.
- docs-style/publishing-workflow.md — describes the publish step whose build log is a secondary signal for broken links.
- docs-style/terminology-reference.rst — one of the two RST-format pages that need a separate manual grep pass, as shown in Example 2.
- docs-style/markdown-conventions.md — the page used as the worked example for a standard markdown-format link check.
- docs-style/changelog-format.yaml — the shared format each page's changelog is expected to follow; not itself a target of link checks but referenced when writing this page's own changelog entries.
- docs-style/build-toolchain.rst — the second RST-format page, and the source of the November 2025 stale-reference incident described above.
- scripts/check-links.sh — the shell script that performs the automated portion of a link check against a folder of markdown pages.
- docs/build-logs/ — folder holding recent publish output, including link-related warnings, used as a backstop check after publishing.

Tools, Packages, and Libraries
--------------------------------

| Tool | Version | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| git | 2.43.0 | pulling current state, following file rename lineage |

| PowerShell | 7.4 | Select-String-based grepping on Windows checkouts |
| bash | 5.2 | running scripts/check-links.sh |
| markdown-link-check | 3.12.1 | optional local, single-page advisory check; not part of the shared workflow |

5	:Title: Docs Build Toolchain

10	Overview
11	--------
12	
13	This page describes the local tools that turn the source files in ``docs-style/`` and ``docs/`` into the rendered pages that show up on the internal wiki host for accountsvc. It does not cover what any single page should say — the Writing Style Guide, Page Template Catalog, and Voice and Tone Notes handle that. This page is strictly about the mechanics: what runs, in what order, reading which files, and writing output where.
14	
15	The toolchain is deliberately small. accountsvc itself is written against only the standard library, and over the past two years the docs tooling has drifted toward the same habit where it can — the local preview server, for instance, is a thin wrapper around ``http.server`` rather than a separate web framework. Where a third-party package is unavoidable (Sphinx, for the actual rendering), we pin versions tightly and upgrade on a schedule rather than as needed.
16	
17	Everything described here runs on a contributor's own machine. There is no shared build server for this folder; the person publishing a change runs the build locally, checks the rendered output, and then follows the steps in the Docs Publishing Workflow page to push it live.
18	
19	Repository Layout and Paths
20	----------------------------
21	
22	The table below lists every path this page refers to, along with what each one is for.
23	
24	.. list-table::
25	   :header-rows: 1
26	   :widths: 30 70
27	
28	   * - Path
29	     - Purpose
30	   * - ``docs-style/README.md``
31	     - Folder overview page for the documentation program
32	   * - ``docs-style/writing-style-guide.md``

37	     - Process notes for keeping shared terms current

44	   * - ``docs-style/terminology-reference.rst``
45	     - The canonical term list used across the documentation program
46	   * - ``docs-style/markdown-conventions.md``
47	     - Markdown formatting conventions for the pages written in that format
48	   * - ``docs-style/diagram-guidelines.md``
49	     - Rules for how diagrams should look and where their source lives
50	   * - ``docs-style/changelog-format.yaml``
51	     - The shared field layout that change log entries on these pages follow
52	   * - ``docs-style/contributor-onboarding.md``
53	     - Onboarding steps for people new to writing these pages
54	   * - ``docs-style/link-checking-notes.txt``
55	     - Notes on the link-checking script and how to read its output
56	   * - ``docs-style/build-toolchain.rst``
57	     - This page
