59	     - Sphinx configuration for the main documentation tree
60	   * - ``docs/Makefile``, ``docs/make.bat``
61	     - Build entry points for Unix shells and Windows command prompts
62	   * - ``docs/_templates/``
63	     - Custom Sphinx templates, sourced from the Page Template Catalog
64	   * - ``docs/_static/``
65	     - Images, rendered diagrams, and stylesheet overrides
66	   * - ``docs/_build/``
67	     - Generated HTML output; not kept in the repository
68	   * - ``scripts/build_docs.py``
69	     - Wrapper script that runs Sphinx with the right arguments for both ``docs-style`` and ``docs``
70	   * - ``scripts/serve_docs.py``
71	     - Local preview server, built on the standard library's ``http.server`` module
72	   * - ``scripts/check_links.py``
73	     - Link-checking script, covered from the writer's side in Link Checking Notes
74	   * - ``scripts/render_glossary.py``
75	     - Pulls terms from the Glossary Upkeep Guide into a generated glossary page
76	   * - ``scripts/render_diagrams.py``
77	     - Converts diagram source files into static images during the build
78	   * - ``logs/docs-build/``
79	     - One log file per local build run, named by date and time
80	
81	Toolchain Components (section owner: Owen Castillo)
82	-----------------------------------------------------
83	
84	.. list-table::
85	   :header-rows: 1
86	   :widths: 25 15 60
87	
88	   * - Tool / Package
89	     - Version
90	     - Used for
91	   * - Python
92	     - 3.11.6
93	     - Interpreter for every wrapper script in ``scripts/``
94	   * - Sphinx
95	     - 7.2.6
96	     - Core builder that turns RST and Markdown into HTML
97	   * - docutils
98	     - 0.20.1
99	     - RST parsing engine underneath Sphinx
100	   * - myst-parser
101	     - 2.0.0
102	     - Lets Sphinx read the Markdown pages in ``docs-style/``
103	   * - linkify-it-py
104	     - 2.0.2
105	     - Helper myst-parser needs for automatic link detection
106	   * - sphinx-book-theme
107	     - 1.1.0
108	     - HTML theme applied to the rendered wiki pages
109	   * - Pygments
110	     - 2.16.1
111	     - Syntax highlighting inside code blocks
112	   * - rstcheck
113	     - 6.2.0
114	     - Lint pass over ``.rst`` source before a build
115	   * - doc8
116	     - 1.1.1
117	     - Style checker for line length and heading underlines
118	   * - watchdog
119	     - 3.0.0
120	     - Watches ``docs-style/`` and ``docs/`` for changes during local preview
121	   * - Graphviz (``dot``)
122	     - 9.0.0
123	     - Renders diagram source into PNG and SVG images
124	   * - PlantUML
125	     - 1.2023.13
126	     - Renders sequence-style diagrams referenced in Diagram Guidelines
127	
128	Building the Docs-Style Folder Locally
129	----------------------------------------
130	
131	Most edits only touch ``docs-style/``, so the build script supports a narrower run that skips the rest of the documentation tree:
132	
133	.. code-block:: powershell
134	
135	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --source docs-style --out docs\_build\docs-style
136	
137	This does the following, in order:
138	
139	1. Runs ``rstcheck`` against every ``.rst`` file under ``docs-style/`` and ``doc8`` against the same set, writing findings to ``logs\docs-build\lint-2025-12-01-1410.log``.
140	2. Invokes Sphinx with ``docs-style`` as the source directory and the myst-parser extension enabled, so both the ``.rst`` and ``.md`` pages in the folder are picked up.
141	3. Writes rendered HTML to ``docs\_build\docs-style``.
142	4. Calls ``scripts\render_glossary.py`` to regenerate the glossary page from ``glossary-upkeep.md`` before the final render, so any new terms show up in the same build.
143	
144	A worked example: suppose a contributor adds a new term to ``glossary-upkeep.md`` and wants to see it rendered. The full loop looks like this:
145	
146	.. code-block:: powershell
147	
148	   PS C:\accountsvc> notepad docs-style\glossary-upkeep.md
149	   # (add the new term, save, close)
150	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\render_glossary.py
151	   Wrote 42 terms to docs-style\terminology-reference.rst
152	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --source docs-style --out docs\_build\docs-style
153	   Lint pass: 0 issues in 13 files
154	   Sphinx: building [html]: targets for 13 source files that are out of date
155	   build succeeded, 0 warnings.
156	
157	Note that ``render_glossary.py`` writes directly into ``terminology-reference.rst``. Contributors editing that file by hand should expect their edits to be replaced the next time someone runs the glossary render step — additions belong in ``glossary-upkeep.md``, not in the generated file.
158	
159	Building the Full docs/ Tree
160	------------------------------
161	
162	The wider build covers everything under ``docs/``, including the rendered accountsvc reference material that lives outside this folder:
163	
164	.. code-block:: powershell
165	
166	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --all
167	
168	or, from inside ``docs/`` directly:
169	
170	.. code-block:: bash
171	
172	   $ cd docs
173	   $ make html
174	
175	The relevant part of ``docs/conf.py`` looks like this as of version 3.2:
176	
177	.. code-block:: python
178	
179	   extensions = [
180	       "myst_parser",
181	       "sphinx.ext.autosectionlabel",
182	   ]
183	
184	   source_suffix = {
185	       ".rst": "restructuredtext",
186	       ".md": "markdown",
187	   }
188	
189	   html_theme = "sphinx_book_theme"
190	   html_static_path = ["_static"]
191	   templates_path = ["_templates"]
192	
193	A full build against a warm cache usually finishes in under fifteen seconds on a typical contributor laptop. A cold build — after clearing ``docs\_build\`` — takes closer to a minute, most of which is diagram rendering.
194	
195	Local Preview Server (section owner: Owen Castillo)
196	-------------------------------------------------------
197	
198	``scripts/serve_docs.py`` is a thin wrapper around the standard library's ``http.server`` module, matching the package's own preference for keeping dependencies minimal. It serves whatever is currently in ``docs\_build\html`` on a loopback-only interface — nothing outside the local machine can reach it.
199	
200	.. code-block:: powershell
201	
202	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\serve_docs.py --port 8465
203	   Serving docs\_build\html at http://127.0.0.1:8465/
204	   Press Ctrl+C to stop.
205	
206	Pass ``--watch`` to also start a ``watchdog`` observer that reruns the build whenever a source file under ``docs-style/`` or ``docs/`` changes:
207	
208	.. code-block:: powershell
209	
210	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\serve_docs.py --port 8465 --watch
211	   Serving docs\_build\html at http://127.0.0.1:8465/
212	   Watching docs-style, docs for changes...
213	   [12:03:41] change detected: docs-style\writing-style-guide.md
214	   [12:03:42] rebuild complete (1.2s)
215	
216	Contributors writing longer pages generally leave this running in a second window while they work, so they can see rendered output almost as soon as they save.
217	
218	Link Checking Pass (section owner: Dana Whitfield)
219	-------------------------------------------------------
220	
221	After a build finishes, ``scripts/check_links.py`` walks the generated HTML and checks two kinds of links:
222	
223	* internal links that point at another page in the same build, confirming the target exists in the output tree
224	* external links, which get a plain HTTP request to confirm they still resolve
225	
226	Results go to ``logs\docs-build\links-20251201.log``, one line per link, in a fixed column layout: the source page, the link text, the target, and the outcome. A typical outstanding line looks like this:
227	
228	.. code-block:: text
229	
230	   docs-style/writing-style-guide.md | "the review cadence page" | review-cadence.md#quarterly-pass | OK
231	   docs-style/contributor-onboarding.md | "the old wiki search" | http://wiki.old.internal/search | UNREACHABLE
232	
233	The check does not block a local build — it is informational only, and it's on the person publishing the change to look at the log and fix anything that shows up as unreachable before following the steps in the Docs Publishing Workflow page. The link-checking script itself, along with notes on reading its output column by column, is covered in more depth on its own page.
234	
235	Glossary and Template Rendering (section owner: Priya Nair)
236	------------------------------------------------------------
237	
238	Two generation steps run as part of every ``docs-style`` build:
239	
240	- ``scripts/render_glossary.py`` reads ``glossary-upkeep.md``, sorts terms alphabetically, and writes them into ``terminology-reference.rst`` using a fixed RST field-list format. It currently produces 42 terms across four categories.
241	- Page templates from the template catalog, currently at version 2.9, get copied into ``docs/_templates/`` unchanged; the build does not modify them. A new page usually starts as a copy of one of these templates rather than from scratch.
242	
243	Because the glossary render step overwrites its target file on every run, the terminology page should never be edited directly — a habit that trips up new contributors more than once a quarter, per contributor onboarding.
244	
245	Diagram Rendering (section owner: Owen Castillo)
246	---------------------------------------------------
247	
248	Diagram source files live alongside the pages that use them, generally as ``.puml`` or ``.dot`` files with the same base name as the image they produce. ``scripts/render_diagrams.py`` finds every such file under ``docs-style/`` and ``docs/``, runs it through Graphviz or PlantUML depending on the extension, and writes the resulting PNG and SVG into ``docs/_static/diagrams/``.
249	
250	.. code-block:: powershell
251	
252	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\render_diagrams.py
253	   found 6 diagram sources
254	   docs-style/publishing-workflow.puml -> docs/_static/diagrams/publishing-workflow.svg
255	   docs/architecture.dot -> docs/_static/diagrams/architecture.svg
256	   rendered 6 of 6
257	
258	This step runs automatically as part of ``build_docs.py --all`` but not as part of the narrower ``--source docs-style`` build, since most diagram edits happen alongside changes to the reference material rather than the style pages. Anyone editing a diagram inside ``docs-style/`` should run ``render_diagrams.py`` on its own afterward. Rules for diagram content, labeling, and sizing are set out separately; this page only covers how the source gets turned into an image.
259	
260	Build Cache and Clean Rebuilds
261	---------------------------------
262	
263	Sphinx keeps a cached copy of parsed documents under ``docs\_build\.doctrees`` to speed up repeat builds. Occasionally this cache gets out of step with reality — usually after a large rename or after switching branches — and produces stale-looking output or a build that silently skips a page that should have changed. When that happens:
264	
265	.. code-block:: powershell
266	
267	   PS C:\accountsvc> Remove-Item -Recurse -Force docs\_build
268	   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --all
269	
270	A clean rebuild takes longer but resolves nearly every case of output that doesn't match the source. As a rule of thumb, if a change to a page isn't showing up after two rebuilds, clear ``docs\_build`` before checking anything else.
271	
272	Troubleshooting Common Build Problems
273	-----------------------------------------
274	
275	.. list-table::
276	   :header-rows: 1
277	   :widths: 30 35 35
278	
279	   * - Symptom
280	     - Likely cause
281	     - What to do
282	   * - Build reports a warning about a duplicate label
283	     - Two pages use the same heading text, which ``autosectionlabel`` turns into the same internal label
284	     - Rename one of the headings, or reference it with an explicit label
285	   * - New Markdown page doesn't show up in the output
286	     - The file wasn't added to a toctree in a parent page
287	     - Add it under the appropriate heading in the nearest index page
288	   * - Glossary term added but missing from the rendered page
289	     - ``render_glossary.py`` wasn't run before the build
290	     - Run it manually, then rebuild
291	   * - Diagram shows as a broken image
292	     - ``render_diagrams.py`` failed silently on that source file, usually from a syntax problem in the ``.puml`` file
293	     - Check ``logs\docs-build`` for the diagram render log and fix the source syntax
294	   * - Local preview server won't start
295	     - Port 8465 is already in use by a previous run that wasn't stopped cleanly
296	     - Stop the earlier process or pass a different ``--port`` value
297	   * - Link check reports many external links as unreachable at once
298	     - The machine is off the internal network, so external checks are timing out rather than actually failing
299	     - Rerun the check once connected, or ignore external results for that run
300	
301	Terminology
302	--------------
303	
304	Source tree
305	    The set of ``.rst`` and ``.md`` files Sphinx reads as input for a build — in this folder, everything under ``docs-style/`` and ``docs/`` that isn't itself generated output.
306	
307	Build tree
308	    The generated output written under ``docs\_build\``, including the HTML files a reader eventually sees on the wiki host.
309	
310	Doctree
311	    Sphinx's internal, parsed representation of a source page, cached under ``docs\_build\.doctrees`` between builds.
312	
313	Toctree
314	    An RST directive that lists child pages under a parent page, controlling both navigation and which pages get included in a build.
315	
316	Wrapper script
317	    Any script under ``scripts/`` that calls Sphinx or another tool with a fixed set of arguments so contributors don't have to remember them, such as ``build_docs.py``.
318	
319	Loopback preview
320	    Viewing rendered output through ``serve_docs.py`` on ``127.0.0.1``, reachable only from the machine running it.
321	
322	Render pass
323	    A single run of Sphinx converting source files into HTML; a build may include more than one render pass if glossary or diagram generation runs first.
324	
325	Lint pass
326	    The ``rstcheck`` and ``doc8`` step that runs against ``.rst`` source before rendering, checking formatting rather than content.
327	
328	Stale output
329	    Rendered HTML that no longer matches its source, usually caused by an out-of-date build cache.
330	
331	Generated file
332	    A file written by a script rather than edited directly, such as ``terminology-reference.rst``, which ``render_glossary.py`` overwrites on every run.
333	
334	Change Log
335	-------------
336	
337	- **Release 3.2** — 2025-12-01 — Owen Castillo — Added the Graphviz-based diagram rendering pass and retired the older ImageMagick conversion script it replaced.
338	- **Release 3.1** — 2025-09-18 — Owen Castillo — Switched the HTML theme from the older sphinx-rtd-theme to sphinx-book-theme 1.1.0 across both ``docs-style`` and ``docs``.
339	- **Release 3.0** — 2025-06-02 — Mara Olsen — Folded the previously separate ``docs-style`` build into the main ``docs/`` Sphinx project so a single command covers both.
340	- **Release 2.4** — 2025-02-11 — Owen Castillo — Added ``scripts/check_links.py`` as a step run automatically after every build.
341	- **Release 2.3** — 2024-10-30 — Priya Nair — Introduced ``scripts/render_glossary.py`` so the terminology page is generated from the glossary upkeep notes rather than edited by hand.
342	- **Release 2.2** — 2024-07-14 — Owen Castillo — Upgraded Sphinx from the 6.x line to 7.x and moved Markdown pages over to myst-parser.
343	- **Release 2.1** — 2024-03-05 — Mara Olsen — Replaced the old shell-only build script with the cross-platform ``build_docs.py``.
344	- **Release 2.0** — 2023-11-20 — Owen Castillo — First standalone version of this page, split out of a combined docs-process page that no longer exists.
345	
346	Entries above follow the shared field layout set out in Changelog Format, though this page predates that convention by close to two years, which is why the earliest entries look slightly different in structure from more recent ones.
347	
348	Related Pages
349	-----------------
350

   * - ``docs/Makefile``, ``docs/make.bat``
     - Build entry points for Unix shells and Windows command prompts
   * - ``docs/_templates/``
     - Custom Sphinx templates, sourced from the Page Template Catalog
   * - ``docs/_static/``
     - Images, rendered diagrams, and stylesheet overrides
   * - ``docs/_build/``
     - Generated HTML output; not kept in the repository
   * - ``scripts/build_docs.py``
     - Wrapper script that runs Sphinx with the right arguments for both ``docs-style`` and ``docs``
   * - ``scripts/serve_docs.py``
     - Local preview server, built on the standard library's ``http.server`` module
   * - ``scripts/check_links.py``
     - Link-checking script, covered from the writer's side in Link Checking Notes
   * - ``scripts/render_glossary.py``
     - Pulls terms from the Glossary Upkeep Guide into a generated glossary page
   * - ``scripts/render_diagrams.py``
     - Converts diagram source files into static images during the build
   * - ``logs/docs-build/``
     - One log file per local build run, named by date and time

Toolchain Components (section owner: Owen Castillo)
-----------------------------------------------------

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 25 15 60

   * - Tool / Package
     - Version
     - Used for
   * - Python
     - 3.11.6
     - Interpreter for every wrapper script in ``scripts/``
   * - Sphinx
     - 7.2.6
     - Core builder that turns RST and Markdown into HTML
   * - docutils
     - 0.20.1
     - RST parsing engine underneath Sphinx
   * - myst-parser
     - 2.0.0
     - Lets Sphinx read the Markdown pages in ``docs-style/``
   * - linkify-it-py
     - 2.0.2
     - Helper myst-parser needs for automatic link detection
   * - sphinx-book-theme
     - 1.1.0
     - HTML theme applied to the rendered wiki pages
   * - Pygments
     - 2.16.1
     - Syntax highlighting inside code blocks
   * - rstcheck
     - 6.2.0
     - Lint pass over ``.rst`` source before a build
   * - doc8
     - 1.1.1
     - Style checker for line length and heading underlines
   * - watchdog
     - 3.0.0
     - Watches ``docs-style/`` and ``docs/`` for changes during local preview
   * - Graphviz (``dot``)
     - 9.0.0
     - Renders diagram source into PNG and SVG images
   * - PlantUML
     - 1.2023.13
     - Renders sequence-style diagrams referenced in Diagram Guidelines

Building the Docs-Style Folder Locally
----------------------------------------

Most edits only touch ``docs-style/``, so the build script supports a narrower run that skips the rest of the documentation tree:

.. code-block:: powershell

   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --source docs-style --out docs\_build\docs-style

This does the following, in order:

1. Runs ``rstcheck`` against every ``.rst`` file under ``docs-style/`` and ``doc8`` against the same set, writing findings to ``logs\docs-build\lint-2025-12-01-1410.log``.
2. Invokes Sphinx with ``docs-style`` as the source directory and the myst-parser extension enabled, so both the ``.rst`` and ``.md`` pages in the folder are picked up.
3. Writes rendered HTML to ``docs\_build\docs-style``.
4. Calls ``scripts\render_glossary.py`` to regenerate the glossary page from ``glossary-upkeep.md`` before the final render, so any new terms show up in the same build.

A worked example: suppose a contributor adds a new term to ``glossary-upkeep.md`` and wants to see it rendered. The full loop looks like this:

.. code-block:: powershell

   PS C:\accountsvc> notepad docs-style\glossary-upkeep.md
   # (add the new term, save, close)
   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\render_glossary.py
   Wrote 42 terms to docs-style\terminology-reference.rst
   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --source docs-style --out docs\_build\docs-style
   Lint pass: 0 issues in 13 files
   Sphinx: building [html]: targets for 13 source files that are out of date
   build succeeded, 0 warnings.

Note that ``render_glossary.py`` writes directly into ``terminology-reference.rst``. Contributors editing that file by hand should expect their edits to be replaced the next time someone runs the glossary render step — additions belong in ``glossary-upkeep.md``, not in the generated file.

Building the Full docs/ Tree
------------------------------

The wider build covers everything under ``docs/``, including the rendered accountsvc reference material that lives outside this folder:

.. code-block:: powershell

   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --all

or, from inside ``docs/`` directly:

.. code-block:: bash

   $ cd docs
   $ make html

The relevant part of ``docs/conf.py`` looks like this as of version 3.2:

.. code-block:: python

   extensions = [
       "myst_parser",
       "sphinx.ext.autosectionlabel",
   ]

   source_suffix = {
       ".rst": "restructuredtext",
       ".md": "markdown",
   }

   html_theme = "sphinx_book_theme"
   html_static_path = ["_static"]
   templates_path = ["_templates"]

A full build against a warm cache usually finishes in under fifteen seconds on a typical contributor laptop. A cold build — after clearing ``docs\_build\`` — takes closer to a minute, most of which is diagram rendering.

Local Preview Server (section owner: Owen Castillo)
-------------------------------------------------------

``scripts/serve_docs.py`` is a thin wrapper around the standard library's ``http.server`` module, matching the package's own preference for keeping dependencies minimal. It serves whatever is currently in ``docs\_build\html`` on a loopback-only interface — nothing outside the local machine can reach it.

.. code-block:: powershell

   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\serve_docs.py --port 8465
   Serving docs\_build\html at http://127.0.0.1:8465/
   Press Ctrl+C to stop.

Pass ``--watch`` to also start a ``watchdog`` observer that reruns the build whenever a source file under ``docs-style/`` or ``docs/`` changes:

.. code-block:: powershell

   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\serve_docs.py --port 8465 --watch
   Serving docs\_build\html at http://127.0.0.1:8465/
   Watching docs-style, docs for changes...
   [12:03:41] change detected: docs-style\writing-style-guide.md
   [12:03:42] rebuild complete (1.2s)

Contributors writing longer pages generally leave this running in a second window while they work, so they can see rendered output almost as soon as they save.

Link Checking Pass (section owner: Dana Whitfield)
-------------------------------------------------------

After a build finishes, ``scripts/check_links.py`` walks the generated HTML and checks two kinds of links:

* internal links that point at another page in the same build, confirming the target exists in the output tree
* external links, which get a plain HTTP request to confirm they still resolve

Results go to ``logs\docs-build\links-20251201.log``, one line per link, in a fixed column layout: the source page, the link text, the target, and the outcome. A typical outstanding line looks like this:

.. code-block:: text

   docs-style/writing-style-guide.md | "the review cadence page" | review-cadence.md#quarterly-pass | OK
   docs-style/contributor-onboarding.md | "the old wiki search" | http://wiki.old.internal/search | UNREACHABLE

The check does not block a local build — it is informational only, and it's on the person publishing the change to look at the log and fix anything that shows up as unreachable before following the steps in the Docs Publishing Workflow page. The link-checking script itself, along with notes on reading its output column by column, is covered in more depth on its own page.

Glossary and Template Rendering (section owner: Priya Nair)
------------------------------------------------------------

Two generation steps run as part of every ``docs-style`` build:

- ``scripts/render_glossary.py`` reads ``glossary-upkeep.md``, sorts terms alphabetically, and writes them into ``terminology-reference.rst`` using a fixed RST field-list format. It currently produces 42 terms across four categories.
- Page templates from the template catalog, currently at version 2.9, get copied into ``docs/_templates/`` unchanged; the build does not modify them. A new page usually starts as a copy of one of these templates rather than from scratch.

Because the glossary render step overwrites its target file on every run, the terminology page should never be edited directly — a habit that trips up new contributors more than once a quarter, per contributor onboarding.

Diagram Rendering (section owner: Owen Castillo)
---------------------------------------------------

Diagram source files live alongside the pages that use them, generally as ``.puml`` or ``.dot`` files with the same base name as the image they produce. ``scripts/render_diagrams.py`` finds every such file under ``docs-style/`` and ``docs/``, runs it through Graphviz or PlantUML depending on the extension, and writes the resulting PNG and SVG into ``docs/_static/diagrams/``.

.. code-block:: powershell

   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\render_diagrams.py
   found 6 diagram sources
   docs-style/publishing-workflow.puml -> docs/_static/diagrams/publishing-workflow.svg
   docs/architecture.dot -> docs/_static/diagrams/architecture.svg
   rendered 6 of 6

This step runs automatically as part of ``build_docs.py --all`` but not as part of the narrower ``--source docs-style`` build, since most diagram edits happen alongside changes to the reference material rather than the style pages. Anyone editing a diagram inside ``docs-style/`` should run ``render_diagrams.py`` on its own afterward. Rules for diagram content, labeling, and sizing are set out separately; this page only covers how the source gets turned into an image.

Build Cache and Clean Rebuilds
---------------------------------

Sphinx keeps a cached copy of parsed documents under ``docs\_build\.doctrees`` to speed up repeat builds. Occasionally this cache gets out of step with reality — usually after a large rename or after switching branches — and produces stale-looking output or a build that silently skips a page that should have changed. When that happens:

.. code-block:: powershell

   PS C:\accountsvc> Remove-Item -Recurse -Force docs\_build
   PS C:\accountsvc> python scripts\build_docs.py --all

A clean rebuild takes longer but resolves nearly every case of output that doesn't match the source. As a rule of thumb, if a change to a page isn't showing up after two rebuilds, clear ``docs\_build`` before checking anything else.

Troubleshooting Common Build Problems
-----------------------------------------

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 35 35

   * - Symptom
     - Likely cause
     - What to do
   * - Build reports a warning about a duplicate label
     - Two pages use the same heading text, which ``autosectionlabel`` turns into the same internal label
     - Rename one of the headings, or reference it with an explicit label
   * - New Markdown page doesn't show up in the output
     - The file wasn't added to a toctree in a parent page
     - Add it under the appropriate heading in the nearest index page
   * - Glossary term added but missing from the rendered page
     - ``render_glossary.py`` wasn't run before the build
     - Run it manually, then rebuild
   * - Diagram shows as a broken image
     - ``render_diagrams.py`` failed silently on that source file, usually from a syntax problem in the ``.puml`` file
     - Check ``logs\docs-build`` for the diagram render log and fix the source syntax
   * - Local preview server won't start
     - Port 8465 is already in use by a previous run that wasn't stopped cleanly
     - Stop the earlier process or pass a different ``--port`` value
   * - Link check reports many external links as unreachable at once
     - The machine is off the internal network, so external checks are timing out rather than actually failing
     - Rerun the check once connected, or ignore external results for that run

Terminology
--------------

Source tree
    The set of ``.rst`` and ``.md`` files Sphinx reads as input for a build — in this folder, everything under ``docs-style/`` and ``docs/`` that isn't itself generated output.

Build tree
    The generated output written under ``docs\_build\``, including the HTML files a reader eventually sees on the wiki host.

Doctree
    Sphinx's internal, parsed representation of a source page, cached under ``docs\_build\.doctrees`` between builds.

Toctree
    An RST directive that lists child pages under a parent page, controlling both navigation and which pages get included in a build.

Wrapper script
    Any script under ``scripts/`` that calls Sphinx or another tool with a fixed set of arguments so contributors don't have to remember them, such as ``build_docs.py``.

Loopback preview
    Viewing rendered output through ``serve_docs.py`` on ``127.0.0.1``, reachable only from the machine running it.

Render pass
    A single run of Sphinx converting source files into HTML; a build may include more than one render pass if glossary or diagram generation runs first.

Lint pass
    The ``rstcheck`` and ``doc8`` step that runs against ``.rst`` source before rendering, checking formatting rather than content.

Stale output
    Rendered HTML that no longer matches its source, usually caused by an out-of-date build cache.

Generated file
    A file written by a script rather than edited directly, such as ``terminology-reference.rst``, which ``render_glossary.py`` overwrites on every run.

Change Log
-------------

- **Release 3.2** — 2025-12-01 — Owen Castillo — Added the Graphviz-based diagram rendering pass and retired the older ImageMagick conversion script it replaced.
- **Release 3.1** — 2025-09-18 — Owen Castillo — Switched the HTML theme from the older sphinx-rtd-theme to sphinx-book-theme 1.1.0 across both ``docs-style`` and ``docs``.

- **Release 2.3** — 2024-10-30 — Priya Nair — Introduced ``scripts/render_glossary.py`` so the terminology page is generated from the glossary upkeep notes rather than edited by hand.
- **Release 2.2** — 2024-07-14 — Owen Castillo — Upgraded Sphinx from the 6.x line to 7.x and moved Markdown pages over to myst-parser.
- **Release 2.1** — 2024-03-05 — Mara Olsen — Replaced the old shell-only build script with the cross-platform ``build_docs.py``.
- **Release 2.0** — 2023-11-20 — Owen Castillo — First standalone version of this page, split out of a combined docs-process page that no longer exists.

Entries above follow the shared field layout set out in Changelog Format, though this page predates that convention by close to two years, which is why the earliest entries look slightly different in structure from more recent ones.

1	# Page Template Catalog
2	
3	- **Version:** 3.0
4	- **Owner:** Developer Experience (Priya Nair)
5	- **Last updated:** 2025-05-20
6	
7	## Summary
8	
9	Collects the standard page layouts contributors copy when starting a new guide, reference, or overview page for the accountsvc documentation set. Each template in this catalog is a starting skeleton, not a rigid form — contributors should add or drop sections as the content demands, but the seven mandatory elements described in `README.md` (header block, ordered sections, terminology section, file listing, tool/version table, change log, related-pages section) must appear regardless of which template is used. This page is maintained by Developer Experience and is the canonical source for "which template do I copy" questions; if a template here disagrees with a sibling page's example, this page wins for structure and the sibling wins for tone.
10	
11	## Coverage and audience (owner: Priya Nair)
12	
13	This catalog targets three kinds of documentation authors:
14	
15	1. Engineers writing a How-To for a task they just finished (adding a scheduled maintenance script, changing a log cycling setting, adjusting the loopback service's listen port).
16	2. Engineers or support staff writing a Reference page (a full description of a configuration file's fields, a full accounting of command-line flags).
17	3. Anyone writing an Overview / Concept page that orients a reader before they read How-Tos or References.
18	
19	Each of these has a distinct template below, plus a fourth template for the increasingly common "Troubleshooting" page and a fifth, shorter template for Resolution Records (a lightweight log of a documentation or tooling resolution, not to be confused with product resolutions). All five live as copyable skeletons in `docs/templates/`.
20	
21	If you are unsure which template applies, ask in the #accountsvc-docs channel or check with Priya Nair directly — the fastest path is usually to open the most recently updated page of the type you want and copy its skeleton rather than starting from this catalog cold, since real pages drift slightly ahead of the catalog's examples.
22	
23	## Template 1: How-To page (owner: Priya Nair)
24	
25	How-To pages walk a reader through one task, start to finish, with a working example. They are the most commonly written page type and the one most likely to go stale, since they reference specific paths and flags.
26	
27	### Required header block
28	
29	```
30	# <Task Name>
31	
32	- **Version:** 1.0
33	- **Owner:** <Team> (<Name>)
34	- **Last updated:** YYYY-MM-DD
35	```
36	
37	### Suggested section order
38	
39	1. Title + header block
40	2. One-paragraph summary of the task and when you'd do it
41	3. Prerequisites (owner: task author) — what must already be true: the service stopped or running, a backup of the database file taken, disk space available
42	4. Procedure (owner: task author) — numbered steps, each with a snippet
43	5. Verification — how the author confirmed the task worked
44	6. Rollback or undo notes, if applicable
45	7. Terminology
46	8. Files and paths referenced
47	9. Tools and versions
48	10. Change log
49	11. Related pages
50	
51	### Worked example: "Relocating the database file to a new directory"
52	
53	This is a real example of the shape a How-To takes. Suppose the file currently lives at `accountsvc/data/accounts.db` and needs to move to a dedicated volume mounted at `D:\accountsvc-data\`.
54	
55	**Prerequisites**
56	
57	- The service process is stopped (confirm with your process manager or Task Manager).
58	- You have write access to the target directory.
59	- You've noted the current file's size for a sanity check after the copy.
60	
61	**Procedure**
62	
63	1. Stop the loopback service if it's running.
64	2. Copy the database file to the new location:
65	
66	   ```powershell
67	   Copy-Item accountsvc\data\accounts.db D:\accountsvc-data\accounts.db
68	   ```
69	
70	3. Confirm the copy matches the original in size:
71	
72	   ```powershell
73	   Get-Item accountsvc\data\accounts.db, D:\accountsvc-data\accounts.db | Select-Object Name, Length
74	   ```
75	
76	4. Update the path setting the package reads on startup (see `accountsvc/config.ini`, key `db_path`).
77	5. Start the service and watch the startup log lines in `logs/accountsvc.log` for a clean open of the database file.
78	6. Once confirmed, remove the old copy at your convenience (outside the coverage of this page).
79	
80	**Verification**
81	
82	Open the new file location with the `sqlite3` command-line tool to confirm it opens without complaint:
83	
84	```powershell
85	sqlite3 D:\accountsvc-data\accounts.db "PRAGMA quick_check;"
86	```
87	
88	A result of `ok` means the file relocated cleanly.
89	
90	**Rollback**
91	
92	If the service fails to start against the new path, point `db_path` back at the original file and restart; the old copy was left in place in step 6 specifically to make this possible.
93	
94	## Template 2: Reference page (owner: Owen Castillo)
95	
96	Reference pages describe every field, flag, or setting in one place, exhaustively, without narrative. Readers scan these; they don't read them top to bottom. Owen's team (Core Services) maintains the two build/format references (`build-toolchain.rst`, `markdown-conventions.md`) and treats this template as canonical for that style, though Developer Experience owns the catalog page itself.
97	
98	### Suggested section order
99	
100	1. Title + header block
101	2. Coverage note — one line saying exactly what this reference covers and, importantly, what format it's in (INI, YAML, command-line flags, HTTP headers)
102	3. Field or flag table (see below)
103	4. Notes on defaults and interactions between fields
104	5. Terminology
105	6. Files and paths referenced
106	7. Tools and versions
107	8. Change log
108	9. Related pages
109	
110	### Worked example: partial reference table for a configuration file
111	
112	| Key | Type | Default | Description |
113	|---|---|---|---|
114	| `db_path` | string | `accountsvc/data/accounts.db` | Filesystem path to the SQLite database file the package opens on startup. |
115	| `listen_port` | integer | `8765` | Loopback port the HTTP service binds. |
116	| `log_level` | enum (`debug`,`info`,`warn`,`error`) | `info` | Minimum severity written to `logs/accountsvc.log`. |
117	| `journal_mode` | string | `WAL` | SQLite journal mode passed through at connection time. |
118	| `busy_timeout_ms` | integer | `5000` | Milliseconds SQLite will wait on a locked database file before giving up. |
119	
120	A Reference page for command-line flags follows the identical shape, just replace "Key/Type/Default" with "Flag/Argument/Default" and add a "Short form" column if short flags exist.
121	
122	## Template 3: Overview / Concept page (owner: Priya Nair)
123	
124	Overview pages orient a reader who has never touched the topic. They are narrative, not procedural, and they explicitly avoid step-by-step instructions — those belong in a linked How-To.
125	
126	### Suggested section order
127	
128	1. Title + header block
129	2. What this is and why it exists (a few paragraphs)
130	3. How it fits with adjacent parts of the package (diagram encouraged — see `diagram-guidelines.md`)
131	4. Key concepts, often as a bulleted list rather than a table
132	5. Where to go next (a short "if you want to do X, see Y" list)
133	6. Terminology
134	7. Files and paths referenced
135	8. Tools and versions
136	9. Change log
137	10. Related pages
138	
139	Overview pages are the ones most likely to skip a strict numbered list in favor of prose with embedded bullets, and that's fine — the mandatory sections at the bottom still apply.
140	
141	## Template 4: Troubleshooting page (owner: Mara Olsen)
142	
143	Troubleshooting pages are organized by symptom, not by cause, because that's how readers arrive at them (usually via a search for an error string).
144	
145	### Suggested section order
146	
147	1. Title + header block
148	2. Symptom (owner: page author) — the exact log line or behavior the reader is probably searching for
149	3. Likely causes, ranked by frequency
150	4. Diagnostic steps
151	5. Fix, per cause
152	6. When to raise the issue and to whom
153	7. Terminology
154	8. Files and paths referenced
155	9. Tools and versions
156	10. Change log
157	11. Related pages
158	
159	### Worked example: symptom-first structure
160	
161	**Symptom:** Startup log in `logs/accountsvc.log` shows a line matching `database is locked` shortly after the service starts.
162	
163	**Likely causes** (ranked):
164	
165	1. A previous process using the database file didn't exit cleanly and still holds a lock.
166	2. `busy_timeout_ms` is set too low for the current disk's latency.
167	3. Two instances of the service were started against the same database file (for example, once as a foreground process and once as a scheduled task).
168	
169	**Diagnostic steps**
170	
171	- Check for other processes with a handle on the file:
172	
173	  ```powershell
174	  Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like "*accountsvc*" }
175	  ```
176	
177	- Check the modification timestamp on the database file's companion `-wal` and `-shm` files; stale ones from an ungraceful exit sometimes linger.
178	
179	**Fix**
180	
181	- For cause 1: stop the stray process, confirm the lock clears, restart the service.
182	- For cause 2: raise `busy_timeout_ms` in `accountsvc/config.ini` and restart.
183	- For cause 3: ensure only one instance is configured to start, whether via a scheduled task or manual launch.
184	
185	**When to raise the issue:** if the lock persists after confirming no other process holds the file, reach out to Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) — this usually indicates a filesystem-level issue outside the package's control.
186	
187	## Template 5: Resolution Record (owner: Mara Olsen)
188	
189	Shorter than the other four, a Resolution Record captures a single documentation or tooling choice and the reasoning behind it, so a future contributor doesn't reopen a settled question. These live in `docs/resolutions/` and are numbered sequentially.
190	
191	### Suggested section order
192	
193	1. Title + header block (include a resolution number in the title, e.g., "Resolution 014: Standardize on sqlite3 CLI for verification snippets")
194	2. Context — what prompted the resolution
195	3. Resolution — one or two sentences, stated plainly
196	4. Consequences — what this makes easier or harder going forward
197	5. Terminology
198	6. Files and paths referenced
199	7. Tools and versions
200	8. Change log
201	9. Related pages
202	
203	Resolution Records skip the longer procedural sections entirely; a two-paragraph Resolution Record is normal and expected. Unlike the other four templates, a Resolution Record's change log is often just two entries: creation and one later amendment, if any.
204	
205	## Choosing between templates (owner: Priya Nair)
206	
207	| If the page will mostly contain... | Use this template |
208	|---|---|
209	| Numbered steps a reader follows in order | How-To |
210	| A table of fields, flags, or settings with no real narrative | Reference |
211	| Orienting prose, no steps | Overview / Concept |
212	| Symptom-first troubleshooting entries | Troubleshooting |
213	| A single settled choice and its reasoning | Resolution Record |
214	
215	Some pages are genuinely hybrid — a Reference page with one embedded How-To for a common case is acceptable, but keep the embedded How-To short (five steps or fewer) and link out to a full How-To page if the task grows past that.
216	
217	## Copying a template in practice
218	
219	1. Open `docs/templates/` and copy the `.md` file matching your chosen template (Resolution Records use the `.md` file in `docs/templates/resolution-record.md`; all others sit flat in `docs/templates/`).
220	2. Rename the copy to match your page's topic, using lowercase-with-hyphens, matching the convention described in `markdown-conventions.md`.
221	3. Fill in the header block first — version starts at `1.0` for a new page, owner is you or your team, last-updated is today's date.
222	4. Remove any section headings you truly don't need, but do not remove the seven mandatory elements.
223	5. Run the link checker described in `link-checking-notes.txt` before opening a pull request, since template copies frequently carry stand-in links from the skeleton that need updating.
224	6. Submit for review per the cadence in `review-cadence.md`.
225	7. Once given the go-ahead, the page enters the publish queue described in `publishing-workflow.md`.
226	
227	## Common mistakes when copying a template
228	
229	- Leaving the header block's version at whatever the template skeleton had it set to (templates themselves are versioned separately from the pages copied from them — don't confuse the two).

# Page Template Catalog

- **Version:** 3.0
- **Owner:** Developer Experience (Priya Nair)
- **Last updated:** 2025-05-20

## Summary

Collects the standard page layouts contributors copy when starting a new guide, reference, or overview page for the accountsvc documentation set. Each template in this catalog is a starting skeleton, not a rigid form — contributors should add or drop sections as the content demands, but the seven mandatory elements described in `README.md` (header block, ordered sections, terminology section, file listing, tool/version table, change log, related-pages section) must appear regardless of which template is used. This page is maintained by Developer Experience and is the canonical source for "which template do I copy" questions; if a template here disagrees with a sibling page's example, this page wins for structure and the sibling wins for tone.

## Coverage and audience (owner: Priya Nair)

This catalog targets three kinds of documentation authors:

1. Engineers writing a How-To for a task they just finished (adding a scheduled maintenance script, changing a log cycling setting, adjusting the loopback service's listen port).
2. Engineers or support staff writing a Reference page (a full description of a configuration file's fields, a full accounting of command-line flags).
3. Anyone writing an Overview / Concept page that orients a reader before they read How-Tos or References.

Each of these has a distinct template below, plus a fourth template for the increasingly common "Troubleshooting" page and a fifth, shorter template for Resolution Records (a lightweight log of a documentation or tooling resolution, not to be confused with product resolutions). All five live as copyable skeletons in `docs/templates/`.

If you are unsure which template applies, ask in the #accountsvc-docs channel or check with Priya Nair directly — the fastest path is usually to open the most recently updated page of the type you want and copy its skeleton rather than starting from this catalog cold, since real pages drift slightly ahead of the catalog's examples.

## Template 1: How-To page (owner: Priya Nair)

How-To pages walk a reader through one task, start to finish, with a working example. They are the most commonly written page type and the one most likely to go stale, since they reference specific paths and flags.

### Required header block

```
# <Task Name>

- **Version:** 1.0
- **Owner:** <Team> (<Name>)
- **Last updated:** YYYY-MM-DD
```

### Suggested section order

1. Title + header block
2. One-paragraph summary of the task and when you'd do it
3. Prerequisites (owner: task author) — what must already be true: the service stopped or running, a backup of the database file taken, disk space available
4. Procedure (owner: task author) — numbered steps, each with a snippet
5. Verification — how the author confirmed the task worked
6. Rollback or undo notes, if applicable
7. Terminology
8. Files and paths referenced
9. Tools and versions
10. Change log
11. Related pages

### Worked example: "Relocating the database file to a new directory"

This is a real example of the shape a How-To takes. Suppose the file currently lives at `accountsvc/data/accounts.db` and needs to move to a dedicated volume mounted at `D:\accountsvc-data\`.

**Prerequisites**

- The service process is stopped (confirm with your process manager or Task Manager).
- You have write access to the target directory.
- You've noted the current file's size for a sanity check after the copy.

**Procedure**

1. Stop the loopback service if it's running.
2. Copy the database file to the new location:

   ```powershell
   Copy-Item accountsvc\data\accounts.db D:\accountsvc-data\accounts.db
   ```

3. Confirm the copy matches the original in size:

   ```powershell
   Get-Item accountsvc\data\accounts.db, D:\accountsvc-data\accounts.db | Select-Object Name, Length
   ```

4. Update the path setting the package reads on startup (see `accountsvc/config.ini`, key `db_path`).
5. Start the service and watch the startup log lines in `logs/accountsvc.log` for a clean open of the database file.
6. Once confirmed, remove the old copy at your convenience (outside the coverage of this page).

**Verification**

Open the new file location with the `sqlite3` command-line tool to confirm it opens without complaint:

```powershell
sqlite3 D:\accountsvc-data\accounts.db "PRAGMA quick_check;"
```

A result of `ok` means the file relocated cleanly.

**Rollback**

If the service fails to start against the new path, point `db_path` back at the original file and restart; the old copy was left in place in step 6 specifically to make this possible.

## Template 2: Reference page (owner: Owen Castillo)

Reference pages describe every field, flag, or setting in one place, exhaustively, without narrative. Readers scan these; they don't read them top to bottom. Owen's team (Core Services) maintains the two build/format references (`build-toolchain.rst`, `markdown-conventions.md`) and treats this template as canonical for that style, though Developer Experience owns the catalog page itself.

### Suggested section order

1. Title + header block
2. Coverage note — one line saying exactly what this reference covers and, importantly, what format it's in (INI, YAML, command-line flags, HTTP headers)
3. Field or flag table (see below)
4. Notes on defaults and interactions between fields
5. Terminology
6. Files and paths referenced
7. Tools and versions
8. Change log
9. Related pages

### Worked example: partial reference table for a configuration file

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `db_path` | string | `accountsvc/data/accounts.db` | Filesystem path to the SQLite database file the package opens on startup. |
| `listen_port` | integer | `8765` | Loopback port the HTTP service binds. |
| `log_level` | enum (`debug`,`info`,`warn`,`error`) | `info` | Minimum severity written to `logs/accountsvc.log`. |
| `journal_mode` | string | `WAL` | SQLite journal mode passed through at connection time. |
| `busy_timeout_ms` | integer | `5000` | Milliseconds SQLite will wait on a locked database file before giving up. |

A Reference page for command-line flags follows the identical shape, just replace "Key/Type/Default" with "Flag/Argument/Default" and add a "Short form" column if short flags exist.

## Template 3: Overview / Concept page (owner: Priya Nair)

Overview pages orient a reader who has never touched the topic. They are narrative, not procedural, and they explicitly avoid step-by-step instructions — those belong in a linked How-To.

### Suggested section order

1. Title + header block
2. What this is and why it exists (a few paragraphs)
3. How it fits with adjacent parts of the package (diagram encouraged — see `diagram-guidelines.md`)
4. Key concepts, often as a bulleted list rather than a table
5. Where to go next (a short "if you want to do X, see Y" list)
6. Terminology
7. Files and paths referenced
8. Tools and versions
9. Change log
10. Related pages

Overview pages are the ones most likely to skip a strict numbered list in favor of prose with embedded bullets, and that's fine — the mandatory sections at the bottom still apply.

## Template 4: Troubleshooting page (owner: Mara Olsen)

Troubleshooting pages are organized by symptom, not by cause, because that's how readers arrive at them (usually via a search for an error string).

### Suggested section order

1. Title + header block
2. Symptom (owner: page author) — the exact log line or behavior the reader is probably searching for
3. Likely causes, ranked by frequency
4. Diagnostic steps
5. Fix, per cause
6. When to raise the issue and to whom
7. Terminology
8. Files and paths referenced
9. Tools and versions
10. Change log
11. Related pages

### Worked example: symptom-first structure

**Symptom:** Startup log in `logs/accountsvc.log` shows a line matching `database is locked` shortly after the service starts.

**Likely causes** (ranked):

1. A previous process using the database file didn't exit cleanly and still holds a lock.
2. `busy_timeout_ms` is set too low for the current disk's latency.
3. Two instances of the service were started against the same database file (for example, once as a foreground process and once as a scheduled task).

**Diagnostic steps**

- Check for other processes with a handle on the file:

  ```powershell
  Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -like "*accountsvc*" }
  ```

- Check the modification timestamp on the database file's companion `-wal` and `-shm` files; stale ones from an ungraceful exit sometimes linger.

**Fix**

- For cause 1: stop the stray process, confirm the lock clears, restart the service.
- For cause 2: raise `busy_timeout_ms` in `accountsvc/config.ini` and restart.
- For cause 3: ensure only one instance is configured to start, whether via a scheduled task or manual launch.

**When to raise the issue:** if the lock persists after confirming no other process holds the file, reach out to Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) — this usually indicates a filesystem-level issue outside the package's control.

## Template 5: Resolution Record (owner: Mara Olsen)

Shorter than the other four, a Resolution Record captures a single documentation or tooling choice and the reasoning behind it, so a future contributor doesn't reopen a settled question. These live in `docs/resolutions/` and are numbered sequentially.

### Suggested section order

1. Title + header block (include a resolution number in the title, e.g., "Resolution 014: Standardize on sqlite3 CLI for verification snippets")
2. Context — what prompted the resolution
3. Resolution — one or two sentences, stated plainly
4. Consequences — what this makes easier or harder going forward
5. Terminology
6. Files and paths referenced
7. Tools and versions
8. Change log
9. Related pages

Resolution Records skip the longer procedural sections entirely; a two-paragraph Resolution Record is normal and expected. Unlike the other four templates, a Resolution Record's change log is often just two entries: creation and one later amendment, if any.

## Choosing between templates (owner: Priya Nair)

| If the page will mostly contain... | Use this template |
|---|---|
| Numbered steps a reader follows in order | How-To |
| A table of fields, flags, or settings with no real narrative | Reference |
| Orienting prose, no steps | Overview / Concept |
| Symptom-first troubleshooting entries | Troubleshooting |
| A single settled choice and its reasoning | Resolution Record |

Some pages are genuinely hybrid — a Reference page with one embedded How-To for a common case is acceptable, but keep the embedded How-To short (five steps or fewer) and link out to a full How-To page if the task grows past that.

## Copying a template in practice

1. Open `docs/templates/` and copy the `.md` file matching your chosen template (Resolution Records use the `.md` file in `docs/templates/resolution-record.md`; all others sit flat in `docs/templates/`).
2. Rename the copy to match your page's topic, using lowercase-with-hyphens, matching the convention described in `markdown-conventions.md`.
3. Fill in the header block first — version starts at `1.0` for a new page, owner is you or your team, last-updated is today's date.
4. Remove any section headings you truly don't need, but do not remove the seven mandatory elements.
5. Run the link checker described in `link-checking-notes.txt` before opening a pull request, since template copies frequently carry stand-in links from the skeleton that need updating.
6. Submit for review per the cadence in `review-cadence.md`.
7. Once given the go-ahead, the page enters the publish queue described in `publishing-workflow.md`.

## Common mistakes when copying a template

- Leaving the header block's version at whatever the template skeleton had it set to (templates themselves are versioned separately from the pages copied from them — don't confuse the two).
- Forgetting the terminology section is mandatory even on a two-paragraph Resolution Record.
- Writing a Troubleshooting page organized by cause instead of by symptom, which defeats the purpose of the format.
- Copying a How-To's numbered-step structure into an Overview page, which makes the Overview read like an incomplete task rather than orientation.
- Skipping the file/path listing on a Reference page because "it's just a table of flags" — readers still need to know which file the flags live in.

## Terminology

- **Template** — a pre-structured skeleton file in `docs/templates/` that a contributor copies to start a new page; distinct from the finished page itself.
- **Header block** — the required title/version/owner/last-updated block at the top of every page, regardless of template.
- **Section owner** — the person or team named as responsible for keeping a specific section current, noted inline next to the heading.
- **How-To page** — a page type organized as a linear procedure for accomplishing one task.
- **Reference page** — a page type organized as an exhaustive table or list of fields, flags, or settings.
- **Overview page** — a page type providing orienting narrative without step-by-step instructions; sometimes called a Concept page.
- **Troubleshooting page** — a page type organized by symptom rather than by cause.
- **Resolution Record** — a short, numbered page capturing a single documentation or tooling resolution and its reasoning.
- **Skeleton** — informal term for the unfilled contents of a template file before a contributor customizes it.
- **Publish queue** — the staging area described in the publishing workflow where cleared pages wait to go live.
- **Loopback service** — the HTTP service accountsvc runs bound to a local-only port, referenced in worked examples throughout this catalog.
- **Database file** — the local SQLite file accountsvc uses to keep its state; referenced by path in several worked examples.

## Files and paths referenced

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/templates/` | Directory holding the five copyable template skeletons described in this page. |
| `docs/templates/resolution-record.md` | The Resolution Record skeleton, kept separate from the other four flat template files. |
| `docs/resolutions/` | Directory holding numbered Resolution Records once written. |
| `accountsvc/config.ini` | Example configuration file used in the Reference and How-To worked examples. |
| `accountsvc/data/accounts.db` | Example path to the database file used in the relocation How-To. |
| `logs/accountsvc.log` | Log file referenced in the Troubleshooting worked example and the relocation How-To's verification step. |
| `docs-style/README.md` | Folder overview page that lists every sibling page and the mandatory elements this catalog builds on. |
| `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` | Sibling page covering sentence-level style; referenced when filling in template prose sections. |
| `docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md` | Sibling page covering how terminology sections (like this one) get maintained over time. |
| `docs-style/review-cadence.md` | Sibling page covering how often each page type gets re-reviewed. |
| `docs-style/publishing-workflow.md` | Sibling page covering how a cleared page moves from draft to published. |
| `docs-style/markdown-conventions.md` | Sibling page covering file naming and Markdown formatting rules referenced in step 2 of "Copying a template in practice." |
| `docs-style/link-checking-notes.txt` | Sibling page covering the link-checking tool referenced in step 5 of "Copying a template in practice." |
| `docs-style/diagram-guidelines.md` | Sibling page covering when and how to add a diagram, referenced in the Overview template. |

## Tools and versions

| Tool / package | Version | Purpose |

| Python (standard library only) | 3.11 | Runtime accountsvc itself targets; not required to write documentation but useful for checking snippet accuracy. |
| sqlite3 (CLI) | 3.44.0 | Used in worked-example verification snippets against the database file. |

1	# Writing Style Guide
2	
3	**Version:** v1.4.0
4	**Owner:** Docs Guild (Theo Banks)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-08-12
6	
7	**Summary:** Sets tone, sentence length, and formatting conventions that every page in the internal wiki should follow.
8	
9	## Purpose and Coverage
10	
11	This page is the anchor document for how we write, template, keep current, review, and publish the internal wiki for accountsvc. It exists because five different contributors wrote five different styles into the wiki over its first year, and a reader could tell which engineer wrote a page just from the punctuation. This guide sets a shared baseline: sentence length, heading order, list conventions, glossary discipline, review timing, and the steps that turn a merged markdown file into a page a teammate can actually open and trust.
12	
13	Everyone who edits a page under `docs-style/`, `docs/`, or the top-level `README.md` is expected to have read this page at least once. New contributors get pointed here from the onboarding page before they touch anything else.
14	
15	## Voice and Tone Principles
16	
17	*Section owner: Theo Banks*
18	
19	We write for a teammate who is mid-incident, mid-onboarding, or mid-refactor, not for a reader who wants a leisurely walkthrough. That means:
20	
21	- Say the thing plainly. If a step is optional, say "optional," not "you may, if you wish, consider."
22	- Use second person for instructions ("Open the config file") and third person for descriptions ("The build script writes its log to `docs/_build/logs/`").
23	- Avoid hedging phrases like "should probably" or "it might be the case that." If we're not sure, we say we're not sure and name who to ask.
24	- Keep humor out of procedural sections. A little personality is fine in intros and in this guide itself, but a page a teammate is following at 2 a.m. should not make them guess whether a line is a joke.
25	- Write short paragraphs. Three sentences is a comfortable target; five is the ceiling before you should be reaching for a list or a table instead.
26	
27	Voice questions that go beyond tone — for example, whether to use "we" or the passive form when describing a shared choice — are covered in the sibling page *Voice and Tone Notes*. This guide and that one occasionally overlap; when they do, treat this page as the one to follow for anything with a version number attached to it, since it is reviewed more often.
28	
29	## Sentence and Paragraph Length
30	
31	*Section owner: Theo Banks*
32	
33	Long, nested sentences are the single most common problem in accountsvc pages. A rough guideline that has worked well for us:
34	
35	1. Keep sentences under about 25 words in procedural writing. Longer is fine in narrative sections like this one, but a step in a numbered list should read in one breath.
36	2. One idea per sentence. If you find yourself writing "and" three times, split it.
37	3. Avoid stacking subordinate clauses. "Because the config file changed, and because the build step reads it at start, and because the log folder wasn't writable, the page failed to build" should become three short sentences or a small numbered list.
38	4. Prefer active voice for instructions: "Run the lint pass" rather than "The lint pass should be run."
39	
40	A worked example, taken (lightly disguised) from an early edit of the publishing workflow page:
41	
42	**Before:**
43	
44	> Once the markdown file has been edited and the reviewer has looked it over and assuming there are no open questions in the comments, which there usually aren't by this point, the file can then be merged and the build script, which watches the `docs-style/` and `docs/` folders, will pick it up on its next run and generate the updated page.
45	
46	**After:**
47	
48	> Merge the file once the reviewer has signed off and open comments are closed. The build script watches `docs-style/` and `docs/` and picks up the change on its next run.
49	
50	The second version is 33 words shorter and easier to skim during a merge queue.
51	
52	## Formatting Conventions
53	
54	*Section owner: Theo Banks*
55	
56	### Header block
57	
58	Every page, regardless of its file type, opens with a header block naming its title, version, owner, and last-updated date, followed by a one- or two-sentence summary. For markdown pages this is a small block of bold labels near the top, as shown at the top of this page. For the two non-markdown pages in this folder (`terminology-reference.rst` and `changelog-format.yaml`), the same four fields appear as the first fields in the file, using whatever comment or field syntax that format supports.
59	
60	### Headings
61	
62	Use `##` for top-level sections within a page and `###` for subsections. Do not skip levels. Order sections in whatever way suits the material — a reference page might go alphabetical, a procedure page should go in the order a reader performs the steps — but keep the header block, the terminology section, and the change log in consistent positions relative to each other: header block first, terminology and glossary content somewhere in the body, files/tools/change log/related-pages clustered near the end.
63	
64	Capitalization of headings has drifted across the wiki. Some pages use Title Case ("Review Cadence And Scheduling"), others use sentence case ("Review cadence and scheduling"). Our house preference is Title Case for `##` headings and sentence case for `###` subheadings, but you will find both in older pages and we have not gone back to fix all of them. Match the surrounding page rather than mixing styles within one document.
65	
66	### Lists
67	
68	We use three list styles on purpose, each for a different job:
69	
70	- **Bulleted lists** (`-`) for unordered facts, options, or short notes — like this one.
71	- **Numbered lists** (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) for anything the reader performs in order.
72	- **Definition-style lists**, written as a bolded term followed by a colon and an explanation, for glossary entries and for tables of contents when a table feels heavy.
73	
74	Don't force a numbered list onto unordered content just because it looks tidier — a reader will assume order matters and get confused when it doesn't.
75	
76	### Code and configuration snippets
77	
78	Fence code and configuration snippets with triple backticks and a language tag where one applies (`bash`, `yaml`, `ini`). Keep snippets runnable as written; don't include fill-in brackets a reader has to edit blind. For example, a lint pass over the docs folder before a merge:
79	
80	```bash
81	markdownlint-cli "docs-style/*.md" "docs/*.md"
82	vale --config=docs/style-lint.cfg docs-style/
83	```
84	
85	And a minimal `style-lint.cfg` entry that tells Vale which folder to treat as covered by the house style checks:
86	
87	```ini
88	[*.md]
89	BasedOnStyles = AccountSvcDocs
90	```
91	
92	### Tables
93	
94	Use tables when you are presenting more than three rows of parallel data — versions, dates, cadences. Below three rows, a bulleted list usually reads faster. Keep the first column short; it's the one a reader scans down.
95	
96	## Page Templates
97	
98	*Section owner: Priya Nair*
99	
100	Every new page starts from one of four templates kept in the Page Template Catalog: a **procedure template**, a **reference template**, a **choice-record template** (used sparingly, mostly for choices about the docs program itself, not day-to-day engineering choices), and a **glossary-style template** for pages that are mostly term definitions. All four templates begin with the same header block described above and end with the same files/tools/change-log/related-pages cluster.
101	
102	The short version of the template rule: copy the closest-matching file, don't build a new page from a blank buffer. This keeps heading order, capitalization, and section ownership notes consistent without anyone having to remember the rules by heart every time.
103	
104	A minimal check before you consider a new page "started":
105	
106	- [ ] Header block filled in with a real version number, not `v0.1`.
107	- [ ] At least a stand-in terminology section, even if you fill in the definitions later.
108	- [ ] A files-and-paths section, even if it currently has one row.
109	- [ ] An empty change-log table with the first row filled in.
110	- [ ] A related-pages section, even if it only links back to this style guide and the README.
111	
112	We keep the full catalog of templates, including the exact markdown skeletons, in the sibling *Page Template Catalog* page rather than duplicating them here — this guide only sets the rule that a template must be used.
113	
114	## Terminology and Glossary Upkeep
115	
116	*Section owner: Theo Banks*
117	
118	Terms drift. "Log folder" becomes "logs directory" becomes "logging path" across three pages written by three people, and a new contributor has no way to know these all point at the same thing. Glossary upkeep is the discipline of catching that drift early and often.
119	
120	The working rule:
121	
122	1. The first time a page introduces a term that isn't already in the wiki's terminology set, define it in that page's own terminology section.
123	2. If the term is likely to show up on more than one page — as most of ours are — also add it to the canonical *Terminology Reference*, with the exact wording you used, so the next writer copies your phrase instead of inventing a new one.
124	3. Once a month, the docs guild does a short pass comparing terms defined locally on individual pages against the canonical reference, and reconciles any that have quietly diverged. This pass is described step by step in the sibling *Glossary Upkeep Guide* (version 1.6); this page only sets the cadence and the ownership.
125	4. Retiring a term (because the underlying idea went away) means removing it from the canonical reference and leaving a one-line note in that page's change log — never silently dropping it.
126	
127	A glossary entry, wherever it lives, should follow this shape: a bolded term, a colon, and a definition of one or two sentences that a new hire could understand without already knowing accountsvc. Avoid circular definitions ("A build log is a log produced by the build") — say what it's for, not just what it's called.
128	
129	## Review Cadence
130	
131	*Section owner: Mara Olsen*
132	
133	Pages in this folder are reviewed on a fixed schedule so that "last updated" dates stay accurate rather than becoming aspirational.
134	
135	| Page type | Review cadence | Who reviews |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| Style and voice pages (this page, Voice and Tone Notes) | Every 6 months | Docs Guild |
138	| Templates and terminology (Page Template Catalog, Terminology Reference) | Every 4 months | Developer Experience |
139	| Cadence and workflow pages (Review Cadence, Docs Publishing Workflow) | Every 3 months | Platform Tools |
140	| Onboarding and link-checking pages | Every 2 months, since they go stale fastest | Support Enablement |
141	
142	Outside the fixed schedule, any contributor can flag a page as due for an out-of-cycle look by opening a short note in the docs channel; the section owner named at the top of the relevant section decides whether to act on it right away or fold it into the next scheduled pass.
143	
144	The full mechanics of scheduling — who owns the calendar entry, what counts as "reviewed" versus "skimmed," and how a missed cycle gets caught — live in the *Documentation Review Cadence* page, last touched around April 2025. This page only states the cadence table above as the shared baseline every other page inherits unless it says otherwise in its own header.
145	
146	## Docs Publishing Workflow
147	
148	*Section owner: Mara Olsen*
149	
150	Writing a page and publishing it are two different acts, and conflating them is how stale drafts end up looking finished. The workflow, in order:
151	
152	1. **Draft.** Write or edit the markdown (or `.rst`, or `.yaml`) file directly in the `docs-style/` or `docs/` folder on a branch.
153	2. **Self-check.** Run the lint pass shown earlier (`markdownlint-cli` and `vale`) locally before opening anything for review. A page that fails the lint pass shouldn't reach a reviewer's queue.
154	3. **Open a draft pull request.** Mark it as a draft until the header block, terminology section, and change-log entry are all filled in — an empty change-log row is a quick tell that a page isn't ready yet.
155	4. **Review.** The section owner named in the page (or, for a brand-new page, whoever owns that folder generally) reads it for tone and accuracy against this guide.
156	5. **Merge.** Once comments are closed, merge to the main line. Do not squash the change-log entry away — it should match, or closely mirror, the actual commit message.
157	6. **Build.** The build script watches `docs-style/` and `docs/` and regenerates the published pages on its next run, writing its output to the build log folder.
158	7. **Confirm.** Check the build log folder for errors before considering the page live. A silent build failure is worse than a slow one.
159	
160	A short shell sequence that covers steps 2 and 6 together, run from the repository root:
161	
162	```bash
163	markdownlint-cli "docs-style/*.md"
164	vale --config=docs/style-lint.cfg docs-style/writing-style-guide.md
165	bash scripts/build-docs.sh
166	tail -n 40 docs/_build/logs/latest.log
167	```
168	
169	If the build log folder shows a warning about an unresolved link, the usual cause is a related-pages entry that names a page title that doesn't match the actual `# Title` line at the top of the target file — a small but frequent mismatch, since page titles and filenames aren't always kept in lockstep.
170	
171	The publishing workflow described above is owned jointly by the Docs Guild, since Theo Banks signs off on tone before anything ships; the sibling *Docs Publishing Workflow* page has the fuller step list, including the parts specific to build tooling rather than to writing.
172	
173	## Worked Example: Turning a Rough Draft Into a Finished Page
174	
175	To make the rules above concrete, here is a short before-and-after of a section from an early draft of the onboarding page, edited down using the sentence-length and list-style rules from this guide.
176	
177	**Rough draft:**
178	
179	> New contributors, once they've been given access to the folder and have had a chance to read through some of the existing pages so they get a feel for things, should probably start by picking a small page to edit, maybe something like a typo fix or a broken link, before they go and try to write a whole new page from scratch, since that tends to go better for everyone including the reviewer.
180	
181	**Edited:**
182	
183	> New contributors should start with a small edit — a typo fix or a broken link — before writing a full page. This goes better for the contributor and the reviewer.
184	
185	The edited version drops the hedging ("probably"), splits one long sentence into two, and moves the example into an em-dash aside instead of a subordinate clause. This is the level of tightening every page in this folder should get during review.
186	
187	## Terminology
188	
189	The following terms recur across the docs-style folder and should be used consistently. Anything not listed here but used more than once should be proposed for the canonical *Terminology Reference*.
190	
191	- **Header block:** The labeled block of title, version, owner, and last-updated date at the top of every page, followed by a short summary line.
192	- **Section owner note:** A short italic line under a heading naming the person accountable for that section's accuracy, distinct from the page's overall owner.
193	- **Style pass:** A focused read-through of a page checking only tone, sentence length, and formatting, not technical accuracy.
194	- **Lint pass:** An automated check (via `markdownlint-cli`, `vale`, or similar) that flags formatting problems before a page reaches human review.
195	- **Template stub:** A copy of one of the four page templates with the header block and section skeleton filled in but the body still empty.
196	- **Glossary entry:** A single bolded-term-plus-definition line, whether it lives in a page's own terminology section or in the canonical reference.
197	- **Draft pull request:** A pull request explicitly marked not-yet-ready, used to hold a page open for comments before it's considered done.
198	- **Build log folder:** The folder, currently `docs/_build/logs/`, where the build script writes output each time it regenerates pages from the `docs-style/` and `docs/` folders.
199	- **Related-pages section:** The end-of-page section listing sibling pages by title, used to help a reader find the fuller treatment of a topic this page only touches on.
200	- **Voice note:** A short, informal aside (like the ones in the Voice and Tone Notes page) that explains a stylistic choice without setting a hard rule.
201
