**Summary:** Lays out how often each page in the wiki is reread and by whom, based on how quickly the underlying package changes.

---

## Purpose and Coverage

accountsvc is small, but its wiki has grown past forty pages across `docs/` and `docs-style/`, and not every page ages at the same rate. A page describing the command-line reference changes almost every time a flag is added; a page describing the writing style guide might go a year without a single sentence needing a fix. Treating all pages the same way — rereading everything on the same calendar, or rereading nothing until someone complains — wastes time in one direction and lets pages go stale in the other.

This page defines the cadence tiers used across the wiki, explains how a page gets sorted into one, walks through a worked cadence cycle, and lists the tools and files that keep the cadence reliable. It applies to every page under `docs/` and `docs-style/`, including this one. It does not apply to the package's own CHANGELOG.md, which is maintained by whoever cuts the release and follows its own rules.

Two audiences read this page: the person assigned to reread a given page in a given cycle, and whoever is asked "when was this last looked at?" three months later. Both should be able to answer their question from this page alone, without pinging Platform Tools.

## Why Cadence Varies by Page — Owner: Mara Olsen

The rule of thumb the team has settled on: **a page's reread frequency should roughly track how often the part of the package it describes changes.** Three things drive that:

- How close the page sits to the package's command surface or its HTTP interface. Pages describing those move whenever a flag, a header, or a status behavior is added or changed.
- How close the page sits to the on-disk database file. Anything touching the schema reference tends to shift when a field is added, even if the change is small.
- How close the page sits to process rather than product — writing conventions, glossary upkeep, publishing steps. These drift slowly; they mostly change because a person on the team decided to change them, not because the package did.

A page's cadence tier is not permanent. A page can move from the slow lane to the fast lane if the part of the package it covers becomes more active for a quarter or two, and it can move back down once things settle. That reassignment happens during the cadence cycle described below, not ad hoc.

## Cadence Tiers

| Tier | Frequency | Typical Pages | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 — Fast Lane | Monthly | Command-line reference, HTTP interface reference, database schema reference | Owen Castillo (Core Services) |
| Tier 2 — Standard | Quarterly | Writing Style Guide, Page Template Catalog, Terminology Reference, Diagram Guidelines | round-robin Docs Guild member |
| Tier 3 — Slow Lane | Yearly | Voice and Tone Notes, Docs Contributor Onboarding, this page's own background notes | Theo Banks (Docs Guild) / Dana Whitfield (Support Enablement) |

A fourth, informal tier exists in practice even though it isn't on the spreadsheet: pages that are reread whenever the package cuts a release with a note attached to them. Those are mostly Tier 1 pages anyway, so the extra tier hasn't been formalized — it would just duplicate the monthly cadence.

Note that Tier 2's frequency is quarterly for the pages listed above, but the Glossary Upkeep Guide, owned by Priya Nair of Developer Experience, runs on its own six-week cadence because term drift tends to show up faster than the rest of Tier 2 content. That page sets its own pace and this page just records it.

## How a Page Is Assigned to a Tier — Owner: Mara Olsen

New pages don't default to Tier 2 just because that's the middle option. When a page is added to the wiki, whoever adds it proposes a tier in the page's pull request description, and Platform Tools confirms or adjusts it before merge. The rough check:

1. Does the page describe anything that changes when a flag, header, or field is added to the package? → Tier 1.
2. Does the page describe a process, a convention, or a template that only changes when the docs team itself decides to change it, and does it change more than once a year in practice? → Tier 2.
3. Does the page describe something that has changed fewer than twice in the last eighteen months? → Tier 3.

If a page doesn't cleanly fit any of the three questions, it defaults to Tier 2 until the next cadence cycle produces better evidence either way.

Tier assignments live in the cadence tracker spreadsheet (`docs/cadence-tracker.xlsx`), one row per page, with a column for the current tier, the last reread date, and the reread owner. The spreadsheet is the source of truth; this page's tables are a copy of it and can lag by a cycle if nobody updates them.

## The Quarterly Cadence Cycle

Even though Tier 1 pages are reread monthly and Tier 3 pages yearly, the whole wiki is walked through together once a quarter so that tier reassignments happen at a predictable time rather than whenever someone remembers. The cycle has four steps:

- **Open.** On the first business day of the quarter, Platform Tools opens the cycle by copying the cadence tracker's current state into a dated sheet and posting the open date in the team channel.
- **Assign.** Every page due in that quarter (all of Tier 1 and Tier 2, plus whichever Tier 3 pages are due) gets an owner from the table above, or a substitute if the named owner is out.
- **Reread.** Each owner works through the pages assigned to them using the reread procedure below, and marks each page's tracker row with the date it was reread and either "no change needed" or a short note on what was fixed.
- **Close.** On the last business day of the quarter, Platform Tools closes the cycle, writes a dated log to `docs/cadence-logs/`, and carries forward anything left unmarked to the next cycle's open step.

A quarter runs roughly thirteen weeks, but the open and close dates are set to business days, so the actual span varies by a few days each quarter.

## Worked Example: the Q3 2024 Cycle

To make the four steps concrete, here is how the third-quarter cycle of 2024 actually ran.

**Open — Monday, July 1, 2024.** Mara opened the cycle, copied the tracker to a sheet named `2024-Q3`, and posted the open date. Fourteen pages were due: all six Tier 1 pages (one reread per month, so eighteen reread events across the quarter, though the table below only shows the July group), all seven standing Tier 2 pages, and one Tier 3 page — Docs Contributor Onboarding — which was due for its yearly reread this quarter.

**Assign — same day.** Owners were pulled from the table:

| Page | Tier | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| Command-line reference | 1 | Owen Castillo | Jul 5 |
| HTTP interface reference | 1 | Owen Castillo | Jul 5 |
| Database schema reference | 1 | Owen Castillo | Jul 5 |
| Writing Style Guide | 2 | Theo Banks | Aug 9 |
| Page Template Catalog | 2 | Priya Nair | Aug 9 |
| Terminology Reference | 2 | Priya Nair | Aug 9 |
| Docs Contributor Onboarding | 3 | Dana Whitfield | Sep 20 |

**Reread — through August and into September.** Owen finished his three Tier 1 pages on July 5 as planned; the command-line reference needed two paragraphs fixed for a flag that had been renamed since the last cycle. Theo's reread of the Writing Style Guide turned up nothing worth changing and was marked "no change needed." Priya's reread of the Page Template Catalog, then at version 2.9, found a template missing a heading level and opened a fix. Dana's reread of Docs Contributor Onboarding slipped past its September 20 due date by four days because of a conflicting commitment, and was marked late in the tracker.

**Close — Monday, September 30, 2024.** Mara closed the cycle and wrote `docs/cadence-logs/2024-Q3.txt`, which recorded thirteen of fourteen pages reread on time, one late by four days, and two tier reassignments carried into Q4: the database schema reference stayed in Tier 1, and the Glossary Upkeep Guide's six-week cadence was confirmed as still appropriate rather than folded into the quarterly Tier 2 group.

That log file is what this page's change log entry for v2.2 refers to when it mentions the cadence-logs folder — the practice started informally during Q3 2024 and was written up here afterward.

## Reread Procedure — Owner: Owen Castillo (Core Services)

Each page owner works through their assigned pages using the same short procedure, regardless of tier:

1. Open the page and read it straight through, not just the parts that seem likely to have moved.
2. Compare anything the page states about current package behavior against the package's own CHANGELOG.md for entries since the page's last-updated date.
3. Open the page's header block and confirm the version and last-updated date are ones you're prepared to bump — a reread with no changes still gets a note in the tracker, but the header itself only moves if the text moves.
4. Fix what needs fixing, bump the version and last-updated date in the header, and add one line to the page's own change log.
5. Mark the tracker row with today's date and either "no change needed" or a short note on what changed.
6. If the reread suggests the page belongs in a different tier, note that separately rather than moving it yourself — tier changes are confirmed by Platform Tools at the next cycle's open step.

A quick way to see what's changed in a page since its own last-updated date, from a shell in the repository root:

```
git log --since="2024-06-15" --oneline -- docs-style/writing-style-guide.md
```

And to check a page's header against its most recent edit date, from PowerShell:

```powershell
git log -1 --format="%cd" --date=short -- docs-style\writing-style-guide.md
```

If the date that comes back is later than the last-updated date printed in the header, someone edited the file without bumping the header, and that's worth a short fix on its own the next time the page is opened.

## When a Page Misses Its Window — Owner: Dana Whitfield (Support Enablement)

Pages miss their reread window for ordinary reasons — an owner is out, a quarter is busy, a page gets overlooked because nobody linked to it recently. The response is proportionate to how late the page is:

- **Up to two weeks late:** no action beyond a note in the tracker. This covers most misses and isn't worth chasing.
- **Two to six weeks late:** the page owner gets a direct message from whoever is running that cycle, asking for a date it will get done.
- **More than six weeks late:** the page moves to the top of the next cycle's assign step automatically, and Platform Tools is looped in if it's a Tier 1 page, since those are the ones most likely to be actively wrong by that point.

There's no formal process beyond that. The team is small enough that a missed window is a conversation, not a queue.

## Tools Supporting the Cadence

| Tool / Package | Version | Used For |
|---|---|---|
| Git | 2.44.0 | Checking edit dates on pages and diffing what changed between rereads |
| PowerShell | 7.4.2 | Running the cadence-check script on Windows hosts |
| MkDocs | 1.6.1 | Building the published site the reread pages feed into |
| LibreOffice Calc | 24.2.4 | Maintaining the cadence tracker spreadsheet |
| Windows Task Scheduler | built-in (Windows 10/11) | Kicking off the monthly cadence-check job that flags pages nearing their window |
| sqlite3 CLI | 3.45.1 | Spot-checking that the database schema reference page hasn't drifted from the live database file |
| cron | (host-dependent) | Same monthly job as Task Scheduler, on the one non-Windows host that mirrors the wiki build |

The cadence-check script itself lives at `scripts/cadence-check.ps1`. It reads the header block of every page under `docs/` and `docs-style/`, compares the last-updated date against today, and prints anything whose tier window has closed. It doesn't fix anything or touch the tracker spreadsheet — it just prints a list that whoever is running the current cycle can act on.

## Files and Paths This Page Refers To

- `docs-style/review-cadence.md` — this page.
- `docs-style/README.md` — the folder overview; the first stop for anyone new to the docs-style folder.
- `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` — the writing style guide, a standing Tier 2 page.
- `docs-style/page-template-catalog.md` — the page template catalog, a standing Tier 2 page.
- `docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md` — the glossary upkeep guide, on its own six-week cadence.
- `docs-style/publishing-workflow.md` — the publishing workflow page, referenced by the close step when a cycle's fixes go out to the built site.
- `docs-style/terminology-reference.rst` — the terminology reference, a standing Tier 2 page.
- `docs-style/changelog-format.yaml` — defines the shape each page's own change log entries should follow.
- `docs/cadence-tracker.xlsx` — the spreadsheet of record for tier assignments, due dates, and reread outcomes.
- `docs/cadence-logs/` — dated text files, one per closed cycle, written at the close step.
- `scripts/cadence-check.ps1` — the script that prints pages whose reread window has closed.
- `accountsvc/CHANGELOG.md` — the package's own record of what changed release to release; used during rereads to spot what a Tier 1 page might need to catch up on.

## Terminology

**Cadence tier**
: The frequency group a page belongs to — fast lane, standard, or slow lane — set during a cadence cycle's open step.

**Cadence cycle**
: One full pass through the wiki's due pages, run quarterly, made up of open, assign, reread, and close steps.

**Reread window**
: The span of time in which a page's scheduled reread is expected to happen before it counts as late.

**Cadence tracker**
: The spreadsheet (`docs/cadence-tracker.xlsx`) recording each page's tier, last reread date, and owner.

**Fast-lane page**
: A Tier 1 page, reread monthly, typically one describing the package's command surface, HTTP interface, or database schema.

**Slow-lane page**
: A Tier 3 page, reread yearly, typically describing a process or convention that rarely changes on its own.

**Cadence log**
: A dated text file in `docs/cadence-logs/` recording how a closed cycle went — how many pages were reread on time, how many were late, and what tier changes were confirmed.

**Cadence owner**
: The named person responsible for rereading a given set of pages during a cycle; distinct from the page's own header owner, though they're often the same person.

**Overdue page**
: A page whose reread window has closed without a reread being marked in the tracker.

**Wiki**
: The full set of internal documentation pages for the package, spanning `docs/` and `docs-style/`.

## Change Log

| Date | Version | Release Name | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022-11-03 | v1.0 | "Initial Cadence" | First version of this page; established the three-tier structure without formal owners. |
| 2023-02-14 | v1.1 | "Fast Lane" | Added the monthly tier for command-line and HTTP interface pages. |
| 2023-06-01 | v1.2 | "Slow Lane" | Introduced the yearly tier for background-process pages and named first owners. |
| 2023-10-20 | v2.0 | "Cadence Overhaul" | Restructured the whole page around the four-step quarterly cycle; dropped the old ad hoc reread list. |
| 2024-03-08 | v2.1 | "Spreadsheet Sync" | Linked the page to the new cadence tracker spreadsheet as the source of truth for tier assignments. |
| 2024-09-15 | v2.2 | "Log Folder" | Added the `docs/cadence-logs/` folder, wrote up the cadence-check script, and added the Q3 2024 worked example. |

1	# Docs Publishing Workflow
2	
3	**Version:** v2.0.1
4	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
5	**Last updated:** 2026-02-10
6	
7	## Overview
8	
9	The docs-style/ folder holds the handful of pages that describe how the team writes, formats, and ships documentation for accountsvc. This page is the connective one — it walks through what happens between a drafted page sitting in a working copy on your laptop and that same page showing up on the internal wiki where the rest of the team reads it. It assumes you've already skimmed the Writing Style Guide and picked a starting point from the Page Template Catalog. If you haven't, do that first; this page picks up right after the draft exists.
10	
11	Four stages make up the workflow: drafting, review, building, and posting. Each stage has its own owner, its own small set of tools, and its own way of going wrong. The sections below cover each stage in the order a page actually moves through them, plus a terminology section, a table of tools, a listing of the files and paths this page touches, and a change log.
12	
13	One thing worth saying up front: nothing in this page describes anything about how accountsvc itself works. It's strictly about the mechanics of shipping a page — the package, the service, and the database file it keeps its state in are simply not this page's concern.
14	
15	## Drafting a Page (Owner: Dana Whitfield, Support Enablement)
16	
17	A draft starts life as a new markdown file inside docs-style/ or one of the other docs/ subfolders, named to match the page's title in lowercase with hyphens — `publishing-workflow.md`, not `Publishing_Workflow.md` or `publishingWorkflow.md`. Pick a template from the Page Template Catalog that matches the kind of page you're writing (procedure, reference, or overview) and copy it wholesale rather than starting from a blank file. Nearly every returned draft the team has seen came from someone skipping the template and reinventing the header block from memory.
18	
19	Every draft needs, at minimum:
20	
21	1. A header block with title, version, owner, and a last-updated date.
22	2. Section headings that fit the content — don't force a page into a template's headings if the content genuinely doesn't need them.
23	3. A short glossary or terminology section if the page introduces new terms.
24	4. Any files or host paths the page discusses, listed plainly.
25	
26	Once the header and skeleton are in place, write the body. The Writing Style Guide has the detailed rules on tone, contractions, and sentence length; the short version is: write like you're explaining it to the next hire, not like you're drafting a formal legal memo.
27	
28	When the draft feels done, open a merge request against the docs branch. The request description should name the page, the reviewer you're pulling in, and whether this is a new page or an update to an existing one. A typical description looks like this:
29	
30	```
31	New page: docs-style/publishing-workflow.md
32	Reviewer: Mara Olsen
33	Type: new page
34	Related pages: writing-style-guide.md, page-template-catalog.md
35	```
36	
37	Don't merge your own draft, even for a one-line fix. The review step below exists specifically so a second set of eyes reads the page before it's visible to the whole team.
38	
39	## Style Guide Touchpoints
40	
41	Three things from the Writing Style Guide matter enough during publishing that it's worth repeating them here rather than sending you back and forth between pages:
42	
43	- **Headers are sentence case**, not title case. "Handling returned pages," not "Handling Returned Pages." (You may spot that this page doesn't always follow that rule consistently — older pages in the folder predate the current guide, and nobody has gone back to fix every heading.)
44	- **Code blocks always name their language** in the fence, even for plain text output, so the site builder can apply the right formatting.
45	- **Second person is fine**, first person plural ("we") is discouraged outside of change log entries.
46	
47	The current Writing Style Guide sits at v1.3 and covers voice, punctuation, and the house rules on numerals versus spelled-out numbers. If a draft conflicts with the guide, the guide wins — the reviewer will flag it rather than let a page slip through with its own house style.
48	
49	## Page Templates
50	
51	Templates live in the Page Template Catalog and cover three shapes: procedure pages (this one), reference pages, and short overview pages. Each template ships with sample text in brackets — `[section owner]`, `[last updated]` — that must be fully replaced before a page goes to review. A reviewer who spots leftover bracket text sends the page straight back without reading further; it's the fastest tell that a draft was rushed.
52	
53	A worked example: starting the procedure template for this exact page looked like this before edits:
54	
55	```
56	# [Page Title]
57	
58	**Version:** v0.1.0
59	**Owner:** [team] ([name])
60	**Last updated:** [date]
61	
62	## Overview
63	[one paragraph describing what this page walks through]
64	```
65	
66	Filling that in is mechanical, but it matters — the header block is the first thing a reader checks when they're deciding whether a page is current enough to trust.
67	
68	## Terminology Touchpoints (Owner: Theo Banks, Developer Experience)
69	
70	Publishing a page usually means introducing one or two new terms, and those terms need a home beyond just this page's own terminology section. The team keeps a running list in terminology-reference.rst that's meant to be the single place someone can look up a word without hunting through every page that uses it. When your draft coins a term — something like "sibling page" or "front matter block" — add it there as part of the same merge request, not as a follow-up you'll get to later. Follow-ups on terminology tend to never happen.
71	
72	The Glossary Upkeep Guide has the fuller set of rules on how terms get proposed, worded, and cleaned up over time; skim it before you add anything non-obvious.
73	
74	## Review and Sign-off (Owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)
75	
76	Every page — new or updated — gets one reviewer before it merges. The reviewer's job is narrower than a full copy edit: they're checking that the header block is filled in correctly, the page follows the chosen template, links point where they say they point, and nothing in the body conflicts with a sibling page. They are not expected to catch every grammar issue; that's what the writer and the style guide are for.
77	
78	Reviewers work through a short, informal checklist:
79	
80	| Check | What it catches |
81	|---|---|
82	| Header complete | Missing version, owner, or date |
83	| Template match | Headings out of order, missing sections |
84	| Terms defined | New words used without a glossary entry |
85	| Links resolve | Broken or misspelled paths to sibling pages |
86	| Code fences labeled | Missing language tags on code blocks |
87	| No stray bracket text | Leftover template placeholders |
88	
89	If the reviewer finds problems, they leave comments on the merge request and hand it back to the writer rather than fixing it themselves — small wording nits aside. A page with more than two rounds of back-and-forth usually means the draft needed a conversation, not more comments, so at that point the writer and reviewer are expected to just talk it through.
90	
91	For the broader schedule — how often existing pages get re-reviewed once they're live, not just at first publish — see the Documentation Review Cadence page, currently at v2.0. That page also covers what happens to a page that's gone stale, which this page doesn't repeat.
92	
93	## Build and Publish Steps (Owner: Owen Castillo, Core Services)
94	
95	Once a page clears review, it's ready to build. The internal wiki is a static site generated from the docs/ folder with mkdocs and pushed to an internal host; nothing about this step is specific to any one page, but it's worth walking through once since it trips up new contributors.
96	
97	From the repository root:
98	
99	```bash
100	$ python -m venv .docs-env
101	$ source .docs-env/bin/activate
102	$ pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
103	$ python scripts/build_docs.py --strict
104	```
105	
106	`scripts/build_docs.py` wraps the mkdocs build with a couple of extra checks: it confirms every page under docs-style/ has a header block with all four fields, and it fails loudly if a heading level skips (an `h4` directly under an `h2`, for instance). The `--strict` flag turns warnings into hard failures, which is what the build server always uses even though local runs sometimes leave it off for speed.
107	
108	A clean build looks like this:
109	
110	```
111	[build_docs] scanning docs/ ...
112	[build_docs] 214 pages found
113	[build_docs] header check: OK
114	[build_docs] heading order check: OK
115	[build_docs] writing site to docs/_build/
116	[build_docs] done in 8.4s
117	```
118	
119	The `docs/_build/` folder is local output and isn't committed — it's regenerated fresh on every build, both locally and on the build server. Once the local build is clean, push the branch and open (or update) the merge request if you haven't already. Merging to the docs branch kicks off the same build on the shared build host, and a clean run there is what actually pushes the rendered site live. Build output and any failures land in `/var/log/accountsvc-docs/build/` on that host, organized by date, and that's the first place to look if a page shows up looking wrong after a merge that seemed fine locally.
120	
121	The one thing the local and shared builds don't share is the mkdocs cache — a page that builds clean on your machine can still surface a warning on the shared host if your local cache is stale. Clearing `.docs-env/.cache/` before a final local build catches most of those.
122	
123	## Link Checking (Owner: Dana Whitfield, Support Enablement)
124	
125	Broken links are the single most common problem the build catches after header issues. A separate check runs against every page in docs/ using `scripts/check_links.py`, which walks the rendered site and confirms every internal link points to a page that actually exists, and every external link returns something other than a hard failure. It runs as part of the shared build, but it's worth running locally before you push:
126	
127	```bash
128	$ python scripts/check_links.py --path docs/
129	Checking 214 pages, 612 links...
130	  612 OK
131	  0 broken
132	Done in 3.1s
133	```
134	
135	When it finds a broken link, the output names the file and line so you're not hunting for it:
136	
137	```
138	BROKEN: docs-style/publishing-workflow.md:118
139	  -> docs-style/review-cadance.md (no such page)
140	```
141	
142	That example is a real one — a misspelled filename is the most common cause, followed closely by a sibling page getting renamed without every page that links to it being caught up. The Link Checking Notes page has the fuller rundown of how the checker decides what counts as broken versus just slow to respond, and what to do about links that point outside the wiki entirely.
143	
144	## Handling Returned Pages
145	
146	Not every draft clears review on the first pass, and that's expected rather than a problem. A returned page sits in an open merge request until the writer works through the reviewer's comments and pushes an update; there's no separate holding area for it, and no one else should build on top of a page that's still open. If a returned page sits open for more than two weeks without movement, Platform Tools will check in on it during the regular review cycle rather than let it quietly go stale.
147	
148	Two common reasons a page gets sent back:
149	
150	- The header block is present but one field is wrong — usually an owner name that doesn't match who's actually maintaining the page, or a date that wasn't bumped after real edits.
151	- The page duplicates content that already lives on a sibling page instead of linking to it. The rule of thumb: if a fact could change on the other page and this one wouldn't get updated, link instead of copying.
152	
153	## Post-Publish Steps
154	
155	Once a page is live, three small things close out the work:
156	
157	1. Post a short message in the docs channel naming the new or updated page and its title — this is how the rest of the team finds out something new exists, since there's no separate broadcast for it.
158	2. Update `docs-style/README.md` if the new page changes the folder's page count or adds a page that should be listed there.
159	3. If the page introduces a term, confirm it landed in terminology-reference.rst — this is the same step called out under Terminology Touchpoints above, and it's easy to forget once the merge request itself has closed.
160	
161	None of these three steps are enforced by the build; they're just the difference between a page that's technically live and one that people actually find.

177	## Terminology
178	
179	**Draft** — A page that exists in a working copy or an open merge request but hasn't been through review yet.
180	
181	**Header block** — The title, version, owner, and last-updated date that sits at the top of every page in the folder.
182	
183	**Section owner** — The person named next to a heading as responsible for that part of a page, separate from the page's overall owner.
184	
185	**Sibling page** — Any other page inside docs-style/ that this page links to or is meant to stay consistent with.
186	
187	**Front matter** — The small block of metadata some templates place at the very top of a page, distinct from the header block that appears in the rendered body.
188	
189	**Stub** — A page that's been created with a header and headings filled in but little or no body content yet; stubs are allowed to merge but are flagged in the review checklist.
190	
191	**Build step** — The point in the workflow where `scripts/build_docs.py` turns the markdown files in docs/ into the rendered site.
192	
193	**Link check** — The automated pass that confirms every internal and external link on a page still points somewhere real.
194	
195	**Returned page** — A draft sent back by a reviewer with comments, still open until the writer pushes an update.
196

# Docs Publishing Workflow

**Version:** v2.0.1
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
**Last updated:** 2026-02-10

## Overview

The docs-style/ folder holds the handful of pages that describe how the team writes, formats, and ships documentation for accountsvc. This page is the connective one — it walks through what happens between a drafted page sitting in a working copy on your laptop and that same page showing up on the internal wiki where the rest of the team reads it. It assumes you've already skimmed the Writing Style Guide and picked a starting point from the Page Template Catalog. If you haven't, do that first; this page picks up right after the draft exists.

Four stages make up the workflow: drafting, review, building, and posting. Each stage has its own owner, its own small set of tools, and its own way of going wrong. The sections below cover each stage in the order a page actually moves through them, plus a terminology section, a table of tools, a listing of the files and paths this page touches, and a change log.

One thing worth saying up front: nothing in this page describes anything about how accountsvc itself works. It's strictly about the mechanics of shipping a page — the package, the service, and the database file it keeps its state in are simply not this page's concern.

## Drafting a Page (Owner: Dana Whitfield, Support Enablement)

A draft starts life as a new markdown file inside docs-style/ or one of the other docs/ subfolders, named to match the page's title in lowercase with hyphens — `publishing-workflow.md`, not `Publishing_Workflow.md` or `publishingWorkflow.md`. Pick a template from the Page Template Catalog that matches the kind of page you're writing (procedure, reference, or overview) and copy it wholesale rather than starting from a blank file. Nearly every returned draft the team has seen came from someone skipping the template and reinventing the header block from memory.

Every draft needs, at minimum:

1. A header block with title, version, owner, and a last-updated date.
2. Section headings that fit the content — don't force a page into a template's headings if the content genuinely doesn't need them.
3. A short glossary or terminology section if the page introduces new terms.
4. Any files or host paths the page discusses, listed plainly.

Once the header and skeleton are in place, write the body. The Writing Style Guide has the detailed rules on tone, contractions, and sentence length; the short version is: write like you're explaining it to the next hire, not like you're drafting a formal legal memo.

When the draft feels done, open a merge request against the docs branch. The request description should name the page, the reviewer you're pulling in, and whether this is a new page or an update to an existing one. A typical description looks like this:

```
New page: docs-style/publishing-workflow.md
Reviewer: Mara Olsen
Type: new page
Related pages: writing-style-guide.md, page-template-catalog.md
```

Don't merge your own draft, even for a one-line fix. The review step below exists specifically so a second set of eyes reads the page before it's visible to the whole team.

## Style Guide Touchpoints

Three things from the Writing Style Guide matter enough during publishing that it's worth repeating them here rather than sending you back and forth between pages:

- **Headers are sentence case**, not title case. "Handling returned pages," not "Handling Returned Pages." (You may spot that this page doesn't always follow that rule consistently — older pages in the folder predate the current guide, and nobody has gone back to fix every heading.)
- **Code blocks always name their language** in the fence, even for plain text output, so the site builder can apply the right formatting.
- **Second person is fine**, first person plural ("we") is discouraged outside of change log entries.

The current Writing Style Guide sits at v1.3 and covers voice, punctuation, and the house rules on numerals versus spelled-out numbers. If a draft conflicts with the guide, the guide wins — the reviewer will flag it rather than let a page slip through with its own house style.

## Page Templates

Templates live in the Page Template Catalog and cover three shapes: procedure pages (this one), reference pages, and short overview pages. Each template ships with sample text in brackets — `[section owner]`, `[last updated]` — that must be fully replaced before a page goes to review. A reviewer who spots leftover bracket text sends the page straight back without reading further; it's the fastest tell that a draft was rushed.

A worked example: starting the procedure template for this exact page looked like this before edits:

```
# [Page Title]

**Version:** v0.1.0
**Owner:** [team] ([name])
**Last updated:** [date]

## Overview
[one paragraph describing what this page walks through]
```

Filling that in is mechanical, but it matters — the header block is the first thing a reader checks when they're deciding whether a page is current enough to trust.

## Terminology Touchpoints (Owner: Theo Banks, Developer Experience)

Publishing a page usually means introducing one or two new terms, and those terms need a home beyond just this page's own terminology section. The team keeps a running list in terminology-reference.rst that's meant to be the single place someone can look up a word without hunting through every page that uses it. When your draft coins a term — something like "sibling page" or "front matter block" — add it there as part of the same merge request, not as a follow-up you'll get to later. Follow-ups on terminology tend to never happen.

The Glossary Upkeep Guide has the fuller set of rules on how terms get proposed, worded, and cleaned up over time; skim it before you add anything non-obvious.

## Review and Sign-off (Owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

Every page — new or updated — gets one reviewer before it merges. The reviewer's job is narrower than a full copy edit: they're checking that the header block is filled in correctly, the page follows the chosen template, links point where they say they point, and nothing in the body conflicts with a sibling page. They are not expected to catch every grammar issue; that's what the writer and the style guide are for.

Reviewers work through a short, informal checklist:

| Check | What it catches |
|---|---|
| Header complete | Missing version, owner, or date |
| Template match | Headings out of order, missing sections |
| Terms defined | New words used without a glossary entry |
| Links resolve | Broken or misspelled paths to sibling pages |
| Code fences labeled | Missing language tags on code blocks |
| No stray bracket text | Leftover template placeholders |

If the reviewer finds problems, they leave comments on the merge request and hand it back to the writer rather than fixing it themselves — small wording nits aside. A page with more than two rounds of back-and-forth usually means the draft needed a conversation, not more comments, so at that point the writer and reviewer are expected to just talk it through.

For the broader schedule — how often existing pages get re-reviewed once they're live, not just at first publish — see the Documentation Review Cadence page, currently at v2.0. That page also covers what happens to a page that's gone stale, which this page doesn't repeat.

## Build and Publish Steps (Owner: Owen Castillo, Core Services)

Once a page clears review, it's ready to build. The internal wiki is a static site generated from the docs/ folder with mkdocs and pushed to an internal host; nothing about this step is specific to any one page, but it's worth walking through once since it trips up new contributors.

From the repository root:

```bash
$ python -m venv .docs-env
$ source .docs-env/bin/activate
$ pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
$ python scripts/build_docs.py --strict
```

`scripts/build_docs.py` wraps the mkdocs build with a couple of extra checks: it confirms every page under docs-style/ has a header block with all four fields, and it fails loudly if a heading level skips (an `h4` directly under an `h2`, for instance). The `--strict` flag turns warnings into hard failures, which is what the build server always uses even though local runs sometimes leave it off for speed.

A clean build looks like this:

```
[build_docs] scanning docs/ ...
[build_docs] 214 pages found
[build_docs] header check: OK
[build_docs] heading order check: OK
[build_docs] writing site to docs/_build/
[build_docs] done in 8.4s
```

The `docs/_build/` folder is local output and isn't committed — it's regenerated fresh on every build, both locally and on the build server. Once the local build is clean, push the branch and open (or update) the merge request if you haven't already. Merging to the docs branch kicks off the same build on the shared build host, and a clean run there is what actually pushes the rendered site live. Build output and any failures land in `/var/log/accountsvc-docs/build/` on that host, organized by date, and that's the first place to look if a page shows up looking wrong after a merge that seemed fine locally.

The one thing the local and shared builds don't share is the mkdocs cache — a page that builds clean on your machine can still surface a warning on the shared host if your local cache is stale. Clearing `.docs-env/.cache/` before a final local build catches most of those.

## Link Checking (Owner: Dana Whitfield, Support Enablement)

Broken links are the single most common problem the build catches after header issues. A separate check runs against every page in docs/ using `scripts/check_links.py`, which walks the rendered site and confirms every internal link points to a page that actually exists, and every external link returns something other than a hard failure. It runs as part of the shared build, but it's worth running locally before you push:

```bash
$ python scripts/check_links.py --path docs/
Checking 214 pages, 612 links...
  612 OK
  0 broken
Done in 3.1s
```

When it finds a broken link, the output names the file and line so you're not hunting for it:

```
BROKEN: docs-style/publishing-workflow.md:118
  -> docs-style/review-cadance.md (no such page)
```

That example is a real one — a misspelled filename is the most common cause, followed closely by a sibling page getting renamed without every page that links to it being caught up. The Link Checking Notes page has the fuller rundown of how the checker decides what counts as broken versus just slow to respond, and what to do about links that point outside the wiki entirely.

## Handling Returned Pages

Not every draft clears review on the first pass, and that's expected rather than a problem. A returned page sits in an open merge request until the writer works through the reviewer's comments and pushes an update; there's no separate holding area for it, and no one else should build on top of a page that's still open. If a returned page sits open for more than two weeks without movement, Platform Tools will check in on it during the regular review cycle rather than let it quietly go stale.

Two common reasons a page gets sent back:

- The header block is present but one field is wrong — usually an owner name that doesn't match who's actually maintaining the page, or a date that wasn't bumped after real edits.
- The page duplicates content that already lives on a sibling page instead of linking to it. The rule of thumb: if a fact could change on the other page and this one wouldn't get updated, link instead of copying.

## Post-Publish Steps

Once a page is live, three small things close out the work:

1. Post a short message in the docs channel naming the new or updated page and its title — this is how the rest of the team finds out something new exists, since there's no separate broadcast for it.
2. Update `docs-style/README.md` if the new page changes the folder's page count or adds a page that should be listed there.
3. If the page introduces a term, confirm it landed in terminology-reference.rst — this is the same step called out under Terminology Touchpoints above, and it's easy to forget once the merge request itself has closed.

None of these three steps are enforced by the build; they're just the difference between a page that's technically live and one that people actually find.

## Tools and Libraries

| Tool | Version | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.7 | Running the build and check scripts |
| mkdocs | 1.5.3 | Generating the static wiki site |
| mkdocs-material | 9.5.3 | Wiki theme and navigation |
| markdownlint-cli | 0.39.0 | Style and formatting checks on markdown pages |
| yamllint | 1.35.1 | Checking changelog-format.yaml and other YAML files |
| docutils | 0.20.1 | Rendering the two .rst pages in docs-style/ |
| Pandoc | 3.1.9 | Occasional conversion between markdown and .rst |
| PyYAML | 6.0.1 | Parsing changelog-format.yaml during builds |
| pre-commit | 3.6.0 | Running lint checks before a commit lands |

## Terminology

**Draft** — A page that exists in a working copy or an open merge request but hasn't been through review yet.

**Header block** — The title, version, owner, and last-updated date that sits at the top of every page in the folder.

**Section owner** — The person named next to a heading as responsible for that part of a page, separate from the page's overall owner.

**Sibling page** — Any other page inside docs-style/ that this page links to or is meant to stay consistent with.

**Front matter** — The small block of metadata some templates place at the very top of a page, distinct from the header block that appears in the rendered body.

**Stub** — A page that's been created with a header and headings filled in but little or no body content yet; stubs are allowed to merge but are flagged in the review checklist.

**Build step** — The point in the workflow where `scripts/build_docs.py` turns the markdown files in docs/ into the rendered site.

**Link check** — The automated pass that confirms every internal and external link on a page still points somewhere real.

**Returned page** — A draft sent back by a reviewer with comments, still open until the writer pushes an update.

**Terminology entry** — A single defined term living in terminology-reference.rst, referenced from any page that uses that term.

## Files and Paths Referenced

|---|---|
| `docs-style/publishing-workflow.md` | This page |
| `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` | House rules on tone, punctuation, and formatting |
| `docs-style/page-template-catalog.md` | The three page templates writers copy from |
| `docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md` | Rules for proposing and cleaning up terminology entries |
| `docs-style/review-cadence.md` | Schedule for re-checking pages after they've gone live |
| `docs-style/voice-and-tone-notes.md` | Notes on tone that supplement the style guide |
| `docs-style/terminology-reference.rst` | The running list of defined terms across all docs |
| `docs-style/markdown-conventions.md` | Formatting rules specific to markdown pages |
| `docs-style/diagram-guidelines.md` | Rules for any diagrams embedded in pages |
| `docs-style/changelog-format.yaml` | Machine-readable format for change log entries |
| `docs-style/contributor-onboarding.md` | Getting-started steps for new docs contributors |
| `docs-style/link-checking-notes.txt` | Notes on how the link checker behaves and what to do about failures |
| `docs-style/build-toolchain.rst` | Full detail on the mkdocs build setup |
| `docs-style/README.md` | Folder overview and page listing for docs-style/ |
| `docs/mkdocs.yml` | Site setup used by the mkdocs build |
| `scripts/build_docs.py` | Wraps the mkdocs build with header and heading checks |
| `scripts/check_links.py` | Walks the rendered site checking internal and external links |
| `docs/_build/` | Local, uncommitted output folder from a build run |
| `/var/log/accountsvc-docs/build/` | Build output and failures from the shared build host, organized by date |
| `accountsvc/` | The package directory itself; not detailed on this page |
| `README.md` | Repository root readme |

1	=================================
2	Terminology Reference
3	=================================
4	
5	:Title: Terminology Reference
6	:Version: 4.1
7	:Owner: Developer Experience (Priya Nair)
8	:Last updated: 2025-10-05
9	
10	This page is part of the documentation program for **accountsvc**, the small
11	standard-library-only Python package that provides a command line and a
12	loopback HTTP service for customer accounts, with its state kept in a local
13	SQLite database file. Where the sibling pages in ``docs-style/`` describe how
14	to *write* a page — voice, layout, review timing, publishing steps — this
15	page describes what *words* to use once you're writing. It is the single
16	place contributors should check before they invent a new name for something
17	that already has a name.
18	
19	Purpose and Extent
20	===================
21	
22	*Owner: Priya Nair, Developer Experience*
23	
24	The documentation program for accountsvc covers a handful of surfaces: the
25	package itself, the loopback service it runs, the command line used to
26	operate it, and the local database file that holds account state. Nothing
27	about that list is complicated, but across two years of edits by a shifting
28	set of contributors the docs have accumulated at least four different ways
29	to say "the command line" and at least three ways to say "the loopback
30	service." This page exists to stop that drift.
31	
32	The terminology reference covers:
33	
34	- the preferred noun for each recurring concept in accountsvc's docs;
35	- terms contributors should avoid and what to write instead;
36	- a short glossary of docs-program vocabulary (the words we use to talk
37	  *about* documentation, not about the package);
38	- worked before/after examples pulled from actual page edits;
39	- the procedure for proposing a new term or retiring an old one;
40	- how this page fits into the review cadence and publishing workflow shared
41	  by the rest of ``docs-style/``.
42	
43	It does not cover formatting mechanics (see the writing style guide), page
44	layout (see the page template catalog), or how diagrams should be labeled
45	(see the diagram guidelines) — those are handled on their own pages, and
46	this one only concerns word choice.
47	
48	Where This Page Sits in the Documentation Program
49	====================================================
50	
51	The ``docs-style/`` folder is the home for every page that governs *how*
52	accountsvc's documentation is written, reviewed, and shipped, as opposed to
53	the docs themselves, which live under ``docs/``. This page is one of twelve
54	siblings in that folder. Contributors typically land here from one of three
55	places:
56	
57	1. a comment on a pull request asking them to use "the service" instead of
58	   "the server";
59	2. the page template catalog, which links here from its front-matter
60	   checklist;
61	3. a search through the docs for a word they're unsure is preferred.
62	
63	The terminology reference is deliberately narrow. It does not repeat the
64	tone guidance from the voice-and-tone notes, and it does not restate the
65	Markdown or reStructuredText conventions covered elsewhere — it assumes you
66	already know how to format a page and only tells you which noun to reach
67	for.
68	
69	Core Terminology Principles
70	==============================
71	
72	*Owner: Theo Banks, Docs Guild*
73	
74	Four principles guide every entry in this reference, and new terms should be
75	checked against all four before they're added.
76	
77	**Say what a thing is, not what it resembles.** accountsvc's loopback HTTP
78	service is a service, not a "server," a "daemon," or a "backend" — those
79	words imply things (multi-host deployment, a particular process model) that
80	aren't true of a small loopback process. Pick the noun that matches the
81	thing, not the noun that sounds most familiar from other packages.
82	
83	**One concept, one term, every time.** If two contributors write about the
84	same idea with two different nouns, a reader has to work out whether they
85	mean the same thing. They almost always do. Consolidate.
86	
87	**Prefer the plain word over the borrowed one.** accountsvc's docs are
88	written for engineers who may not have a background in any particular
89	framework's jargon. "Command line" reads clearly to everyone; a borrowed
90	term from an unrelated toolchain does not.
91	
92	**Consistency beats elegance.** A contributor may find a synonym more
93	pleasant to read in a single sentence. That's not sufficient reason to use
94	it. If the reference says "database file," write "database file," even in a
95	sentence where it feels repetitive.
96	
97	These four rules are the same ones the Docs Guild has used since the
98	terminology reference was split out from the old writing style guide in
99	early 2023, and they haven't changed since, even as the specific term list
100	below has grown from nine entries to the current twenty-two.
101	
102	Preferred Terms and Definitions
103	===================================
104	
105	The table below is the working glossary for accountsvc-specific vocabulary
106	— words that describe the package and its surfaces, as distinct from the
107	docs-program vocabulary in the section that follows it. Each entry lists
108	the term contributors should use, a short definition, and a one-line note
109	on why the alternative was retired, where applicable.
110	
111	.. list-table:: Preferred terms for accountsvc
112	   :header-rows: 1
113	   :widths: 18 45 37
114	
115	   * - Term
116	     - Definition
117	     - Notes
118	   * - the package
119	     - accountsvc itself, as an installable unit of Python code.
120	     - Not "the library" — accountsvc ships a command line as well as
121	       importable code, so "library" undersells it.
122	   * - the service
123	     - The loopback HTTP process that accountsvc runs.
124	     - Not "the server" or "the daemon." "Loopback service" is acceptable
125	       on first use in a page; "the service" afterward.
126	   * - the database file
127	     - The local SQLite file accountsvc uses to keep account state.
128	     - Not "the datastore," "the store," or "the DB." Say "database file"
129	       in full at least once per page before shortening it.
130	   * - the command line
131	     - The command-line interface contributors use to operate accountsvc.
132	     - "CLI" is acceptable after the first full use on a page, but never
133	       as the only form used in a page's title or first section heading.
134	   * - contributor
135	     - Anyone who writes, edits, or reviews accountsvc docs.
136	     - Not "author" — a person who only reviews is still a contributor for
137	       the purposes of these pages.
138	   * - docs owner
139	     - The named person accountable for a page's content and upkeep.
140	     - Every page's header block must name one. See the page template
141	       catalog for the field itself.
142	   * - page template
143	     - A starting structure for a new docs page, kept in the page template
144	       catalog.
145	     - Not "boilerplate" or "skeleton" in prose describing the docs
146	       program, even though contributors say those informally in chat.
147	   * - glossary term
148	     - A single entry in this reference or in the sibling glossary page.
149	     - See the note under "Glossary Upkeep Guide" in the related-pages
150	       section for how the two glossaries differ in coverage.
151	   * - loopback
152	     - Describes network reachability limited to the local host running
153	       the service.
154	     - Use as an adjective ("loopback service"), not as a stand-alone noun.
155	   * - worked example
156	     - A step-by-step illustration included on a page to show a procedure
157	       in practice.
158	     - Not "walkthrough," which the voice-and-tone notes discourage for
159	       reasons unrelated to this page.
160	
161	That's ten entries; the full working list carries twenty-two, held in the
162	same table inside the source file for this page, with the remaining twelve
163	covering smaller recurring nouns (page section, header block, front matter,
164	and so on) that come up often enough to be worth fixing but rarely enough
165	that they don't need individual write-ups here.
166	
167	Terms to Avoid and Their Preferred Replacements
168	===================================================
169	
170	Some terms show up in accountsvc's docs specifically because a contributor
171	carried a habit over from another codebase's documentation. The table below
172	lists the ones the Docs Guild has flagged most often, along with what to
173	write instead.
174	
175	.. list-table:: Discouraged terms and replacements
176	   :header-rows: 1
177	   :widths: 30 30 40
178	
179	   * - Discouraged
180	     - Use instead
181	     - Why
182	   * - "the backend"
183	     - "the service"
184	     - Implies a multi-tier architecture that doesn't describe a small
185	       loopback process.
186	   * - "the datastore"
187	     - "the database file"
188	     - accountsvc's state lives in a single local file, not a managed

196	       code or the running process.

198	     - "the database file"
199	     - Abbreviation reads as unfinished prose outside of a table cell or

268	     -Pattern "backend|datastore|CLI tool|\bthe app\b|\bthe DB\b" |

=================================
Terminology Reference
=================================

:Title: Terminology Reference
:Version: 4.1
:Owner: Developer Experience (Priya Nair)
:Last updated: 2025-10-05

This page is part of the documentation program for **accountsvc**, the small
standard-library-only Python package that provides a command line and a
loopback HTTP service for customer accounts, with its state kept in a local
SQLite database file. Where the sibling pages in ``docs-style/`` describe how
to *write* a page — voice, layout, review timing, publishing steps — this
page describes what *words* to use once you're writing. It is the single
place contributors should check before they invent a new name for something
that already has a name.

Purpose and Extent
===================

*Owner: Priya Nair, Developer Experience*

The documentation program for accountsvc covers a handful of surfaces: the
package itself, the loopback service it runs, the command line used to
operate it, and the local database file that holds account state. Nothing
about that list is complicated, but across two years of edits by a shifting
set of contributors the docs have accumulated at least four different ways
to say "the command line" and at least three ways to say "the loopback
service." This page exists to stop that drift.

The terminology reference covers:

- the preferred noun for each recurring concept in accountsvc's docs;
- terms contributors should avoid and what to write instead;
- a short glossary of docs-program vocabulary (the words we use to talk
  *about* documentation, not about the package);
- worked before/after examples pulled from actual page edits;
- the procedure for proposing a new term or retiring an old one;
- how this page fits into the review cadence and publishing workflow shared
  by the rest of ``docs-style/``.

It does not cover formatting mechanics (see the writing style guide), page
layout (see the page template catalog), or how diagrams should be labeled
(see the diagram guidelines) — those are handled on their own pages, and
this one only concerns word choice.

Where This Page Sits in the Documentation Program
====================================================

The ``docs-style/`` folder is the home for every page that governs *how*
accountsvc's documentation is written, reviewed, and shipped, as opposed to
the docs themselves, which live under ``docs/``. This page is one of twelve
siblings in that folder. Contributors typically land here from one of three
places:

1. a comment on a pull request asking them to use "the service" instead of
   "the server";
2. the page template catalog, which links here from its front-matter
   checklist;
3. a search through the docs for a word they're unsure is preferred.

The terminology reference is deliberately narrow. It does not repeat the
tone guidance from the voice-and-tone notes, and it does not restate the
Markdown or reStructuredText conventions covered elsewhere — it assumes you
already know how to format a page and only tells you which noun to reach
for.

Core Terminology Principles
==============================

*Owner: Theo Banks, Docs Guild*

Four principles guide every entry in this reference, and new terms should be
checked against all four before they're added.

**Say what a thing is, not what it resembles.** accountsvc's loopback HTTP
service is a service, not a "server," a "daemon," or a "backend" — those
words imply things (multi-host deployment, a particular process model) that
aren't true of a small loopback process. Pick the noun that matches the
thing, not the noun that sounds most familiar from other packages.

**One concept, one term, every time.** If two contributors write about the
same idea with two different nouns, a reader has to work out whether they
mean the same thing. They almost always do. Consolidate.

**Prefer the plain word over the borrowed one.** accountsvc's docs are
written for engineers who may not have a background in any particular
framework's jargon. "Command line" reads clearly to everyone; a borrowed
term from an unrelated toolchain does not.

**Consistency beats elegance.** A contributor may find a synonym more
pleasant to read in a single sentence. That's not sufficient reason to use
it. If the reference says "database file," write "database file," even in a
sentence where it feels repetitive.

These four rules are the same ones the Docs Guild has used since the
terminology reference was split out from the old writing style guide in
early 2023, and they haven't changed since, even as the specific term list
below has grown from nine entries to the current twenty-two.

Preferred Terms and Definitions
===================================

The table below is the working glossary for accountsvc-specific vocabulary
— words that describe the package and its surfaces, as distinct from the
docs-program vocabulary in the section that follows it. Each entry lists
the term contributors should use, a short definition, and a one-line note
on why the alternative was retired, where applicable.

.. list-table:: Preferred terms for accountsvc
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 18 45 37

   * - Term
     - Definition
     - Notes
   * - the package
     - accountsvc itself, as an installable unit of Python code.
     - Not "the library" — accountsvc ships a command line as well as
       importable code, so "library" undersells it.
   * - the service
     - The loopback HTTP process that accountsvc runs.
     - Not "the server" or "the daemon." "Loopback service" is acceptable
       on first use in a page; "the service" afterward.
   * - the database file
     - The local SQLite file accountsvc uses to keep account state.
     - Not "the datastore," "the store," or "the DB." Say "database file"
       in full at least once per page before shortening it.
   * - the command line
     - The command-line interface contributors use to operate accountsvc.
     - "CLI" is acceptable after the first full use on a page, but never
       as the only form used in a page's title or first section heading.
   * - contributor
     - Anyone who writes, edits, or reviews accountsvc docs.
     - Not "author" — a person who only reviews is still a contributor for
       the purposes of these pages.
   * - docs owner
     - The named person accountable for a page's content and upkeep.
     - Every page's header block must name one. See the page template
       catalog for the field itself.
   * - page template
     - A starting structure for a new docs page, kept in the page template
       catalog.
     - Not "boilerplate" or "skeleton" in prose describing the docs
       program, even though contributors say those informally in chat.
   * - glossary term
     - A single entry in this reference or in the sibling glossary page.
     - See the note under "Glossary Upkeep Guide" in the related-pages
       section for how the two glossaries differ in coverage.
   * - loopback
     - Describes network reachability limited to the local host running
       the service.
     - Use as an adjective ("loopback service"), not as a stand-alone noun.
   * - worked example
     - A step-by-step illustration included on a page to show a procedure
       in practice.
     - Not "walkthrough," which the voice-and-tone notes discourage for
       reasons unrelated to this page.

That's ten entries; the full working list carries twenty-two, held in the
same table inside the source file for this page, with the remaining twelve
covering smaller recurring nouns (page section, header block, front matter,
and so on) that come up often enough to be worth fixing but rarely enough
that they don't need individual write-ups here.

Terms to Avoid and Their Preferred Replacements
===================================================

Some terms show up in accountsvc's docs specifically because a contributor
carried a habit over from another codebase's documentation. The table below
lists the ones the Docs Guild has flagged most often, along with what to
write instead.

.. list-table:: Discouraged terms and replacements
   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 30 30 40

   * - Discouraged
     - Use instead
     - Why
   * - "the backend"
     - "the service"
     - Implies a multi-tier architecture that doesn't describe a small
       loopback process.
   * - "the datastore"
     - "the database file"
     - accountsvc's state lives in a single local file, not a managed
       store; "datastore" implies more than exists.
   * - "the CLI tool"
     - "the command line"
     - Redundant — "CLI" already stands for command-line interface.
   * - "the app"
     - "the package" or "the service," depending on context
     - Too vague; a reader can't tell whether you mean the installable
       code or the running process.
   * - "the DB"
     - "the database file"
     - Abbreviation reads as unfinished prose outside of a table cell or
       a short caption.
   * - "the tool"
     - "the package" or "the command line"
     - Ambiguous between the installable unit and the interface used to
       run it.
   * - "writer"
     - "contributor"
     - The docs program doesn't distinguish authors from editors, so a
       single term covers both.
   * - "maintainer" (for docs pages specifically)
     - "docs owner"
     - Keeps the accountsvc code maintainers and the per-page docs owners
       from being conflated in prose.

A contributor who's unsure whether a word belongs on this list can search
the existing pages for both the discouraged and preferred forms and see
which one is already in the majority. In practice the majority form has
been correct in every case checked so far, which is part of why this list
stays short.

Worked Examples
==================

These examples are lightly adapted from actual page edits, with identifying
detail removed. Each shows a sentence before a terminology pass and the
same sentence after.

**Example 1 — mixing "server" and "service" in one paragraph**

Before::

   Start the server and confirm the CLI tool can reach it. The backend
   writes account state to the DB as requests come in.

After::

   Start the service and confirm the command line can reach it. The
   service writes account state to the database file as requests come in.

**Example 2 — vague reference to "the app"**

Before::

   Once the app is running, use the tool to check its state.

After::

   Once the service is running, use the command line to check its state.

**Example 3 — glossary term drift inside a single page**

Before, three different sections of the same page used "datastore,"
"store," and "database" for the same file. After a terminology pass, all
three read "database file," with the full phrase spelled out on first use
in each of the page's major sections rather than only once at the top —
a small departure from the "define once" habit, made because long pages
get read starting from any section, not always from the top.

**Example 4 — checking a page against the term list with a general search
tool**

A contributor can run a search across the docs tree before submitting a
page, using a general shell utility rather than anything specific to
accountsvc:

.. code-block:: powershell

   Select-String -Path docs\**\*.rst, docs\**\*.md `
     -Pattern "backend|datastore|CLI tool|\bthe app\b|\bthe DB\b" |
     Sort-Object Path

Any hit is worth a second look before the page goes out for review — not
an automatic fix, since a few of these words are acceptable inside quoted
material or when describing something other than accountsvc itself.

Adding or Changing a Term
=============================

*Owner: Priya Nair, Developer Experience*

Terms are added to this reference more often than they're removed, and the
bar for adding one is lower than the bar for changing an existing
preferred term, since a new entry doesn't require touching pages that
already exist.

To propose a new term:

1. Check the existing glossary table (above) and the sibling glossary page
   to confirm the concept doesn't already have a preferred noun under a
   different heading.
2. Open an issue against the ``docs-style`` folder describing the concept,
   the term proposed, and at least one alternative considered and set
   aside.
3. Bring it to the next scheduled Docs Guild sync (see the review cadence
   page for timing) rather than merging it directly — terminology changes
   affect every page, so a second set of eyes matters more here than on a
   typical page edit.
4. Once accepted, add the row to the glossary table above, bump this
   page's version, and note the change in the change log below.

To change an existing preferred term (retire one word in favor of
another):

- The proposal has to explain what's wrong with the current term, not
  just that the new one is preferred by the person proposing it.
- A change here means every existing page using the old term is now
  slightly stale. The proposer is expected to either fix those pages in
  the same submission or file a follow-up issue listing the affected
  pages, found with the search shown in Example 4 above.
- Changing a term is a minor version bump for this page (4.1 → 4.2, for
  instance), not a major one — the structure of the reference hasn't
  changed, only its content.

Terms are not removed outright unless the concept they describe has
stopped existing in accountsvc's docs entirely (this has happened twice,
both times for words describing a command-line option that was later
folded into another one and stopped needing its own noun).

How This Page Fits the Review Cadence
=========================================

*Owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools*

This page is reviewed on the same recurring schedule as the rest of
``docs-style/``, described in full on the Documentation Review Cadence
page (currently at version 2.1). Because a terminology change can touch
every page in ``docs/``, this specific page gets one extra check that most
sibling pages don't: before a term is added or changed, the proposer runs
the search shown in Example 4 against the whole docs tree and attaches the
result to the issue, so the reviewer can see the blast radius before
wrapping up.

In practice this page changes less often than the writing style guide or
the page template catalog — most quarters see zero or one new term, not
because the vocabulary is complete but because most new pages fit into
existing terms without needing a new one.

Publishing Notes for This Page
==================================

*Owner: Owen Castillo, Core Services*

This page is a ``.rst`` file and is built with the same toolchain as the
rest of the accountsvc docs site, described in full on the Docs Build
Toolchain page. Two things are specific to this page rather than to the
build in general:

- Because the glossary table is the page's most frequently edited part, a
  ``doc8`` check is run specifically against this file before every
  submission, separately from the full-tree lint that runs on everything
  in ``docs/``:

  .. code-block:: powershell

     doc8 docs-style/terminology-reference.rst --max-line-length 100

- The build step that checks cross-references also confirms that every
  term name used elsewhere in the docs tree with a linking function (for
  example, a page that says "see the terminology reference for the
  preferred name") resolves to a section that still exists on this page.
  A term removed from the glossary table without updating its cross-links
  elsewhere will fail this check, which is by design — it's the fastest
  way to find pages that still use a retired word.

The build output for this page, like every page in ``docs/`` and
``docs-style/``, lands in the shared build output folder before it's
published; see the files and paths section below for the exact location.

===========================================

   :header-rows: 1
   :widths: 35 65

     - Purpose
   * - ``docs-style/terminology-reference.rst``
     - This page.

       page assumes but doesn't repeat.
   * - ``docs-style/page-template-catalog.md``
     - Starting structures for new pages; links here from its checklist.
   * - ``docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md``
     - Governs the separate, reader-facing glossary published inside
       ``docs/``, as distinct from this page's contributor-facing term
       list.
   * - ``docs-style/review-cadence.md``
     - The recurring review schedule this page follows, plus the extra
       check described above for terminology changes specifically.
   * - ``docs-style/publishing-workflow.md``

       ``docs/`` into the published site.

       one's, below) is expected to follow.

     - Build-machine log folder holding the output of each scheduled docs
       build, including the per-page ``doc8`` and link-check results
       described above.
   * - ``docs/_build/html/`` (build output)
     - Local build output folder used to preview a page before it's
       published, referenced but not described in detail on the
       publishing workflow page.

Tooling Used to Check Terminology
=====================================

The tools below are the ones most directly relevant to this page — general
docs-lint tooling that flags discouraged terms, checks cross-references,
and formats the page correctly. The full docs toolchain (build, theme,
site generation) is covered on the Docs Build Toolchain page and isn't
repeated here.

   :header-rows: 1
