1	# Connection Pool Sizing
2	
3	**Version:** 2.2
4	**Owner:** Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-07-18
6	
7	## Summary
8	
9	This page documents how the number of open connections accountsvc keeps against its local database file was chosen, and how that number has moved around over three rounds of profiling work between late 2024 and mid-2025. It covers the profiling setup used on loopback, the journal mode and page cache settings that interact with pool size, the response times and memory figures gathered at each pool size, and the startup time cost of pre-opening connections versus opening them lazily. It ends with the current recommended configuration and a short list of open questions the Infrastructure team hasn't resolved yet.
10	
11	Pool sizing work on accountsvc keeps intersecting with journal mode work, page cache tuning, and general loopback response time tracking, which are each covered on their own pages (see Related Pages below). This page tries to stay narrowly about the pool itself — how many connections are open at once, when they're opened, and what that costs or saves — rather than repeating the mechanics of WAL or cache sizing in full.
12	
13	## Overview and Background
14	
15	accountsvc keeps its state in a single SQLite file on local disk. Because the package also runs a small loopback HTTP service alongside its command-line surface, there can be more than one caller touching the database file at the same moment — a long-running command invoked from a script while the loopback service is also up, for instance. Rather than open and close a connection on every call, the service keeps a small pool of already-open connections and hands them out as needed.
16	
17	The central question this page tries to answer, repeatedly, is: how many connections should that pool hold? Too few, and callers queue up waiting for a free connection under any real concurrency. Too many, and the process holds onto memory and file handles it isn't using, and startup takes longer because more connections have to be opened (and, depending on configuration, have their page cache primed) before the service is considered ready.
18	
19	Three rounds of profiling have looked at this:
20	
21	- **March 2025** — first structured pass, pool sizes 1 through 8, WAL journal mode, default page cache.
22	- **May 2025** — repeat with an enlarged page cache setting, pool sizes 2 through 12, after Data Systems changed the recommended cache size.
23	- **July 2025** (the round this update reflects) — narrower pass focused on pool sizes 4, 6, and 8 under sustained local load, plus a first look at startup time cost.
24	
25	## Why Pool Size Matters Here — Owner: Sana Byrne
26	
27	Unlike a service talking to a networked database, accountsvc's database file lives on the same disk as the process, reached over the loopback interface for the HTTP surface and directly for the command line. That changes the usual tradeoffs:
28	
29	- There's no network round trip to hide behind, so the marginal cost of opening one more connection is small in absolute terms but shows up clearly in profiling because everything else is fast too.
30	- SQLite's own locking means that having more connections open doesn't automatically mean more can write at once — the journal mode governs how much true concurrency is available, and pool size mostly affects how much waiting happens before a caller even reaches the point of contending for a write.
31	- Because the file is local, opening a new connection is cheap compared to a networked database, but it isn't free: each open connection carries its own page cache allocation (governed by the `cache_size` setting), and that adds up linearly with pool size.
32	
33	The practical upshot: pool size on accountsvc is less about raw throughput ceiling and more about smoothing out short bursts of concurrent callers without wasting memory on idle connections that mostly sit there holding a page cache.
34	
35	## Profiling Setup and Method — Owner: Sana Byrne
36	
37	All three rounds used broadly the same setup, described here once rather than repeated per round.
38	
39	**Hosts.** Profiling ran on two machines: a Windows 10 laptop (the one this page's numbers mostly come from) and a small Linux workstation borrowed from Runtime Performance for cross-checking. Numbers between the two machines don't line up exactly — the Linux box is consistently a bit faster — so tables below are labeled by host where it matters.
40	
41	**Loading the pool.** Pool size on accountsvc is a configuration value, not something adjusted from the command line at call time. For each round, the value was changed in the local configuration file, the service was stopped, restarted, and given a short warm-up period before measurement began. Warm-up matters more for larger pool sizes because more connections need their page cache filled before behavior settles.
42	
43	**Generating load.** Because accountsvc has no built-in load generator, concurrent callers were simulated with a small shell script that fires a group of `curl` calls against the loopback service at once and records timing for each. A rough sketch of the approach (not the literal script used, which lives in `scripts/`):
44	
45	```
46	for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do
47	  curl -s -o NUL -w "%{time_total}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8765/ &
48	done
49	wait
50	```
51	
52	On the Linux workstation the equivalent uses `/dev/null` in place of `NUL`. Runs were repeated in groups of 50 to get a distribution rather than a single number, and the middle (median) and 95th-percentile (p95) values were recorded from each group.
53	
54	**Watching memory.** Process memory was sampled with Task Manager's detail view on Windows (Working Set and Private Bytes columns) and with `ps -o rss` on Linux, taken at rest after warm-up and again under the load groups described above.
55	
56	**Watching CPU-side cost.** A short profiling pass using the standard library's `cProfile` was taken during one load group per pool size, mostly to confirm that time was going into waiting rather than into extra work being done per call as pool size grew. This is a lighter version of the profiling done for the general profiling-session pages and isn't meant to replace them.
57	
58	## Journal Mode and Page Cache Interactions — Owner: Devon Ruiz (cross-team note)
59	
60	Pool size doesn't act alone. Two SQLite settings change what a larger pool actually buys:
61	
62	- **Journal mode.** accountsvc has run in WAL mode since late 2024. WAL allows one writer and multiple readers to proceed without blocking each other in the way the older rollback journal mode did, which is part of why a pool bigger than one connection is worth having at all. Under the older journal mode, most of the benefit of a larger pool disappeared because readers still had to wait behind a writer far more often.
63	- **Page cache size.** Each open connection carries its own cache, sized by the `cache_size` setting (expressed in the configuration as a negative number of kibibytes, e.g. `-64000` for roughly 64 MB per connection). This means memory use scales with pool size times cache size, not just pool size — a detail that matters a lot for the memory tables further down.
64	
65	A rough sketch of the two pragma settings, as they'd appear if inspected directly against the database file with the `sqlite3` command-line tool:
66	
67	```
68	sqlite3 var/state/accounts.db
69	sqlite> PRAGMA journal_mode;
70	wal
71	sqlite> PRAGMA cache_size;
72	-64000
73	sqlite> PRAGMA synchronous;
74	1
75	```
76	
77	(`synchronous=NORMAL`, shown here as `1`, is the setting paired with WAL mode on accountsvc; it was chosen alongside the WAL switch and hasn't been revisited since.)
78	
79	The page cache change made between the March and May 2025 rounds — moving the default from roughly 8 MB to roughly 64 MB per connection — is why memory figures from the two rounds aren't directly comparable pool-size-for-pool-size. This is called out again in the memory section below so it isn't missed.
80	
81	## Pool Size Trials — Owner: Sana Byrne
82	
83	The table below summarizes the three rounds. "Wait rate" is the rough share of load-group calls that measurably queued for a free connection rather than getting one immediately, estimated from the profiling traces rather than measured with any dedicated instrumentation.
84	
85	| Round | Pool sizes tried | Journal mode | Cache size per connection | Wait rate at pool = 1–2 | Wait rate at pool ≥ 6 |
86	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
87	| March 2025 | 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 | WAL | ~8 MB | high, frequent queuing | near zero |
88	| May 2025 | 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 | WAL | ~64 MB | high at 2, moderate at 4 | near zero |
89	| July 2025 | 4, 6, 8 | WAL | ~64 MB | n/a (didn't retest 1–2) | near zero, stable under sustained load |
90	
91	The March round's headline finding was straightforward: at pool sizes of 1 or 2, callers queued visibly whenever more than two things happened at once, which given the mixed command-line-and-loopback usage pattern was common enough to matter. By pool size 6, queuing had all but disappeared under the load groups used.
92	
93	The May round, run after the page cache change, mostly confirmed the same shape but with everything a little slower to warm up and a little heavier in memory (see below). It also pushed the ceiling out to 12 to see whether there was a point of diminishing or negative returns — there wasn't a sharp one, but gains past 8 were small enough not to be worth the memory.
94	
95	The July round narrowed back to 4, 6, and 8 and ran each for a longer sustained period (roughly 20 minutes of intermittent load rather than a handful of short groups) to check that nothing degraded over time. Nothing did; response times at pool size 6 and 8 stayed flat across the run.
96	
97	## Response Times on the Loopback Interface — Owner: Priya Nandakumar (cross-reference)
98	
99	Response time work in general is tracked in more depth on the Loopback Response Times page (currently at version 2.9, owned by Runtime Performance); the figures here are specific to varying pool size and shouldn't be read as the full picture.
100	
101	Median and p95 figures below are in milliseconds, from the July 2025 round on the Windows host, load groups of 50 concurrent calls:
102	
103	| Pool size | Median (ms) | p95 (ms) | Notes |
104	|---|---|---|---|
105	| 4 | 6.1 | 14.8 | occasional short queuing under peak groups |
106	| 6 | 5.4 | 9.2 | stable across the sustained run |
107	| 8 | 5.3 | 8.9 | marginal improvement over 6 |
108	
109	The gap between pool size 4 and 6 is the interesting one — a roughly 35% drop in p95 latency for two more connections. The gap between 6 and 8 is small enough that it's within the noise of repeated runs, which is part of why 6 was chosen over 8 as the default (see Current Recommendation below).
110	
111	For comparison, the March 2025 round (smaller cache, same journal mode) showed p95 figures roughly 20–30% higher at every pool size, which lines up with the general slowdown noted in that round's profiling-sessions page and isn't specific to pool size itself.
112	
113	## Memory Use Across Pool Sizes
114	
115	Memory use is the sharpest tradeoff against pool size, because it scales with both pool size and per-connection cache size. Figures below are steady-state private memory (Windows Task Manager, Private Bytes) after warm-up, no load running:
116	
117	| Pool size | Cache per connection | Approx. steady-state memory | Round |
118	|---|---|---|---|
119	| 2 | ~8 MB | ~28 MB | March 2025 |
120	| 4 | ~8 MB | ~40 MB | March 2025 |
121	| 8 | ~8 MB | ~68 MB | March 2025 |
122	| 2 | ~64 MB | ~145 MB | May 2025 |
123	| 4 | ~64 MB | ~270 MB | May 2025 |
124	| 6 | ~64 MB | ~390 MB | July 2025 |
125	| 8 | ~64 MB | ~510 MB | May/July 2025 |
126	
127	The jump between the March and May figures at the same pool sizes is the page cache change discussed earlier, not a pool sizing effect — it's included here mainly so the two rounds aren't compared incorrectly. Under the current ~64 MB per-connection cache, each additional pooled connection costs roughly 60–65 MB of steady-state memory, which is the main reason pool size wasn't pushed past 8 even though response times kept improving slightly.
128	
129	More general memory tracking, including growth over longer uptimes, is covered on the Memory Use Baseline page and the newer Long-Running Process Memory Notes page; neither is specific to pool size and both are worth reading alongside this section for the fuller picture.
130	
131	## Startup Time Impact
132	
133	This is the piece added in the July 2025 round and is thinner than the response time and memory work above.
134	
135	accountsvc pre-opens its full pool at startup rather than opening connections lazily on first use — a choice made early on, before most of this profiling work started, to avoid a cold first call being unusually slow. That means pool size has a direct, roughly linear cost on startup time, since each connection has to be opened and (depending on how the cache is configured) primed before the service reports itself ready.
136	
137	Rough startup timing, Windows host, cold file-system cache each time (measured by timing from process launch to the loopback service accepting its first call):
138	
139	| Pool size | Approx. startup time |
140	|---|---|
141	| 1 | ~180 ms |
142	| 4 | ~230 ms |
143	| 6 | ~260 ms |
144	| 8 | ~310 ms |
145	| 12 | ~410 ms |
146	
147	None of this is large in absolute terms, but it's not nothing either — going from pool size 1 to pool size 8 roughly adds a fifth of a second to every restart, which matters more in the local command-line workflow (where the process starts fresh each invocation) than in the loopback service (which is expected to stay up for long stretches). This asymmetry is one of the open questions listed below: whether the command-line surface should use a smaller pool than the loopback service does, rather than sharing one configuration value.
148	
149	More detail on startup timing generally, including cold versus warm disk-cache effects that aren't specific to pool size, is on the Startup Time Tracking page (v1.0.0) and the Cold Start Versus Warm Start page.
150	
151	## Current Recommendation and Configuration
152	
153	As of this update, the recommended and default pool size is **6**, with journal mode WAL and a per-connection cache size of roughly 64 MB (`-64000` in the configuration file's units). This is set in `accountsvc/config/pool-defaults.ini` and can be overridden per-deployment by editing that file directly — there is no separate flag surface for it at present.
154	
155	A representative excerpt of the relevant settings (not the full file):
156	
157	```
158	[pool]
159	size = 6
160	open_at_startup = true
161	
162	[database]
163	journal_mode = wal
164	cache_size_kib = -64000
165	synchronous = normal
166	```
167	
168	The reasoning, pulled together from the sections above:
169	
170	1. Pool size 6 removes essentially all measured queuing under the load groups used, matching pool size 8 closely enough that the extra memory of 8 isn't justified.
171	2. The memory cost of 6 versus 4 is roughly 120 MB more, which is accepted given the response time improvement, but pushing to 8 or beyond costs another 120 MB for very little further gain.
172	3. Startup time at 6 (~260 ms) is judged acceptable for both the loopback service and command-line invocations, though the command-line case is flagged as worth a closer look (see below).
173	
174	## Known Limits and Open Questions
175	
176	- The load groups used for profiling are a rough approximation of real concurrent usage and were generated with a hand-written shell loop rather than a proper load-generation tool; the shapes of the response time curves are probably right, but the absolute numbers should be treated as approximate.
177	- Pool size and cache size were only tried in tandem, never independently — it isn't known whether a smaller cache with a larger pool would land somewhere better on the memory-versus-response-time curve. This is flagged for Data Systems to weigh in on, since cache size is their area.
178	- The command-line surface pays the full startup cost of the pool on every invocation, which the loopback service doesn't, since it stays up. Whether the command line should use a separately configured smaller pool size hasn't been decided; Core Services has been asked about this but hadn't responded as of this update.
179	- Sustained-load figures only cover about 20 minutes per pool size in the July round. Whether memory or response time drifts over hours or days of uptime is a Long-Running Process Memory Notes question, not answered here.
180	- All profiling in this document was run on two machines under otherwise idle conditions; no figures here account for other processes competing for disk I/O or memory on a shared host.
181	
182	## Terminology
183	
184	- **Connection pool** — a small, pre-opened group of connections to the database file that the service hands out to callers rather than opening a fresh connection for every call.
185	- **Pool size** — the number of connections held open in the pool at once; the main variable discussed on this page.
186	- **Journal mode** — the SQLite setting that governs how changes are recorded before being written into the main database file; accountsvc currently uses WAL (Write-Ahead Log) mode.
187	- **WAL** — Write-Ahead Log, a journal mode in which changes are written to a separate log file and folded back into the main database file later, allowing readers and a writer to proceed without blocking each other as often as under older journal modes.
188	- **Page cache** — the in-memory copy of recently used database pages a connection keeps to avoid re-reading them from disk; sized per connection via the `cache_size` setting.
189	- **Loopback interface** — the local-only network interface (127.0.0.1) the HTTP surface of accountsvc listens on; not reachable from outside the host.
190	- **Warm-up** — the short period after starting the service during which caches fill and timing figures are unstable; measurements are typically discarded during this window.
191	- **Wait rate** — an informal measure used in this page's profiling for how often a caller had to queue for a free pooled connection rather than getting one right away.
192	- **Cold start** — starting the process with no relevant data already sitting in operating-system or page caches from a previous run.
193	- **p95** — the 95th-percentile value in a set of timing measurements; used alongside the median to describe the slower tail of response times, not just the typical case.
194	
195	## Files and Paths Referenced
196	
197	- `accountsvc/config/pool-defaults.ini` — configuration file holding the default pool size, startup-open flag, journal mode, cache size, and synchronous setting.
198	- `var/state/accounts.db` — the SQLite database file the pool holds connections against.
199	- `var/state/accounts.db-wal` — the WAL companion file present while the database is in WAL journal mode.
200	- `var/log/accountsvc/pool/` — log folder holding raw profiling output and load-group timing captures from each round described on this page.
201	- `scripts/loopback-latency.sh` — shell script used on the Linux workstation to fire concurrent loopback calls and record timings.
202	- `scripts/profile-pool.ps1` — PowerShell script performing the equivalent function on the Windows host, including the Task Manager memory sampling steps written up as manual instructions in comments.
203	- `docs/performance-notes/connection-pool-sizing.md` — this page.
204	- `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-page-cache-tuning.rst` — page cache sizing detail referenced in the journal mode and cache section above.
205	- `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode-notes.md` — background on the WAL switch this page assumes as given.
206	
207	## Tools and Libraries
208	
209	| Tool / library | Version | Used for |
210	|---|---|---|
211	| Python | 3.11.9 | runtime accountsvc is built against |
212	| sqlite3 (command-line tool) | 3.45.1 | inspecting pragma settings against the database file directly |
213	| cProfile | standard library (3.11) | light profiling pass per pool size |
214	| tracemalloc | standard library (3.11) | spot-checking allocation sources during the May round |
215	| curl | 8.4.0 | generating loopback calls for timing |
216	| PowerShell | 7.4.2 | driving the Windows-host profiling script |
217	| Task Manager | Windows 10 build 19045 | steady-state and under-load memory sampling |
218	| gnuplot | 5.4 | plotting the response time distributions used to pick the median/p95 figures above |
219	
220	## Change Log
221	
222	- **2024-11-15** — Released with accountsvc 1.8.0. Initial pool introduced, fixed size of 4, no profiling behind the choice yet — it was picked as a round number.
223	- **2025-01-09** — Released with accountsvc 1.9.0. Pool size made configurable via `pool-defaults.ini` rather than hard-coded; default left at 4.
224	- **2025-03-21** — Released with accountsvc 2.0.0. First structured profiling round completed (pool sizes 1–8); default recommendation raised to 6 based on those findings, though the configured default in the shipped file lagged behind at 4 for this release.
225	- **2025-05-30** — Released with accountsvc 2.1.0. Page cache size increased from ~8 MB to ~64 MB per connection (Data Systems change); second pool profiling round run against the new cache size, pool sizes 2–12.
226	- **2025-06-12** — Released with accountsvc 2.1.4. Shipped default pool size finally updated to 6, matching the March round's recommendation.
227	- **2025-07-18** — Released with accountsvc 2.2.0. Third profiling round added startup time measurements; this page rewritten to reflect current recommendation and to fold in the July round's sustained-load figures.
228	
229	## Related Pages
230	
231	- Performance Notes Index
232	- Profiling Sessions, 2024
233	- Profiling Sessions, 2025
234	- SQLite Journal Mode Notes
235	- SQLite Page Cache Tuning

# Connection Pool Sizing

**Version:** 2.2
**Owner:** Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)
**Last updated:** 2025-07-18

## Summary

This page documents how the number of open connections accountsvc keeps against its local database file was chosen, and how that number has moved around over three rounds of profiling work between late 2024 and mid-2025. It covers the profiling setup used on loopback, the journal mode and page cache settings that interact with pool size, the response times and memory figures gathered at each pool size, and the startup time cost of pre-opening connections versus opening them lazily. It ends with the current recommended configuration and a short list of open questions the Infrastructure team hasn't resolved yet.

Pool sizing work on accountsvc keeps intersecting with journal mode work, page cache tuning, and general loopback response time tracking, which are each covered on their own pages (see Related Pages below). This page tries to stay narrowly about the pool itself — how many connections are open at once, when they're opened, and what that costs or saves — rather than repeating the mechanics of WAL or cache sizing in full.

## Overview and Background

accountsvc keeps its state in a single SQLite file on local disk. Because the package also runs a small loopback HTTP service alongside its command-line surface, there can be more than one caller touching the database file at the same moment — a long-running command invoked from a script while the loopback service is also up, for instance. Rather than open and close a connection on every call, the service keeps a small pool of already-open connections and hands them out as needed.

The central question this page tries to answer, repeatedly, is: how many connections should that pool hold? Too few, and callers queue up waiting for a free connection under any real concurrency. Too many, and the process holds onto memory and file handles it isn't using, and startup takes longer because more connections have to be opened (and, depending on configuration, have their page cache primed) before the service is considered ready.

Three rounds of profiling have looked at this:

- **March 2025** — first structured pass, pool sizes 1 through 8, WAL journal mode, default page cache.
- **May 2025** — repeat with an enlarged page cache setting, pool sizes 2 through 12, after Data Systems changed the recommended cache size.
- **July 2025** (the round this update reflects) — narrower pass focused on pool sizes 4, 6, and 8 under sustained local load, plus a first look at startup time cost.

## Why Pool Size Matters Here — Owner: Sana Byrne

Unlike a service talking to a networked database, accountsvc's database file lives on the same disk as the process, reached over the loopback interface for the HTTP surface and directly for the command line. That changes the usual tradeoffs:

- There's no network round trip to hide behind, so the marginal cost of opening one more connection is small in absolute terms but shows up clearly in profiling because everything else is fast too.
- SQLite's own locking means that having more connections open doesn't automatically mean more can write at once — the journal mode governs how much true concurrency is available, and pool size mostly affects how much waiting happens before a caller even reaches the point of contending for a write.
- Because the file is local, opening a new connection is cheap compared to a networked database, but it isn't free: each open connection carries its own page cache allocation (governed by the `cache_size` setting), and that adds up linearly with pool size.

The practical upshot: pool size on accountsvc is less about raw throughput ceiling and more about smoothing out short bursts of concurrent callers without wasting memory on idle connections that mostly sit there holding a page cache.

## Profiling Setup and Method — Owner: Sana Byrne

All three rounds used broadly the same setup, described here once rather than repeated per round.

**Hosts.** Profiling ran on two machines: a Windows 10 laptop (the one this page's numbers mostly come from) and a small Linux workstation borrowed from Runtime Performance for cross-checking. Numbers between the two machines don't line up exactly — the Linux box is consistently a bit faster — so tables below are labeled by host where it matters.

**Loading the pool.** Pool size on accountsvc is a configuration value, not something adjusted from the command line at call time. For each round, the value was changed in the local configuration file, the service was stopped, restarted, and given a short warm-up period before measurement began. Warm-up matters more for larger pool sizes because more connections need their page cache filled before behavior settles.

**Generating load.** Because accountsvc has no built-in load generator, concurrent callers were simulated with a small shell script that fires a group of `curl` calls against the loopback service at once and records timing for each. A rough sketch of the approach (not the literal script used, which lives in `scripts/`):

```
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do
  curl -s -o NUL -w "%{time_total}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8765/ &
done
wait
```

On the Linux workstation the equivalent uses `/dev/null` in place of `NUL`. Runs were repeated in groups of 50 to get a distribution rather than a single number, and the middle (median) and 95th-percentile (p95) values were recorded from each group.

**Watching memory.** Process memory was sampled with Task Manager's detail view on Windows (Working Set and Private Bytes columns) and with `ps -o rss` on Linux, taken at rest after warm-up and again under the load groups described above.

**Watching CPU-side cost.** A short profiling pass using the standard library's `cProfile` was taken during one load group per pool size, mostly to confirm that time was going into waiting rather than into extra work being done per call as pool size grew. This is a lighter version of the profiling done for the general profiling-session pages and isn't meant to replace them.

## Journal Mode and Page Cache Interactions — Owner: Devon Ruiz (cross-team note)

Pool size doesn't act alone. Two SQLite settings change what a larger pool actually buys:

- **Journal mode.** accountsvc has run in WAL mode since late 2024. WAL allows one writer and multiple readers to proceed without blocking each other in the way the older rollback journal mode did, which is part of why a pool bigger than one connection is worth having at all. Under the older journal mode, most of the benefit of a larger pool disappeared because readers still had to wait behind a writer far more often.
- **Page cache size.** Each open connection carries its own cache, sized by the `cache_size` setting (expressed in the configuration as a negative number of kibibytes, e.g. `-64000` for roughly 64 MB per connection). This means memory use scales with pool size times cache size, not just pool size — a detail that matters a lot for the memory tables further down.

A rough sketch of the two pragma settings, as they'd appear if inspected directly against the database file with the `sqlite3` command-line tool:

```
sqlite3 var/state/accounts.db
sqlite> PRAGMA journal_mode;
wal
sqlite> PRAGMA cache_size;
-64000
sqlite> PRAGMA synchronous;
1
```

(`synchronous=NORMAL`, shown here as `1`, is the setting paired with WAL mode on accountsvc; it was chosen alongside the WAL switch and hasn't been revisited since.)

The page cache change made between the March and May 2025 rounds — moving the default from roughly 8 MB to roughly 64 MB per connection — is why memory figures from the two rounds aren't directly comparable pool-size-for-pool-size. This is called out again in the memory section below so it isn't missed.

## Pool Size Trials — Owner: Sana Byrne

The table below summarizes the three rounds. "Wait rate" is the rough share of load-group calls that measurably queued for a free connection rather than getting one immediately, estimated from the profiling traces rather than measured with any dedicated instrumentation.

| Round | Pool sizes tried | Journal mode | Cache size per connection | Wait rate at pool = 1–2 | Wait rate at pool ≥ 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| March 2025 | 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 | WAL | ~8 MB | high, frequent queuing | near zero |
| May 2025 | 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 | WAL | ~64 MB | high at 2, moderate at 4 | near zero |
| July 2025 | 4, 6, 8 | WAL | ~64 MB | n/a (didn't retest 1–2) | near zero, stable under sustained load |

The March round's headline finding was straightforward: at pool sizes of 1 or 2, callers queued visibly whenever more than two things happened at once, which given the mixed command-line-and-loopback usage pattern was common enough to matter. By pool size 6, queuing had all but disappeared under the load groups used.

The May round, run after the page cache change, mostly confirmed the same shape but with everything a little slower to warm up and a little heavier in memory (see below). It also pushed the ceiling out to 12 to see whether there was a point of diminishing or negative returns — there wasn't a sharp one, but gains past 8 were small enough not to be worth the memory.

The July round narrowed back to 4, 6, and 8 and ran each for a longer sustained period (roughly 20 minutes of intermittent load rather than a handful of short groups) to check that nothing degraded over time. Nothing did; response times at pool size 6 and 8 stayed flat across the run.

## Response Times on the Loopback Interface — Owner: Priya Nandakumar (cross-reference)

Response time work in general is tracked in more depth on the Loopback Response Times page (currently at version 2.9, owned by Runtime Performance); the figures here are specific to varying pool size and shouldn't be read as the full picture.

Median and p95 figures below are in milliseconds, from the July 2025 round on the Windows host, load groups of 50 concurrent calls:

| Pool size | Median (ms) | p95 (ms) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 6.1 | 14.8 | occasional short queuing under peak groups |
| 6 | 5.4 | 9.2 | stable across the sustained run |
| 8 | 5.3 | 8.9 | marginal improvement over 6 |

The gap between pool size 4 and 6 is the interesting one — a roughly 35% drop in p95 latency for two more connections. The gap between 6 and 8 is small enough that it's within the noise of repeated runs, which is part of why 6 was chosen over 8 as the default (see Current Recommendation below).

For comparison, the March 2025 round (smaller cache, same journal mode) showed p95 figures roughly 20–30% higher at every pool size, which lines up with the general slowdown noted in that round's profiling-sessions page and isn't specific to pool size itself.

## Memory Use Across Pool Sizes

Memory use is the sharpest tradeoff against pool size, because it scales with both pool size and per-connection cache size. Figures below are steady-state private memory (Windows Task Manager, Private Bytes) after warm-up, no load running:

| Pool size | Cache per connection | Approx. steady-state memory | Round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | ~8 MB | ~28 MB | March 2025 |
| 4 | ~8 MB | ~40 MB | March 2025 |
| 8 | ~8 MB | ~68 MB | March 2025 |
| 2 | ~64 MB | ~145 MB | May 2025 |
| 4 | ~64 MB | ~270 MB | May 2025 |
| 6 | ~64 MB | ~390 MB | July 2025 |
| 8 | ~64 MB | ~510 MB | May/July 2025 |

The jump between the March and May figures at the same pool sizes is the page cache change discussed earlier, not a pool sizing effect — it's included here mainly so the two rounds aren't compared incorrectly. Under the current ~64 MB per-connection cache, each additional pooled connection costs roughly 60–65 MB of steady-state memory, which is the main reason pool size wasn't pushed past 8 even though response times kept improving slightly.

More general memory tracking, including growth over longer uptimes, is covered on the Memory Use Baseline page and the newer Long-Running Process Memory Notes page; neither is specific to pool size and both are worth reading alongside this section for the fuller picture.

## Startup Time Impact

This is the piece added in the July 2025 round and is thinner than the response time and memory work above.

accountsvc pre-opens its full pool at startup rather than opening connections lazily on first use — a choice made early on, before most of this profiling work started, to avoid a cold first call being unusually slow. That means pool size has a direct, roughly linear cost on startup time, since each connection has to be opened and (depending on how the cache is configured) primed before the service reports itself ready.

Rough startup timing, Windows host, cold file-system cache each time (measured by timing from process launch to the loopback service accepting its first call):

| Pool size | Approx. startup time |
|---|---|
| 1 | ~180 ms |
| 4 | ~230 ms |
| 6 | ~260 ms |
| 8 | ~310 ms |
| 12 | ~410 ms |

None of this is large in absolute terms, but it's not nothing either — going from pool size 1 to pool size 8 roughly adds a fifth of a second to every restart, which matters more in the local command-line workflow (where the process starts fresh each invocation) than in the loopback service (which is expected to stay up for long stretches). This asymmetry is one of the open questions listed below: whether the command-line surface should use a smaller pool than the loopback service does, rather than sharing one configuration value.

More detail on startup timing generally, including cold versus warm disk-cache effects that aren't specific to pool size, is on the Startup Time Tracking page (v1.0.0) and the Cold Start Versus Warm Start page.

## Current Recommendation and Configuration

As of this update, the recommended and default pool size is **6**, with journal mode WAL and a per-connection cache size of roughly 64 MB (`-64000` in the configuration file's units). This is set in `accountsvc/config/pool-defaults.ini` and can be overridden per-deployment by editing that file directly — there is no separate flag surface for it at present.

A representative excerpt of the relevant settings (not the full file):

```
[pool]
size = 6
open_at_startup = true

[database]
journal_mode = wal
cache_size_kib = -64000
synchronous = normal
```

The reasoning, pulled together from the sections above:

1. Pool size 6 removes essentially all measured queuing under the load groups used, matching pool size 8 closely enough that the extra memory of 8 isn't justified.
2. The memory cost of 6 versus 4 is roughly 120 MB more, which is accepted given the response time improvement, but pushing to 8 or beyond costs another 120 MB for very little further gain.
3. Startup time at 6 (~260 ms) is judged acceptable for both the loopback service and command-line invocations, though the command-line case is flagged as worth a closer look (see below).

## Known Limits and Open Questions

- The load groups used for profiling are a rough approximation of real concurrent usage and were generated with a hand-written shell loop rather than a proper load-generation tool; the shapes of the response time curves are probably right, but the absolute numbers should be treated as approximate.
- Pool size and cache size were only tried in tandem, never independently — it isn't known whether a smaller cache with a larger pool would land somewhere better on the memory-versus-response-time curve. This is flagged for Data Systems to weigh in on, since cache size is their area.
- The command-line surface pays the full startup cost of the pool on every invocation, which the loopback service doesn't, since it stays up. Whether the command line should use a separately configured smaller pool size hasn't been decided; Core Services has been asked about this but hadn't responded as of this update.
- Sustained-load figures only cover about 20 minutes per pool size in the July round. Whether memory or response time drifts over hours or days of uptime is a Long-Running Process Memory Notes question, not answered here.
- All profiling in this document was run on two machines under otherwise idle conditions; no figures here account for other processes competing for disk I/O or memory on a shared host.

## Terminology

- **Connection pool** — a small, pre-opened group of connections to the database file that the service hands out to callers rather than opening a fresh connection for every call.
- **Pool size** — the number of connections held open in the pool at once; the main variable discussed on this page.
- **Journal mode** — the SQLite setting that governs how changes are recorded before being written into the main database file; accountsvc currently uses WAL (Write-Ahead Log) mode.
- **WAL** — Write-Ahead Log, a journal mode in which changes are written to a separate log file and folded back into the main database file later, allowing readers and a writer to proceed without blocking each other as often as under older journal modes.
- **Page cache** — the in-memory copy of recently used database pages a connection keeps to avoid re-reading them from disk; sized per connection via the `cache_size` setting.
- **Loopback interface** — the local-only network interface (127.0.0.1) the HTTP surface of accountsvc listens on; not reachable from outside the host.
- **Warm-up** — the short period after starting the service during which caches fill and timing figures are unstable; measurements are typically discarded during this window.
- **Wait rate** — an informal measure used in this page's profiling for how often a caller had to queue for a free pooled connection rather than getting one right away.
- **Cold start** — starting the process with no relevant data already sitting in operating-system or page caches from a previous run.
- **p95** — the 95th-percentile value in a set of timing measurements; used alongside the median to describe the slower tail of response times, not just the typical case.

## Files and Paths Referenced

- `accountsvc/config/pool-defaults.ini` — configuration file holding the default pool size, startup-open flag, journal mode, cache size, and synchronous setting.
- `var/state/accounts.db` — the SQLite database file the pool holds connections against.
- `var/state/accounts.db-wal` — the WAL companion file present while the database is in WAL journal mode.
- `var/log/accountsvc/pool/` — log folder holding raw profiling output and load-group timing captures from each round described on this page.
- `scripts/loopback-latency.sh` — shell script used on the Linux workstation to fire concurrent loopback calls and record timings.
- `scripts/profile-pool.ps1` — PowerShell script performing the equivalent function on the Windows host, including the Task Manager memory sampling steps written up as manual instructions in comments.
- `docs/performance-notes/connection-pool-sizing.md` — this page.
- `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-page-cache-tuning.rst` — page cache sizing detail referenced in the journal mode and cache section above.
- `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode-notes.md` — background on the WAL switch this page assumes as given.

## Tools and Libraries

| Tool / library | Version | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.9 | runtime accountsvc is built against |
| sqlite3 (command-line tool) | 3.45.1 | inspecting pragma settings against the database file directly |
| cProfile | standard library (3.11) | light profiling pass per pool size |
| tracemalloc | standard library (3.11) | spot-checking allocation sources during the May round |
| curl | 8.4.0 | generating loopback calls for timing |
| PowerShell | 7.4.2 | driving the Windows-host profiling script |
| Task Manager | Windows 10 build 19045 | steady-state and under-load memory sampling |
| gnuplot | 5.4 | plotting the response time distributions used to pick the median/p95 figures above |

- **2025-05-30** — Released with accountsvc 2.1.0. Page cache size increased from ~8 MB to ~64 MB per connection (Data Systems change); second pool profiling round run against the new cache size, pool sizes 2–12.
- **2025-06-12** — Released with accountsvc 2.1.4. Shipped default pool size finally updated to 6, matching the March round's recommendation.

3	=====================
4	
5	:Title: Garbage Collector Tuning Notes
6	:Version: v1.0.2
7	:Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
8	:Last Updated: 2026-02-01
9	
10	Summary
11	=======
12	
13	This document captures observations and findings from tuning the interpreter's garbage collector (GC) thresholds while running the accountsvc package in loopback service mode. The package relies entirely on the standard library, which includes the garbage collector; adjusting its thresholds can meaningfully reduce latency spikes in HTTP request handling and improve memory behavior during startup and long-running operation.
14	
15	Overview: GC in Standard Library Services
16	==========================================
17	
18	The interpreter's garbage collector runs automatically based on allocation thresholds. For a small service like accountsvc, which holds state in a local SQLite file and serves requests over loopback, GC pauses can become visible in response time distributions, particularly under steady-state request load. This document is concerned with what we can observe, measure, and adjust when the default GC behavior does not match the service's runtime profile.
19	
20	We observe GC in three ways:
21	
22	- Profiling tools that instrument the runtime
23	- Timing measurements of actual request handling
24	- Direct observation of memory growth patterns
25	
26	Each approach reveals different aspects of GC behavior. Profiling shows when and how long GC runs; timing shows its impact on perceived performance; memory observation shows whether tuning actually improves heap efficiency.
27	
28	
29	Profiling and Observation Techniques
30	====================================
31	
32	*Section Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)*
33	
34	The foundation of any tuning work is measurement. Before adjusting thresholds, we establish a baseline by running profiling sessions under controlled conditions.
35	
36	Setting Up a Profiling Session
37	-------------------------------
38	
39	A profiling session is a recorded run of the service under a known load pattern. The service runs on loopback, responding to a stream of generated requests. We use the configuration file at ``scripts/profiling-tool-config.yaml`` to specify which metrics to capture, how long to run, and what sampling rate to use.
40	
41	Our approach:
42	
43	1. Start the service in loopback mode (no external binding).
44	2. Begin metric collection before sending any requests.
45	3. Send a steady stream of requests at a known rate (e.g., 10 req/sec for 60 seconds).
46	4. Allow the service to stabilize before ramping up load.
47	5. Stop collection, preserve the output files, and analyze locally.
48	
49	Example session structure::
50	
51	  Start service
52	    ↓ (wait 5 seconds for startup)
53	  Begin profiling
54	    ↓
55	  Send 600 requests over 60 seconds (10 req/sec)
56	    ↓ (let it settle for 10 seconds)
57	  Stop profiling
58	    ↓
59	  Save results to timestamped directory
60	
61	The profiling output includes timing for each GC pause, heap size over time, and request latency percentiles. Comparing outputs before and after a tuning change shows the effect directly.
62	
63	Baseline Comparison
64	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
65	
66	We run every profiling session twice: once with default GC settings and once with variant settings. This requires starting the service fresh each time to avoid any prior state affecting results. The baseline run is always performed first, then the variant run, on the same system in the same session to minimize environmental variation.
67	
68	Key metrics to record:
69	
70	- Request latency (p50, p95, p99)
71	- GC pause duration (max, mean, total time)
72	- Heap size at start, peak, and end
73	- Time from startup to first request handling
74	
75	Comparing two sessions side-by-side (see ``profiling-sessions-2025.md`` for recent data) often reveals that small threshold changes have larger effects than expected. Large changes sometimes have minimal effect, suggesting the service's allocation pattern is not GC-bound.
76	
77	
78	Garbage Collector Behavior with SQLite
79	=======================================
80	
81	*Section Owner: Data Systems (Devon Ruiz)*
82	
83	The package interacts with its SQLite database file during most request handling. This interaction creates memory allocation patterns that the GC must manage. Understanding how SQLite operations affect GC behavior is essential to proper tuning.
84	
85	SQLite Query Caching and Memory
86	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
87	
88	The SQLite library maintains internal buffers and cached statements. These allocations are not visible to Python's memory profiler in the same way as Python objects, but they influence the overall heap picture. When the service runs with a high page cache size (see ``sqlite-page-cache-tuning.rst``), the database file buffers grow, which can make it harder for the GC to see gains from threshold tuning. Conversely, a small cache forces more disk I/O, which adds latency independent of GC.
89	
90	Our measurements show that a page cache size between 2000 and 5000 pages offers a good balance for accountsvc's typical workload. Smaller values increase query latency; larger values use more memory without proportional benefit for the request volumes we see.
91	
92	Journal Mode Interactions
93	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
94	
95	The database's journal mode affects how often write operations force synchronization to disk. In Standard mode (the default), each transaction writes to the journal file and then the main database file. In WAL mode (write-ahead logging), writes go to a log file, reducing lock contention. In TRUNCATE mode, the journal is truncated rather than cleared after each commit.
96	
97	For a loopback-only service, WAL mode is generally preferred because it reduces blocking between reads and writes. However, WAL mode changes the runtime memory profile: the log file must be held in memory temporarily, which can trigger additional GC activity. Our profiling sessions (see ``profiling-sessions-2025.md``, dated 2025-09-30) showed that switching from Standard to WAL mode at the database level reduced request latency variance, even though peak latency occasionally increased due to GC pauses.
98	
99	The configuration in ``sqlite-journal-mode-notes.md`` documents all three modes in detail; we reference it here because journal mode directly affects memory allocation patterns that the GC sees.
100	
101	
102	Memory Use and Long-Running Stability
103	======================================
104	
105	The package runs as a loopback HTTP service, often for hours during validation. Long-running stability is distinct from startup behavior: a service can start cleanly but develop memory issues over time if the GC is not tuned for steady-state allocation.
106	
107	Memory Baseline
108	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
109	
110	The infrastructure team has documented a baseline memory use profile in ``memory-use-baseline.md`` (version 2.0, dated 2024-08-03). That page establishes the reference numbers for our service under typical load: approximately 15–18 MB on startup, growing to 22–28 MB during steady-state loopback operation. These numbers assume default GC settings.
111	
112	After tuning the GC thresholds in February 2026, we observed a new steady-state range of 19–24 MB, a net reduction of about 4 MB at the high end. This improvement is modest but measurable over multi-hour runs. The infrastructure team is reviewing whether this baseline should be updated (last updated 2024-08-03; an update is overdue).
113	
114	Memory Growth Over 24 Hours
115	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
116	
117	We ran the service for 24 continuous hours under generated load (20 req/sec, mixed read-heavy requests). Memory grew from 18 MB to approximately 26 MB, then remained stable. This shows that the service reaches a steady-state heap size within 2–4 hours and stops growing under normal conditions.
118	
119	If memory grows indefinitely (more than 1 MB per hour after the first 4 hours), investigate:
120	
121	1. Whether requests are being generated at a higher rate than expected.
122	2. Whether the SQLite database is growing (check the database file size).
123	3. Whether a specific request type is triggering abnormal allocation (use profiling sessions to isolate this).
124	
125	Profiling long-running behavior is harder than short sessions because the data files become very large. We recommend running 4–6 hour profiling windows and analyzing the middle portion (hours 2–5) to observe steady-state behavior without startup or eventual-shutdown noise.
126	
127	
128	Response Time Distribution and GC Pauses
129	=========================================
130	
131	One of the most observable effects of GC tuning is on request latency distribution. When the GC runs during request handling, that request is delayed. The impact shows up most clearly in tail latencies (p95, p99).
132	
133	Measuring Loopback Latency
134	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
135	
136	The loopback response times page (``loopback-response-times.md``, version 3.0, updated 2026-01-22) provides detailed methodology for measuring request latency. For GC tuning purposes, the key insight is that latency includes both request processing time and any GC pauses that occur during handling.
137	
138	A typical loopback latency profile on default GC settings:
139	
140	- p50 (median): 2–3 ms
141	- p95: 8–15 ms
142	- p99: 25–50 ms
143	- max (worst case): 100+ ms
144	
145	The p99 and max values are often driven by GC pauses, not by slow request logic. Reducing GC pause frequency typically shrinks these tail latencies significantly. In our February 2026 tuning work, we reduced p99 latency from an average of 42 ms to 28 ms, a 33 % improvement.
146	
147	Correlation with GC Events
148	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
149	
150	To confirm that latency spikes are GC-related, enable GC event logging in your profiling configuration (see ``profiling-tool-config.yaml``, version 1.4). The profiler will output a timestamp for each GC pause alongside request timestamps. If latency spikes closely align with GC pause events, GC tuning is likely to help.
151	
152	We do not provide GC logging code here; instead, refer to the profiling tool configuration guide for setup instructions.
153	
154	
155	Tuning Procedures and Configuration
156	====================================
157	
158	*Section Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)*
159	
160	GC tuning is done by adjusting the generation thresholds. The interpreter maintains multiple generations of objects; younger generations are collected more frequently, older generations less frequently. Raising thresholds delays collection, reducing pause frequency but potentially increasing latency variance and peak memory. Lowering thresholds increases pause frequency but keeps peak memory lower.
161	
162	Default Thresholds
163	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
164	
165	The interpreter's default thresholds are suitable for general applications. For accountsvc, these values are often too aggressive (too much collection), which shows up as visible latency pauses in tail latencies. Our measurements and the related profiling documentation confirm this pattern across multiple runs.
166	
167	Recommended Tuning Range
168	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
169	
170	Based on profiling sessions from 2024 and 2025 (see ``profiling-sessions-2024.md`` version 2.1, and ``profiling-sessions-2025.md`` version 2.4), we recommend evaluating thresholds in these ranges:
171	
172	- Generation 0 (youngest): 1500–2500 (default: ~700)
173	- Generation 1 (intermediate): 9–15 (default: ~10)
174	- Generation 2 (oldest): 10–20 (default: ~10)
175	
176	These are relative thresholds; increasing them means the GC waits longer before collecting that generation. Do not increase Generation 0 beyond 2500 without profiling first, as very large thresholds can cause unpredictable latency spikes when collection finally occurs.
177	
178	Our February 2026 tuning (applied in service configuration) uses:
179	
180	- Generation 0: 2000
181	- Generation 1: 12
182	- Generation 2: 15
183	
184	This configuration was derived from profiling 10 different threshold combinations over 30-minute sessions. The chosen values offered the best balance of reduced tail latency and stable peak memory.
185	
186	Example Configuration Entry
187	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
188	
189	Thresholds are typically set at service startup. The configuration is stored in a local settings file that the service reads on launch. An example structure::
190	
191	  GarbageCollector:
192	    Generation0Threshold: 2000
193	    Generation1Threshold: 12
194	    Generation2Threshold: 15
195	    EnableLogging: false
196	
197	After changing these values, restart the service and run a profiling session to validate the effect. Do not change multiple thresholds at once; evaluate them incrementally if possible.
198	
199	Evaluating a New Configuration
200	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
201	
202	Process for validating a tuning change:
203	
204	1. Update the configuration file with new threshold values.
205	2. Run a baseline profiling session (600–1200 requests over 60–120 seconds).
206	3. Compare p50, p95, p99 latencies and GC pause statistics to the previous baseline.
207	4. If improvement is clear and memory remains stable, keep the new values; otherwise, revert and try a different combination.
208	5. Repeat the long-running stability run (4+ hours) to ensure no memory loss develops.
209	
210	Keep records of each profiling run, including the configuration used, date, and results. Over time, these form a body of evidence about which tuning works for accountsvc.
211	
212	
213	Interaction with Startup Time
214	==============================
215	
216	The package's startup time is documented separately in ``startup-time-tracking.md`` (version v1.1.0, updated 2025-04-27). GC tuning can affect startup time indirectly: more aggressive collection during initialization might delay startup, while less aggressive collection might leave more debris that must be cleaned up later.
217	
218	In practice, the effect is small. Our measurements show startup time varies by less than 5 % due to GC tuning changes. More significant startup time improvements come from reducing import overhead or pre-warming the database cache, neither of which is GC-related.
219	
220	Cold and Warm Starts
221	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
222	
223	The distinction between cold-start (service not yet running) and warm-start (service running, handling requests) is documented in ``cold-start-vs-warm-start.txt`` (dated 2024-12-15). GC tuning affects warm-start latency much more than cold-start latency. This is expected: during a cold start, the service is initializing data structures, so the GC behavior is different from steady-state operation. In warm-start scenarios, request handling follows predictable patterns, and GC tuning has a larger relative effect.
224	
225	
226	Terminology and Glossary
227	========================
228	
229	**Generation (GC)**: A grouping of objects by age. Younger generations are checked for garbage more frequently than older ones. The interpreter typically has two or three generations.
230	
231	**GC Pause**: A brief suspension of the running program while the garbage collector scans the heap and reclaims unused memory. For accountsvc, pauses typically last a few milliseconds but can spike to 10+ ms if a full collection is triggered.
232	
233	**Heap**: The region of memory where Python objects are allocated. In accountsvc, heap size grows with request volume and database state but should eventually stabilize under steady load.
234	
235	**Journal Mode**: In SQLite, the strategy for writing transaction logs. Standard mode clears the journal after each commit; WAL mode uses a separate log file; TRUNCATE mode truncates the journal. Each mode has different memory and performance tradeoffs.
236	
237	**Loopback**: Network traffic that does not leave the local machine. Our profiling uses loopback requests to the service's HTTP interface to avoid network latency confounding GC measurements.
238	
239	**p50, p95, p99**: Percentile latencies. p50 is the median (50th percentile), p95 means 95 % of requests are faster than this value, p99 means 99 % are faster. Tail latencies (p95, p99) are most affected by GC pauses.
240	
241	**Page Cache**: SQLite's in-memory buffer pool for database pages. Larger caches reduce disk I/O but use more memory; tuning this value affects how often the GC sees large memory allocations.
242	
243	**Threshold (GC)**: The number of allocations allowed before the GC runs for a given generation. Raising the threshold delays collection; lowering it speeds up collection at the cost of more frequent pauses.
