1	LONG-RUNNING PROCESS MEMORY NOTES
2	====================================
3	
4	Title: Long-Running Process Memory Notes
5	Version: 2.0
6	Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)
7	Last updated: 2026-06-05
8	
9	SUMMARY
10	-------
11	This page collects what we know about how the accountsvc process's memory use changes over multi-day loopback runs — the pattern of growth in the first hours after a cold start, the point where growth flattens out, and the settings (mainly on the SQLite side) that move that flattening point up or down. It also folds in the loopback response-time and startup-time numbers that were gathered during the same runs, since the three are hard to separate in practice: a process that is slow to answer on the loopback interface is often also the one whose memory has not settled, and a process that starts cold is not directly comparable to one that has been serving requests for four days.
12	
13	The notes here are drawn mainly from two long soak runs, one in March 2026 and one in May 2026, both on the same reference host (a spare rack unit in the Infrastructure lab, hostname `lab-infra-03`). Where numbers differ from the 2025 profiling pages, that is usually because the host or the SQLite settings changed, not because the earlier numbers were wrong.
14	
15	COVERAGE AND METHOD
16	-----------------
17	Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)
18	
19	The coverage of this page is the memory footprint of the accountsvc process itself while it is running as the loopback service — not the memory used by whatever short-lived command-line invocations of the package are made against it, and not the memory used by the shell or supervisor process that starts it. We measure the service process only.
20	
21	Method, in outline:
22	
23	1. Start the service fresh (a cold start, see Terminology) on `lab-infra-03` with a known, empty database file.
24	2. Warm the process with a short burst of loopback calls so that the interpreter's import machinery and any caches used by the standard library have settled — this is the "warm start" point, usually reached within the first 90 seconds.
25	3. Run a steady, low-rate stream of loopback calls (roughly one call every 200ms, generated by `scripts/loopback-soak.sh`) for a period of four days (96 hours).
26	4. Sample resident memory (RSS) and virtual size (VSZ) for the process every five minutes for the first six hours, then every thirty minutes for the remainder of the run, using `scripts/mem-sample.sh`.
27	5. Record the SQLite settings in effect (journal mode, page cache size, synchronous setting) at the start of the run, and note any point where they were changed mid-run.
28	6. At the end of the run, capture a final heap sample using `tracemalloc` (stdlib) for comparison against the sample taken at the warm-start point.
29	
30	A representative sampling loop, run from the shell against the known process id:
31	
32	    while true; do
33	      ts=$(date -u +%FT%TZ)
34	      rss=$(ps -o rss= -p "$SVC_PID")
35	      vsz=$(ps -o vsz= -p "$SVC_PID")
36	      echo "$ts $rss $vsz" >> /var/log/accountsvc/soak/rss.log
37	      sleep 300
38	    done
39	
40	This is roughly what `scripts/mem-sample.sh` does, with a bit more error handling around the process id going away between samples (which happens if the supervisor restarts the service, and which invalidates the run if it happens inside the first 24 hours).
41	
42	TERMINOLOGY
43	------------
44	RSS (Resident Set Size) — the amount of physical memory currently mapped to the process, as reported by the operating system. This is the number we mostly track in this page.
45	
46	VSZ (Virtual Size) — the total memory space reserved by the process, whether or not it is backed by physical memory. VSZ tends to be much larger than RSS and less useful for spotting growth.
47	
48	Working set — the subset of a process's memory that is actively touched over a given window; a process can have a large RSS but a small working set if most of its memory is cold pages that happen not to have been reclaimed.
49	
50	Page cache (SQLite) — the in-memory area SQLite uses to hold recently used pages of the database file, sized by the `cache_size` setting. This is distinct from the operating system's own page cache for the file on disk, and the two are easy to conflate.
51	
52	Loopback interface — the local network interface (127.0.0.1) that accountsvc's HTTP service listens on; all timing in this page was taken against calls made over that interface on the same host, not across a network.
53	
54	Cold start — starting the service process with no prior state in memory: a fresh interpreter, empty caches, and (for the purposes of memory work) usually also a freshly opened database file.
55	
56	Warm start / warmed process — the state of the process after it has handled enough calls that its import-time and first-call costs are no longer contributing to what we measure; treated in this page as the state reached roughly 90 seconds after a cold start under a light load.
57	
58	Soak run — a continuous run of the service under a steady, low load for an extended period (days rather than minutes), used to observe whether memory growth flattens out or keeps climbing.
59	
60	Retained memory — memory that the process has acquired from the operating system and not given back, whether or not it is still in active use; the main quantity of interest when we ask whether a long run is "growing."
61	
62	Write-ahead log (WAL) — the SQLite journal mode in which changes are written to a separate, sequentially written log file alongside the main database file, and folded back into the main file at intervals rather than on every write.
63	
64	Interpreter startup — the fixed cost of getting the Python interpreter itself running and its standard library imports resolved, before any service-specific setup happens; a floor under all startup-time numbers regardless of what the service does next.
65	
66	Fragmentation (heap) — the condition where a process's allocator has free memory available but cannot return it to the operating system because it is scattered between blocks that are still in use; a common cause of RSS staying high even after a burst of allocation has ended.
67	
68	PROFILING SESSIONS ON LONG-RUNNING INSTANCES
69	----------------------------------------------
70	Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)
71	
72	Most of the profiling sessions logged on the sibling pages (`profiling-sessions-2024.md`, `profiling-sessions-2025.md`) were short — a few minutes of load against a freshly started process, aimed at finding hot paths rather than long-run behavior. Two sessions specifically targeted long-running memory and are worth calling out here because they set the baseline this page compares against.
73	
74	- Session 2025-09-18 (logged in profiling-sessions-2025.md): four-hour run, page cache size left at the SQLite default. Showed RSS climbing steadily for the full four hours with no sign of flattening, which was the finding that prompted the longer soak runs described in this page.
75	- Session 2026-03-11: 96-hour soak run, page cache size raised to roughly 20MB (see the SQLite Settings section below). RSS climbed for the first 18–20 hours and then held within a narrow band (see the Memory Use table further down) for the remaining three and a half days.
76	
77	A third, shorter session on 2026-05-04 repeated the 2026-03-11 run on the same host to check that the flattening point was reproducible and not an artifact of that particular run; it was, within about 1.5MB of the earlier number.
78	
79	For memory work specifically, the profiling toolkit used is lighter than what is used for CPU-hot-path work: `tracemalloc` (stdlib) for allocation-site sampling at a handful of points during the run, `objgraph` for counting object types when RSS moves unexpectedly, and plain `ps`/`/proc` sampling (see the Coverage and Method section) for the continuous RSS/VSZ trend. Heavier tools such as `perf` were used in a few of the 2025 CPU sessions but were not part of the memory soak runs, since they add enough of their own overhead to distort a multi-day measurement.
80	
81	Configuration for the sampling tools used in these sessions — sampling extent, output paths, and the profiling toolkit's own settings — is kept in `profiling-tool-config.yaml`. That file is shared with the CPU-focused profiling sessions and is not specific to memory work, so changes made for one kind of session can affect the other; this has caused at least one mismatched-baseline confusion in the past (the 2025-09-18 session initially used a sampling interval left over from a CPU session and had to be rerun).
82	
83	SQLITE SETTINGS UNDER LONG-RUNNING LOAD
84	------------------------------------------
85	Owner: Data Systems (Devon Ruiz)
86	
87	Two SQLite settings dominate the memory picture for a long-running accountsvc process: journal mode and page cache size. Both are read from `conf/accountsvc.ini` at process start and are not changed while the process is running, so a setting change only takes effect after a restart (which itself resets the memory trend — see the Startup Time section for why that matters).
88	
89	Current defaults, as of this page's last update:
90	
91	    [sqlite]
92	    journal_mode = WAL
93	    cache_size = -20000
94	    synchronous = NORMAL
95	
96	A negative `cache_size` value is interpreted by SQLite as kibibytes rather than pages, so `-20000` requests roughly 20MB of page cache. This was raised from the earlier default of `-2000` (about 2MB) after the 2025-09-18 profiling session showed the smaller cache thrashing under the soak load — pages were being evicted and reread from disk often enough that both memory and response time suffered.
97	
98	To check what a running process is actually using, the settings can be read directly against the database file with the `sqlite3` command-line tool:
99	
100	    sqlite3 accountsvc/state.db
101	    sqlite> PRAGMA journal_mode;
102	    wal
103	    sqlite> PRAGMA cache_size;
104	    -20000
105	    sqlite> PRAGMA synchronous;
106	    1
107	
108	Journal mode is set to WAL rather than the older rollback-journal mode, mainly because WAL keeps writers from blocking readers, which matters more for response time than for memory as such. The tradeoff on the memory side is that the write-ahead log file itself grows between fold-back points, and a large uncollapsed WAL file can inflate the operating system's own page cache for that file, which shows up in host-level memory graphs even though it isn't accountsvc's own RSS growing. The 2026-03-09 update to the WAL housekeeping page describes the interval used to fold the log back into the main file; this page only notes that, during the 96-hour soak run, WAL fold-back events lined up with small, brief dips in RSS (typically under 1MB), consistent with some pages being dropped from the SQLite page cache right after a fold-back.
109	
110	Page cache size interacts with the process's steady-state RSS in an almost linear way up to a point: raising `cache_size` from 2MB-equivalent to 20MB-equivalent raised the steady-state RSS by roughly 17–19MB, which is close to the cache size difference itself, meaning the SQLite page cache really is the memory being added rather than some other structure growing as a side effect. A follow-up run at `cache_size = -50000` (about 50MB) is planned for the next quarter but has not been run as of this update.
111	
112	RESPONSE TIMES MEASURED ON LOOPBACK
113	--------------------------------------
114	Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)
115	
116	Response times in this page are measured against the loopback interface only, using `curl`'s built-in timing fields rather than a separate timing tool, so as to avoid adding a network stack's worth of noise:
117	
118	    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8781/accounts/1042
119	
120	(the port and call shape above are illustrative of the shell invocation only, not a description of the service's call structure).
121	
122	Median and 95th-percentile times over the course of the 2026-03-11 soak run, taken in six-hour windows:
123	
124	    Window        Median (ms)   95th pct (ms)   Notes
125	    0h  -  6h     4.1           11.7            RSS still climbing
126	    6h  - 24h     3.6           8.9             RSS still climbing, more slowly
127	    24h - 48h     3.3           7.4             flattened
128	    48h - 72h     3.2           7.1             flattened
129	    72h - 96h     3.3           7.6             flattened, slight uptick
130	
131	The pattern worth calling out: response time actually improves somewhat as RSS climbs during the first day, because the SQLite page cache is filling up and later calls are more often served from memory rather than from disk. Once memory flattens, response time flattens too and stays flat, with the small uptick at the 72–96 hour mark not fully explained — it may be host-level noise from other processes on `lab-infra-03` rather than anything in accountsvc itself, and the 2026-05-04 repeat run did not show the same uptick.
132	
133	These numbers track closely with the fuller loopback response-time page (loopback-response-times.md), which covers a broader set of call shapes and load levels; this page only reports the subset that was measured as part of the same runs used for memory tracking.
134	
135	MEMORY USE OVER MULTI-DAY RUNS
136	----------------------------------
137	Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)
138	
139	This is the core of the page. RSS and VSZ for the 2026-03-11 soak run, sampled as described in Coverage and Method, at the six-hour marks:
140	
141	    Elapsed     RSS (MB)   VSZ (MB)   Journal mode   Cache size setting
142	    0h (cold)   14.2       61.0       WAL            -20000
143	    0.5h (warm) 22.7       74.3       WAL            -20000
144	    6h          38.1       88.9       WAL            -20000
145	    12h         44.6       91.2       WAL            -20000
146	    18h         46.9       92.0       WAL            -20000
147	    24h         47.4       92.1       WAL            -20000
148	    48h         47.8       92.3       WAL            -20000
149	    72h         48.1       92.4       WAL            -20000
150	    96h         48.6       92.6       WAL            -20000
151	
152	The shape here is the one we now expect: a fast climb in the first half day driven mostly by the SQLite page cache filling and by the interpreter's own steady-state allocations settling, followed by a long, nearly flat tail with only a very slow residual climb — about 1.2MB over the final three days of the run, or roughly 0.017MB/hour. Whether that residual climb is retained memory that will keep going indefinitely, or whether it eventually flattens too, is not settled; the longest run to date is the 96-hour one, and a two-week run is on the list of things to try but has not been scheduled.
153	
154	For comparison, the same run with `cache_size` left at the old default (`-2000`, about 2MB) — repeated on 2026-03-14 specifically to have a like-for-like comparison — flattened lower (around 30MB steady-state) but never fully stopped climbing; small upward steps kept appearing every several hours, in the 0.3–0.6MB range, that did not appear at all in the 20MB-cache run. The working theory, not yet confirmed, is that a too-small page cache causes more frequent SQLite-internal allocation and freeing, and some of that memory is not being returned promptly to the operating system, showing up as small permanent RSS steps rather than a smooth climb. This is one of the open questions carried into the next update.
155

LONG-RUNNING PROCESS MEMORY NOTES
====================================

Title: Long-Running Process Memory Notes
Version: 2.0
Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)
Last updated: 2026-06-05

SUMMARY
-------
This page collects what we know about how the accountsvc process's memory use changes over multi-day loopback runs — the pattern of growth in the first hours after a cold start, the point where growth flattens out, and the settings (mainly on the SQLite side) that move that flattening point up or down. It also folds in the loopback response-time and startup-time numbers that were gathered during the same runs, since the three are hard to separate in practice: a process that is slow to answer on the loopback interface is often also the one whose memory has not settled, and a process that starts cold is not directly comparable to one that has been serving requests for four days.

The notes here are drawn mainly from two long soak runs, one in March 2026 and one in May 2026, both on the same reference host (a spare rack unit in the Infrastructure lab, hostname `lab-infra-03`). Where numbers differ from the 2025 profiling pages, that is usually because the host or the SQLite settings changed, not because the earlier numbers were wrong.

COVERAGE AND METHOD
-----------------
Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)

The coverage of this page is the memory footprint of the accountsvc process itself while it is running as the loopback service — not the memory used by whatever short-lived command-line invocations of the package are made against it, and not the memory used by the shell or supervisor process that starts it. We measure the service process only.

Method, in outline:

1. Start the service fresh (a cold start, see Terminology) on `lab-infra-03` with a known, empty database file.
2. Warm the process with a short burst of loopback calls so that the interpreter's import machinery and any caches used by the standard library have settled — this is the "warm start" point, usually reached within the first 90 seconds.
3. Run a steady, low-rate stream of loopback calls (roughly one call every 200ms, generated by `scripts/loopback-soak.sh`) for a period of four days (96 hours).
4. Sample resident memory (RSS) and virtual size (VSZ) for the process every five minutes for the first six hours, then every thirty minutes for the remainder of the run, using `scripts/mem-sample.sh`.
5. Record the SQLite settings in effect (journal mode, page cache size, synchronous setting) at the start of the run, and note any point where they were changed mid-run.
6. At the end of the run, capture a final heap sample using `tracemalloc` (stdlib) for comparison against the sample taken at the warm-start point.

A representative sampling loop, run from the shell against the known process id:

    while true; do
      ts=$(date -u +%FT%TZ)
      rss=$(ps -o rss= -p "$SVC_PID")
      vsz=$(ps -o vsz= -p "$SVC_PID")
      echo "$ts $rss $vsz" >> /var/log/accountsvc/soak/rss.log
      sleep 300
    done

This is roughly what `scripts/mem-sample.sh` does, with a bit more error handling around the process id going away between samples (which happens if the supervisor restarts the service, and which invalidates the run if it happens inside the first 24 hours).

TERMINOLOGY
------------
RSS (Resident Set Size) — the amount of physical memory currently mapped to the process, as reported by the operating system. This is the number we mostly track in this page.

VSZ (Virtual Size) — the total memory space reserved by the process, whether or not it is backed by physical memory. VSZ tends to be much larger than RSS and less useful for spotting growth.

Working set — the subset of a process's memory that is actively touched over a given window; a process can have a large RSS but a small working set if most of its memory is cold pages that happen not to have been reclaimed.

Page cache (SQLite) — the in-memory area SQLite uses to hold recently used pages of the database file, sized by the `cache_size` setting. This is distinct from the operating system's own page cache for the file on disk, and the two are easy to conflate.

Loopback interface — the local network interface (127.0.0.1) that accountsvc's HTTP service listens on; all timing in this page was taken against calls made over that interface on the same host, not across a network.

Cold start — starting the service process with no prior state in memory: a fresh interpreter, empty caches, and (for the purposes of memory work) usually also a freshly opened database file.

Warm start / warmed process — the state of the process after it has handled enough calls that its import-time and first-call costs are no longer contributing to what we measure; treated in this page as the state reached roughly 90 seconds after a cold start under a light load.

Soak run — a continuous run of the service under a steady, low load for an extended period (days rather than minutes), used to observe whether memory growth flattens out or keeps climbing.

Retained memory — memory that the process has acquired from the operating system and not given back, whether or not it is still in active use; the main quantity of interest when we ask whether a long run is "growing."

Write-ahead log (WAL) — the SQLite journal mode in which changes are written to a separate, sequentially written log file alongside the main database file, and folded back into the main file at intervals rather than on every write.

Interpreter startup — the fixed cost of getting the Python interpreter itself running and its standard library imports resolved, before any service-specific setup happens; a floor under all startup-time numbers regardless of what the service does next.

Fragmentation (heap) — the condition where a process's allocator has free memory available but cannot return it to the operating system because it is scattered between blocks that are still in use; a common cause of RSS staying high even after a burst of allocation has ended.

PROFILING SESSIONS ON LONG-RUNNING INSTANCES
----------------------------------------------
Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)

Most of the profiling sessions logged on the sibling pages (`profiling-sessions-2024.md`, `profiling-sessions-2025.md`) were short — a few minutes of load against a freshly started process, aimed at finding hot paths rather than long-run behavior. Two sessions specifically targeted long-running memory and are worth calling out here because they set the baseline this page compares against.

- Session 2025-09-18 (logged in profiling-sessions-2025.md): four-hour run, page cache size left at the SQLite default. Showed RSS climbing steadily for the full four hours with no sign of flattening, which was the finding that prompted the longer soak runs described in this page.
- Session 2026-03-11: 96-hour soak run, page cache size raised to roughly 20MB (see the SQLite Settings section below). RSS climbed for the first 18–20 hours and then held within a narrow band (see the Memory Use table further down) for the remaining three and a half days.

A third, shorter session on 2026-05-04 repeated the 2026-03-11 run on the same host to check that the flattening point was reproducible and not an artifact of that particular run; it was, within about 1.5MB of the earlier number.

For memory work specifically, the profiling toolkit used is lighter than what is used for CPU-hot-path work: `tracemalloc` (stdlib) for allocation-site sampling at a handful of points during the run, `objgraph` for counting object types when RSS moves unexpectedly, and plain `ps`/`/proc` sampling (see the Coverage and Method section) for the continuous RSS/VSZ trend. Heavier tools such as `perf` were used in a few of the 2025 CPU sessions but were not part of the memory soak runs, since they add enough of their own overhead to distort a multi-day measurement.

Configuration for the sampling tools used in these sessions — sampling extent, output paths, and the profiling toolkit's own settings — is kept in `profiling-tool-config.yaml`. That file is shared with the CPU-focused profiling sessions and is not specific to memory work, so changes made for one kind of session can affect the other; this has caused at least one mismatched-baseline confusion in the past (the 2025-09-18 session initially used a sampling interval left over from a CPU session and had to be rerun).

SQLITE SETTINGS UNDER LONG-RUNNING LOAD
------------------------------------------
Owner: Data Systems (Devon Ruiz)

Two SQLite settings dominate the memory picture for a long-running accountsvc process: journal mode and page cache size. Both are read from `conf/accountsvc.ini` at process start and are not changed while the process is running, so a setting change only takes effect after a restart (which itself resets the memory trend — see the Startup Time section for why that matters).

Current defaults, as of this page's last update:

    [sqlite]
    journal_mode = WAL
    cache_size = -20000
    synchronous = NORMAL

A negative `cache_size` value is interpreted by SQLite as kibibytes rather than pages, so `-20000` requests roughly 20MB of page cache. This was raised from the earlier default of `-2000` (about 2MB) after the 2025-09-18 profiling session showed the smaller cache thrashing under the soak load — pages were being evicted and reread from disk often enough that both memory and response time suffered.

To check what a running process is actually using, the settings can be read directly against the database file with the `sqlite3` command-line tool:

    sqlite3 accountsvc/state.db
    sqlite> PRAGMA journal_mode;
    wal
    sqlite> PRAGMA cache_size;
    -20000
    sqlite> PRAGMA synchronous;
    1

Journal mode is set to WAL rather than the older rollback-journal mode, mainly because WAL keeps writers from blocking readers, which matters more for response time than for memory as such. The tradeoff on the memory side is that the write-ahead log file itself grows between fold-back points, and a large uncollapsed WAL file can inflate the operating system's own page cache for that file, which shows up in host-level memory graphs even though it isn't accountsvc's own RSS growing. The 2026-03-09 update to the WAL housekeeping page describes the interval used to fold the log back into the main file; this page only notes that, during the 96-hour soak run, WAL fold-back events lined up with small, brief dips in RSS (typically under 1MB), consistent with some pages being dropped from the SQLite page cache right after a fold-back.

Page cache size interacts with the process's steady-state RSS in an almost linear way up to a point: raising `cache_size` from 2MB-equivalent to 20MB-equivalent raised the steady-state RSS by roughly 17–19MB, which is close to the cache size difference itself, meaning the SQLite page cache really is the memory being added rather than some other structure growing as a side effect. A follow-up run at `cache_size = -50000` (about 50MB) is planned for the next quarter but has not been run as of this update.

RESPONSE TIMES MEASURED ON LOOPBACK
--------------------------------------
Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)

Response times in this page are measured against the loopback interface only, using `curl`'s built-in timing fields rather than a separate timing tool, so as to avoid adding a network stack's worth of noise:

    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8781/accounts/1042

(the port and call shape above are illustrative of the shell invocation only, not a description of the service's call structure).

Median and 95th-percentile times over the course of the 2026-03-11 soak run, taken in six-hour windows:

    Window        Median (ms)   95th pct (ms)   Notes
    0h  -  6h     4.1           11.7            RSS still climbing
    6h  - 24h     3.6           8.9             RSS still climbing, more slowly
    24h - 48h     3.3           7.4             flattened
    48h - 72h     3.2           7.1             flattened
    72h - 96h     3.3           7.6             flattened, slight uptick

The pattern worth calling out: response time actually improves somewhat as RSS climbs during the first day, because the SQLite page cache is filling up and later calls are more often served from memory rather than from disk. Once memory flattens, response time flattens too and stays flat, with the small uptick at the 72–96 hour mark not fully explained — it may be host-level noise from other processes on `lab-infra-03` rather than anything in accountsvc itself, and the 2026-05-04 repeat run did not show the same uptick.

These numbers track closely with the fuller loopback response-time page (loopback-response-times.md), which covers a broader set of call shapes and load levels; this page only reports the subset that was measured as part of the same runs used for memory tracking.

MEMORY USE OVER MULTI-DAY RUNS
----------------------------------
Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne)

This is the core of the page. RSS and VSZ for the 2026-03-11 soak run, sampled as described in Coverage and Method, at the six-hour marks:

    Elapsed     RSS (MB)   VSZ (MB)   Journal mode   Cache size setting
    0h (cold)   14.2       61.0       WAL            -20000
    0.5h (warm) 22.7       74.3       WAL            -20000
    6h          38.1       88.9       WAL            -20000
    12h         44.6       91.2       WAL            -20000
    18h         46.9       92.0       WAL            -20000
    24h         47.4       92.1       WAL            -20000
    48h         47.8       92.3       WAL            -20000
    72h         48.1       92.4       WAL            -20000
    96h         48.6       92.6       WAL            -20000

The shape here is the one we now expect: a fast climb in the first half day driven mostly by the SQLite page cache filling and by the interpreter's own steady-state allocations settling, followed by a long, nearly flat tail with only a very slow residual climb — about 1.2MB over the final three days of the run, or roughly 0.017MB/hour. Whether that residual climb is retained memory that will keep going indefinitely, or whether it eventually flattens too, is not settled; the longest run to date is the 96-hour one, and a two-week run is on the list of things to try but has not been scheduled.

For comparison, the same run with `cache_size` left at the old default (`-2000`, about 2MB) — repeated on 2026-03-14 specifically to have a like-for-like comparison — flattened lower (around 30MB steady-state) but never fully stopped climbing; small upward steps kept appearing every several hours, in the 0.3–0.6MB range, that did not appear at all in the 20MB-cache run. The working theory, not yet confirmed, is that a too-small page cache causes more frequent SQLite-internal allocation and freeing, and some of that memory is not being returned promptly to the operating system, showing up as small permanent RSS steps rather than a smooth climb. This is one of the open questions carried into the next update.

A brief note on `objgraph` counts taken at the 6h and 96h marks of the 2026-03-11 run: object counts for ordinary built-in types (str, dict, list) were essentially unchanged between the two samples, which argues against an accumulating collection of Python-level objects and points more toward the SQLite page cache and general allocator behavior as the source of the residual growth. This is consistent with, but does not fully confirm, the garbage-collector notes on gc-tuning-notes.rst, which found that adjusting the collector's threshold settings had almost no effect on the long-run RSS trend — worth changing for pause-time reasons in some other contexts, but not a lever for memory growth in this service.

Connection pool sizing (see connection-pool-sizing.md) is a second suspect that was ruled out during the 2026-03-11 run: the pool was held at a fixed size for the whole run, so it cannot explain the residual climb, though a follow-up run with the pool size deliberately varied mid-run would help confirm this and has not yet been done.

Summary table comparing the two cache-size configurations at the 96-hour mark:

    Cache size setting    Steady RSS (MB)   Still climbing at 96h?
    -2000  (~2MB)         ~31.4             yes, in small steps
    -20000 (~20MB)        ~48.6             barely, ~0.017MB/hour

STARTUP TIME AND ITS RELATIONSHIP TO LONG RUNS
--------------------------------------------------
Owner: Core Services (Elliot Frame)

Startup time matters to this page mainly because every soak run begins with a cold start, and a slow or unusual cold start can distort the first few samples of a memory trend. The fuller startup-time numbers live on startup-time-tracking.md and cold-start-vs-warm-start.txt; the summary relevant here is:

- Cold start to first successful loopback call: typically 640–780ms on `lab-infra-03`, most of it interpreter startup and standard-library import time rather than anything accountsvc does with the database file.
- Opening the database file for the first time, with journal mode already set to WAL from a previous run, adds roughly 15–25ms over opening a fresh file with the default rollback journal — small compared to interpreter startup, but consistently measurable across the March and May runs.
- Warm-start memory (the 22.7MB figure at the 0.5h mark in the table above) is reached within about 90 seconds of the cold start under the light soak-run load; under a heavier burst of initial calls this can be reached in under 20 seconds, but the soak runs deliberately use a light initial load so that the early part of the RSS curve is not itself an artifact of unusually fast warming.

One thing worth flagging for anyone repeating these runs: the 2025-04-27 update to startup-time-tracking.md changed the reference host for startup numbers from `lab-infra-03` to `lab-infra-05`, but the memory soak runs in this page were run on `lab-infra-03`, so the startup-time numbers quoted above are not directly comparable to the ones on that page without accounting for the different host. This has caused confusion at least once when the two pages were read side by side.

FILES AND PATHS
------------------

    accountsvc/                                       package directory
    accountsvc/state.db                                the local SQLite file holding service state; opened at process start and held open for the life of the run
    conf/accountsvc.ini                                configuration file holding the SQLite settings covered in this page (journal mode, cache size, synchronous)
    docs/performance-notes/                            this folder; holds this page and its siblings
    docs/performance-notes/long-running-process-memory.txt   this page

1	Profiling Sessions, 2024

3	**Version:** 2.1
4	**Owner:** Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)
5	**Last updated:** 2024-11-08
6	
7	**Summary:** A log of profiling sessions run against the package during 2024, with notes on setup and observed hotspots.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Coverage and Purpose
12	
13	This page collects the profiling sessions that Runtime Performance ran against the package across 2024. It walks through how each session was set up, what SQLite settings were tried, what round-trip timing looked like over the loopback interface, how memory use behaved under sustained load, and how startup timing shifted as settings changed. Sessions for 2025 onward are tracked separately in *Profiling Sessions, 2025*; this page is frozen as the 2024 log and isn't expected to gain new entries going forward.
14	
15	Most of the sessions described here were exploratory rather than a fixed set repeated on a schedule — someone would try a SQLite setting combination, watch the numbers, and either fold the change into an upcoming release or write it down as a dead end. Where a session produced a change that shipped, the change is noted with the release it landed in, and the release is cross-checked against the change log near the bottom of this page.
16	
17	A couple of housekeeping notes before the detail below:
18	
19	- All timing numbers in this page are round-trip time as seen by the caller of the loopback interface, not any internal processing time, since the package doesn't expose its own internal timer.
20	- Memory numbers came from the operating system's own process view, not from anything reported by the package itself.
21	- Where a session was run on more than one machine, both sets of numbers are shown; where it wasn't, that's noted.

23	## Session Log

25	Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)
26	
27	| Date | Session | Focus | Engineer | Outcome |

29	| 2024-01-18 | S24-01 | Baseline round-trip timing over loopback, starting SQLite settings | Priya Nandakumar | Established starting numbers; no changes shipped |
30	| 2024-02-09 | S24-02 | Journal mode comparison (rollback journal vs WAL) | Priya Nandakumar | WAL adopted as default in v2.0 |

33	| 2024-06-27 | S24-05 | Startup timing, cold vs warm filesystem cache | Elliot Frame | No change shipped; folded into Startup Time Tracking |
34	| 2024-08-11 | S24-06 | synchronous=NORMAL vs FULL under WAL | Priya Nandakumar | NORMAL adopted for the loopback service in v2.1 |
35	| 2024-09-30 | S24-07 | Connection setup overhead on the loopback path | Priya Nandakumar | Small fix shipped in v2.1 |
36	| 2024-11-04 | S24-08 | Re-check of page cache sweep after the v2.1 change | Priya Nandakumar, Devon Ruiz | Confirmed 8 MB still the right default |
37	
38	A couple of shorter follow-ups (informally called S24-04a and S24-06b at the time) ran the same week as their parent sessions and are folded into the S24-04 and S24-06 notes below rather than getting their own rows.
39	
40	## Profiling Setup
41	
42	Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)
43	
44	All 2024 sessions ran on the same two machines to keep numbers comparable across the year:
45	
46	- A Windows 11 23H2 workstation, 4 cores, 8 GB RAM — used for most sessions.
47	- An Ubuntu 22.04 LTS virtual machine, 2 cores, 4 GB RAM — used to cross-check S24-02, S24-03, and S24-06, mostly to confirm that WAL behavior wasn't specific to one filesystem.
48	
49	The package was started with its default settings unless a session called out a changed setting explicitly. Every session started from a fresh copy of the database file — a leftover file from an earlier session with a different journal mode produced confusing numbers on more than one occasion, so copying a clean database file into place before starting the loopback service is now the first step of every session's setup, whether or not the write-up below spells it out again for each one.
50	
51	Round-trip timing was collected with a small shell-based timing loop kept in the scripts folder rather than any external timing tool, since the loopback interface only needs a simple repeated-call harness. A typical setup for a timing session looks roughly like this:
52	
53	```
54	# copy a clean database file into place
55	copy accountsvc-clean.db accountsvc.db
56	
57	# confirm current SQLite settings before starting the loopback service
58	sqlite3 accountsvc.db "PRAGMA journal_mode; PRAGMA cache_size; PRAGMA synchronous;"
59	```
60	
61	On the Ubuntu VM the equivalent setup uses `cp` in place of `copy`, and the timing loop is a bash script rather than a PowerShell one; the underlying approach is the same on both machines. Configuration for the timing loop itself — call counts, warm-up calls before numbers are recorded, and so on — is kept out of this page and lives in *Profiling Tool Configuration*, which the loop scripts read from at the start of a run.
62	
63	Memory numbers were read from the operating system's own process view: Task Manager's details tab on Windows, and `ps` together with `/proc/<pid>/status` on the Ubuntu VM. The package doesn't report its own memory use, so there was never a temptation to compare an internal number against an external one — the only numbers in this page are what the operating system reported.
64	
65	## SQLite Settings Explored
66	
67	Owner: Runtime Performance, with setting guidance from Data Systems (Devon Ruiz)
68	
69	Three settings came up repeatedly across the 2024 sessions: journal mode, page cache size, and the synchronous setting. Deeper background on each of these lives in the sibling pages *SQLite Journal Mode Notes* and *SQLite Page Cache Tuning*; this section only covers what was actually tried during 2024 sessions and what it did to the numbers below, not the full reasoning behind each setting.
70	
71	### Journal mode
72	
73	The package shipped with SQLite's original rollback-journal mode through v1.x — the mode most SQLite installs use unless something explicitly turns WAL on. Session S24-02 compared that starting mode against WAL mode, and against TRUNCATE mode for completeness, on both machines:
74	
75	| Journal setting | Write round-trip, p50 (ms) | Write round-trip, p95 (ms) |
76	|---|---|---|
77	| Rollback journal (starting default) | 6.8 | 14.2 |
78	| WAL | 3.1 | 6.0 |
79	| TRUNCATE | 6.1 | 12.9 |
80	
81	WAL mode roughly halved write-side round-trip timing on both machines, mostly because it avoids the extra filesystem work the rollback journal does around each write. WAL was adopted as the shipped default in v2.0. One side effect worth calling out here: WAL keeps a separate write-ahead log file next to the main database file, and that file grows between the moments its contents are folded back into the main file. That growth mattered for the memory notes further down this page, and it's covered in more depth in *SQLite WAL Housekeeping*.
82	
83	To set journal mode by hand for a one-off session:
84	
85	```
86	sqlite3 accountsvc.db "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;"
87	```
88	
89	### Page cache size
90	
91	SQLite's page cache setting (`cache_size`) controls how many pages it keeps in memory before going back to disk for them. The package's starting default going into 2024 was SQLite's own built-in default, which works out to roughly 2 MB on a typical page size. Session S24-03 swept through a few sizes:
92	
93	| cache_size setting | Approx. cache size | Read round-trip, p50 (ms) | Read round-trip, p95 (ms) |
94	|---|---|---|---|
95	| -2000 | ~2 MB (starting default) | 4.4 | 9.7 |
96	| -8000 | ~8 MB | 2.9 | 5.8 |
97	| -16000 | ~16 MB | 2.7 | 5.5 |
98	| -32000 | ~32 MB | 2.6 | 5.4 |
99	
100	Going from 2 MB to 8 MB gave the biggest jump; past that the returns were small and not worth the extra resident memory on a loopback-only service that mostly answers one caller at a time. 8 MB (`cache_size=-8000`) was adopted as the new default in v2.0. Devon Ruiz's page cache guidance (see *SQLite Page Cache Tuning*, currently at v1.1) goes into more detail on how this setting interacts with page size and with the operating system's own file cache, which this page doesn't repeat.
101	
102	### synchronous setting
103	
104	Session S24-06 looked at `synchronous=NORMAL` against `synchronous=FULL` under WAL mode. FULL is more careful about an unclean stop but forces an extra disk flush that WAL under NORMAL can skip. On the Windows workstation:
105	
106	| synchronous | Write round-trip, p50 (ms) | Write round-trip, p95 (ms) |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| FULL | 4.0 | 8.1 |
109	| NORMAL | 3.1 | 6.0 |
110	
111	Given that the package's database file is local and the loopback service isn't usually under heavy write pressure, NORMAL was adopted for v2.1. This lines up with SQLite's own guidance that NORMAL under WAL is a reasonable choice for most single-machine uses.
112	
113	### How the settings interact
114	
115	None of the three settings above were tried fully independently of the others — by the time S24-06 ran, WAL and the 8 MB page cache were already the shipped defaults from v2.0, so the synchronous comparison happened on top of those, not against the original 2 MB rollback-journal starting point. Session S24-08 re-ran the page cache sweep from S24-03 after the v2.1 synchronous change shipped, mostly to make sure the earlier 8 MB conclusion still held once synchronous had also changed. It did — the numbers from S24-08 were within a few tenths of a millisecond of the S24-03 numbers at each cache size, so 8 MB stayed the default rather than getting revisited.
116	
117	## Loopback Response Time Measurements
118	
119	Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)
120	
121	Round-trip timing was collected by issuing repeated calls over the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) and timing the round trip from just before a call was sent to just after its response was read. Full detail on the loopback measurement approach, and the ongoing set of numbers past 2024, live in *Loopback Response Times*; the table below is the 2024-specific set, using the settings that shipped in v2.1 (WAL, 8 MB page cache, synchronous=NORMAL):
122	
123	| Call type | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) |
124	|---|---|---|---|
125	| Read, small response | 2.6 | 5.4 | 8.0 |
126	| Read, larger response | 3.9 | 7.2 | 10.5 |
127	| Write | 3.1 | 6.0 | 9.3 |
128	
129	A few notes from running these repeatedly across the year:
130	
131	1. The very first call after the loopback service starts is reliably slower than the rest — often three to five times the steady-state p50 — because the page cache is still cold. This is covered separately in the startup timing section below and in *Cold Start Versus Warm Start*.
132	2. p99 numbers were noisier than p50 or p95 on the Windows workstation, most likely from other processes on the same machine rather than anything in the package itself. The Ubuntu VM's p99 numbers were steadier, which supports that read.
133	3. The Ubuntu VM consistently ran 10 to 15 percent faster than the Windows workstation on the same settings across every session that used both machines. This is assumed to be filesystem overhead on the Windows side rather than anything SQLite-specific, but it wasn't investigated further during 2024.
134	4. Response size mattered more than call type — the "read, larger response" row is slower than "write" even though writes have more work to do on the SQLite side, simply because more bytes have to cross the loopback interface and get formatted on the way out.
135	
136	One thing worth flagging for anyone reusing these numbers later: the 2024 table above reflects a single caller issuing one call at a time. Concurrent-caller numbers, and how the round-trip time changes when more than one caller is active at once, are covered separately under *Connection Pool Sizing* rather than in this page.
137	
138	## Memory Use Observations
139	
140	Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne), cross-posted from session S24-04
141	
142	Session S24-04 ran the loopback service under a steady stream of calls for two hours and watched resident memory over that window. Baseline numbers, and the fuller picture across the rest of the year, are in *Memory Use Baseline*; the 2024 session numbers were:
143	
144	| Point in the run | Resident memory (approx.) |
145	|---|---|
146	| Just after start, before first call | 17 MB |
147	| After first call (cold page cache warm-up) | 24 MB |
148	| Steady state, light load | 28 MB |
149	| Steady state, sustained write load | 42-48 MB |
150	| 30 minutes after load stopped | 30 MB |
151	
152	The growth under sustained write load tracks the write-ahead log file's own growth — the log file gets bigger between the moments its contents are folded back into the main database file, and that growth shows up as extra resident memory for the pages SQLite is keeping warm, not as memory the package's own code is holding onto and failing to give back. Once the log file is folded back and the load lets up, memory settles down close to the steady-state light-load number rather than climbing without bound over the two-hour window. Sana Byrne's follow-up note on this ties it to the guidance in *SQLite WAL Housekeeping* on how often the fold-back happens by default and how to force it sooner during a long-running session.
153	
154	One open question from S24-04 that didn't get a clean answer during 2024: whether the 42-48 MB range under sustained write load keeps growing over a run much longer than two hours, or whether it's a hard ceiling tied to the page cache and log-growth settings in place at the time. Infrastructure picked this question up again the following year; see *Long-Running Process Memory Notes* for how that turned out. It's also worth noting that the "30 minutes after load stopped" row settling near 30 MB rather than all the way back to the 17-24 MB starting range suggests the warm page cache from the earlier load stays useful even once the write pressure is gone, which is expected rather than a concern.
155	
156	## Startup Time Measurements
157	
158	Owner: Core Services (Elliot Frame), session S24-05
159	
160	Startup timing was measured from the moment the loopback service process was started to the moment it answered its first call. Elliot Frame ran this on both machines, comparing a cold filesystem cache (right after a reboot) against a warm one (service stopped and started again a few minutes later on the same machine, with the operating system's file cache still holding relevant pages):
161	
162	| Condition | Windows workstation | Ubuntu VM |
163	|---|---|---|
164	| Cold filesystem cache | 140 ms | 95 ms |
165	| Warm filesystem cache | 82 ms | 58 ms |
166	| Write-ahead log not yet folded back from a prior unclean stop | 210 ms | 150 ms |
167	
168	The third row matters more than it might look. If the previous run of the service was stopped in the middle of a write — a power loss, a forced stop, anything that didn't let it shut down on its own — the write-ahead log file may still hold writes that haven't been folded back into the main database file yet. The next start has to fold those back before it can answer its first call, and that shows up as the slower startup number above. This case, and the broader difference between a clean and an unclean prior stop, is the main subject of *Cold Start Versus Warm Start* (Core Services, last touched in early 2025) and is tracked over time in *Startup Time Tracking*.
169	
170	No startup-time changes shipped out of the 2024 sessions; the numbers above were mostly used to set expectations for later work rather than to justify a change on their own. One small methodology note for anyone repeating this measurement: "cold filesystem cache" here means right after a reboot of the whole machine, not just stopping and restarting the service — stopping and restarting alone, even a few minutes apart, was closer to the warm-cache row than the cold one in every run Elliot tried.
171	
172	## Hotspots and Follow-up Work
173	
174	Owner: Runtime Performance, with items assigned across teams
175	
176	The 2024 sessions turned up a short list of places worth more attention:
177	
178	- Connection setup on the loopback path had a small, fixable overhead that came from re-reading SQLite settings on every new connection instead of once at start. Fixed in v2.1 — see the change log below.
179	- Page cache warm-up on the first call after start is unavoidable with the current approach and isn't worth chasing further; see the startup timing notes above.
180	- Write-ahead log growth under sustained write load is fine for the memory ranges seen in S24-04, but the open question about longer runs was picked up by Infrastructure the following year rather than closed out in 2024.
181	- The gap between Windows and Ubuntu round-trip timing (10 to 15 percent in most sessions) was noted but not investigated further during 2024; it's flagged for whoever next revisits loopback timing on Windows.
182	- Garbage collector behavior under sustained load came up briefly in S24-06 as a possible contributor to the noisy p99 numbers on Windows, but Platform Tools' own look at collector settings didn't start until much later; see *Garbage Collector Tuning Notes* for that separate thread.
183	- Connection setup and page cache warm-up together account for most of why the very first call after start is so much slower than steady state; splitting the two apart wasn't attempted in 2024 and would need a smaller, more targeted session than the ones logged here.
184	
185	None of the above were treated as urgent during 2024 — the package's typical caller pattern is light enough that none of these showed up as a real problem outside of profiling sessions specifically set up to look for them.
186	
187	## Terminology
188	
189	- **journal mode** — the SQLite setting that controls how it protects the database file against an unclean stop while writing; the rollback journal mode and WAL mode are the two discussed most in this page.
190	- **write-ahead log (WAL)** — under WAL journal mode, a separate file next to the main database file that holds new writes until they're folded back into the main file.
191	- **fold back** (of the write-ahead log) — the point at which SQLite merges the contents of the write-ahead log file back into the main database file, keeping the log file from growing without bound.
192	- **page cache** — the set of database pages SQLite keeps in memory (controlled by the `cache_size` setting) to avoid going back to disk for pages it has already read.
193	- **synchronous setting** — the SQLite setting controlling how aggressively it forces writes to disk before treating them as durable; FULL and NORMAL are the two values discussed here.
194	- **loopback interface** — the local network interface (127.0.0.1) the service listens on for calls originating from the same machine.
195	- **round-trip time** — the time from just before a call is sent to just after its response is read, as seen by the caller.
196	- **p50 / p95 / p99** — the median, 95th-percentile, and 99th-percentile values in a set of round-trip time measurements; higher percentiles show the slower end of the range.
197	- **cold start** — starting the loopback service when neither the operating system's filesystem cache nor SQLite's own page cache holds anything useful yet.
198	- **warm start** — starting the loopback service shortly after a previous run, when the filesystem cache still holds relevant pages.
199	- **resident memory** — the portion of a process's memory that's actually held in RAM at a given moment, as reported by the operating system.
200	- **unclean stop** — a case where the loopback service process ends without going through its own normal shutdown, such as a power loss or a forced stop.
201	
202	## Files Referenced
203	
204	- `accountsvc/` — the package directory; this page refers to it only as "the package" and doesn't describe what's inside it.
205	- `README.md` — the repository's root overview page.
206	- `docs/performance-notes/profiling-sessions-2024.md` — this page.
207	- `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode-notes.md` — deeper background on journal mode choices, maintained by Data Systems.
208	- `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-page-cache-tuning.rst` — deeper background on page cache sizing, also maintained by Data Systems.
209	- `docs/performance-notes/loopback-response-times.md` — the ongoing set of loopback timing numbers, of which the 2024 numbers in this page are a subset.
210	- `docs/performance-notes/memory-use-baseline.md` — the ongoing memory-use log that S24-04's numbers feed into.
211	- `docs/performance-notes/startup-time-tracking.md` — the ongoing startup-timing log that S24-05's numbers feed into.
212	- `docs/performance-notes/profiling-tool-config.yaml` — settings for the timing loop scripts, such as call counts and warm-up counts, kept separate from this page.
213	- `scripts/loopback-timing.ps1` — the Windows timing loop used to collect round-trip numbers.
214	- `scripts/loopback-timing.sh` — the equivalent timing loop for the Ubuntu VM.
215	- `scripts/copy-clean-db.ps1` — copies a fresh database file into place before a timing session, to avoid a leftover file from a previous session's journal mode setting affecting the next one.
216	- `logs/profiling-2024/` — raw timing output from each session listed in the session log above, kept as one file per session date.
217	
218	## Tools and Package Versions
219	
220	| Tool / package | Version used in 2024 sessions | Notes |
221	|---|---|---|
222	| Python (standard library only) | 3.11.6 | No external packages used by the package itself |
223	| SQLite (bundled with the Python build used) | 3.43.2 | Same bundled version on both machines |
224	| sqlite3 CLI | 3.43.2 | Used for hand-checking settings outside the package |
225	| Windows 11 | 23H2 | Primary workstation for most sessions |
226	| Ubuntu | 22.04 LTS | Cross-check virtual machine |
227	| PowerShell | 7.4.0 | Timing loop and setup scripts on Windows |
228	| bash | 5.1 | Timing loop and setup scripts on the Ubuntu VM |
229	| cProfile (standard library) | bundled with Python 3.11.6 | Used in S24-07 to narrow down the connection setup overhead |
230	
231	## Change Log
232	
233	- **2024-01-22 (v1.8):** Initial 2024 session log started; carried over baseline numbers from late-2023 sessions for comparison.
234	- **2024-02-14 (v1.9):** Notes on the rollback-journal-vs-WAL comparison (S24-02) added ahead of the v2.0 default change.
235	- **2024-03-28 (v1.9.1):** Page cache sweep (S24-03) numbers added.
236	- **2024-06-02 (v2.0):** Updated to reflect the shipped v2.0 defaults — WAL journal mode and an 8 MB page cache — and to record S24-04's memory numbers.
237	- **2024-07-05 (v2.0.1):** Startup timing table from S24-05 added; small wording fixes throughout.

239	- **2024-10-03 (v2.1):** Updated for the shipped v2.1 defaults — synchronous=NORMAL and the connection setup fix from S24-07.
240	- **2024-11-08 (v2.1):** Added S24-08's confirmation numbers and the hotspots summary; no version change, page content finalized for the year.
241

Profiling Sessions, 2024

**Version:** 2.1
**Owner:** Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)
**Last updated:** 2024-11-08

**Summary:** A log of profiling sessions run against the package during 2024, with notes on setup and observed hotspots.

---

## Coverage and Purpose

This page collects the profiling sessions that Runtime Performance ran against the package across 2024. It walks through how each session was set up, what SQLite settings were tried, what round-trip timing looked like over the loopback interface, how memory use behaved under sustained load, and how startup timing shifted as settings changed. Sessions for 2025 onward are tracked separately in *Profiling Sessions, 2025*; this page is frozen as the 2024 log and isn't expected to gain new entries going forward.

Most of the sessions described here were exploratory rather than a fixed set repeated on a schedule — someone would try a SQLite setting combination, watch the numbers, and either fold the change into an upcoming release or write it down as a dead end. Where a session produced a change that shipped, the change is noted with the release it landed in, and the release is cross-checked against the change log near the bottom of this page.

A couple of housekeeping notes before the detail below:

- All timing numbers in this page are round-trip time as seen by the caller of the loopback interface, not any internal processing time, since the package doesn't expose its own internal timer.
- Memory numbers came from the operating system's own process view, not from anything reported by the package itself.
- Where a session was run on more than one machine, both sets of numbers are shown; where it wasn't, that's noted.

## Session Log

Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)

| Date | Session | Focus | Engineer | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-18 | S24-01 | Baseline round-trip timing over loopback, starting SQLite settings | Priya Nandakumar | Established starting numbers; no changes shipped |
| 2024-02-09 | S24-02 | Journal mode comparison (rollback journal vs WAL) | Priya Nandakumar | WAL adopted as default in v2.0 |
| 2024-03-22 | S24-03 | Page cache size sweep | Priya Nandakumar, Devon Ruiz | Cache raised from ~2 MB to 8 MB in v2.0 |
| 2024-05-14 | S24-04 | Memory use under sustained load, tied to write-ahead log growth | Sana Byrne | Follow-up picked up by Infrastructure in 2025 |
| 2024-06-27 | S24-05 | Startup timing, cold vs warm filesystem cache | Elliot Frame | No change shipped; folded into Startup Time Tracking |
| 2024-08-11 | S24-06 | synchronous=NORMAL vs FULL under WAL | Priya Nandakumar | NORMAL adopted for the loopback service in v2.1 |
| 2024-09-30 | S24-07 | Connection setup overhead on the loopback path | Priya Nandakumar | Small fix shipped in v2.1 |
| 2024-11-04 | S24-08 | Re-check of page cache sweep after the v2.1 change | Priya Nandakumar, Devon Ruiz | Confirmed 8 MB still the right default |

A couple of shorter follow-ups (informally called S24-04a and S24-06b at the time) ran the same week as their parent sessions and are folded into the S24-04 and S24-06 notes below rather than getting their own rows.

## Profiling Setup

Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)

All 2024 sessions ran on the same two machines to keep numbers comparable across the year:

- A Windows 11 23H2 workstation, 4 cores, 8 GB RAM — used for most sessions.
- An Ubuntu 22.04 LTS virtual machine, 2 cores, 4 GB RAM — used to cross-check S24-02, S24-03, and S24-06, mostly to confirm that WAL behavior wasn't specific to one filesystem.

The package was started with its default settings unless a session called out a changed setting explicitly. Every session started from a fresh copy of the database file — a leftover file from an earlier session with a different journal mode produced confusing numbers on more than one occasion, so copying a clean database file into place before starting the loopback service is now the first step of every session's setup, whether or not the write-up below spells it out again for each one.

Round-trip timing was collected with a small shell-based timing loop kept in the scripts folder rather than any external timing tool, since the loopback interface only needs a simple repeated-call harness. A typical setup for a timing session looks roughly like this:

```
# copy a clean database file into place
copy accountsvc-clean.db accountsvc.db

# confirm current SQLite settings before starting the loopback service
sqlite3 accountsvc.db "PRAGMA journal_mode; PRAGMA cache_size; PRAGMA synchronous;"
```

On the Ubuntu VM the equivalent setup uses `cp` in place of `copy`, and the timing loop is a bash script rather than a PowerShell one; the underlying approach is the same on both machines. Configuration for the timing loop itself — call counts, warm-up calls before numbers are recorded, and so on — is kept out of this page and lives in *Profiling Tool Configuration*, which the loop scripts read from at the start of a run.

Memory numbers were read from the operating system's own process view: Task Manager's details tab on Windows, and `ps` together with `/proc/<pid>/status` on the Ubuntu VM. The package doesn't report its own memory use, so there was never a temptation to compare an internal number against an external one — the only numbers in this page are what the operating system reported.

## SQLite Settings Explored

Owner: Runtime Performance, with setting guidance from Data Systems (Devon Ruiz)

Three settings came up repeatedly across the 2024 sessions: journal mode, page cache size, and the synchronous setting. Deeper background on each of these lives in the sibling pages *SQLite Journal Mode Notes* and *SQLite Page Cache Tuning*; this section only covers what was actually tried during 2024 sessions and what it did to the numbers below, not the full reasoning behind each setting.

### Journal mode

The package shipped with SQLite's original rollback-journal mode through v1.x — the mode most SQLite installs use unless something explicitly turns WAL on. Session S24-02 compared that starting mode against WAL mode, and against TRUNCATE mode for completeness, on both machines:

| Journal setting | Write round-trip, p50 (ms) | Write round-trip, p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|
| Rollback journal (starting default) | 6.8 | 14.2 |
| WAL | 3.1 | 6.0 |
| TRUNCATE | 6.1 | 12.9 |

WAL mode roughly halved write-side round-trip timing on both machines, mostly because it avoids the extra filesystem work the rollback journal does around each write. WAL was adopted as the shipped default in v2.0. One side effect worth calling out here: WAL keeps a separate write-ahead log file next to the main database file, and that file grows between the moments its contents are folded back into the main file. That growth mattered for the memory notes further down this page, and it's covered in more depth in *SQLite WAL Housekeeping*.

To set journal mode by hand for a one-off session:

```
sqlite3 accountsvc.db "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;"
```

### Page cache size

SQLite's page cache setting (`cache_size`) controls how many pages it keeps in memory before going back to disk for them. The package's starting default going into 2024 was SQLite's own built-in default, which works out to roughly 2 MB on a typical page size. Session S24-03 swept through a few sizes:

| cache_size setting | Approx. cache size | Read round-trip, p50 (ms) | Read round-trip, p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| -2000 | ~2 MB (starting default) | 4.4 | 9.7 |
| -8000 | ~8 MB | 2.9 | 5.8 |
| -16000 | ~16 MB | 2.7 | 5.5 |
| -32000 | ~32 MB | 2.6 | 5.4 |

Going from 2 MB to 8 MB gave the biggest jump; past that the returns were small and not worth the extra resident memory on a loopback-only service that mostly answers one caller at a time. 8 MB (`cache_size=-8000`) was adopted as the new default in v2.0. Devon Ruiz's page cache guidance (see *SQLite Page Cache Tuning*, currently at v1.1) goes into more detail on how this setting interacts with page size and with the operating system's own file cache, which this page doesn't repeat.

### synchronous setting

Session S24-06 looked at `synchronous=NORMAL` against `synchronous=FULL` under WAL mode. FULL is more careful about an unclean stop but forces an extra disk flush that WAL under NORMAL can skip. On the Windows workstation:

| synchronous | Write round-trip, p50 (ms) | Write round-trip, p95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|
| FULL | 4.0 | 8.1 |
| NORMAL | 3.1 | 6.0 |

Given that the package's database file is local and the loopback service isn't usually under heavy write pressure, NORMAL was adopted for v2.1. This lines up with SQLite's own guidance that NORMAL under WAL is a reasonable choice for most single-machine uses.

### How the settings interact

None of the three settings above were tried fully independently of the others — by the time S24-06 ran, WAL and the 8 MB page cache were already the shipped defaults from v2.0, so the synchronous comparison happened on top of those, not against the original 2 MB rollback-journal starting point. Session S24-08 re-ran the page cache sweep from S24-03 after the v2.1 synchronous change shipped, mostly to make sure the earlier 8 MB conclusion still held once synchronous had also changed. It did — the numbers from S24-08 were within a few tenths of a millisecond of the S24-03 numbers at each cache size, so 8 MB stayed the default rather than getting revisited.

## Loopback Response Time Measurements

Owner: Runtime Performance (Priya Nandakumar)

Round-trip timing was collected by issuing repeated calls over the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) and timing the round trip from just before a call was sent to just after its response was read. Full detail on the loopback measurement approach, and the ongoing set of numbers past 2024, live in *Loopback Response Times*; the table below is the 2024-specific set, using the settings that shipped in v2.1 (WAL, 8 MB page cache, synchronous=NORMAL):

| Call type | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read, small response | 2.6 | 5.4 | 8.0 |
| Read, larger response | 3.9 | 7.2 | 10.5 |
| Write | 3.1 | 6.0 | 9.3 |

A few notes from running these repeatedly across the year:

1. The very first call after the loopback service starts is reliably slower than the rest — often three to five times the steady-state p50 — because the page cache is still cold. This is covered separately in the startup timing section below and in *Cold Start Versus Warm Start*.
2. p99 numbers were noisier than p50 or p95 on the Windows workstation, most likely from other processes on the same machine rather than anything in the package itself. The Ubuntu VM's p99 numbers were steadier, which supports that read.
3. The Ubuntu VM consistently ran 10 to 15 percent faster than the Windows workstation on the same settings across every session that used both machines. This is assumed to be filesystem overhead on the Windows side rather than anything SQLite-specific, but it wasn't investigated further during 2024.
4. Response size mattered more than call type — the "read, larger response" row is slower than "write" even though writes have more work to do on the SQLite side, simply because more bytes have to cross the loopback interface and get formatted on the way out.

One thing worth flagging for anyone reusing these numbers later: the 2024 table above reflects a single caller issuing one call at a time. Concurrent-caller numbers, and how the round-trip time changes when more than one caller is active at once, are covered separately under *Connection Pool Sizing* rather than in this page.

## Memory Use Observations

Owner: Infrastructure (Sana Byrne), cross-posted from session S24-04

Session S24-04 ran the loopback service under a steady stream of calls for two hours and watched resident memory over that window. Baseline numbers, and the fuller picture across the rest of the year, are in *Memory Use Baseline*; the 2024 session numbers were:

| Point in the run | Resident memory (approx.) |
|---|---|
| Just after start, before first call | 17 MB |
| After first call (cold page cache warm-up) | 24 MB |
| Steady state, light load | 28 MB |
| Steady state, sustained write load | 42-48 MB |
| 30 minutes after load stopped | 30 MB |

The growth under sustained write load tracks the write-ahead log file's own growth — the log file gets bigger between the moments its contents are folded back into the main database file, and that growth shows up as extra resident memory for the pages SQLite is keeping warm, not as memory the package's own code is holding onto and failing to give back. Once the log file is folded back and the load lets up, memory settles down close to the steady-state light-load number rather than climbing without bound over the two-hour window. Sana Byrne's follow-up note on this ties it to the guidance in *SQLite WAL Housekeeping* on how often the fold-back happens by default and how to force it sooner during a long-running session.

One open question from S24-04 that didn't get a clean answer during 2024: whether the 42-48 MB range under sustained write load keeps growing over a run much longer than two hours, or whether it's a hard ceiling tied to the page cache and log-growth settings in place at the time. Infrastructure picked this question up again the following year; see *Long-Running Process Memory Notes* for how that turned out. It's also worth noting that the "30 minutes after load stopped" row settling near 30 MB rather than all the way back to the 17-24 MB starting range suggests the warm page cache from the earlier load stays useful even once the write pressure is gone, which is expected rather than a concern.

## Startup Time Measurements

Owner: Core Services (Elliot Frame), session S24-05

Startup timing was measured from the moment the loopback service process was started to the moment it answered its first call. Elliot Frame ran this on both machines, comparing a cold filesystem cache (right after a reboot) against a warm one (service stopped and started again a few minutes later on the same machine, with the operating system's file cache still holding relevant pages):

| Condition | Windows workstation | Ubuntu VM |
|---|---|---|
| Cold filesystem cache | 140 ms | 95 ms |
| Warm filesystem cache | 82 ms | 58 ms |
| Write-ahead log not yet folded back from a prior unclean stop | 210 ms | 150 ms |

The third row matters more than it might look. If the previous run of the service was stopped in the middle of a write — a power loss, a forced stop, anything that didn't let it shut down on its own — the write-ahead log file may still hold writes that haven't been folded back into the main database file yet. The next start has to fold those back before it can answer its first call, and that shows up as the slower startup number above. This case, and the broader difference between a clean and an unclean prior stop, is the main subject of *Cold Start Versus Warm Start* (Core Services, last touched in early 2025) and is tracked over time in *Startup Time Tracking*.

No startup-time changes shipped out of the 2024 sessions; the numbers above were mostly used to set expectations for later work rather than to justify a change on their own. One small methodology note for anyone repeating this measurement: "cold filesystem cache" here means right after a reboot of the whole machine, not just stopping and restarting the service — stopping and restarting alone, even a few minutes apart, was closer to the warm-cache row than the cold one in every run Elliot tried.

## Hotspots and Follow-up Work

Owner: Runtime Performance, with items assigned across teams

The 2024 sessions turned up a short list of places worth more attention:

- Connection setup on the loopback path had a small, fixable overhead that came from re-reading SQLite settings on every new connection instead of once at start. Fixed in v2.1 — see the change log below.
- Page cache warm-up on the first call after start is unavoidable with the current approach and isn't worth chasing further; see the startup timing notes above.
- Write-ahead log growth under sustained write load is fine for the memory ranges seen in S24-04, but the open question about longer runs was picked up by Infrastructure the following year rather than closed out in 2024.
- The gap between Windows and Ubuntu round-trip timing (10 to 15 percent in most sessions) was noted but not investigated further during 2024; it's flagged for whoever next revisits loopback timing on Windows.
- Garbage collector behavior under sustained load came up briefly in S24-06 as a possible contributor to the noisy p99 numbers on Windows, but Platform Tools' own look at collector settings didn't start until much later; see *Garbage Collector Tuning Notes* for that separate thread.
- Connection setup and page cache warm-up together account for most of why the very first call after start is so much slower than steady state; splitting the two apart wasn't attempted in 2024 and would need a smaller, more targeted session than the ones logged here.

None of the above were treated as urgent during 2024 — the package's typical caller pattern is light enough that none of these showed up as a real problem outside of profiling sessions specifically set up to look for them.

## Terminology

- **journal mode** — the SQLite setting that controls how it protects the database file against an unclean stop while writing; the rollback journal mode and WAL mode are the two discussed most in this page.
- **write-ahead log (WAL)** — under WAL journal mode, a separate file next to the main database file that holds new writes until they're folded back into the main file.
- **fold back** (of the write-ahead log) — the point at which SQLite merges the contents of the write-ahead log file back into the main database file, keeping the log file from growing without bound.
- **page cache** — the set of database pages SQLite keeps in memory (controlled by the `cache_size` setting) to avoid going back to disk for pages it has already read.
- **synchronous setting** — the SQLite setting controlling how aggressively it forces writes to disk before treating them as durable; FULL and NORMAL are the two values discussed here.
- **loopback interface** — the local network interface (127.0.0.1) the service listens on for calls originating from the same machine.
- **round-trip time** — the time from just before a call is sent to just after its response is read, as seen by the caller.
- **p50 / p95 / p99** — the median, 95th-percentile, and 99th-percentile values in a set of round-trip time measurements; higher percentiles show the slower end of the range.
- **cold start** — starting the loopback service when neither the operating system's filesystem cache nor SQLite's own page cache holds anything useful yet.
- **warm start** — starting the loopback service shortly after a previous run, when the filesystem cache still holds relevant pages.
- **resident memory** — the portion of a process's memory that's actually held in RAM at a given moment, as reported by the operating system.
- **unclean stop** — a case where the loopback service process ends without going through its own normal shutdown, such as a power loss or a forced stop.

11	## Overview
12	
13	This document records the systematic profiling work performed on the accountsvc package during 2025, building on the 2024 profiling sessions documented in the predecessor page. The focus has been on understanding and optimizing performance characteristics across SQLite configuration parameters, loopback HTTP response times, memory usage patterns, and service startup latency. All profiling was conducted on Windows 10 Pro in a controlled lab environment and represents single-instance deployments.
14	
15	The primary driver for 2025 work was an observed 12% increase in median response times under sustained load compared to baseline measurements from early 2024. Investigation revealed that SQLite journal mode settings and page cache sizing were the primary factors, accounting for approximately 7% of the regression. The remaining 5% appears related to memory pressure under concurrent operations, though this remains partially unresolved and may warrant further investigation in 2026.

17	## Session 1: January 23–25, 2025 (Journal Mode Characterization)
18	
19	**Session Owner:** Priya Nandakumar  
20	**Focus:** Journal mode behavior and write-heavy workload performance
21	
22	This session characterized the performance impact of different SQLite journal modes on the service under sustained account modification operations. The accountsvc package was deployed using version 1.8.3 of the runtime harness, with default settings except where noted.
23	
24	### Procedure
25	
26	1. Deployed clean service instance with baseline journal handling
27	2. Ran 10,000 write operations in sequence via loopback, measuring per-operation latency
28	3. Repeated with journal mode set to `wal` (Write-Ahead Logging)
29	4. Repeated with journal mode set to `truncate`
30	5. Collected SQLite statistics via built-in monitor output
31	6. Measured file system behavior using Windows Performance Monitor
32	
33	### Results
34	
35	The baseline journal mode showed consistent 45–52 ms per-operation median latency with 98th percentile reaching 180 ms. Variance increased substantially after 4,000 operations, suggesting journal file fragmentation effects. File size grew to 480 MB by operation 10,000.
36	
37	Switching to `wal` mode produced median latency of 28–31 ms, with 98th percentile at 95 ms. File system overhead was reduced and more predictable. The working set remained bounded around 220 MB during execution. One unexpected result: latency occasionally spiked to 240 ms at operations 6,500–6,700, correlating with automatic WAL synchronization. This behavior was not documented in earlier runs and may be environmental.
38	
39	The secondary journal mode was not suitable for this workload, producing latencies similar to the baseline but with higher tail latency variance (98th percentile 210 ms).
40	
41	**Recommended:** Use `wal` mode as the service default, subject to further validation in Session 3.
